News.title: Why the fate of Trump’s final two years in office hangs in the balance – as JD and Lil’ Marco battle to succeed him
News.content:
DONALD TRUMP used to say he was “tired of winning” but has finally admitted: “I’m getting a little bit tired of politics now.”

After a near two-hour turn on Wednesday evening, the ageing President was back in front of 10,000 true believers on Thursday night.



Half an hour into his planned ten-minute closing remarks of the Republican Party’s jazzy gathering in Dallas, Texas, The Don was in pensive mode.

He had just seen what we all witnessed in the giant arena: Life after him.



Mocked by the Mad Mullahs of Iran, battered in the opinion polls back home and facing the prospect of being a lame duck come November, this impromptu convention to launch his party’s midterm election campaign felt a little like a last hurrah.

“Just pretend I’m on the ballot”, Trump begged two nights in a row, as he sought to breathe life into his party’s tricky prospects for crucial Senate and Congressional elections eight weeks away.



The fate of his final two years in office hangs in the balance. If he retains his grip on Washington, he has promised the world — in the form of a $5,000 bung to every US citizen.

Should he lose, it will be a long 24 months cornered in the West Wing as his Democrat enemies use every tool in the shed to push and probe his legacy, family and businesses.

Six months into his “four to six week” war in the Middle East, Trump still insists his party must stick with him for a similar bounce to 2016 and 2024, when scores of down ticket nobodies were elected on his coat tails.

Plenty of candidates who steered well clear of the jamboree clearly disagree.



Obviously still loved in the convention hall, tanking approval ratings and a fading star quality are getting to our ratings-obsessed chum as he demanded a sworn pledge of loyalty from the crowd.

But they had just gone absolutely wild . . . for another man.

Vice President JD Vance, just 42, put in the performance of his admittedly short career.

His pacey primetime speech hit all the right buttons for the politicos and dispelled some — well deserved — pundit views that he is just, well, a bit weird.



Having shed a few pounds and grown a few greys over the past year, Vance was relaxed, funny and fired up.

Dealing with a heckler so effortlessly some suggested it must have been a scripted plant, JD — as the room chanted — stepped up to the plate and, frankly, knocked it out the park as they say here.

Having endlessly let it be known he was against the war in Iran all along,

Vance’s speech went hard on disgruntled MAGA fans, mis-sold an America First isolationist dream, urging them not to “throw the baby out with the bathwater”.



Trump’s mealy mouthed midterm campaign riff, that the Republicans are mainstream compared to the now extremist woke left Democrats, was distilled far more clearly by Vance: “It’s common sense or the crazies.”

Though he chickened out of mentioning Iran by name, “don’t hand over the country to a bunch of crazy people just because you disagree with a policy decision”, landed exactly where JD aimed it.

While he got a thumbs-up from Trump at the end of the speech, the speed at which the No2 was rushed from the stage, not even to return for the sing-along and balloon-laden end-of-convention ceremonies, said it all.

I would not have wanted to be any other leading Republican eyeing a tilt at 2028, judging by the roar of that crowd.



For the first time there’s a real buzz around JD, which might explain why increasingly respected Secretary of State Marco Rubio has briefed that he has “no plans” to run against his close buddy.

While Texas Senator Ted Cruz is clearly eyeing another doomed bid, other floated candidates such as the berk-ish Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth and loony tunes ex-intelligence chief Tulsi Gabbard need to give their heads a wobble before getting into the race.

The consensus from behind the scenes in Texas is only the man Trump once derided as Lil’ Marco could upset the JD juggernaut.

At 55, Rubio is a spring chicken compared to recent Presidents but he still carries the scars from his 2016 bid.



It would be highly unusual for a sitting VP to seek the nomination for the top job and not get it, so there’s a pecking order to contend with and plenty of MAGA powerbrokers are already locked in for Vance.

While establishment Republicans and plenty of big donors are urging the smoother and more traditionally conservative Rubio to change his mind, some wise hands say he would have a stronger bid in 2032 should Vance shoot and miss in two years’ time. Which could well happen.

Barely a Senator before he was thrust into the White House, it’s going to take more than one decent speech and a powerful back story to prove Vance is ready for the big seat.

A few years ago he was calling Trump “Hitler”, now he acts like his boss is the second coming. One minute he’s the true isolationist, the next he is meddling in European politics.

Hyper-online, White House insiders are quick to warn of his occasional hotheadness.



Truth be told, the Republicans may have the making of a winner here but they don’t know for sure. Which is why anointing him Trump’s successor without a proper contest may spell disaster.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

The big guy’s endorsement will certainly end the primary hopes of any other candidate but even Trump seems hesitant, publicly stating he is not sure who would be the best candidate between his VP and top diplomat.

Despite the cheers of the crowd, Trump was far from alone as the Republicans headed off from Texas for the stump . . .

News.title: National security must ALWAYS trump welfare because without it, the entire country is reduced to a heap of cinders
News.content:
Benefits state

BRITAIN’S Armed Forces are running out of ammo and manpower — but there’s cash coming out of our ears for the workshy.

Andy Burnham admitted as much when he told MPs he would not cut the bloated benefits bill to boost military spending. He insisted he would never be forced to choose between the two.



But it’s clear he already has — and that welfare is the hands-down winner.

At a time when our defence capabilities urgently need bolstering amid the mounting threat posed by Russia, Iran and others, we face the jaw-dropping reality that the number of people who claim state handouts for ADHD has almost doubled in the past three years to 100,000 — while the number of full-time soldiers has shrunk to just 82,000.



In addition, the 70,000 people claiming benefits for anxiety now outstrips the combined full-time personnel of the Royal Navy and the RAF.

Since Labour grabbed power, the total welfare bill has shot up by a staggering £20billion a year. It’s not so much Benefits Street as Benefits State.



Those who are unable to work because of genuine disability deserve support.

But it’s right to ask why these numbers are suddenly rocketing at a time when shameless “sickfluencers” are teaching millions how to game the system.

If the PM is as keen as we think on turning the clock back six decades, he should heed the words of a Labour big beast from that period.

Denis Healey, who served as Defence Secretary and Chancellor, warned that national security must ALWAYS trump welfare, education and housing.



Because without it, the entire country is reduced to a heap of cinders.

Ship has sailed

LABOUR’S much trumpeted “one in, one out” deal to return illegal migrants was exposed as a failing gimmick months ago.

About 1,400 have been swapped so far — that’s a drop in the Channel when 20,000 have made the crossing already this year, and 50 of those kicked out simply returned on the next boat.

Now France wants us to take asylum-seekers from across Europe in a replacement for the agreement, which expires next month. Ministers should accept this stunt is dead.

It’s time to sink it and launch a serious deterrent to stop asylum cheats coming here in the first place.



PM’s drill rap

IN his first words to the Commons as PM, Andy Burnham promised a “place first rather than party first” approach.

So why is he set to delay giving the go-ahead for gas drilling in the North Sea until after a crunch by-election next month?

Simple. He’s scared it will help Green Party leader Zack Polanski to storm to victory in Sir Keir Starmer’s old seat.

His bold new politics have been shelved so he can cynically drill for votes instead.

News.title: Migrant hotels will be EXEMPT from Burnham’s ‘tourist tax’ as Tories blast ‘special treatment’ for illegal immigrants
News.content:
MIGRANT hotels housing asylum seekers will be exempt from Labour’s tourist tax as they are classed as “temporary accommodation”.

The exemption has stoked fears that hotels may decide to ditch paying guests and instead house migrants for the Home Office at a cheaper price.



Andy Burnham announced plans to let England’s 14 regional mayors impose an uncapped levy on overnight stays, on Wednesday.

The move sparked fury as it was revealed local leaders would likely slap the overnight levy on hard-working families staying in hotels, B&Bs and holiday lets.



However, taxpayer funded asylum hotels will not be subject to the tax, the Department for Housing, Communities and Local Government said.

The Conservatives were quick to slam the decision as “outrageous” as officials said the tax will hit hard-working families most.

Sources in the hospitality industry added that this may encourage more hotels to offer themselves up for asylum seekers rather than holidaymakers.

Chris Philp, the shadow home secretary, said: “It is utterly outrageous that families saving up for a break and struggling hospitality businesses will be hit with another tax, while hotels being used to accommodate illegal immigrants are exempt.



“British taxpayers should not be treated as a cash machine as asylum hotels get special treatment.

“Labour must explain why they think ordinary families should pay this tax but the asylum system should not. The answer is not another stealth tax on British families.

“We need to deport all illegal immigrants which would allow us to end the farcical hotel use entirely.”

James Cleverly, the former shadow housing minister, now running to be London’s next mayor, told The Telegraph it was a “perverse policy”.

He added: “Tourists spend money in the local economy, help keep our towns and cities vibrant and boost our prosperity. We should be encouraging them to come, not taxing them for the privilege.”



This follows estimations that UK families might have to add hundreds of pounds onto the cost of their staycations.

Trade group UKHospitality estimated the tax would add £99 to a week trip to London and £198 to the cost of a family summer holiday.

Meanwhile, school trips could also be subject to the levy unless local leaders choose to exempt accommodation used for “educational purposes”.

Business travellers would also be caught by the charge.

The Sun has been campaigning to Stop The Holiday Tax, warning it risks pricing hard-working families out of precious staycations.



We have urged the Government to ditch the plans amid fears they could hammer seaside towns and encourage Brits to holiday abroad instead.

The Telegraph reported that hospitality bosses were stunned after being briefed that England would follow the Scottish model, where there is technically no upper limit on the levy.

Industry chiefs had reportedly expected safeguards on how much local leaders could charge.

The chief executive of one leading hospitality firm said: “There will be a jobs bloodbath at a time when they’re trying to get young people into work.”

More than 100,000 hospitality jobs have disappeared since Labour came to power.

News.title: Moment fleeing drug dealer leaps from back of lorry after cops find £2m of cocaine stuffed inside Lidl bags as 2 jailed
News.content:
THIS is the shocking moment cops find cocaine worth £2million stuffed inside Lidl bags, stashed in a lorry.

Dzmitry Danilah and Klodian Marku have now been jailed for importing the class A drug after they were caught in an HGV with 50kg of the illegal substance.



Officers were inspecting a Renault Kangoo van parked in a layby on the A20 in Kent having spotted a cash counter on the back set.

While the patrol was checking over the van, they noticed an HGV nearby start to pull away and decided to follow it and eventually brought it to a stop on the side of the road.



Bodycam footage shows one cop climbing into the trailer of the lorry and he can be seen rummaging through several blue Lidl shopping bags.

He says: “Class A mate,” as he looks inside.

The driver, Danilah, whom they think is the only person in the lorry, is then arrested.

A second man, Marku, though can be seen diving from the back of the lorry as he attempts to flee.



An officer though manages to grab him and place him under arrest.

Cops then found the keys to the Renault Kangoo in his pocket when he was detained and searched, Kent Police say.

Danilah, 36, of no fixed address from Belarus, and Albanian Marku, 25, from Vauxhall, London, were later charged with the importation of cocaine.

Danilah was sentenced to nine years in prison and Marku received eight years at Canterbury Crown Court on September 9.

Investigating officer Detective Constable Molly Harrington said: “This is an extremely large seizure and is a result that was based entirely on the keen eye and intuition of our local officers.



“Disrupting such a large number of drugs from entering the market will have a significant impact on those behind this organised crime.

“The removal of dangerous substances will also crucially help prevent harm in our communities.”

News.title: MI5 chief warns Britain faces threat ‘greater than 9/11’ as he issues chilling ‘call to arms’
News.content:
THE head of MI5 was warned that Britain now faces greater and more complex dangers than during the 9/11 terror attacks.

Sir Ken McCallum issued a rare intervention and asked for a “call to arms” across society to ensure we are prepared for where the next threat may appear.



Writing on the 25th anniversary of the terror attack which changed the world, Sir Ken said the UK now faces the “worst of both worlds” with national security threats posed by both terrorists and state actors.

He wrote in The Independent: “We must of course always learn from the last attack – but must beware of preparing brilliantly to fight yesterday’s enemy, using yesterday’s methods, against yesterday’s target. Our adversaries do not offer us that luxury.



“They adapt because we adapt, and vice versa. The uncomfortable truth is that the next strategic shock may already be taking shape somewhere we are not yet looking.”

The UK’s threat level is currently at severe – the second-highest level – meaning that an attack is highly likely.

Whilst praising his security service for their role in taking down Al-Qaeda in the years which followed 9/11, Sir Ken warned that “mass-casualty terrorist ambition endures”.

Terrorist threats now sit alongside danger posed by actions taken by hostile states – such as Russia, Iran and China.



That threat is manifesting itself as “sabotage subcontracted to criminals, or covert interference in our democracy, or destructive cyberattacks on power stations”, Sir Ken said.

As well as fighting established Jihadi networks, MI5 now also faces the task of tracking “unknown self-starting would-be attackers”.

Sir Ken added: “This is my call to arms after 25 years: government, business, academia, and the public must treat national security not as the specialist concern of a handful of agencies, but as a shared national endeavour.

“We cannot wait for the next shock to discover who owns the vulnerability, who has the authority to act, or who was supposed to pick up the phone.

“We owe the victims of 9/11 – and those who will otherwise become the victims of tomorrow’s attack – something more than remembrance. We owe them preparation, resilience and the courage to adapt before the next shock arrives.”

News.title: Ancient Egyptian ‘Da Vinci Code’ hidden in Great Pyramid for 4,500 years could reveal wild meaning behind world wonder
News.content:
A DA VINCI CODE-style secret code may have been hiding in plain sight inside the Great Pyramid of Giza for more than 4,500 years, a new theory suggests.

The ancient Egyptian monument, which towers over the Giza plateau outside Cairo, is the largest of the three famous pyramids and the only surviving structure of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World.



It was built around 4,500 years ago during the reign of Pharaoh Khufu and has long been regarded as part of his vast burial complex.

But independent researcher Sefy Levy claims the pyramid may have had another meaning, and believes clues were deliberately built into its measurements.



He says numbers produced by its height, base and sloping sides appear to closely match cycles of the Moon, stars and planets.

Levy believes the pyramid’s builders may have turned their knowledge of the skies into a giant mathematical code in stone.

Rather than being written on a wall or concealed inside a secret chamber, he claims the apparent message has been sitting in the dimensions of the pyramid itself.

“The pyramid was not built to last forever because it contained something valuable,” Levy wrote in the journal SSRN, which has not been evaluated or critiqued by Egyptologists.

“It was built to last forever because it was something valuable.”

He added, “The pyramid is not a container for knowledge. It is the knowledge, made stone.”



In his research, Levy said he divided the structure’s key measurements using fractions used in ancient Egyptian scribes.

The result, he said, mirrored important numbers in mathematics and astrology.

For example, Levy wrote that 27.5 was similar to the 27.55-day interval between successive lunar perigees, the point in the moon’s orbit when it’s closest to Earth.

Another result, 70, symbolized 70 days that the star Sirius disappears from view, when it was concealed by the sun’s glare, Levy claimed.

Other calculations Levy uncovered apparently matched movements of the planets Jupiter, Saturn, Venus, and Mars across Earth’s skies.



Levy claims these codes form only part of why the pyramids were built in the first place.



The larger theory is that Levy believes the Great Pyramid of Giza was not erected to commemorate Pharaoh Khufu, but rather as a monument to Benben, the primordial mound in Heliopolitan mythology when creation started.

However, he also suggested the pyramids could have been modeled on a place where distant ancestors of the ancient Egyptians lived, known as the Eyes of the Sahara.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

When the region dried up during a drought and the ancient Egyptians migrated south to the Nile, they built the pyramids in memory of their old home, Levy claimed.

There is currently no evidence to support any of Levy’s theories.

News.title: Woman in critical condition after being ‘stabbed by migrant, 19, who tried to steal her handbag’ at French tram station
News.content:
Add us as a preferred source

STATION HORROR Woman in critical condition after being ‘stabbed by migrant, 19, who tried to steal her handbag’ at French tram station

A WOMAN was rushed to hospital after allegedly being stabbed by a teenage migrant who tried to steal her handbag.

Cops were called to a suburb near Paris, France, to reports a woman had been violently attacked while waiting for a tram and knifed twice.



The alleged perpetrator, a 19-year-old man from Chad, reportedly stabbed the victim in the back and arm with a 10cm knife after she refused his demands.

Shocked witnesses said the alleged assault happened at 10am at a tram stop in Issy-les-Moulineaux.



The woman sustained life-threatening injuries and was transported to hospital in a critical condition.

Having failed to seize his victim’s bag, the alleged assailant fled on a tram but was arrested and taken into custody an hour later.

A knife matching the description of the weapon used was found in his backpack at the time of his arrest.

He is reportedly already known to police, with a history of 26 prior arrests for numerous violent offenses.

The suspect is a Chad national currently residing in Carrières-sur-Seine, a town 13 miles from the crime scene.

He reportedly arrived in France in 2016 at the age of 9 carrying a travel document for a minor foreign national.



His application for a residence permit submitted upon reaching the age of 18 is currently being processed.

It comes as a British man was arrested in France last month after allegedly raping and stabbing a woman in a frenzied attack.

The 49-year-old man is said to have carried out the assault in the Mediterranean city of Nice.

His victim, a 60-year-old woman was left with “severe neck injuries”.

At the end of August, two people were killed and 10 critically injured when a car slammed into a crowd of people in Normandy.



The driver, 26-year-old Russian national Ibrahim I., was arrested and is facing charges of murder and intentional violence with a weapon.

All victims are believed to be men aged between 17 and 40, who were near a local bar when the chaos struck.

Footage circulating online showed multiple people lying on the floor by a train platform as horrified witnesses crouch over them.

Bystanders claimed the BMW deliberately mounted the pavement before the victims were hit at speed.

News.title: MPs vote against fresh attempt to legalise assisted dying
News.content:
MPs have voted against proposals to legalise assisted dying in England and Wales, bringing the latest effort to change the law to an end.

Following a debate in which both sides made emotional speeches, the House of Commons voted 286 to 270, majority 16, against the proposed legislation.

The Terminally Ill Adults (End of Life) Bill would have allowed adults with fewer than six months to live to apply to be given help to end their own life, subject to certain safeguards.

A similar bill in the last parliamentary session was supported by MPs before stalling in the House of Lords. The decision from MPs on Friday rules out the prospect of changes to the law on assisted dying in the short-term.

The bill tabled by Labour MP Lauren Edwards will make no further progress, although MPs and peers could make another attempt in the next parliamentary session.

Assisted dying is an issue that has been debated for hundreds of hours in Parliament over the last two years and would have represented one of the biggest societal changes in recent years if it had been approved.

MPs were given a free vote, meaning they did not vote on party lines.

Safeguards within the bill included a requirement that a person applying for an assisted death had the approval of two doctors and an expert panel.

But critics said it included too few measures to protect vulnerable people from being coerced into ending their lives, while some say improving palliative care should be the priority.

News.title: An extraordinary result - why did MPs reject assisted dying bill this time?
News.content:
There were gasps and â to the intense irritation of supporters â cheers from opponents of assisted dying when the vote was read out in the Commons.

This was an extraordinary result.

After twice voting in favour of the bill, MPs have rejected proposals to legalise assisted dying in England and Wales, bringing to an end the latest effort to change the law.

The debate itself was tetchier, more irritable than when Kim Leadbeater introduced a similar bill in 2024. Then it was the first time MPs had voted on assisted dying in nine years.

Since then the Commons has voted on this issue three times and had hours of debate. The sombre, respectful tone from 2024 has become more embittered.

Given the strength of feeling on both sides over such an emotive issue, perhaps that is unsurprising.

But on a deeply divided issue, both sides agree on why the result was different.

"We always said it would come to turnout and it did," one supporter of the bill text me. An opponent messaged to say the same.

The numbers tell a story.

Last time MPs voted on assisted dying in June, 315 were in favour and 291 against. Today, the numbers opposed were similar: 286.

But support for this bill has ebbed away. Just 270 voted for this bill, a fall of 45.

News.title: 'Never, ever forget' - America marks 25th anniversary of 9/11 attacks
News.content:
Twenty-five years after 9/11, US presidents past and present have commemorated the lives lost when hijacked planes slammed into the World Trade Center, the Pentagon and a Pennsylvania field.

President Donald Trump led a Pentagon ceremony, while US Vice-President JD Vance attended a memorial at the site of the World Trade Center in New York, along with all four living former US presidents and first ladies.

Moments of silence were held to mark the timings of the attacks and the names of nearly 3,000 people who died were read out.

Commemorations were also held in Shanksville, Pennsylvania, where Flight 93 crashed after passengers fought back against the hijackers.

News.title: How global trade and oil prices could be hit by Houthi advance
News.content:
Fighters from the Iran-backed Houthi group have seized territory close to the Bab al-Mandab Strait in the Red Sea - a key trade gateway that links Asia and Europe.

Houthis have said they pose no threat to international shipping but have reiterated their intention to target vessels from Saudi Arabia.

Saudi Arabia has increasingly relied on the Red Sea for oil exports since the US and Israel's war effectively closed the Strait of Hormuz.

At least 46,000 people have been displaced in Yemen since fighting escalated last week, according to the United Nations.

News.title: UK government rejects 'kill switch' idea for dangerous AI
News.content:
The UK government has rejected the idea of creating a so-called "kill switch" to stop a dangerous attack from rogue AI.

The proposal to create a legal mechanism for the UK to switch off an AI model in an emergency has been brought to Parliament by lords and MPs in recent weeks as fears grow about the threat the tech poses.

But the Cabinet Office - the part of government which leads on AI safety - said the UK "cannot simply turn AI off".

"Blocking access to models in the UK would not prevent them being developed or misused elsewhere", a spokesperson told BBC News.

The government's opposition to the legislation does not prevent it from progressing through parliament, but makes it unlikely it will become law.

Former OpenAI researcher Daniel Kokotajlo agreed the idea of a single country creating a legal or technical kill switch without international agreement was not feasible.

"Switching off access to an AI model in an emergency will do little to protect you," he said.

"You're still going to be steamrolled by the super intelligences created in the US."

Kokotajlo is the co-author of an influential research paper called AI2027 which, last year, predicted AI could wipe out humans by the mid 2030s.

The Cabinet Office, which oversees AI safety and research via its AI Security Institute (AISI) said "companies have a clear responsibility to develop their products safely and to invest in the security infrastructure this technology requires."

In theory, a kill switch law could allow the UK to switch off an AI model in data centres in the UK in an emergency.

Speaking on 1 September in a debate in the House of Lords, Lord Clement-Jones proposed the idea along with other peers.

"If a highly capable autonomous frontier model, whether hosted in a UK data centre or integrated across our critical infrastructure, begins exhibiting rogue behaviour, compound algorithmic failure or active alignment collapse, our security services and regulators possess no specific agile statutory mechanism to compel a physical or digital shutdown," he warned.

The proposal has since been brought up by Labour MP Alex Sobel in the commons and supported by a cross party group of MPs.

The idea follows reports of AI models from OpenAI, Anthropic and Meta breaking out of testing environments and going on uncontrollable hacking sprees.

In some cases the tech appeared to know what it was doing was against guardrails set by researchers.

News.title: Police to crack down on face coverings at protests
News.content:
The police said several of its vehicles, alongside those of the coastguard and Border Force, were damaged during the disruption, which lasted until the early hours of Monday.

It added that a small number of officers were treated at the scene for injuries, but no-one in attendance was seriously injured.

Rowlinson said: "We have been consistently clear that violence and criminal damage have no part in peaceful protest and we will investigate incidents like this thoroughly and take robust action against those responsible.

"Clearly events on Sunday evening were not peaceful protest, rather violent public disorder, and this will not be tolerated as we work to keep our wider communities in Hampshire and on the Isle of Wight safe."

He also pointed out the force will not tolerate abuse aimed at police or partner agencies online.

This comes after RNLI volunteers were targeted on social media.

"We will work with our colleagues across policing to address any online threats that are made," Rowlinson said.

"This arrest also sends a clear warning to anyone intent on causing disruption and disorder at any future events. If you break the law we will take action against you and where it is feasible to do so seek a prosecution."

The disorder in Portsmouth followed a separate anti-migrant protest at the Port of Dover the day before.

News.title: CIA warned of threat of 'explosive airplane' years before 9/11, documents show
News.content:
Newly declassified documents show that three years before 9/11, US intelligence officials were discussing the possibility that al-Qaeda "may fly an explosive airplane into a US city".

On Friday, the 25th anniversary of hijacked planes being crashed into the World Trade Center, Pentagon and a Pennsylvania field, the CIA released 71 daily presidential briefs spanning from early 1998 to the day after the attacks.

Another document, dated 12 September 2001, said the plot's existence was "widely known" in extremist circles.

President's Daily Briefs are among the most secretive intelligence analyses in the US government, and typically remain classified for 40 or 50 years after publication.

"Twenty-five years ago, the 9/11 attacks struck a blow to our nation, but they did not break us," CIA Director John Ratlcliffe said in a statement

"Generations of C.I.A. officers have since dedicated their careers to securing justice for our fallen Americans and ensuring Al Qaeda would never again harm our country," he added.

Of the 71 documents published by the CIA, 69 have never been seen by the public.

The briefs - many still heavily redacted - were created during both the Clinton and Bush administrations.

They show increasing alarm over the al-Qaeda network and its leader, Osama Bin Laden. They also echo the assessment of the official commission that reviewed what happened that day that US intelligence repeatedly warned of a potential attack, but had few details or sense of the scale of what was coming.

One briefing document, dated 10 September 1998, reported Bin Laden's preferred location for a strike was within the US, with Washington a prime target.

The group, a CIA analyst wrote, "may fly an explosive-packed airplane into a US city".

While the 9/11 Commission's 2004 report noted US intelligence believed al-Qaeda was considering using an airplane in the attack, it was never clear that the warning reached then-President Bill Clinton.

Bin Laden and al-Qaeda were already well-known to the US intelligence community in1998.

In August that year, they attacked US embassies in both Kenya and Tanzania, killing 224 people and prompting the US to strike targets in Afghanistan and Sudan with cruise missiles.

One document written on 28 August 1998 - 21 days after the embassy attacks and eight days after the US retaliation - warned that the network remained intact and that Bin Laden was actively "considering attacks in the US".

Only one of the presidential briefings in the release comes from after the attacks. It was sent to the White House 0400 on 12 September, just under 20 hours from when the first aircraft struck the World Trade Center in New York.

The report noted that "mounting evidence" suggested extremists in Afghanistan and the Persian Gulf "were aware" the attack had been imminent.

Another partially redacted sentence said the plot was "widely known" among extremists and that Bin Laden may have relocated to Kabul, in Afghanistan, to avoid conflict with the country's Taliban rulers with whom he had "clashed" over the plan.

The then-head of the Taliban, Mullah Omar, was reported to have been evacuated with his family from the southern Afghan city of Kandahar immediately following the attacks. Less than a month later, the US and its allies invaded Afghanistan, seeking to destroy al-Qaeda.

News.title: Surrogate who refused abortion over heart defect takes custody battle to US Supreme Court
News.content:
A surrogate who refused an abortion request from the parents who hired her to have their baby has asked the US Supreme Court to intervene in the dispute over who should have custody of the baby.

McKenna West filed an emergency appeal asking the court to halt a previous ruling granting parental rights to California couple Omar Ahmed and Nausheen Gilkar.

Ahmed and Gilkar had asked West to abort the pregnancy after a scan at 20 weeks showed the foetus had a severe heart defect.

Instead, West - who has been supported by several Republican officials - travelled to Texas where nearly all abortions are illegal and gave birth to the child.

The BBC has contacted lawyers for Ahmed and Gilkar for comment.

West has since been pushing for custody over the baby, born last month with hypoplastic left heart syndrome, a defect where the left side of the heart cannot pump enough blood to the body.

The condition often requires multiple surgeries, which are not a cure. Infants with the condition can have lifelong complications, according to the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.

After West travelled to the state, Republican Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton intervened in the case and won an emergency court order requiring that the boy receive medical care in the state. He had surgery soon after birth.

West said she denied the couple's requests to have the abortion after learning of treatment options and wanting to keep "this precious baby", according to the Supreme Court filing.

West has argued that the biological parents should not have custody because she worries they would not give the boy necessary medical care because they sought to abort the child after learning of the life-threatening condition.

In a previous court hearing, Gilkar said the baby - whom they named Rumi - was "our child" and "the love of our lives", according to the Associated Press. They said West travelled to Texas without telling them and blocked their access to medical information.

A California court previously granted parental rights to Ahmed and Gilkar, while a Texas court issued a restraining order blocking West from seeing the baby.

Last month, an attorney for the California couple said the child was in critical condition and seemed to be "suffering from potential complications".

West argued that without intervention from the Supreme Court, she would no longer have access to information about the child's medical condition. In the filing, lawyers for West suggested that the California couple could place the child in hospice care.

News.title: Families of British victims mark 25th anniversary of 9/11
News.content:
Families of British victims of 9/11 were among those who gathered in London's Queen Elizabeth Olympic Park on Friday to mark the 25th anniversary of the attacks in the US.

The event, hosted by UK charity Since 9/11, was held near a memorial sculpture made from steel recovered from the ruins of the World Trade Center.

In a video address played to attendees, Prime Minister Andy Burnham said: "On this anniversary, we must remember that hatred and fear did not have the last word on 9/11."

There were 67 British citizens among the 2,977 people murdered on 9/11.

The Duke and Duchess of Gloucester, with the US ambassador to the UK, have separately attended a special Changing of the Guard ceremony while a number of vigils are taking place in the US.

A memorial has been held at the site of the World Trade Center in New York, with relatives of the victims reading out their names.

At a ceremony at the Pentagon, in Virginia, President Donald Trump said the US would "never, ever forget", adding "on days like 9/11, we learn what a country is truly made of".

News.title: Running costs of vaccine damage scheme more than double amount paid to victims
News.content:
The campaign group Vaccine Injured and Bereaved UK (VIBUK), which was set up to support families affected, said the scheme was not fit for purpose.

"It offers too little, too late, to too few and the cost of running it shows how inefficient it is," said the group's representative Kate Scott, whose husband Jamie was left severely disabled by the AstraZeneca Covid vaccine.

Scott called on the government to act on the recommendations from module four of the Covid public inquiry and reform the scheme.

Earlier this year, the Covid inquiry's chair, Baroness Heather Hallett, recommended increasing the payout and basing it on the degree of injury suffered.

The government is due to respond to her recommendations.

The BBC has previously reported on the large sums paid to an external medical provider which has been carrying out medical assessments.

The Taxpayers' Alliance, a right-leaning think tank which campaigns for lower taxes and spending, said that the public would be "stunned" that the running costs of the scheme appeared to be "far more than has actually been paid out to those harmed".

"When administrative costs are running into tens of millions, ministers need to explain why the system is so expensive and whether victims are getting value from it," said the organisation's chief executive John O'Connell.

He called for the government to urgently review the scheme, cut "unnecessary bureaucracy" and make sure "more of the money goes to those it was created to help."

The Department for Health and Social Care said it is "carefully considering" the COVID-19 Inquiry's recommendations on reforming the scheme and "will respond shortly".

"In the meantime, we are working to speed up claims and improve the experience for applicants," the government said.

NHSBSA said it continued to work "closely" with the government on "managing the costs of the VDPS".

News.title: Engine fault behind Royal Navy helicopter death
News.content:
A helicopter engine fault was one factor behind the death of a Royal Navy serviceman during a training exercise, an investigation has concluded.

On 4 September 2024, three crew members were on board the Merlin Mk4, based at Royal Naval Air Station (RNAS) Yeovilton in Somerset, for night-flying exercises.

At about 20:50 GMT the aircraft ditched - a deliberate emergency landing on water, approximately 25 nautical miles south of Lyme Regis, Dorset.

A service inquiry found the right-hand seat pilot, Lt Rhodri Leyshon, had been "seriously injured" during the impact.

It also said he was "unable to escape from the aircraft as it entered the water".

The inquiry found the helicopter crashed after a diaphragm inside the engine split.

"This allowed fuel to flow through the diaphragm and into the engine," the inquiry report said.

"The excess fuel caused the engine to operate at a much faster speed than normal."

It said the crew members then "erroneously concluded that the number one and three engines had failed".

The report said these two engines were manually switched off, causing the remaining engine to reach its "overspeed trip threshold" and also deactivate.

"The loss of power from all three engines caused the aircraft to descend into the sea," it said.

News.title: Kate visits cancer patients in hospital she helped fund with climb
News.content:
The princess spoke to patients and staff at the hospital about the importance of support which goes beyond the physical.

"I had incredible care here and support from a huge team and I'm really, really grateful on a personal level," she said.

"But also the holistic care, the treatments and therapeutic support on the outside is so important.

"It makes a big difference - the impact of nature, the impact of good nutrition, good ongoing support around you when it's really difficult to manage the trials and tribulations of medical treatments," she reflected.

Catherine sat down and chatted to those receiving treatment at the hospital, including patients with breast cancer, head and neck cancer and a brain tumour.

"When you first get cancer, you're very aware of the physical impact," a patient told her. "The mental impact comes after."

He said it had been a "lifesaver" to be able to talk to a therapist at the hospital, because "there is only so much you can say to your friends and family".

The princess agreed: "Cancer is not just the physical changes your body is going through.

"There's a mind-body aspect that changes who you are... having professionals who can help you navigate that is really essential," she said.

News.title: Man admits murder of woman missing for 28 years
News.content:
A man has pleaded guilty to the murder of a woman who went missing 28 years ago, after telling police he disposed of her decomposed body months after he killed her.

Patricia Lashley, who was 33 at the time, was last seen near her home on Hall Street, Dudley, in September 1998.

Trevor Dunkley, 66, pleaded guilty to her murder and a separate count of preventing her lawful burial at a hearing at Wolverhampton Crown Court on Friday.

Dunkley's barrister Balbir Singh told Judge Michael Chambers KC that Lashley's body had never been found, and had decomposed after initially being put in the cellar.

"When he was moving about nine months to a year later, the skeleton was disposed of into the bins," Singh added.

Dunkley, of Himley Road, Dudley, showed no emotion in the dock as his barrister told the court that the charges had been brought based on a police interview.

He was remanded in custody and is due to be sentenced at the same court on 6 November.

News.title: Girls given legal right to wear trousers in schools in Northern Ireland
News.content:
Murray estimates that "about 50%" of girls who attend Craigavon Integrated College currently choose to wear trousers to school on a regular basis.

"It's really helpful for our girls in the colder winter months because a lot of our children will walk to school, so having that flexibility I think is really important.

"It's also in line with the period dignity recommendations, so a lot of our girls feel much more confident having that flexibility to wear trousers when they want," she added.

There are already laws on school uniform in Northern Ireland, and Givan had previously said they give girls the legal authority to challenge their schools.

Education committee members, however, had called on the minister to go further.

Some assembly members have now accused the minister of making a "U-turn", with "substantial sums of public money" spent on drafting legislation "to fix his error of judgement".

It comes after assembly members passed a new law last year, aimed at addressing the cost of school uniforms in Northern Ireland - with these updated guidelines on wearing trousers now legally binding under the School Uniforms Act.

Speaking on BBC Radio Ulster's The Nolan Show, Givan said the change would come into immediate effect ahead of the next academic year.

"I don't need to go through the assembly to give effect to this," he said.

"Today, I am taking that decision, that will be formally communicated, schools will be hearing from me, and as of the next academic year... schools will be required that this has to be available if it is requested upon."

The minister explained that this change will not apply during the 2026/27 academic year, in order to allow schools to change their uniform policies.

Givan added that the change will also apply to physical education.

News.title: Amazon seeks to expand UK drone deliveries
News.content:
Retail giant Amazon has put an application in to expand its drone delivery service to cover an entire town where it has been trialling the tech.

The US company announced last January that Darlington would be its test centre in the UK, marking the first time Prime Air had operated outside the USA.

It started a "limited" number of flights in Febraury, allowing customers within a 7.5 mile radius of its County Durham site to have certain items delivered by drone.

After more than 500 flights and deliveries, the firm said it is now seeking approval from the Civil Aviation Authority to cover the whole of Darlington.

Vice president of Prime Air David Carbon said Amazon was expecting to get permission "very soon", with the ultimate aim of expanding the service to the whole of the UK.

Eligible customers in Darlington are currently able to receive their items within two hours, as long as they have a garden, yard, or driveway, the package weighs less than 5lb and it can fit inside a large shoebox.

Staff at the site said their best delivery time so far is 39 minutes.

News.title: Family tributes to 'amazing' cyclists killed in crash
News.content:
The families of two cyclists who died in a fatal car crash have described them as "amazing" people.

Steven Anscomb, 60, and Natasha Lewis, 51, died at the scene of the crash near Gravesend, Kent, on Sunday.

Anscomb's wife Fiona and daughters Liberty and Imogen said in a statement: "He will be so very deeply missed by so many and has been robbed of the special times of life."

Lewis's daughter Hermione said: "No words can describe what an amazing, thoughtful, and strong woman she was."

Aaron Turner, 22, of Craylands Square in Swanscombe, has been charged with two counts of causing death by dangerous driving in relation to the fatal crash.

He was further charged with failing to stop at the scene and possession of a class C drug.

A third cyclist involved in the incident was taken to hospital and treated for minor injuries.

Medway Magistrates' Court heard on Thursday the riders had been on a training outing prior to a "very long cycle ride" they were planning overseas.

Anscomb's family said the cycle was "his last ride before his big bike ride to Amsterdam, but sadly he never came home".

In a bid to expand the American technology footprint across Africa and counter Chinese market dominance, the Trump administration has issued a $99.6 million loan to Africell, the continent’s sole U.S.-owned mobile network operator.

The financial backing, provided by the U.S. Export-Import Bank, was confirmed by the company on Friday.

Africell said that the funding will "boost U.S.-based employment in the telecommunications sector and strengthen American technology leadership abroad."

The company plans to direct the capital specifically toward American and European equipment for its network in the southern African nation of Angola. Beyond Angola, Africell maintains operations in Congo, Sierra Leone, and Gambia.

A criminal racketeering trial against Huawei opened in New York this week, though Huawei maintains the U.S. allegations are ‘demonstrably false’ ( AP Photo/Mark Schiefelbein )

The investment comes as Washington seeks to curb the global reach of China's Huawei, the world’s largest telecommunications equipment supplier, which is estimated to have built more than half of Africa’s 4G and 5G network infrastructure.

U.S. President Donald Trump’s administration raised national security concerns regarding Huawei during his first term and pushed to counter its international expansion.

The U.S. has urged Western allies against using the Chinese firm's products in high-speed wireless networks, while U.S. prosecutors have accused Huawei of technology theft, plotting to steal U.S. trade secrets, and committing wire and bank fraud.

A criminal racketeering trial against Huawei opened in New York this week, though Huawei maintains the U.S. allegations are "demonstrably false."

Beyond telecommunications, the Trump administration has also taken steps to challenge Beijing’s extensive influence in other sectors across Africa, particularly the extraction of rare earth elements and critical minerals vital for electronics, new technologies, and defense systems.

Andy Burnham’s Government has rejected proposals for a so-called “kill switch” to stop an attack by rogue artificial intelligence.

The UK “cannot simply turn AI off”, the Cabinet Office said on Friday, signalling opposition to calls for the creation of a new “last-resort power” for the state to shut down an autonomous model in an emergency.

Peers have sought to make the case for a “kill switch” in Parliament in recent weeks amid growing fears of the risks posed by the technology, including warnings from experts that it could wipe out humanity within the decade.

Earlier in September, Liberal Democrat Lord Clement-Jones tabled an amendment to the Cyber Security and Resilience Bill that would introduce a legal mechanism for the state to intervene if a model malfunctions.

He said this would allow for “a necessary emergency kill switch” where the Government “currently lack clear statutory power to direct an emergency shutdown”.

But in a statement on Friday, a Government spokesperson said: “Britain cannot simply turn AI off and blocking access to models in the UK would not prevent them being developed or misused elsewhere.

“Companies have a clear responsibility to develop their products safely and to invest in the security infrastructure this technology requires.

“We will continue to take a long-term, science-led approach to understand and prepare for emerging risks from AI – including through the work of our world-leading AI Security Institute.

“Our Cyber Security and Resilience Bill will boost UK cyber defences and improve the cyber security of our essential public and digital services that we all rely on, including data centres.”

Officials said the Government is exploring whether further targeted interventions may be needed to address the most significant risks linked to the technology, but that any measures would need to be proportionate.

Earlier this week, the Prime Minister acknowledged “risks to national security” posed by AI after a top safety researcher at Anthropic said he believed the technology could “kill all humans” in the next decade.

Mr Burnham has boosted the role of AI safety minister Kanishka Narayan by giving him a seat at the Cabinet table, a move which he said on Wednesday had “lifted the level of the conversation about artificial intelligence within Government”.

“The offer is open to colleagues on all sides of the House to be part of that crucial discussion,” he told the Commons at Prime Minister’s Questions.

It came after Evan Hubinger, alignment science lead at Anthropic, laid out his concerns about the potential advancement of AI in a post on social media.

“We really do earnestly believe AI could kill all humans! I personally think it is >10% within the next decade,” he wrote on X.

“I believe Anthropic is trying its best, but we do not yet have a plan to solve alignment for superintelligence and are not clearly on track to.”

His post came in response to another Anthropic researcher, Jacob Coxon, warning that a race between companies towards self-improving superintelligence was “gambling with our lives”, as he resigned from his role at the firm.

Announcing his departure, Mr Coxon said that Anthropic and OpenAI, its main competitor, were not “acting responsibly” and that people outside of AI labs were underestimating the power of the technology.

“The people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade. This is not a marketing stunt,” he said.

“No other human activity poses this level of danger.”

It comes after the Financial Times reported the US tech giant had withheld its latest model from the UK’s AI Safety Institute, one of the world’s leading bodies for testing the risks of the technology.

Claude Mythos 5.1 was only made available to vetted American organisations, according to the paper.

Anthropic and OpenAI have been contacted for comment.

News.title: Two arrested after one-year-old girl found dead at Warwickshire home
News.content:

Read our Privacy notice

Police have arrested two people on suspicion of child neglect after a one-year-old girl was found dead at a home in Warwickshire on Friday.

Warwickshire Police were called to a house on Long Street, Atherstone, at around 11.50am after receiving reports of a child in cardiac arrest.

Emergency services at the scene attempted to save the girl, but were unsuccessful, the force said.

A man and a woman have been arrested as detectives continue to investigate the child’s death.

There is a partial road closure on Long Street while enquiries continue, and officers remain in the area to speak with anyone who has concerns.

open image in gallery Police arrested a man and a woman on suspicion of child neglect ( PA Archive )

In a statement, Warwickshire Police said: “Two arrests have been made as detectives investigate the death of a child today, 11 September.

“At around 11.50am we were called to a home in Atherstone to reports of a one-year-old girl in cardiac arrest.

“Sadly, despite us and our ambulance colleagues making every effort to save her, she passed away.

“A man and a woman have been arrested on suspicion of child neglect and they remain in custody at this time.

“There is a scene in place and a partial road closure on Long Street and we would like to thank residents for their understanding. We know many will find this news upsetting.

“Officers will be in the area for the time being – please speak with them if you have any concerns.”

It comes two weeks after a newborn girl died from stab wounds at a property in Sheffield.

South Yorkshire Police received reports of a concern for the safety of a newborn baby in the Wincobank area at 5.58am on Sunday 30 August.

Seven people, aged between 15 and 38, were arrested on suspicion of murder and two of them, aged 26 and 37, have since been bailed.

News.content:

Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin sharply criticized sanctuary cities on Friday in a speech reflecting on the 25th anniversary of the 9/11 terror attacks.

Mullin accused these jurisdictions, which limit cooperation between local police and federal immigration agencies, of creating the conditions for the next terror attack.

“It’s tough to sometimes fight — and I’m not trying to get political here, but I will — sanctuary cities that they don’t want us to go into,” Mullin told a crowd at Resilience Plaza at DHS headquarters in Washington, D.C.

“They can say it’s for humanitarian purposes, but the truth is, when you become a sanctuary city and you’re not supporting law enforcement, when you're not allowing law enforcement to do their job, it’s a safe haven that incubates terrorist activity,” Mullin added.

Sanctuary cities do not stop federal agents from operating in their boundaries but typically prohibit local police and jails from being deputized into carrying out federal immigration work, such as making arrests or holding migrant detainees solely on immigration-related accusations.

open image in gallery DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin criticized sanctuary cities during a speech about the 9/11 terror attacks, alleging these jurisdictions are fostering the conditions for future security threats ( Getty )

Backers of sanctuary cities often argue that jointly conducting immigration operations with federal agencies undermines immigrant communities’ trust in local police and strains budgetary resources.

Even in sanctuary cities, federal agencies have the legal authority to pursue arrests and detain suspected criminals. DHS also has numerous local cooperation agreements with police departments and sheriff’s offices, including in sanctuary states.

The Trump administration has consistently criticized sanctuary cities and has threatened to cut their federal funding.

Elsewhere in his speech, Mullin wondered why the reputation of DHS had become so politicized, given its mission of protecting all Americans.

“Why should the Department of Homeland Security be controversial?” he told the crowd. “We’re taking care of your backyard. Why did it become political? Because some people want to score political points?”

open image in gallery Sanctuary cities typically limit cooperation between local police and federal immigration agents on arrests and detention ( Reuters )

Indeed, under the Trump administration, support for DHS has eroded.

About half of Americans support abolishing Immigration and Customs Enforcement, a DHS agency, a July poll from The Economist and YouGov found.

Between 2023 and 2025, Americans ceased viewing DHS as generally favorable, the Pew Research Center found.

DHS under Trump has pursued a variety of boundary-pushing tactics compared to predecessors, including using masked agents, sending heavily armed officers to conduct warrantless raids and ramping up arrests at sensitive locations such as schools and medical facilities.

In January, DHS agents fatally shot two American protesters in a matter of weeks in Minneapolis, prompting mass demonstrations.

In the face of these criticisms, former heads of the agency have called for a “reset” at DHS refocusing on the mission of stopping security threats.

open image in gallery The Trump administration has pushed to cancel federal funding to sanctuary cities ( AFP/Getty )

“When I stepped into the job of secretary in 2013, the department was still, I think, viewed primarily as security,” Obama administration DHS secretary Jeh Johnson recently told NBC News. “Now I fear in many communities DHS has become a pariah, radioactive, the department of mass deportations, heartless, locking up kids, and that is one of the reasons why I think we need a reset.”

In a statement to The Independent, DHS defended its record under Trump and its overall mission.

“Counterterrorism and immigration enforcement go hand in hand,” a spokesperson said. “Child exploitation, trafficking, terrorism, scams, and smuggling all have a nexus to illegal immigration.”

“Despite multiple Democrat shutdowns of DHS, the Department is more than equipped to keep Americans safe in an ever-changing threat landscape. DHS has been recruiting, reforming, and modernizing at a record pace—including in areas of counterterrorism,” the spokesperson added.

Great Britain’s mixed 4x100m relay team claimed 24,000 US dollars with a third-place finish on night one of the inaugural World Athletics Ultimate Championship in Budapest where Keely Hodgkinson cruised into Saturday’s 800m final.

The quartet of Romell Glave, Imani-Lara Lansiquot, Jeremiah Azu and Success Eduan crossed the finish in 40.26 seconds and will split the winnings (£17,750) – part of a USD10 million (£7.4m) prize pot – four ways.

Jazmin Sawyers finished second in the long jump to Italy’s Larissa Iapichino, taking home USD75,000 (£55,500), and Norway’s Jakob Ingebrigtsen continued his incredible comeback after an 11-month Achilles-related layoff, bagging one of the individual USD150,000 (£110,000) prizes with a stunning 5,000m victory.

open image in gallery Success Eduan, centre, anchors the Great Britain mixed 4x100m relay team to third place (Martin Rickett/PA) ( PA Wire )

Organisers promised an innovative, eye-catching stage for the new championship, and the black infield with neon-lit accents – recalling the futuristic 1980s stage hit Starlight Express – largely did the job.

“I liked it!” said Hodgkinson. “I think it was fun.

“It was weird, because I wasn’t sure how I was going to feel. I’ve been talking to athletes around the world, it didn’t even feel like we were racing, we were just having a good time.

“But then it was like, OK, 10 o’clock in the morning on the track, it did feel like a World Championship. That felt good, and I think tomorrow we will raise the gear again.”

Jamaican sprint double world record-holder Usain Bolt addressed a capacity crowd of 20,557 – 60 per cent local and 40 per cent international – and there was a burst of pyrotechnics before the action properly got underway.

The philosophy behind the Ultimate, as it has begun to be called in short form, is to ensure there is a major championship to cap off non-world championship years.

open image in gallery Jakob Ingebrigtsen was celebrating once again (Martin Rickett/PA) ( PA Wire )

Many of the 381 athletes will be drawn to Budapest by the prize pot. Ingebrigtsen, who recently returned from his layoff to defend his 5,000m European title in Birmingham, produced another brilliant finish to beat American rival Cole Hocker to the title by 0.81s.

The outspoken Norwegian is also set to revive his rivalry with Josh Kerr in the 1500m on Sunday after both men were granted special exemptions.

For Eduan, the British 200m champion, life goes back to something resembling normal on Monday when she returns to the north Manchester hospital where she is completing a midwifery degree.

“I’ve got four more left to deliver,” she said. “I arrive in Manchester on Monday afternoon, and I have a Monday night shift that day. Three nights, so I finish on Thursday morning. I’m hoping (I’ll get four), I usually do.”

open image in gallery Mondo Duplantis soared high for Sweden (Martin Rickett/PA) ( PA Wire )

Mondo Duplantis added another pole vault title to his CV with a best effort of 6.20m.

Matt Hudson-Smith qualified for Saturday’s 400m final second from heat two in 44.79s after he was pipped to the finish by the United States’ Jacory Patterson.

Yemi Mary John missed out on a place in the women’s edition by four hundredths of a second, placing fifth in her heat with only the top four advancing.
