Roma were awarded a penalty in the 68th minute when ​Kerem Akturkoglu was ‌penalised for a ​foul on Paulo ​Dybala, but a VAR check ruled that the challenge had taken place outside the area. Fenerbahce came closest to grabbing a winner late on when Nathan Aké headed against the Roma crossbar.

Fenerbahce will travel to Aston Villa and host Liverpool in two of their remaining league phase games – whether Kartal will be in charge or not remains to be seen.

Sports.title: Champions League opening data shows English dominance and too few shocks
Sports.content:
The 2026-27 Champions League is under way. There are still 126 matches to play until we know which 24 teams will feature in the knockout phase but that doesn’t mean we haven’t learned anything yet. Here are the key data talking points from week one.

England good, Italy bad?

Premier League teams took five of the eight automatic qualification spots in 2025-26. England’s representatives all won this week to take a step toward repeating that feat. Arguably the biggest winners were Liverpool, as they were the only English team to play an opponent drawn from pot one.

They were at home, though, so perhaps the away victories for Arsenal, Aston Villa and Manchester City were more impressive. Regardless of which club can be most pleased, the Premier League’s dominance was absolute. English teams collectively out-shot their opponents 102-44, put 28 more efforts on target and had 24 shots deemed by Opta to be big chances while conceding only five.

They topped the expected goal difference by country too, a chart that has Italy at the bottom. Como won, Roma drew at Fenerbahce while Napoli and Inter faced Arsenal and Real Madrid respectively. All is far from lost, but Serie A’s numbers were not pretty.

Inter dominated Real Madrid

It wasn’t all bad for Inter. They were one of two teams who had at least 57 touches in the opposition penalty area this week. It’s an incredibly high tally – one that has only been topped once in the Premier League this season, where the average is 24.6 per team per game. For Paris Saint-Germain to be so strongly camped in the Slovan Bratislava box was hardly a surprise. For Inter to be so busy in the Real Madrid penalty area at the Santiago Bernabéu was more worthy of comment.

It would be easy to dismiss this as classic Real; they did not play well in the Champions League but won regardless. And they mustered an enormous nine big chances, missing seven of them, so might have won more comfortably with sharper finishing. But as Inter had the most shots of any visiting team in the league or Europe (in a 90-minute match) for eight years, Real might have lost too.

The only player among the back four who was there last season was 21-year-old Dean Huijsen, which may help explain how Inter were able to have so many attempts at goal. José Mourinho called it “mad, and not a madness I like”. He wasn’t wrong.

Few even games

There were no draws in the first two nights of action. Ismail Kartal resigned as Fenerbahce head coach on Thursday after his side drew 1-1 with Roma, presumably because he was so shocked that the match had finished level.

There were not even many close games on the underlying numbers, with only four of the 18 matches having an expected goal margin between the two teams that was below one. Every team that won deserved to, at least according to the xG.

With so many games still to play, a relative lack of draws this week may prove insignificant. However, it will affect the points tally required to reach the playoff round if the trend continues. There were 25 draws in the 2025-26 league phase, with the team in 24th (Benfica) finishing on nine points. But there were only 18 the season before when Club Brugge finished with 11 points when taking the final playoff spot. Fewer draws mean more teams earn three points, which lifts the bar for competitiveness. We’re currently on track for 16 draws, so keep an eye on how many matches end all square when match week two rolls around.

No surprises

Despite 16 of the 18 matches being won, there were no shocks. For the bloated league phase to generate serious excitement, it needs major upsets. Only two wins were secured by the underdog according to bookmakers, and one of those was Europa League champions Aston Villa beating Club Brugge. Hardly an upset when you compare their finances.

The surprise of the week based on pre-match prediction was Real Betis winning 3-2 at Lille. They are 49th and 52nd respectively in Opta’s Power Rankings, so Betis did not overcome an insurmountable challenge. The early weeks of last season had Qarabag winning at Benfica and Galatasaray beating Liverpool. We need more of those types of results.

Sports.title: Former Premier League footballer Nathaniel Mendez-Laing, 34, charged with beating his wife as he appears in court
Sports.content:
Former Premier League footballer Nathaniel Mendez-Laing, 34, charged with beating his wife as he appears in court

See more Daily Mail on Google - save us as a Preferred Source

Ex-Premier League winger Nathaniel Mendez-Laing has appeared in court after being charged with beating his wife.

The 34-year-old, who currently plays for MK Dons, was accused of assaulting his spouse, Saira Mendez-Laing back in June at their Staffordshire home.

He was arrested after police were called to the property in Shenstone and charged with assault by beating. The Crown Prosecution Service then authorised those charges last month.

Mendez-Laing appeared in Cannock magistrates' court on Friday and denied the charge.

Mendez-Laing and Saira, who is the mother of his child, have only been married for a year having tied the knot last summer.

He was seen entering the court on crutches and confirmed his name, age and address, without speaking further.

Nathaniel Mendez-Laing, pictured with his wife Saira, denies the charge of beating her

The court heard that Mendez-Laing was accused of hitting his wife over the head repeatedly and injuring her arm in the alleged incident.

The dispute between the couple started over a 'disagreement about a phone', but the footballer insists the confrontation did not turn into a physical assault.

The case will go to trial in January next year and the judge, Joseph O'Connor, allowed Mendez-Laing conditional bail rather than remanding him in custody.

MK Dons have said they cannot comment on an ongoing case and are struggling in League One this season.

Mendez-Laing played in the Premier League for Cardiff in 2019-20 and scored four times in 20 games for the Welsh side.

He also turns out for Guatemala, who he qualifies for through his mother and maternal grandmother.

Mendez-Laing has not been seen on the pitch since the opening day of the League One campaign. He moved to MK Dons after spending three years at Derby, during which time he scored 19 goals in 131 games.

Sports.title: Debutant Razaullah hits sensational knock as Pakistan FINALLY show guts and heart to make England pay for their lack of variety for the first time in the series, writes LAWRENCE BOOTH
Sports.content:
After a few weeks in which Pakistan’s batsmen have headed lemming-like to their doom, they finally made England’s bowlers look mortal, unexpectedly dragging this third and final Test into a fourth morning thanks to a raucous stand of 121 between tailenders Razaullah and Mohammad Abbas.

Barring more madness on Saturday, it will still not be enough to avoid the 3-0 whitewash that has looked almost inevitable from the opening day of the series. Pakistan’s lead is just 130, and this pitch remains the best batting strip of the summer, though that isn’t saying much.

But a total of 449 after five successive surrenders below 200 made a welcome change for their supporters and provided England’s bowlers with a useful reality check ahead of stiffer challenges in South Africa this winter. Ollie Robinson’s bowling average for the series even nudged above eight, for goodness sake.

When the dismissal of Razaullah for 81 off 63 balls, stumped as he tried to swing Dan Lawrence for what would have been a tenth six, triggered the close at 7pm, he walked off to a standing ovation from fans of both sides – relieved, regardless of affiliation, to have finally seen some kind of contest. The applause felt like the highlight of the series.

At none for two after two balls of their second innings on Thursday afternoon, no one could rule out another two-day finish in this era of fast-forward Tests. Instead, Pakistan found previously hidden reserves of guts and heart on an Edgbaston surface that was badly betrayed by their first-innings collapse of 133.

And the manner in which Razaullah counter-attacked, while Abbas carefully compiled a career-best 42, was a reminder that for all the excellence of England’s seamers, their lack of a frontline spinner is a weakness opponents will seek to exploit.

Debutant Razaullah (left) ensured Pakistan finally showed some fight against England

There are concerns around England's lack of front-line spinner and how they may fare in less helpful conditions

Lawrence had struck earlier in the day with his loopy off-breaks when Azan Awais tickled his second ball down the leg side to end a third-wicket stand of 125 with Shan Masood. But as Razaullah used the pace of the quick bowlers to launch one six after another, it was clear, for the first time in this series, that England were paying for their lack of variety.

At first, it seemed like a bit of fun. He had walked out into a hopeless situation after Gus Atkinson had removed Ghazi Ghori and Mohammad Imran in successive overs to reduce Pakistan to 318 for eight, still one run short of an innings defeat.

But he ensured England would bat again by pulling Josh Tongue for six, then pulled and drove Atkinson for three meaty sixes in four balls. A straight six off Jofra Archer brought up a 43-ball half-century, and another next ball Pakistan’s 400.

Razaullah, one of four members of this team drafted in at the last minute following the Pakistan board’s chaotic decimation of their touring party, swung Archer for another six, before even Abbas got in on the act, bringing up the 100 lead with a straight six off a startled Atkinson.

Perhaps the pick of Razaullah’s strokes was a flat-batted thrash over extra cover off Atkinson, by which point England and Joe Root were looking worryingly devoid of ideas. It almost came as a surprise when Abbas cut Tongue to Atkinson at point to end the most entertaining passage of play of the Test summer.

Razaullah had time for one more blow, heaving Lawrence over midwicket towards the building site, before he was stumped by Jordan Cox, who enjoyed an excellent day with the gloves in the absence of the injured Jamie Smith. He walked off cursing his demise, though there was no need for self-reproach.

With the exception of Robinson, who went at 2.34 an over and will finish the series with a remarkable haul of 21 wickets at 8.76, England’s other quicks went the distance. Between them, Archer, Atkinson and Tongue conceded 335 runs at nearly five an over while taking six wickets, and did little to quieten those who have wondered how they might fare in less helpful conditions.

They remain a quartet full of potential, able to pose different threats despite their mutual right-handedness. But the comparisons to England’s 2005 Ashes-winning foursome of Steve Harmison, Matthew Hoggard, Andrew Flintoff and Simon Jones look, on this evidence anyway, to be premature.

Ollie Robinson will finish the series with a remarkable haul of 21 wickets at 8.76

Earlier, they had been held up by Masood, who seemed set to become the first centurion on either side in this series, only to be brilliantly caught low in the cordon by Lawrence off Atkinson on 95.

Babar Azam, having played nicely for 76, then got into a flap against the short stuff, eventually gloving an unconvincing pull off Tongue down the leg side off Cox. Archer then bounced out Saud Shakeel, Pakistan’s best batsman on this trip, with a brute, and England seemed set for a three-day win when Atkinson had Ghori and Imran caught behind off inside edges.

But the 21-year-old Razaullah, who scored a hundred opening the batting for Peshawar against Islamabad in November, was determined not to go down without a fight.

He had already marked his debut with the wicket of Root in his first over, adding three more to finish with Pakistan’s best figures. Now he batted with a freedom that suggested a new star may have emerged from the debris of a troubled tour.

He has already enjoyed a debut to remember. If he can make England fight for their runs, Pakistan may even fly home with a spring in their step.

Sports.title: George Russell sounds the alarm over 'mental' Madrid track ahead of Spanish GP after Max Verstappen labelled circuit a 'car-killer'
Sports.content:
George Russell sounds the alarm over 'mental' Madrid track ahead of Spanish GP after Max Verstappen labelled circuit a 'car-killer'

See more Daily Mail on Google - save us as a Preferred Source

'Mental,' said George Russell of the new track in Madrid that gets its first outing this weekend, and he sighed. He was not nervous, or at least not betraying nerves, but he wanted to express the verdict.

Over on a screen at this very moment an 'orange ball' that has stalked and fascinated Formula One fans for years lit up.

That is how it was in the Madrid paddock, on the fringes of this great city hosting its first F1 race for 45 years, as he sat next to me and we stared at the monitor while he held his breath.

A day before, Russell had called this new race the 'most risky' in the sport. The track is surrounded by concrete walls and he and his 'pals' are circumnavigating it at far higher speeds than they do in the similarly confined Monaco streets. 'A car-killer,' reckoned Max Verstappen, the four-time world champion, perhaps the most fearless competitor on the grid.

This so-called orange ball came in practice for F1's feeder series, F2, when Thai driver Tasanapol Inthraphuvasak's car caught fire after he hit barriers at Turn 19.

The 20-year-old escaped straight away as Russell watched on. The red flag was waved. Marshals arrived on the scene. The fire was extinguished. The driver was fine.

George Russell has warned fans that the new circuit for the Spanish Grand Prix is 'mental'

Formula Two driver Tasanapol Inthraphuvasak saw his car go up in flames following a crash

A few hours later Arvid Lindblad pranged his Racing Bulls car at Turn 13 in practice for tomorrow's F1 race. The 19-year-old Briton was uninjured. This incident added to the state of concern over the track, though it may, in truth, be less dangerous possibly than Jeddah, home of the Saudi Arabian Grand Prix.

Russell, who is 66 points adrift of his Mercedes team-mate and championship-leader Kimi Antonelli, exclaimed: 'Wow.'

He looked at the TV screen ahead of him.

'This circuit is mental, and this corner… it is a fast right hander,' he added.

'There are a lot of really fast corners. The barriers come back on to the track. So, if you are going to go wide, you're not hitting it at the same angle as the car is going.

'The car is going towards the wall but the wall is coming in at you. Another element of the challenge here, which probably won't cause major crashes, there'll be a lot of lock-ups.

'You have got three corners where you're turning and braking, and if you lock up, the wall is right in front of you, which is very reminiscent of the – Oh, my God (as he watched the TV replay) – the 15th corner in Baku.

'We've got three corners that are very similar to that Baku corner.

Russell explained how there are 'a lot of really fast corners' - but there are no concerns that the track could be too dangerous

'When I heard about the 20 red flags in F3, it was surprising. This circuit has less margin than Monaco. Purely because of the speed. In Monaco, the walls are closer, but because you're going far slower, if you make a mistake, you're not into the wall as quickly. And you can recover it sometimes, a small lock-up you can get over. Here, I think there's less room for error.'

Is there any concern that this track is too dangerous?

'Not at the moment, but the view on that question will definitely be interesting after this weekend,' said Russell, who was fifth quickest in practice under blue, with affairs led by Antonelli; an ominous sign for the Englishman, yet again.

Of the fire-ball incident and, linked to that, a sense of hazard, Russell added: 'I don't think too much to be honest… I'm sure my mother worries more than I do on seeing any crash.

'But I'm content with whatever happens. This is part of the risk. You can hurt yourself doing anything. My biggest incident where I probably hurt myself the most was on a vehicle when I was playing with my three-year-old nephew. He was on a quad and I was on an electric bike racing him through the garden.

'I was next to him, and he looked at me, and, as he looked, he turned, and he wiped me out, and he's gone barrel-rolling on the quad. I've gone barrel-rolling on the electric bike. That was the one when I hurt myself the most.'

Let's hope it stays that way, as F1 ponders its new track in Madrid.

Sports.title: How Aaron Ramsdale fell to become FOURTH-CHOICE in the Championship: Insiders speak out on ex-Arsenal keeper - now playing in front of just 246 fans after transfers worth £80m
Sports.content:
How Aaron Ramsdale fell to become FOURTH-CHOICE in the Championship: Insiders speak out on ex-Arsenal keeper - now playing in front of just 246 fans after transfers worth £80m

See more Daily Mail on Google - save us as a Preferred Source

When Aaron Ramsdale was in the early days of his career, he would often turn to the fans behind him and tell them a joke.

Sometimes a cracker, sometimes not. He was in the lower leagues back then so the supporters were so close to the goal he could almost feel the breath from their laughter. For Ramsdale, it was his way of coping with the pressure of being in the eye of the storm.

Those exchanges with the crowd became a release valve that remained with him ever since. He slid on his knees in front of the Manchester United fans. He joined in with Leicester supporters' chants of 'You're s***, ahhh' after his goal-kicks. He kissed the Arsenal badge in front of Spurs fans after the north London derby, though one of them climbed the hoardings and kicked him in the back.

It was his way, too, of staying focused. Three years ago, he revealed to an astonished Ian Wright how he was unable to keep his mind dialled in from the first whistle to the last. 'To concentrate on a game of football for 90 minutes, I'm finished, I can't do it,' said Ramsdale.

'That's why I get involved with the fans. I sing along with the songs. Someone's giving me abuse, I'll turn around and give it back. I've had my two, three minutes of madness in my head, straight back to the football and I've got 10-15 minutes of pure concentration again.'

Whatever your view of the methodology, it's one that has, until now, kept him in the eye of ever greater, more prominent storms. Five England caps. On the bench at Euro 2020, Euro 2024 and the World Cup in 2022. Arsenal's No 1. Named in the PFA team of the year in 2023 when the Gunners finished second under Mikel Arteta for the first time.

Aaron Ramsdale is effectively fourth-choice goalkeeper at Southampton in the Championship

Ramsdale was one Arsenal's No 1 and named as the Premier League's finest goalkeeper

Back in March, while on loan at Newcastle, he stood between the posts in front of nearly 60,000 in the Nou Camp in the last-16 of the Champions League. Five months later, on the Friday night before Southampton began their post-Spygate campaign still in the Championship, Ramsdale strolled out of the tunnel at Eastleigh's Silverlake Stadium for Saints Under 21s and their Premier League Cup opener against Blackburn. The official attendance was 246 and none of them paid to get in.

Ramsdale, who joined from Arsenal in a deal worth up to £25million after Saints' promotion in 2024, has not featured in a single matchday squad for Tonda Eckert this season. It was at Ramsdale's request that he played for the kids. He is now, this once Arsenal record goalkeeper signing and England international whose cumulative transfer fees hit almost £80m, seemingly fourth choice at second-tier Southampton.

Daniel Peretz, who arrived on loan from Bayern Munich last January and joined permanently this summer for around £6m, has been superb. He is now Eckert's No 1 and the Saints boss has made that clear to him. George Long, who also joined on loan while Ramsdale was at Newcastle last season before turning his stay permanent in June, has been told he's Eckert's No 2. Southampton also followed the recent trend of hiring an older third-choice keeper to help mentor the others so Ramsdale also finds himself behind 37-year-old Jamie Jones.

'That group worked really well together last year and this is the way that we will go forward,' said Eckert last week. He likes the unit. He likes the characters.

And that, really, is the nub of the predicament in which Ramsdale – and Saints - now find themselves. Southampton expected Ramsdale would leave in the summer and planned for his departure without really considering the prospect of him staying.

They have, as it stands, made a commitment to a new No 1 and Ramsdale, as he's shown before, is not a goalkeeper content to sit on the bench. Were he wired differently, Ramsdale could well have a Premier League winners' medal now. He was hugely popular at Arsenal among the players and staff, a big personality, and an early catalyst for getting the fans on board with Arteta's revolution.

The goalkeeper lives in Bournemouth with his wife Georgina (pictured together)

Aaron and Georgina are pictured on a summer family holiday together earlier this year

Ramsdale signed a long-term deal at Arsenal in May 2023 after which he declared he wanted to be their keeper for the next decade. 'I want to be a mainstay at this club and do special things, win trophies and see what this team can do,' he said at the time. 'Hopefully we can stay together for a number of years.'

Three months later they signed David Raya on loan and quickly, despite Arteta's protestations that he had 'no No 1s', took his place. Ramsdale was gutted. His dad said his son 'lost his smile'.

Arsenal's view was that, in Ramsdale, they had, as one insider put it, a 'f***ing good keeper and a great lad'. They just felt they had a better one in Raya. A year later, he was gone.

'If I was sitting on the bench, winning a trophy wouldn't have meant that much to me,' said Ramsdale after his move to Saints. 'I just wanted to play football. As a kid I wanted to play football, not to just sit on a bench.'

Right now, he's not even doing that. The question is whether that will change.

Eckert admitted last week he held 'honest conversations' with Ramsdale over the summer, though it is understood none of them involved telling Ramsdale the door is closed. The two are said to have a good relationship.

Ramsdale is seen arriving for Southampton training in July - carrying a big bag of tea

Now he is playing in front of just 246 fans - and none of them even paid to get in

Newcastle had the option of signing him after his loan spell last season. The Magpies spent around £4m on the loan fee to bring him in as competition for a faltering Nick Pope, with the view that Ramsdale was better with the ball at his feet, despite it being a figure that raised a few eyebrows among the Newcastle bean counters.

Ramsdale, again, became a much-loved figure among the squad - the stream of messages from his Newcastle team-mates on social media when he announced his return to Saints showed that - but when he got his chance on the pitch, he struggled to seize it.

While the public stance was that Ramsdale's future would be decided at the end of the season, there was a growing feeling internally as the campaign progressed that they would not be activating the option to buy him, especially as it's understood the figure to do so was well above the keeper's current market value.

RAMSDALE'S BIG TRANSFERS 2017: Sheffield United-Bournemouth (£1m) 2020: Bournemouth-Sheffield United (£18.5m) 2021: Sheffield United-Arsenal (£30m) 2024: Arsenal-Southampton (£25m) 2025: Southampton-Newcastle (loan - £4m)

No other moves materialised. Ramsdale made it clear he was keen to stay at Southampton, where he's a big character in the dressing room, and challenge for his place. His high wages are understood to be 'manageable' thanks to a relegation clause.

Ramsdale had enough of moving around clubs to what would be a fourth new side in three years so he only wanted to do so if the offer was too good to refuse and turned down interest throughout the window, including interest from Scotland, Spain and Germany.

Leeds had him firmly in their sights had their ambitious bid to bring in James Trafford not materialised and, had they failed to do so, would likely have landed him. A potential return to Bournemouth, where he lives, was also floated but the Cherries eventually plumped for Juventus keeper Michele Di Gregorio on loan.

Newcastle spent around £4m on the loan fee but didn't make the move permanent

Ramsdale had little interest in moving abroad and a Premier League transfer didn't materialise

Ramsdale had little interest in a loan move abroad, with Serie A sides like Como and Torino also sniffing around him, after his wife recently gave birth to a baby girl, nor did he want to stay in the Championship, go to a big club as a No 2, or join a struggling Premier League side.

The stick that's often used to beat Ramsdale is that he has already suffered three top-flight relegations with three different teams: Bournemouth, Sheffield United and Southampton. At the first two, he was named player of the season despite the drop.

And yet, despite all the noise, Ramsdale was named in Saints' 25-man squad submitted to the Football League. Perhaps there is a future after all?

He trains with the group and has been more involved in recent weeks. There's also a feeling among those around the club that were Peretz to suffer injury, it's likely Eckert would parachute Ramsdale straight into his place.

Sources close to Ramsdale say the 28-year-old still believes he has a big part to play in getting Southampton back to the Premier League.

It may take time, but Ramsdale believes he'll get his chance. Sources described his current fourth-choice predicament as only 'circumstantial'. Ones, perhaps, he might still be able to change.

Sports.title: Former Man United star under investigation for 'offensive' gesture in Copa Libertadores clash
Sports.content:
Former Man United star under investigation for 'offensive' gesture in Copa Libertadores clash

See more Daily Mail on Google - save us as a Preferred Source

Former Manchester United forward Memphis Depay is facing disciplinary action from CONMEBOL after making an 'offensive' gesture during a game.

The forward, who played 53 times for the Red Devils between 2015 and 2017, now plies his trade in Brazil with Corinthians.

His side have qualified for the quarter-finals of the Copa Libertadores, and are favourites to reach the last four after drawing 1-1 away at Estudiantes in the first leg.

But it didn't come without controversy. Alexis Castro had just scored to put Depay and Co behind in the first-half, but in the second period, Kaio Cesar equalised, which triggered a response from Depay towards the home fans.

The Corinthians players were running to the corner to celebrate the goal, but Depay still had time to put his middle finger up to the supporters.

There are now fears the 32-year-old could face a ban, with it currently unclear what game – or games – he will miss, if any.

WARNING: GRAPHIC CONTENT

Che Brasuca, y este gesto ?? pic.twitter.com/TVvcKCzBJy — Kid Lapicera (@kidlapicera) September 10, 2026

Memphis Depay is being investigated after making an indecent gesture during a game

Home fans responded with loud boos, with Depay then approaching the referee to claim an object had been thrown in his direction.

Estudiantes, though, were taking no prisoners. The club said after the game that they have 'filed a complaint with the CONMEBOL disciplinary unit regarding the offensive gestures made by opposing player Memphis Depay, which were undeniably directed towards our stands'.

Corinthians have moved to defend their player, suggesting that it would be impossible for Depay to be banned for the second leg because the deadline for any defence is the day after the game.

They said: 'The deadline for submitting a defense, set by CONMEBOL, is September 17, one day after the Copa Libertadores quarter-final second leg. Therefore, any potential sanction would only be applied after the ruling, which will take place following the presentation of the defense. Respecting the deadline, Corinthians will present this defense to avoid any type of sanction against Memphis Depay.'

He therefore seems set to play the second leg, but could miss other games.

It was as recent as this summer that Depay hit out at Corinthians for their 'unacceptable behaviour' at not honouring an alleged agreement between both parties for him to sign a new contract at the club.

After it had seemed he was set to leave the club, he wrote on social media: 'Very disappointed to read that Corinthians decided not to honour our agreement in place to extend my contract for two more years.

'This renewal was explicitly agreed upon by the president as well as the sporting, legal and financial department. Some people decided however to breach this engagement.

Having played for Manchester United between 2015 and 2017, Depay is now plying his trade at Corinthians in Brazil

'I didn't want this situation and always respected the club throughout the process, but now I am forced to react strongly in order to preserve my interests.

'In the upcoming days I will speak publicly but rest assured that I will not leave this unacceptable behaviour unsanctioned.'

Corinthians said they could not extend Depay's deal due to their finances, but a new deal was eventually agreed when the player agreed a significant pay cut.

Sports.title: Former Sky Sports reporter Bianca Westwood says she's NEVER going to work in football again after she was made redundant
Sports.content:
Former Sky Sports reporter Bianca Westwood has revealed she's not likely to ever work in football again.

Westwood, 51, worked for the broadcaster for 22 years before taking redundancy in 2023.

The West Ham fan, who had a high-profile relationship with Ronnie O'Sullivan in 2001, has now pivoted to creating more female-led content and spoke in depth about leaving the world of sport in a recent TikTok video.

She told her 46.5k followers: 'I wanted to set a few things straight because I still get a lot of messages asking about Sky. When am I going back to Sky? When am I doing the football again? The compliments are really nice, I do appreciate them, but I'm not going back to Sky.

'It's funny because I get so many compliments now about what a good reporter I was, which is lovely, how I was the best football presenter, blah, blah, blah... and yet when I was doing it, especially when I first started, everyone said I was s***. So, work that out.

'The thing is, I'm not going back to Sky and I'm probably never going to work in football again. I had a feeling, probably about a year before I left Sky that the opportunities were becoming few and far between, they didn't really rate me, that's why I started doing the fashion, beauty and skincare, things that I love as a woman.

Former Sky Sports reporter Bianca Westwood said she's unlikely to work in football again

Westwood, pictured with Chris Kamara (right) and Jeff Stelling (left) was the first female reporter on Sky Sports' Soccer Saturday

'All my content now is geared towards women so I don't even know why I get new male followers because the football has gone. I love what I do now so I just wanted to let you know what that's all about.

'Three years ago, Sky offered me redundancy, I decided to take it. Jeff (Stelling) was leaving at the same time, I thought it was probably the best time to go and that was basically the reasons behind my decision so I'm not really going to go back.'

Westwood, who was the first female reporter on Soccer Saturday, went on to explain that she would have kept going as a football reporter if the right opportunity had arisen and lamented the lack of close access to top stars today.

She continued: 'If at the time, three years ago, I'd have been offered another job in football, and I did try, then I probably would still be working in football today, but there weren't any opportunities offered to me and if I'm honest my heart wasn't really in it anymore.

'Football kind of wasn't the same sport that I watched as a kid, even working in football is different now, there's hardly any access. When I first started reporting, you could go out, take players to different locations for interviews, go golfing or sailing or clay pigeon shooting, paintballing, you name it, I've done it.

'But now you literally get shoved into a room, especially in the Premier League, with a light, there's probably about 10 other broadcasters globally who are either going before you or waiting for you to finish.

'The player half the time doesn't want to be there, he's answering the same question, it just didn't feel the same to me and I thought, "I think I'm finished with this".

And Westwood's relationship with the game itself has also changed.

Westwood now makes female-led content and does not envisage a return to football

She added: 'Since I've left Sky, I haven't watched football that much either. I took a break from it, I still love the game but just not kind of how it is now.

'I haven't watched West Ham either because we've been rubbish. So if you're expecting me to talk about football, it's just not going to happen.

'All my content now is going to be about fashion, skincare, women, menopause, grief now I've got that experience recently losing my mum. But football is done... unless a really, really good exciting, challenging job came up but I'm not holding my breath.'

Sports.title: Kylian Mbappe responds to dictator memes as Real Madrid and France star claims viral trend shows a 'lack of awareness' from fans
Sports.content:
Kylian Mbappe has admitted to having mixed feelings over memes depicting him as a dictator, with the star suggesting it showcases a 'lack of awareness' from people. The Real Madrid and France star has been shown in military uniform in the meme, which was reproduced by several fans at the FIFA World Cup in the summer. The origin of the meme is unconfirmed, but there has been speculation the trend emerged amid reports that Mbappe enjoyed significant power at PSG during his time at the French club. It has also been suggested that it originated after Mbappe took legal action against a kebab shop owner in 2024 after they used his name in the description of a sandwich without permission. Mbappe was asked for his response to the memes by L'Equipe in an interview in the build-up to this year's Ballon d'Or, where the 27-year-old is among the favourites. While acknowledging it is largely 'light-hearted', Mbappe expressed a view that people were showing a lack of awareness due to the misery several dictators have caused throughout history. Kylian Mbappe has claimed memes depicting him as a dictator are largely 'light-hearted', but show a 'lack of awareness' Mbappe expressed a view that people were showing a lack of awareness due to the misery several dictators have caused throughout history Some fans had displayed the memes during the World Cup, with the suggestion the trend emerged due the power Mbappe is said to have at both club and international level 'Part of it is funny because you can tell that for some people it’s all in good fun,' Mbappe told France Football. 'Part of it is a little less funny because we know the damage people like that have caused throughout history. 'So being compared to people who murder people, who have made millions and millions of people miserable. 'I don’t think I’ve ever done that in my life, so there’s a mix of things where you think to yourself: “I know it’s meant in a light-hearted way” 'It doesn’t go that far but it sometimes showcases that there’s a lack of awareness, sometimes political, sometimes human among people.' Mbappe also addressed the nickname 'Mobutu', which was given to him by his France and former PSG team-mate Ousmane Dembele. The nickname was made in reference to Mobutu Sese Seko, the dictator who was president of DR Congo, then Zaire, between 1965 and 1997. 'Ousmane, it’s something else, he took it from social media, so no, with him it’s just for fun,' Mbappe said.

Sports.title: I've seen JJ Gabriel's supreme talent develop first-hand: This is why he MUST be fast-tracked into Man United's squad for the Carabao Cup, the team-mates he's wowing at Carrington and the real reason he's deleted his United photos on Instagram
Sports.content:
To watch JJ Gabriel at work inside a near-empty Leigh Sports Village each week feels akin to being given the first look at the next Oscar-winning movie from the back room of your local cinema.

There are only ever a hundred or so in attendance, half a stand is all they open these days, but all of those that go regularly know that Gabriel is destined to take his talents to the very biggest stage.

I have seen Gabriel score on his competitive debut at Old Trafford, netting in front of the Stretford End in the FA Youth Cup to become the club’s youngest scorer in that competition. I was also there when Gabriel dazzled away at Oxford United, which had my colleague Oliver Holt in awe.

I was there when Gabriel scored on his Under 21s debut earlier this season, a stunning scoop over the Ipswich Town goalkeeper from outside the box. And I was there in the rain on Thursday when Gabriel made light work of his UEFA Youth League debut, surpassing Rayan Cherki as the competition’s youngest-ever hat-trick scorer at 15 years and 339 days.

As he scooped the ball out of the net at full-time, he casually strode towards team-mate Yuel Helafu, gave it a toss into the air, and flashed a signature smile. Another record to add to his collection.

Make no mistake – Gabriel is a supreme talent. His 840,000 Instagram followers – more than, for example, the official accounts of Ipswich Town or Coventry City – suggest his ability is widely known.

Manchester United's 15-year-old JJ Gabriel completes his hat-trick for their Under 21s against Sabah in the UEFA Youth League on Thursday

Gabriel became the Youth League's youngest hat-trick scorer, surpassing Rayan Cherki, now of Manchester City

Top executives at Nike, who beat competition from adidas for Gabriel's signature, have had him on their radar as a top-tier talent since he was 10.

It was why in one key meeting they outlined why they believe he is ‘next in line to Cristiano Ronaldo’s throne’ as the face of their 'Mercurial' brand. It was, in Nike’s mind, a safe bet, even before he kicked a ball at Under-18s level.

And yet watching him up close, it really feels like the masses still don’t quite know just what a phenomenon is waiting to be unleashed. The days of watching his artistry in front of a hundred-plus crowd are undoubtedly coming to an end.

‘He’s a scary talent,’ one youth football source raved to me recently.

‘Players cannot get near him, it’s remarkable. He’s got the chance to be one of the best players this country has ever produced,’ said another after Gabriel’s Under 21s debut, where he added a pair of assists to his goal.

One recent training session had £50million summer signing Andrey Santos with hands on his head as he watched Gabriel’s technique in a small-sided drill.

Others such as Bryan Mbeumo, Marcus Rashford and Bruno Fernandes have been keen to take the 15-year-old under their wing.

‘He’s often with us in training and you can feel and see that he’s got something special,’ Mbeumo said earlier this year. ‘Everything is easy for him. He has a lot of composure in front of goal, he has a good shot, and he’s technically strong.’

But back to Leigh Sports Village and an historic afternoon which put Europe – and United’s top execs – on notice. His first goal was instinctive, the ball ricocheting off a defender after Nathanial Junior Brown’s initial effort, before Gabriel took it on his chest and volleyed in with his right foot.

Gabriel scores the first goal of his hat-trick, a right-foot volley, against Sabah

‘Players cannot get near him, it’s remarkable,' says one youth football source. 'He’s got the chance to be one of the best players this country has ever produced’

His second was even better, with some intricate footwork in the box allowing him to skip inside to pick out the bottom corner after he seemingly evaded everyone to meet Amir Ibragimov’s pass.

Then came the clincher. A ball over the top by Jim Thwaites picked out Gabriel, by now drifting in from the left, who ran clear and lifted it over the goalkeeper. Match ball secured.

It’s a modest set-up at Leigh. Team-sheets are like gold dust – we got just two between a group of seven on Thursday – and there is often a who’s who in attendance in the boxes above.

Michael Carrick is a regular, as is his assistant Steve Holland. Director of football Jason Wilcox and Matt Hargreaves, head of football negotiations, were both there on Thursday, along with recruitment chief Christopher Vivell.

It was Wilcox and Hargreaves that intervened in June 2025 to ensure United didn’t lose one of Europe’s most gifted young players. The meeting, first revealed by Daily Mail Sport, was decisive. The pathway was laid out to Gabriel and his family. The first team, by that stage, were already well aware of the teenager.

Now there are legitimate questions being asked as to whether the 15-year-old should make his first matchday squad with the first team for Wednesday’s Carabao Cup clash against Brighton. It's a must. He looks ready.

Gabriel isn’t 16 until October 6 so has ample opportunity to become the club’s youngest-ever player, breaking the record held by goalkeeper David Gaskell, who was 16 years and 19 days old when he debuted for United in 1956.

So, just how difficult, or scary, is it to have the responsibility of coaching a player many inside United believe is destined to become world class?

‘He’s often with us in training and you can feel and see that he’s got something special,’ Bryan Mbeumo (second left) has said of Gabriel

Only days ago United legend Ryan Giggs called Gabriel a ‘generational talent’

‘It’s my job not to ruin him,’ said Under 21s boss Adam Lawrence, who will also manage the Under 19s in the Youth League, on Thursday. ‘When you have a talented player like JJ and the other lads, of course, you don’t want to stifle their freedom and their creativity.

‘I try to set the team up to allow the talent to function and to play free at the right moments. It's enjoyable working with him and challenging as a coach because the best players challenge you – in a good way. Of course there’s things he can keep working on, but he's in a real good place.’

The noise around Gabriel is relentless. Overnight there were questions asked why he had wiped his Instagram account clean. Those close to him insist it’s merely to remove any distractions from his game.

Only days ago United legend Ryan Giggs called Gabriel a ‘generational talent’. Rio Ferdinand simply called Gabriel’s talent ‘ridiculous’ to comprehend.

Others, who don’t speak to those he works with each day, sometimes bring up attitude as a negative. But having spoken to coaches right through the academy, a set-up Gabriel joined at the age of nine, they are effusive in their praise. The criticism couldn’t be further from the truth.

'JJ's an amazing talent and his enthusiasm for football, that he brings to the pitch every day to learn, want to play, be on the ball, he's been a pleasure to work with,’ Under 18s boss Darren Fletcher told me last season.

‘He’s a fantastic kid. He's desperate to do better, to improve, to learn. He takes constructive criticism fantastically and I've got a great relationship with him.'

Carrick, too, has a pep in his step when it comes to Gabriel, describing the young teen as ‘one of the boys’.

‘It’s my job not to ruin him,’ Under 21s boss Adam Lawrence says. ‘When you have a talented player like JJ, you don’t want to stifle their freedom and their creativity'

‘He’s a fantastic kid,' says Under 18s boss Darren Fletcher. 'He's desperate to do better, to improve, to learn. He takes constructive criticism fantastically'

Sir Jim Ratcliffe even made sure to see this burgeoning superstar for himself in a Premier League Cup match at Carrington last season. Naturally, Gabriel scored that day, too.

It was Ratcliffe that once said he wants United to produce their own superstars, their own Kylian Mbappe, rather than going out to sign the finished article. There is no doubt in my mind they’ve got one in the building.

'It's not for us to create robots here,' academy director Stephen Torpey told me in a chat at Carrington back in March. 'It's for us to allow individuals to flourish and express themselves.'

The joy of watching Gabriel is that he tries things, and can do things with the ball, that others cannot. A refreshing antidote to the ‘robots’ we can often see in the Premier League. It feels inevitable that Gaskell’s record will be shattered in the weeks ahead.

Sports.title: 'Brutal, searing and punishing heat' - Babb on playing for Ireland at USA '94
Sports.content:
While none of the home nations qualified for the 1994 World Cup, the Republic of Ireland did.

It was a second successive appearance at the tournament for the Boys in Green, who were again led by 1966 World Cup winner Jack Charlton.

At Italia '90, the weather had been hot - but at USA '94, it was a different kettle of fish altogether.

The iconic image of Charlton launching an open bottle of water in the direction of Andy Townsend and Tommy Coyne always provides a reminder of that.

Image: Jack Charlton led the Republic of Ireland at Italia '90 and USA '94

He clashed with FIFA over their policy that bottles could not be thrown to the players on the pitch, so took to throwing the contents instead before FIFA later relented and allowed water bags to be thrown.

"They trust me to do what is right for them and I will continue to do it," Charlton said. "We have been right in pursuing this matter and FIFA's change of heart proves that."

Charlton was rarely seen without his white baseball cap that summer. Steve Staunton famously even wore one during the national anthem before the second group game against Mexico.

One of the players in the Ireland squad that summer was Phil Babb. The defender, then 23, had just completed his second full Premier League season at Coventry.

He made his international debut in a 0-0 friendly draw with Russia in March 1994, then played in the next four friendlies leading up to the tournament.

Image: Phil Babb played in all four of the Republic of Ireland's games at the 1994 World Cup

Nothing was set in stone, but he knew he would at least have a decent chance of being included in Charlton's 22-man squad, so started to physically prepare himself.

"A coach at Coventry asked me if I wanted to do anything specific - we ended up doing 12-minute sessions in a sauna!" Babb recalls, with a smile.

"We were doing burpees, press-ups, just trying to acclimatise to that intense heat. We did about six sessions - but I wouldn't recommend it for anyone now!

"I was a fit lad and had played pretty much all the Premier League games Coventry had played that season. I adapted to the heat pretty well, but I know some of the older lads really struggled."

Babb started alongside Paul McGrath in the heart of defence for Ireland's tournament opener at Giants Stadium in New Jersey.

Image: Ray Houghton's stunning strike earned a shock 1-0 win over Italy

That Saturday, they shocked an Italy side that featured Paolo Maldini, Franco Baresi and Roberto Baggio. John Aldridge's stunner sealed a memorable 1-0 win.

It was an achievement made all the more impressive by the fact the Azzurri went on to finish as runners-up - but also given the fact it was played in temperatures exceeding 30C.

"When we walked out onto the field, about two hours before kick-off, you could tell it was going to be absolutely roasting," he recalls.

"You could tell that straight away and we didn't stay out long. I just checked the grass to see which studs I wanted, then I went straight back in. I know some of the lads were walking around and taking the atmosphere in, but I thought: 'This is too hot'.

"I didn't go out for a warm-up with the rest of the lads, either. I stayed in the changing room. It was built for NFL, so they had a 40m sprint track. I warmed up in there and waited until we went out. It was brutal, it was searing, it was punishing.

"It affected everyone's game. You were saturated after just 10 minutes walking onto a pitch, so you had to conserve energy at the right times.

"Recovery was very basic and there was very little ball work because of the demands of the actual games and the fluids you lose. When you're that dehydrated, it's quite difficult. You want a drink, but you don't feel hungry and that is a key part of the recuperation."

Image: Babb, whose Ireland were knocked out by Dennis Bergkamp's Netherlands, joined Liverpool later that summer

Thirty-two years on from that tournament, football has evolved exponentially.

Sports science has taken on a key role in the game and, this summer, is likely to play into the way teams approach games tactically due to the heat. A slower tempo is expected in many.

Charlton was not prepared to facilitate the same in 1994, though.

"We only played one way, so if you tried to go off-piste, Jack would certainly let you know!" adds Babb.

"We had one style of play, with a lone striker. If it wasn't Tommy Coyne, it might have been Niall Quinn up there and we'd be putting long balls up to him, with either willing runners out wide or the midfield bombing on.

"That was the Irish way back then. Tommy ran tirelessly, to the point where he actually collapsed with heat exhaustion on the plane home.

"I think Jack's sports science was a barrel of Guinness in his room and he'd call the lads in and have a pint! I'm sure there's a high calorific content in that, so maybe he was ahead of his time!"

In spite of that, Babb's memories of the tournament are largely positive.

"I enjoyed it, I have to admit! I'd rather play in the searing heat than a wet Tuesday night in Hull," he says.

"I was a fit lad and it was quite easy for me playing alongside Paul McGrath, who was imperious in that tournament. I learned a lot from him and how he conserved his energy.

"I felt I got stronger because I got used to it. I guess our 0-0 draw against Norway would probably attest to the heat and the style of play.

"It all comes down to the individual. Footballers are supreme athletes now and they leave nothing to chance, so I think they'll cope a lot better than we did in the mid-90s."

The methods may have moved on since Charlton was throwing water onto the pitch, but Babb's memories from USA '94 provide a reminder this World Cup will be a battle against more than just the opposition.

Sports.title: Ogbene earns Republic of Ireland draw with Canada
Sports.content:
Chiedozie Ogbene's equaliser ensured the Republic of Ireland continued their good run of results as they drew 1-1 with World Cup co-hosts Canada in Montreal.

Canada went ahead in the 24th minute from an own goal by defender Jake O'Brien, heading a failed clearance into his own net from Stephen Eustaquio's corner.

Ireland were then awarded a penalty in the second half after Cyle Larin - who signed a two-year deal with Southampton earlier in the day - took out Jamie McGrath.

Canada goalkeeper Maxime Crepeau saved Troy Parrott's initial attempt, but Ogbene was on hand to slam home the rebound and tie the game in the 60th minute.

Image: Ireland's Jake O'Brien heads the ball into his own net

Ireland, who failed to qualify for this summer's World Cup, went close to a winner but Crepeau denied a charging run from Mason Melia late on.

The Orlando City goalkeeper missed out on the 2022 World Cup in Qatar after breaking his leg while playing in the MLS Cup final.

Canada, managed by former Leeds boss Jesse Marsch, officially open the World Cup on June 12 in Toronto against Bosnia and Herzegovina, before facing Qatar on June 18 and Switzerland on June 24.

They remain without captain Alphonso Davies, who is still nursing a hamstring injury he sustained while playing for Bayern Munich.

Sports.title: Republic of Ireland edge past Qatar in friendly as both sides end with 10
Sports.content:
Captain Nathan Collins headed the Republic of Ireland to a 1-0 friendly victory over World Cup-bound Qatar as both sides were reduced to 10 men.

Collins ensured Ireland got the better of a side managed by his former Wolves boss Julen Lopetegui with an early header.

However, just how the evening might have panned out had Jack Moylan not been dismissed as half-time approached, a sparse crowd inside the Aviva Stadium will never know.

Heimir Hallgrimsson's side, whose hopes of making it to the World Cup finals were dashed in heartbreaking fashion in March when they lost their play-off semi-final to the Czech Republic on penalties, were in complete control until Moylan's premature exit.

Qatar substitute Almoez Ali suffered the same fate 12 minutes from time.

Image: Jack Moylan was sent off before half-time at the Aviva Stadium

The game was played out against the backdrop of ongoing unease at the forthcoming Nations League clashes with Israel, and play was interrupted on several occasions during the first half as 'Stop the Game' protesters among a crowd of 28,981 repeatedly hurled tennis balls on to the pitch.

Ireland will now head for Montreal and their friendly against World Cup co-hosts Canada on June 6, while Qatar continue their preparations for the finals - they launch their Group B campaign against Switzerland in San Francisco on June 13 - against El Salvador in Los Angeles on the same day.

The Republic took the lead with just five minutes gone when, having been fouled by Ayoub Al-Oui wide on the left, Moylan curled the resulting free-kick on to the head of Collins, who glanced the ball effortlessly past 'keeper Mahmoud Abunada.

Image: Qatar's Almoez Ali was also sent off

There was a brief interruption after the protesters made their presence felt for the first time as Qatar's Pedro Miguel underwent treatment for injury, but once order had been restored, Troy Parrott whipped a first-time shot wide after being picked out by Seamus Coleman.

The Qataris simply could not get anywhere near Hallgrimsson's men and a mid-half drinks break did little to improve matters for the visitors with Abunada having to field Jayson Molumby's deflected 24th-minute shot from distance.

Lopetegui could not hide his frustration on the sideline and only the bravery of defender Ahmed Fathi denied Chiedozie Ogbene a second goal as he attempted to latch on to Liam Scales' header back across goal.

But the home side's night took a turn for the worse on the stroke of half-time when Northern Irish referee Jamie Robinson deemed Moylan's challenge on Jassem Gaber worthy of a red card, much to the Lincoln frontman's clear astonishment.

Image: Former Wolves and West Ham boss Julen Lopetegui is now in charge of Qatar

With defender James Abankwah having replaced Dara O'Shea at half-time, the 10 men found themselves under pressure for the first time on their return, although Coleman very nearly caught Abunada off his line with an audacious 52nd-minute attempt from the right wing.

Edmilson Junior dragged a long-range effort wide two minutes later after Molumby went down in midfield under Fathi's challenge and it took a fine 71st-minute reaction save by Caoimhin Kelleher - his first of the night - to keep out Yusuf Abdurisag's deflected shot.

However, Qatari hopes of salvation were dashed with 12 minutes remaining when Ali struck out at Molumby off the ball on several occasions and was also sent off.

Sports.title: Parrott out of luck as Republic of Ireland draw with North Macedonia
Sports.content:
Troy Parrott had two goals disallowed as the Republic of Ireland played out a stalemate against North Macedonia on the night on which they had hoped to book a trip to the World Cup finals.

Five days after their dreams came to an end for another four years in Prague, Ireland drew 0-0 with the Macedonians in a friendly encounter neither side wanted as the Czech Republic and Denmark fought for the big prize.

Even a third successive home victory for the first time since the 2015-16 campaign would have provided scant consolation for Thursday night's disappointment but Heimir Hallgrimsson's men had to make do with a disappointing draw.

AZ Alkmaar striker Parrott came closest to breaking the deadlock as 37-year-old defender Seamus Coleman received a standing ovation from a crowd of 39,560 at the Aviva Stadium when he was replaced during the second half of what could yet prove to be his final appearance for his country.

Nevertheless, the squad will reconvene for a series of friendlies at the end of the season ahead of next season's Nations League campaign and later Euro 2028 qualification having restored a measure of pride and established a momentum they hope will serve them well when they return to competitive action.

The hosts went on to the offensive from the off, although they were unable to find the final ball to allow either Parrott or Chiedozie Ogbene to threaten.

John Egan could not direct an 11th-minute corner at goal and Ogbene saw his snapshot deflected over three minutes later, but goalkeeper Caoimhin Kelleher had to parry Enis Bardhi's 21st-minute free-kick after it flicked off the defensive wall, with Bardhi volleying high over after the resulting corner had been only half-cleared.

Macedonia keeper Stole Dimitrievski saved Parrott's 23rd-minute header comfortably after Dara O'Shea and Finn Azaz had sparked a concerted attack, and Azaz failed to make the most of a free-kick two minutes later after he had been tripped just outside the penalty area.

Parrott was played into a promising position by Knight nine minutes before the break, only to miss the target by some distance.

The in-form striker - he scored his sixth goal in three games in Prague - might have done better again two minutes later after Azaz's clipped pass had caused problems for the Macedonian defence but he snatched at his attempt and fired high and wide.

Parrott twice had the ball in the net as time ran down but an offside flag stalled his celebrations on each occasion.

Ireland were unfortunate not to take the lead with 52 minutes gone when Azaz accepted Seamus Coleman's pass and found Parrott, who turned smartly before shooting against the upright.

Azaz curled an effort just wide and Tihomir Kostadinov denied Parrott a clear run on goal as the hosts began to turn the screw but it was veteran Coleman's 61st-minute departure as

Hallgrimsson made changes which attracted the biggest cheer of the night to that point.

Wholesale changes did not help the flow of the game, which rather petered out as the whistle approached, although Ireland substitute Johnny Kenny passed up a glorious opportunity to win it at the end with a weak shot at the keeper.

Sports.title: Szmodics out of hospital and 'on the mend' after collision
Sports.content:
Republic of Ireland forward Sammie Szmodics has been released from hospital in Prague after being knocked unconscious during Thursday's World Cup play-off defeat by the Czech Republic.

The 24-year-old, who is currently on loan at Derby from Ipswich, was hurt in a collision with defender Stepan Chaloupek just two minutes after his introduction as an extra-time substitute at the Fortuna Arena, sparking concerned medics to rush to his aid.

Szmodics was carried from the field on a stretcher and taken straight to hospital, where Ireland head coach Heimir Hallgrimsson later revealed he would spend the night under observation.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Danyal Khan looks back on the heartbreaking result for the Republic of Ireland who lost their World Cup qualifying play-off against Czech Republic on penalties

A Football Association of Ireland spokesperson said on Friday morning: "Sammie Szmodics was transferred to hospital yesterday having sustained a head injury during extra time of the play-off against Czechia.

"Following further tests and a period of observation, he has been safely discharged from hospital and will continue his recovery under the care of the Republic of Ireland and Derby County medical teams."

Szmodics, who Hallgrimsson confirmed would have taken a penalty in the shoot-out which Ireland ultimately lost 4-3, took to social media to express his thanks to those who had helped him.

He posted on X: "Gutted the way it ended. Fans and boys immense all evening!! Appreciate everyone's messages. And thank you to the medical staff who acted so quickly to help me. On the mend."
