Centum Investment Company PLC has appointed Thomas Omondi-Achola as acting group chief executive, tapping an internal candidate to succeed long-serving CEO James Mworia, who is leaving to head Kenya’s newly established National Infrastructure Fund (NIF).

The transition, effective immediately, marks the end of an 18-year tenure during which Mworia transformed Centum from a small investment firm into East Africa’s largest diversified investment platform, the company said in a statement.

World.title: Ruto: Kenya to end raw mineral exports
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

President William Ruto during a thanksgiving service in South Horr, Samburu County on September 6, 2026. [PCS]

President William Ruto says Kenya will no longer allow its mineral wealth to leave the country in raw form, coming days after the controversial saga surrounding Tata Chemicals’ operations at Lake Magadi.

Ruto defended the government’s decision to suspend Tata Chemicals’ operations at Lake Magadi, Kajiado County, arguing that Kenya has not been receiving sufficient value from the natural resource and that more investors should be given an opportunity to develop the area.

“We want to give five, six or even 10 companies an opportunity to use the resources there to create jobs, value, create wealth and reduce poverty,” Ruto said.

The President made the remarks during a thanksgiving service in South Horr, Samburu County, on Sunday, where he announced a broader government policy aimed at shifting Kenya from exporting raw materials to processing them locally.

“Going into the future, our position as the government. Whether we are talking about Magadi Soda or oil or all our minerals, we have taken the decision that we will no longer export raw materials,” Ruto said.

“We are going to process all minerals available in Kenya.”

The declaration puts the long-running Lake Magadi dispute at the centre of a much wider economic strategy.

Tata Chemicals has been associated with soda ash production at the lake for more than a century. Its Kenyan operations trace their history to 1911, when the Magadi Soda Company began extracting trona from Lake Magadi.

Operations were suspended on July 28, 2026, following a directive from the Ministry of Mining, Blue Economy and Maritime Affairs over compliance and licensing issues.

Ruto has argued that the resource should generate greater benefits for Kenyans through expanded investment, job creation and local value addition.

He accused the existing model of allowing valuable resources to leave the country while Kenya receives less economic benefit than it could.

The President’s comments reflect a longstanding challenge facing Kenya’s extractive sector: how to turn mineral deposits into manufacturing opportunities rather than simply exporting commodities.

Under the proposed approach, minerals such as gold, limestone, iron ore, graphite, titanium and soda ash would be processed or refined in Kenya before being exported.

The government says this would create industrial jobs, strengthen local supply chains and increase the value of exports.

Ruto cited planned cooperation with Nigerian businessman Aliko Dangote as an example of the investment model the government wants to pursue.

He said talks were underway to establish an oil refinery and petrochemical complex in Lamu, alongside efforts to attract investors into mineral refining.

“It is imprudent for any government to export raw materials, create jobs and value in other countries while we have a big population of young people who need jobs,” Ruto said.

World.title: Sifuna condemns abduction of Standard Group Associate Editor
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

Busia County Senator Okiya Omtata, Nairobi Senator Edwin Sifuna, Bumula MP Jack Wamboka during the burial service of Mary Gorreti Okiya at Kabula, in Bumula on September 5,2026. [Benjamin Sakwa, Standard]

Nairobi Senator Edwin Sifuna has declared that the fight to restore democracy, media freedom and the rule of law following the abduction of Standard Group Senior Editor will form the centrepiece of the Linda Mwananchi government vowing to defeat President William Ruto in the 2027 General Election.

Sifuna accused President Ruto’s administration of undermining constitutional freedoms and creating an atmosphere of fear, saying the country must be returned to what he described as “the rail of the six important values” enshrined in the Constitution.

Speaking in Bumula Constituency, Kakamega County during the burial of Mary Goreti, the sister of Busia Senator Okiya Omtatah, Sifuna strongly condemned the abduction and arrest of a Standard Group Associate Editor, Alex Kiprotich, arguing that journalists must be protected if Kenya is to remain a democratic country.

“It is impossible that you are driving on the road and you are taken away the way the way the Standard Group Journaliat and Editor Alex Kiprotich was taken. Kenyans want to live in a free country. We do not want to live in fear,” said Sifuna.

He questioned the circumstances surrounding the incident and accused the Government of failing to protect media freedom, adding that the Linda Mwananchi movement would seek to restore institutions and constitutional safeguards if elected to power, arguing that democracy could not survive where citizens, journalists and political opponents lived in fear.

"You cannot just arrest a senior journalist in the middle of the road with police carrying firearms, then you dump him some 500kilometres near the dam, a country cannot have democracy if media is not being respected and allowed to do it's work as per the constitution," said Sifuna.

He said the movement’s agenda was not merely about removing the current administration from power but it's main plan is rebuilding systems of governance around constitutionalism, democracy, individual freedoms and the rule of law.

“With less than 11 months remaining, we want to tell Kenyans that our entire plan is to return this country to the rails of the six important values contained in our Constitution, including democracy, freedom of citizens and the rule of law,” said Sifuna.

Sifuna also accused the Government of using threats against political opponents, saying leaders should not threaten citizens with arrest, expulsion or other forms of intimidation.

He challenged religious leaders to remind politicians that the power to determine the length of a person's life belongs to God.

Sifuna further linked the rule of law to economic growth, warning that investors would be reluctant to establish businesses in Kenya if government could arbitrarily order them to leave.

He said Kenya could not rely on government alone to create employment for millions of young people, arguing that the country needed both local and foreign investors.

“No investor can bring his project to a country where he can wake up one day and the President tells him, ‘Pack and go.’ It is impossible,” Sifuna said.

He argued that investor confidence was also affected by the possibility of commercial disputes being referred to foreign jurisdictions because investors lacked confidence in Kenya’s legal system.

Sifuna also criticised the government over the ongoing nurses and midwives strike, saying the rule of law required the State to honour agreements signed with workers.

World.title: Murkomen reaffirms IG Kanja's command of National Police Service
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

Interior Cabinet Secretary Kipchumba Murkomen has reaffirmed that the Inspector General of Police retains constitutional command of the National Police Service, saying the government will continue to respect the independence of the office.

Speaking during the passing-out parade of new Administration Police recruits in Nairobi, Murkomen said the Inspector General has authority over key operational matters within the service, including investigations, promotions and deployment of officers.

“Your Excellency, the Inspector General of Police retains the command of the National Police Service, especially on matters of investigation, promotion and deployment of officers without interference from anyone, including the Cabinet Secretary. We will continue respecting Article 245 of the Constitution,” Murkomen said.

His remarks come amid public debate over the relationship between the Interior Ministry and the National Police Service, particularly allegations that political leaders sometimes issue direct instructions to police officers.

Murkomen dismissed criticism directed at the office of the Inspector General, describing some of its proponents as tribalists and propagandists. He maintained that the Inspector General is carrying out his responsibilities and said he had confidence in the leadership of the police service.

“I have full faith in the IG and believe that every act that is done by the National Police Service is guided by the Constitution,” he said.

The Cabinet Secretary also addressed concerns over his role in directing the police, saying that his responsibility is primarily to provide policy direction rather than interfere with the operational command of the service.

“When required to give policy direction, I always give it in writing and we will continue to support the independence of the National Police Service from external interference,” Murkomen said.

During the ceremony, Murkomen also cautioned the newly graduated officers against corruption, excessive alcohol consumption and conduct that could undermine the reputation of the police service.

He urged the recruits to uphold discipline and protect the dignity of the police uniform, noting that the respect they receive from members of the public would depend largely on their conduct.

The Cabinet Secretary encouraged the officers to understand the responsibility that comes with joining the National Police Service and to discharge their duties within the confines of the Constitution and the law.

The passing-out ceremony marked the entry of the new recruits into the police service that made the CS use the occasion to emphasize professional conduct and respect for the constitutional framework governing policing in Kenya.

World.title: Egypt announces closure of the Pyramid of Menkaure
World.content:
Egypt’s Supreme Council of Antiquities has announced the temporary closure of the Pyramid of Menkaure, coinciding with the reopening of the Pyramid of Khafre to visitors as part of a routine rotation system for maintenance across the Giza Pyramids.

This decision falls under the Council’s strategy to conduct periodic maintenance and preservation work, ensuring the world-renowned archaeological site remains accessible to tourists without interruption.

The Pyramid of Khafre, the second-largest of the three Great Pyramids of Giza and a hallmark of ancient Egyptian civilization, was built for King Khafre of the Fourth Dynasty. Originally standing at approximately 143.5 meters tall, it is notably distinct for retaining a portion of its original limestone casing at its apex.

The Supreme Council of Antiquities emphasized that the rotational opening and closing system strikes a balance between artifact conservation and visitor access. By conducting necessary maintenance in cycles, preservation goals are met without disrupting tourist flow.

By contrast, the Pyramid of Menkaure is the smallest of the trio, constructed for the Fourth Dynasty King Menkaure. With an original height of roughly 65 meters, it is famous for the granite blocks used on part of its outer casing.

The largest of the set, the Great Pyramid of King Khufu, remains the primary focal point in size and height, standing as the only surviving wonder of the ancient world. Built during the Fourth Dynasty, its original height reached approximately 146.6 meters, with its current height measuring around 139 meters.

World.title: In an unprecedented move, Egypt to launch sky-high tethered balloon ride at Giza Pyramids
World.content:
Visitors to the Giza Plateau will soon catch a bird’s-eye view of the ancient world’s last surviving wonder, courtesy of a new tethered hot air balloon attraction.

Announced by Egyptian tourism authorities, the high-flying entertainment concept—the first to land near the iconic monuments—promises panoramic vistas from 150 meters up.

The proposal, however, has reignited a fierce conversation among conservationists about visual pollution and ecological balance near world heritage sites.

In response to growing public scrutiny, Tourism Minister Sherif Fathy visited the site on Sunday to audit safety preparations before the attraction begins test runs. Officials insist the 15-minute aerial experience will blend entertainment with education, delivering historical commentary to passengers floating above the desert floor.

Addressing concerns over the site’s historical integrity, the developer emphasized that the infrastructure was engineered to leave no footprint on ancient soil.

Built entirely out of modular, light-gauge components anchored above ground, the setup avoids sub-surface digging and concrete work. Located more than two kilometers clear of both the Pyramids and the Sphinx, the vertically tethered system aims to offer modern thrills without compromising the ancient skyline.

World.title: Egypt Foreign Minister emphasizes unified strategic cooperation with Saudi Arabia
World.content:
Egyptian Foreign Minister Badr Abdelatty affirmed that contacts between the leaderships of Egypt and Saudi Arabia are ongoing within the framework of continuous consultations between the two countries regarding regional developments, RT Arabic reported.

In televised remarks on Thursday evening, Abdelatty stated that the recent phone call between Egyptian President Abdel Fattah El-Sisi and Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman was “brotherly and initiated by Prince Mohammed bin Salman.” He added that both leaders agreed on “continuing, strengthening, and deepening consultations between the two nations, as well as enhancing communication.”

The Egyptian minister emphasized that “the relationship between Egypt and the Kingdom is an eternal one, defined not only by the bonds between the two brotherly peoples or historical ties, but also by a shared destiny and common interests.”

He added, “The security of the Kingdom is integral to the security of Egypt, and likewise, the security of Egypt is integral to the security of the Kingdom, falling within the framework of integration between Egyptian security and Gulf state security.”

Last week, the Egyptian President received a phone call from the Saudi Crown Prince discussing overall bilateral relations. President El-Sisi emphasized the importance of continuing to drive and strengthen various areas of bilateral cooperation to achieve shared interests and meet the aspirations of both brotherly nations and peoples toward development, prosperity, and improved regional conditions.

The official spokesperson for the Egyptian Presidency stated that the President congratulated the Saudi Crown Prince on the upcoming Saudi National Day, expressing his wishes for continued stability and prosperity for the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia.

The spokesperson noted that El-Sisi also stressed the unity of destiny between Egypt and Saudi Arabia, underlining the importance of joint action to overcome the challenges facing the region and its nations, while reiterating that the security of Saudi Arabia and all Arab states is an extension of Egyptian national security.

World.title: Landmark ancient Egypt exhibition welcomed 600 thousand visitors in Hong Kong
World.content:
Hong Kong’s captivated public has bidden farewell to ‘Ancient Egypt Unveils Its Secrets: Treasures from Egyptian Museums,’ which wrapped up a blockbuster nine-month run at the Hong Kong Palace Museum.

Drawing over 600,000 visitors between November 18, 2025, and August 31, 2026, the exhibition’s impressive turnout serves as a striking reminder of the world’s endless fascination with the land of the Pharaohs.

Marking the exhibition’s grand finale and the start of the artifacts’ journey home, Hisham al-Leithy, Secretary-General of the Supreme Council of Antiquities—representing Minister of Tourism and Antiquities Sherif Fathy—joined museum leadership at a joint press conference in Hong Kong alongside Dr. Ahmed Hameeda, Head of the Museums Sector.

The showcase offered a sweeping narrative of ancient Egyptian life, bringing together 250 masterworks drawn from eight Egyptian museums and key archaeological sites.

Among the showstoppers were a monumental quartzite statue of King Tutankhamun weighing nearly 2.7 tons from the Egyptian Museum in Tahrir, a imposing granite likeness of King Merneptah, and a dazzling gilded mummy mask on loan from the Hurghada Museum.

Alongside these heavyweights, visitors marveled at intimate glimpses of daily life, including delicate papyrus scrolls, intricate gold jewelry, stone carvings, and even preserved specimens of ancient Egyptian bread.

Reflecting on the exhibition’s triumph, Al-Leithy noted that international showcases remain a powerful engine for cross-cultural connection and a vital showcase for Egypt’s cultural tourism. With logistics, packing, and high-security transport now underway, the priceless collection is set to return home to Egypt, closing out a seamless collaborative effort between museum, restoration, and diplomatic teams across both regions.

World.title: President Sisi arrives in New Delhi for 18th BRICS Summit
World.content:
President Abdel Fattah El-Sisi arrived on Friday, in the Indian capital, New Delhi, to participate in the 18th BRICS Summit.

The official spokesperson for the Presidency of the Republic stated on his official Facebook page: “President Abdel Fattah El-Sisi arrived safely today in the Indian capital, New Delhi, to participate in the 18th BRICS Summit.”

The official spokesperson added that President El-Sisi was received upon his arrival at Palam Air Force Station airport in New Delhi by Sanjay Seth, Indian Minister of State for Defence; Air Commodore Vijay Rao, Commander of Palam Air Force Station; Ambassador Suresh Kumar, Joint Secretary for West Asia and North Africa at the Indian Ministry of External Affairs; Nisha Dhwal, Indian protocol officer; Ambassador Kamel Galal, Ambassador of the Arab Republic of Egypt to the Republic of India; and members of the Egyptian Embassy in New Delhi.

World.title: Trump makes an extraordinary offer of $5,000 payments, and other takeaways from RNC convention’s first night
World.content:
President Donald Trump vowed to pay every American adult $5,000 if Republicans retain their House and Senate majorities in November’s midterm elections – an extraordinary offer as he tries to keep his party in power.

But he offered no details on how he would pay for such a move, which he equated to companies paying shareholders dividends and the extra $1,776 checks his administration issued to members of the military last year.

“Here is my promise: If the Republicans win the House of Representatives and the United States Senate, both of them,” Trump said, “I will issue a dividend to every adult citizen in the United States of America for $5,000.”

He stressed that the payment — which he named “the Trump dividend” — comes with a condition: It must be spent in the United States.

Trump’s pledge came in a speech to Republicans who gathered in Dallas on Wednesday for the first night of an unusual midterm convention.

The president is seeking to overcome lagging approval ratings, economic headwinds and historic trends against the party in power in his bid to retain the GOP’s majorities – and stave off a slew of likely Democratic investigations and fierce opposition to his agenda – for his final two years in office.

The effort would have the US take on an enormous cost as there are an estimated 270 million adults in the nation. When Trump previously proposed issuing $2,000 tariff rebate checks to most Americans, his treasury secretary noted, “We need legislation for that.”

Vice President JD Vance last night attempted to explain how the US would pay for the dividend, suggesting that the money would come from tariffs.

“We’re taking in an extraordinary amount of revenue because the president of the United States is actually standing up to both foreign companies, but also foreign countries,” Vance said in an interview with Fox News. “What the president is just saying is … if you keep us in power and allow us to continue to do these things, then you’re going to share in some of the benefit of this incredible wealth that we are creating.”

The president, in his speech that concluded the first of the convention’s two nights, also went on to rail against Democrats, calling them “dumocrats.” He touted his border security efforts and bragged about the political potency of his opposition to transgender women participating in women’s sports. And as his political operation begins spending tens of millions of dollars, Trump vowed to campaign hard for the GOP through November 3.

“I’m asking you to pretend that I’m on the ballot,” he said. “I’m on the ballot. Just one more time.”

Here are takeaways from the first night of the convention dubbed by the president’s supporters as “Trump-a-palooza”:

Campaigning for, and mocking, Paxton

Trump told Republicans he would hit the campaign trail aggressively this fall, holding events with about 35 House and Senate candidates in competitive races as the GOP fights to keep its congressional majorities and Trump looks to buck the historic trend of poor performance by the sitting president’s party in midterm elections.

“We’re going to have rallies just like this. We’re going to have big arenas, loaded up with people,” Trump said.

He urged Texans to rally around Ken Paxton, the Republican attorney general who ousted the more moderate Sen. John Cornyn in the primary. Trump’s endorsement played an important role in tipping the race in Paxton’s favor — but also set up a tough general election against the much better-funded Democratic state Rep. James Talarico.

Texas Republican Senate candidate Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton walks on stage on the first day of the 2026 Republican National Convention at the American Airlines Center in Dallas on Wednesday. Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images

In a now-familiar riff, Trump mocked Paxton, even as he acknowledged that doing so was “so insulting.”

He said Texans “may not like the way he dresses. I don’t.” (He did compliment the suit Paxton wore Tuesday night.)

Trump also said voters “may not like the way he talks. I could see that, yeah.”

But, Trump said, Paxton is “maybe the top attorney general in the whole United States.”

“We have to elect Ken Paxton. We have to,” Trump said. “And if I have to, I’ll come back twice or three times.”

Fetterman makes a surprise virtual appearance

Several Republican senators in competitive races — including Maine Sen. Susan Collins and Alaska Sen. Dan Sullivan — skipped the convention, seeking to showcase their independence from their party and president.

But a swing-state Democratic senator did make a virtual appearance.

Sen. John Fetterman recorded a video introducing his Pennsylvania colleague, Republican Sen. Dave McCormick. In the video, recorded outside a US Steel plant, Fetterman said he is a Democrat but rejects “the extremes of socialism” and “the anti-American way of life.”

Fetterman introduced McCormick as a “great American, great senator, and yes, he is in a different party, but I’m proud to count him as my great friend.”

The introduction highlighted one of the Senate’s odd couples — a friendship forged between two senators whose swing state seats are sure to be targets of the other party when they are next on the ballot: Fetterman’s seat in 2028; McCormick’s in 2030.

The Democrat’s introduction of the Republican received one of the biggest rounds of applause of the night. And Fetterman received a loud cheer again when McCormick asked the crowd: “How great is John Fetterman, right?”

Fetterman, in particular, has been the subject of speculation about a potential party switch in recent months. He’s been one of the most vocal critics of the progressive insurgency that has swept the party’s primaries this year.

He’s repeatedly rejected talk of a party switch – and addressed it again in a statement after the video aired.

“I’m a lifelong Democrat who votes overwhelmingly with my party – and should the Senate flip in November, I will still be the 51st vote that I ran on,” the statement said.

Iran and gas prices

The war Trump launched with Iran has sent gas prices soaring. The price of oil hit $100 per barrel earlier in the day, for the first time since July.

Democrats have hammered GOP candidates on high costs. At the convention, Republicans did attempt to home in on a message of affordability, praising Trump’s 2025 tax law that included eliminating taxes on tips and overtime for eligible workers.

Wisconsin Rep. Derrick Van Orden, whose 3rd District seat is a Democratic target this fall, praised Trump’s tax cuts and the One Big Beautiful Bill Act’s rural health care funding.

“He is fighting to make quality health care a reality for everyday Americans,” he said.

Michael Whatley, the Republican Senate nominee in North Carolina who faces Democratic former Gov. Roy Cooper in another key race, praised Trump for putting “thousands of dollars back into the hands of families and seniors.”

The most direct acknowledgement of the war in Iran and its impact on gas prices came from Trump himself, when he said prices would drop as soon as the United States wins the war. He then said the Strait of Hormuz should be renamed the “Trump Strait.”

Progressive insurgents become a top target

Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic Senate nominee in Michigan, might have been the most frequently mentioned member of his party.

El-Sayed’s race against Republican former Rep. Mike Rogers is one of the most important Senate contests in November’s midterms — and perhaps the GOP’s best chance of flipping a Democratic-held seat. Democrats need a net gain of four seats to win a Senate majority.

“He hates part of his own state. He’s not sure Israel should exist,” South Carolina Sen. Tim Scott, the chairman of the National Republican Senatorial Committee, said of El-Sayed in a fiery speech. El-Sayed is a critic of Israel’s war in Gaza following Hamas’ October 7, 2023, attacks and declined to answer whether he believes the state of Israel has a right to exist, describing the question as a distraction.

Scott speaks at the Republican National Midterm Convention in Dallas on Wednesday. Brian Snyder/Reuters

Republicans broadly sought to portray democratic socialists who have won a handful of House primaries and progressives like El-Sayed as anathema to American values — describing them as extremists, communists and terrorist sympathizers.

And they sought to tie the entire Democratic Party to progressive figures like El-Sayed, New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani and Minnesota Rep. Ilhan Omar. All three are Muslim.

“This election is very clear: it’s the mainstream vs. the extreme. Because there’s another political movement in our country right now that doesn’t believe that America is or ever was great,” said Texas Rep. Brandon Gill, who has previously said Muslims should be banned from immigrating to the US. “They sometimes call themselves socialists, some even call themselves communists. But most of them simply go by Democrats.”

Speakers focus on cultural issues

Republicans made clear that they see cultural issues — particularly Democrats’ positions around transgender Americans’ rights — as their strongest line of attack.

Republicans played a video mashup focusing on Trump’s push to bar “men from playing in women’s sports” that included podcaster Joe Rogan calling the move “common sense.”

They also highlighted Democrats’ past rhetoric about transgender people.

“James Talarico claims there are six genders. He believes God is non-binary. He thinks God needs special woke pronouns,” Scott, the NRSC chairman, said of the Democratic Senate nominee in Texas. Talarico on Wednesday told Fox News that he “missed the mark on some of (his) past statements,” including his comment on the number of genders.

Paxton, his rival, claimed Talarico “wants to transition your kids.”

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent lambasted Democrats who he said are “relentless in their pursuit to remake America in the image of every socialist hellscape of the last century.”

Immigration enforcement on the agenda

Most Republicans didn’t directly advocate for Trump’s efforts to ramp up deportations. But they portrayed Democrats as to blame for lax immigration enforcement under former President Joe Biden and for the crimes committed by undocumented immigrants.

Georgia Rep. Mike Collins, who is running against Democratic Sen. Jon Ossoff, said Ossoff wouldn’t help him pass a bill named after Laken Riley, the Georgia nursing student who was murdered by an undocumented immigrant in 2024 — even though Ossoff voted for the measure, which was signed into law by Trump in 2025.

“He wouldn’t lift a finger to help me. He forgot her name until it was politically convenient,” Collins said.

This story has been updated with additional information.

World.title: Exclusive: This small island off Yemen is now a strategic prize in the widening Iran war
World.content:
Perim Island, Yemen —

Stepping on to the Yemeni island of Perim is to relive history.

Its barren sand and rock moonscape feels for all the world like the land that time forgot. Its location, however, has put it at the heart of a very modern conflict.

For Perim Island sits in the Strait of Bab al-Mandab, a geopolitical pinch-point that’s taken on an outsized importance since US President Donald Trump’s war with Iran effectively shuttered the Strait of Hormuz.

To help keep global energy supplies flowing, and prices down, Saudi Arabia diverted its oil exports from Hormuz to the Red Sea.

But now Yemen’s Huthi rebels, Iran’s most powerful regional proxy, have begun an offensive that could land them control of Perim – and with it the ability to prevent ships passing through this narrow gateway from the Red Sea.

Regional sources told CNN Thursday that the Huthis were making major push to capture the town of Mocha, a crucial coastal location some 50 miles to the north of Perim.

On a recent day, an honor guard of Yemeni troops, patiently shuffling in the scorching sun, watched while a weathered officer’s outstretched hand helped arrivals to Perim off an aging gunboat. A CNN crew was among them, granted exclusive access to this dusty outpost.

The tableau, reminiscent of a bygone era, has likely played out here for centuries. The island’s position – at the narrowest point of a strait which brings the Horn of Africa within 12 miles of the Arabian Peninsula – has made it valuable to empires and regional powers for generations. Once a coaling station for ships of the British Empire sailing to India, Perim’s imperial past is still visible in its crumbling ruins.

Bumping along a rocky road to the island’s highest point, the officer – one hand on the wheel of his decrepit army truck – points to Eritrea and Djibouti across the water, on the African side of the strait. A veteran member of a brigade loyal to Yemen’s internationally recognized government, he knows his mission, defending Perim, also known as Mayyun, now carries far greater stakes than before.

‘It’s geopolitical now’

For more than a decade, Yemen’s civil war appeared to be a distant regional conflict. But as fighting intensifies and the Iran-backed Huthi rebels launch attacks towards the Red Sea coast, that distinction is disappearing. Yemen, with Perim at the center, is becoming another potential front line in the confrontation between Washington and Tehran, and a reminder that the consequences of its war no longer stop at its shores.

Already, the Huthis control Yemen’s capital, swaths of the country’s northwest, and much of its Red Sea coastline north of the island.

If history is any guide, Bab al-Mandab – the smaller twin of the Strait of Hormuz and now a crucial alternative to it – could be where Iran, through its proxy, tightens the economic and political screws on Trump next, driving up oil prices and damaging Republican prospects in the US midterm elections in November.

“We told the world that this is an Iranian project, but no one listened to Yemenis back then… It’s geopolitical now,” Tarik Saleh, a vice president in Yemen’s beleaguered, internationally recognized government, told CNN in an exclusive interview.

Saleh, a nephew of the ousted president Ali Abdullah Saleh and a former ally of the Huthis, is a rarity among Yemen’s political class: the only leader and military commander who remains inside the country while many others have fled. He says he has survived several assassination attempts and says Iran wants him dead. Meetings with him are arranged at short notice, in random locations, and are over fast.

Speaking to CNN from a tent on a remote Yemeni beach in late August, Saleh said he was receiving no help from the United States, “only talk.” He warned that if the Huthis seized Perim Island and gained control of the Bab al-Mandab Strait, “then a massive (international) force and the navies will be needed” to dislodge them.

Even reaching Perim Island is a lesson in the dangers of this often one-sidedly high-tech war.

As the CNN team set out for the two-mile crossing from the mainland, warnings of an imminent Huthi drone attack forced the gunboat carrying the crew to turn back. Preparing for a possible attack, the gunner fired a heavy-caliber round from his rusting weapon.

‘In bed together’

Yemen’s civil war began in 2014, when Huthi rebels seized the capital, Sanaa, and drove the internationally recognized government into exile. Saudi Arabia led a military campaign the following year to dislodge the rebels. Iran has supplied the Huthis with weapons and training, and exercises some influence on the rebel group’s decisions.

The result is a fractured country, with the Huthis controlling the capital and the northwest, and the government and allied factions holding much of the south and east. Some 22 million people, roughly half of the population, need humanitarian assistance to this day.

Following the October 7 Hamas attack on Israel and the ensuing war on Gaza, the Huthis joined the conflict. They launched attacks on Israel in solidarity with Palestinians in Gaza and targeted shipping in the Red Sea. The US and Israel launched airstrikes on the group that destroyed key assets. The Trump administration designated the Huthis as a terror group in 2025.

The latest Huthi offensive against Yemen’s government began in July. It ruptured a tacit four-year truce between the Huthis and Saudi Arabia and drew Yemen’s conflict into the wider war involving Iran.

Soldiers of the National Resistance Forces are seen in Mocha in late August. In recent weeks, fighting has intensified between the forces of the internationally recognized government and the Huthi rebels. Michael Pratt/CNN

In a rare exception to restrictions it has enforced over Yemeni airspace since intervening in 2015, Saudi Arabia permitted an Iranian passenger plane to land in Sanaa. The plane – the first direct air link between Tehran and Sanaa in about a decade – then carried a Huthi delegation to the funeral of Ali Khamenei, Iran’s former supreme leader, who was killed alongside several members of his family in the opening US-Israeli strikes of February 28.

But when the aircraft returned 10 days later, Saudi Arabia denied it permission to land in Sanaa amid concerns that it was also carrying Iranian Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps personnel and military equipment. Saudi aircraft struck the airport’s runway, forcing the plane to divert to the Huthi-controlled Yemeni port city of Hodeidah.

The episode became a turning point, unraveling diplomacy that had largely preserved the informal truce and halted Huthi attacks on Saudi territory. Against the backdrop of the collapsing US-Iran ceasefire, the Huthis retaliated by declaring a naval blockade against Saudi Arabia and threatening ships carrying Saudi exports through Bab al-Mandab. They also launched missiles and drones at the kingdom’s oil infrastructure, airports and other civilian sites.

An image taken from video broadcast by Al-Masirah TV, a Huthi-controlled news channel, shows an explosion at the Sanaa International Airport compound during what the Iranian-backed Huthi rebels in Yemen said were several Saudi airstrikes on July 13, 2026. Al-Masirah TV/AP

The timing of the new Huthi offensive could benefit Iran by increasing pressure on Trump. Mohammed Al-Basha, a former Yemeni government press officer and Washington, DC-based risk analyst, described the relationship between Tehran and the Huthis as “not a submissive relationship – but they are in bed together.”

Nonetheless, observers caution against framing the Huthis’ recent intervention as merely executing Iran’s regional agenda.

“The Huthis needed a war as diversion from domestic problems. They wanted to say they can fight Saudi Arabia into negotiating with them again. And of course, if it is going to help an old friend, like Iran, which at one point was the only friend they had, then why not?” said Farea Al-Muslimi, a Chatham House think tank research fellow.

The Huthi attacks on Israel, and the weakening of other Iranian allies in the region like Hezbollah in Lebanon, as well as the fall of the Assad regime in Syria, have elevated the Yemeni faction’s standing in the so-called axis of resistance and the Huthis wanted to capitalize on their new position, he added.

Sanaa officials have not responded to CNN’s request for comment. Huthi leaders have maintained in previous statements that their current offensive inside and outside Yemen is in response to “Saudi aggression and blockade.”

In a statement on Thursday, Nasr al-Din Amer, head of the Huthi-run state news agency Saba, told CNN that the aim of the rebels’ military campaign is to “break the siege unjustly imposed by the Saudi enemy for 12 years.”

Amer claimed the Huthis have control of Bab al-Mandab Strait and parts of the Red Sea through firepower, saying the operations are limited to Saudi vessels.

“We also target the troops mobilized by the Saudis for a territorial advance against us and the weapons the Saudis send to them,” he said.

Strikes on port, fishermen

Oil flows past Perim have already fallen sharply amid this maritime roulette. Three years ago, about 10% of the world’s seaborne oil trade passed through Bab al-Mandab. Kpler data indicates that volume has since fallen by half, and a sustained Huthi campaign could choke the route further.

Yemen’s fishermen are also victims of Huthi drone attacks. Dozens were evacuated from an island north of Perim after one such attack killed and injured several people, according to Yemeni government officials.

As fishermen wrestled their catches out of flimsy fiberglass boats near a makeshift shoreside market recently, several stopped to talk with CNN, complaining that the war is ruining business.

On normal days, one trader said, “there would be many ships out there,” but “because of the attack of the Huthi there are no ships right now.”

Children played in the Red Sea’s lukewarm waves. Apparently unconcerned about their parents’ worries, they jostled to get into the visiting journalists’ pictures.

But the image that emerges here is of an already war-weary, fragile and poor country being pushed ever closer to a breaking point.

A few miles up the coast, evidence of that is mounting.

The port of Mocha remains closed following a Huthi attack in August that killed 16 people. Ships, boats, equipment and platforms were destroyed in the attack. Michael Pratt/CNN

The port of Mocha, the most northerly government-held city of significance on the Red Sea, is being hit hard. A few weeks ago, more than 25 Huthi rockets slammed into the sprawling harbor as commercial ships were unloading, according to port director Abdel Malek Al-Sharaabi.

In the water, half-sunk ships lie at improbable angles, while the concrete on land is scarred with holes deep enough to hide a large dog. Heaps of scorched motorcycle frames lie beside piles of semi-melted engines.

Sixteen people were killed and 22 injured that day, the port director told CNN, while six commercial ships were sunk and 14,000 motorcycles lost. The Huthis, he said, want to destroy the economy.

“The port had a big role in development and commerce,” Al-Sharaabi said. “This attack aims at hurting this development and stopping services.”

Over the past year, the Huthis have repeatedly fired at targets as far as Israel, more than 1,000 miles away. They claim to possess hypersonic missiles and have an arsenal that includes long-range, sea-skimming anti-ship missiles designed to evade radar. They also possess surface-to-air missiles capable of downing high-altitude US drones and threatening crewed aircraft.

‘Higher price in the future’

On Yemen’s front lines, fighting between Huthi and government forces is intensifying. Government troops are flying new, first-person-view, or FPV, quadcopter drones, attacking concealed Huthi bunkers.

“Our troops have improved due to training and new resources like drones,” Saleh told CNN.

But for every step the government takes, officials say, Iran is trying to keep the Huthis ahead. A journey in a vehicle with blacked-out windows to a heavily guarded warehouse at a secret location offered a glimpse of that challenge – and what the government says is evidence of the scale of Iranian support for the Huthis, including the provision of weapons capable of threatening tanker traffic in the Red Sea.

Abdel Nasser El Mamlouh, the director of Saleh’s military media operation, led CNN through what he said was an Iranian-made weapons shipment captured before smugglers could deliver it to the Huthis.

The National Resistance Forces of Yemen’s internationally recognized government say they regularly seize advanced weapons smuggled at sea to their Huthi foes. Michael Pratt/CNN

The cache included enormous, 18-foot-long missiles, complex long-range radar systems, drone engines and optical equipment, even bullets hidden inside a truck battery. Everything, El Mamlouh said, had been disguised as commercial equipment to evade detection.

And what they captured, he readily acknowledged, was only a fraction of what is believed to have made it through. Smugglers “confessed that before this one they had smuggled 11 shipments similar in size and content,” he said, amounting to 750 tons.

If the Huthis seized Perim and gained a foothold in Bab al-Mandab, he warned, they would no longer need long-range weapons to threaten shipping.

“They would mine the strait, just like (Iran) did in Hormuz,” he said.

Along Yemen’s government-held stretch of Red Sea coast, officials have little doubt that their civil war has become part of something much larger.

“(We are) fighting this war on behalf of the Arab world and the international community,” Mamlouh said.

Before hurrying away from his tent on the beach, Saleh was asked what would happen if US support never came.

“We will pay a higher price in the future,” to dislodge the Huthis, he replied. And so, he warned, would “the American army, the international community and international trade.”

CNN’s Sarah El Sirgany contributed to this report.

World.title: ‘Gambling with our lives’: Another AI employee quits over safety concerns
World.content:
“The people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade.”

That blunt admission from former Anthropic employee Jacob Coxon made waves Tuesday, as the just-quit 27-year-old AI researcher spilled the beans on his way out the door in a resignation thread on X.

As alarming and serious as Coxon’s revelations sound (“These will soon be superhuman systems that can hack anything, revolutionize any field overnight, and acquire real power and resources”), they’re also not new. Anthropic got its start in exactly this way, as OpenAI employees concerned about the company’s safety protocols left Sam Altman’s startup to launch their own AI company, arguing their approach was more responsible.

The concerns are becoming commonplace. A number of AI employees have loudly quit their companies over safety concerns over the past several months and years. Others have publicly voiced worries that the technology is moving too quickly and will one day outpace humans’ ability to control it.

In July, nearly 1,400 AI company employees signed an open letter urging the US government to regulate the technology to rein in Big Tech and slow the pace of AI to ensure its safety. And two days ago, OpenAI Chief Scientist Jakub Pachocki warned that AI capabilities are advancing faster than researchers’ ability to reliably monitor and control them.

Now, a relatively junior researcher has become the latest to sound the alarm.

“They are racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives,” Coxon posted.

Coxon’s post gained attention after a more senior Anthropic employee, Evan Hubinger, commented that Coxon was correct.

“We really do earnestly believe AI could kill all humans!” Hubinger posted on X. He said he personally believes the chance is under 10% over the next decade, and despite Anthropic’s good intentions it doesn’t have a plan to avoid so-called superintelligence that could exceed humans’ ability to control AI. Superintelligence, a state at which AI surpasses human capabilities, is a widely debated theoretical milestone with no benchmark that some AI researchers believe has already been achieved and others believe will never come.

Hubinger shortly after clarified his statement in a follow-up post that Anthropic’s own Risk Report acknowledges the concern but says present AI poses little chance of gaining such power.

“We have always been transparent that AI will bring both enormous benefits and unprecedented risks,” an Anthropic spokesperson said in a statement. “To address these risks, we continue to build models with some of the strongest safeguards in the industry.”

Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei has also repeatedly warned that the race to move fast on the technology could unintentionally result in a catastrophic human-caused error that causes a company to lose control of its AI.

“This is a complex engineering problem and I think something will go wrong with someone’s AI system. Hopefully not ours,” Amodei told the New York Times in February.

Regulation stagnation

Despite the constant stream of warnings, regulation seems far off. The Trump administration has actively worked to undermine state AI regulations and Congress has so far been unwilling to rein in the technology. A common refrain: Any effort to regulate AI represents a capitulation to China, which is under no such constraints.

Except China has introduced AI regulation, particularly aimed at risk management and safety. Last year, the government required AI companies to label AI-generated content to make it transparent and traceable. However, China has resisted the kind of stringent regulation that would prevent the kind of problems Silicon Valley researchers have raised.

In the meantime, in the US at least, AI companies are more or less responsible for policing themselves.

The White House has moved toward a voluntary framework to review certain AI models before launch, sources familiar with a meeting last month between the Trump administration and several top AI companies told CNN.

Among the representatives were those from OpenAI, Anthropic, Google and Meta, according to multiple sources familiar with the situation. The details of the framework will not be released publicly and many of the standards set within it will be classified, according to a June executive order on the framework.

In July, Altman suggested it may be time to slow AI development, saying in the Invest Like The Best podcast that the recent testing incidents involving advanced models were raising “long-term questions” about how AI companies should manage rapid advances in capabilities.

“We may have to pace the rate of AI development to give ourselves enough time for society to harden around these new capability levels,” Altman said.

Anthropic, in a statement on Wednesday, concurred with Altman.

“We believe the world would benefit from the industry adopting a lawful, verifiable way to work together to pace how we release powerful models.”

World.title: U.S. Embassy Marks 25 Years Since 9/11 With Memorial Walk in Monrovia
World.content:
Monrovia — The United States Embassy in Monrovia on Friday commemorated the 25th anniversary of the September 11, 2001 terrorist attacks on the United States, honoring the 2,977 people who lost their lives in one of the deadliest attacks in U.S. history.

By Gerald C. Koinyeneh, [email protected]

The commemoration began with the lowering of the U.S. flag at the embassy, followed by a moment of silence led by U.S. Chargé d’Affaires Joe Zadrozny at 8:46 a.m.—the exact time American Airlines Flight 11 crashed into the North Tower of the World Trade Center in New York.

A member of the United States Marine Corps then did a beautiful rendition of the U.S. national anthem, before Zadrozny delivered remarks reflecting on the lives lost, the bravery of first responders and the international solidarity that followed the attacks.

“At 8:46 AM, the world shifted in an instant,” Zadrozny said. “What began as a bright September morning transformed into a day of unprecedented tragedy.”

He said the anniversary was an opportunity to remember the 2,977 innocent civilians, first responders and service members killed at the World Trade Center, the Pentagon and in a field near Shanksville, Pennsylvania.

The Chargé d’Affaires also paid tribute to firefighters, police officers and paramedics who rushed toward danger, as well as passengers aboard United Airlines Flight 93 who resisted the hijackers before the aircraft crashed in Pennsylvania.

“We remember the courage of the firefighters, police officers, and paramedics who ran toward danger so that others might live,” Zadrozny said. “We remember the ordinary citizens on Flight 93, who performed extraordinary acts of bravery.”

Liberia’s Solidarity Remembered

Zadrozny also recalled Liberia’s response to the tragedy, noting that the Liberian government organized an intercessory service and declared three days of national mourning for the victims, including at least one Liberian.

He described Liberia’s solidarity with the United States following the attacks as an enduring element of the two countries’ relationship.

“Our Liberian hosts and international partners stood together with the United States in our grief, reminding us that we do not stand alone,” he said. “That solidarity remains a cornerstone of our work together today.”

Zadrozny said the anniversary should serve not only as a moment to remember the past but also as a reminder of the values of resilience, public service and unity.

“As our flag flies at half-staff, we carry a duty not only to remember the past, but to live out the values of resilience, public service, and unity that defined the days after 9/11,” he said.

2,977 Steps in Memory of 2,977 Lives

At 9:03 a.m., marking the moment United Airlines Flight 175 struck the South Tower of the World Trade Center, participants began a symbolic 2,977-step memorial walk.

The walk started at the embassy flagpole, proceeded through the main gate and around the embassy compound along UN Drive and Benson Street.

Each step represented one of the 2,977 people who died in the September 11 attacks.

Despite a heavy downpour, Zadrozny joined the walk alongside Liberian government officials, U.S. Embassy staff and members of the press.

The memorial concluded with participants returning to the embassy grounds, where they gathered for coffee and refreshments.

The 9/11 attacks killed 2,977 people after four hijacked commercial aircraft were used in coordinated attacks against the World Trade Center in New York, the Pentagon in Arlington, Virginia, and a target that was not reached after Flight 93 crashed in Shanksville, Pennsylvania.

World.title: Liberia: Boakai Shuffles Cabinet: New Acting Defense, Commerce Ministers; Gender Deputy Suspended
World.content:
Monrovia – President Joseph Nyuma Boakai Sr. has shaken up several government ministries and agencies, announcing a wave of new appointments this week.

Cllr. Oswald Natu Tweh takes over as Acting Minister of National Defense, stepping in for Geraldine J. George. Over at Commerce and Industry, Stephen Marka Yekeson Jr. steps into the acting minister role, replacing Magdalene E. Dagoseh. Both George and Dagoseh will be reassigned to other government positions.

The president also tapped Christopher Ben Bailey to serve as Acting Superintendent of Grand Gedeh County. At the National Food Assistance Agency, Mike Khailelu B. Jabateh moves into the role of Acting Deputy Director General for Publicity.

In another appointment, Daniel Frank Gould II has been named to the Board of Commissioners of the Public Procurement and Concessions Commission, though his nomination still needs Senate confirmation.

On the disciplinary side, Frederick S. Cooper, Deputy Minister for Administration at the Ministry of Gender, Children and Social Protection, has been suspended for 60 days without pay. The Executive Mansion says the move stems from conduct it considers incompatible with Cooper’s role as a public official.

Boakai used the moment to send a broader message to his administration, warning officials that public office comes with real accountability — and that conduct undermining government integrity or public trust won’t be tolerated.

World.title: Liberia: A Mystery Vessel, a Prison, and a Warning Nobody Answered
World.content:
MONROVIA — There is a version of this story in which the boat behind the Monrovia Central Prison is nothing more than a stray vessel, pushed toward shore by the tide and forgotten within days.

By Rodney D. Sieh, [email protected] and Gerald C. Koinyeneh, [email protected]

But Thursday’s discovery is difficult to view in isolation.

Five weeks ago, the prison’s Deputy Superintendent for Operations, Jackson K. Kolako, publicly warned that he believed a plan was being developed to facilitate a mass jailbreak—potentially freeing foreign nationals detained in connection with Liberia’s largest cocaine investigation.

Now, before dawn on Thursday, a vessel of disputed ownership and unexplained movements was found at the beach behind the same prison.

Coincidence is possible. But the timing has raised questions that authorities have yet to fully answer.

What Kolako Actually Said

Kolako’s account dates to August 1, when, according to him, two men arrived at the prison claiming to be National Security Agency officers. He said the men were dressed in a manner inconsistent with prison security rules and sought access to one of the foreign nationals detained in connection with the drug case.

Kolako said he questioned whether the prison’s chief superintendent and the Assistant Minister of Justice for Corrections had authorized the visit.

He says he was arrested later that day, in front of his officers, on the orders of a senior Justice Ministry official.

According to Kolako, he spent six days in custody without giving a statement and was pressured to surrender his phones and passwords. Following his release, he publicly raised his concerns and appealed to President Joseph Boakai to consider moving detainees connected to the drug investigation to a more secure facility outside Liberia, suggesting Morocco as one possible destination.

Kolako’s account, however, remains contested.

He has not publicly produced evidence establishing that an actual jailbreak plot was underway, while officials he implicated have not publicly addressed all of his allegations. Ministry of Justice records have reportedly presented a different explanation for his suspension, saying he was sanctioned over alleged obstruction of a lawful operation rather than for raising security concerns.

The competing accounts have yet to be reconciled.

On Thursday, Kolako again took to social media, emphasizing the need for heightened coordination among the Liberia National Police, Armed Forces of Liberia and corrections authorities.

Kolako, using the name Gertrude’s Pap on Facebook, said the detention of people connected to sensitive and high-profile cases requires preparedness, coordination and vigilance.

“Security is stronger when institutions work together,” Kolako wrote.

Mystery Vessel Sparks Calls for Independent Probe

The vessel’s appearance has now triggered calls for an independent investigation.

Liberian activist Martin K. N. Kollie, whose network first reported the boat, is calling for an independent inquiry into how the unidentified vessel came to be at the beach behind the Monrovia Central Prison, commonly known as South Beach.

Kollie has described the vessel as a “ghost boat” and questioned conflicting accounts surrounding its ownership, origin and movements.

He has specifically called for an investigation outside the Liberia National Police, including Inspector General Gregory Coleman, arguing that the circumstances require investigators viewed as independent by the public.

The vessel was later moved toward the Miami Beach area, according to accounts surrounding the incident, further raising questions about who controlled it and why it had initially been positioned near the prison.

The Question of the Boat

Kollie has also challenged claims that the vessel found at South Beach belongs to a person identified publicly only as “Charlie,” who reportedly described himself during a radio interview as a Canadian miner.

Kollie maintains that images circulated by people claiming ownership show a different vessel from the one found behind the prison.

That claim has not been independently verified by FrontPage Africa.

The unresolved questions are nevertheless straightforward: Who owns the vessel? Where did it come from? Who was operating it? When did it leave the St. Paul River? How did it reach South Beach? And was anyone aboard at any point during the journey?

Those questions become more consequential because of the vessel’s location.

The beach behind the prison sits within a highly sensitive security environment, particularly as the facility houses detainees linked to Liberia’s ongoing drug-trafficking investigation.

A Country That Has Seen This Boat Before

The episode comes against a backdrop of growing scrutiny over Liberia’s maritime security.

In June, a vessel identified as the IB Atlantic IV remained off the coast of Grand Cape Mount County for several days as Liberian authorities considered how to respond before the vessel eventually moved away and was later intercepted and seized in Ivorian waters.

No drugs were officially reported recovered from the vessel.

The episode nevertheless became another example of the challenges facing Liberia in monitoring and securing its coastline.

The latest vessel presents a different but related set of questions.

Despite competing ownership claims, authorities have not publicly established who owns the boat, how it reached South Beach or whether it was carrying anything when it arrived.

Nor has any official investigation publicly established a connection between the vessel and the ongoing drug-trafficking cases.

What Remains Unanswered

For now, the boat remains less an answer than a question.

There is no publicly established evidence that the vessel was part of a jailbreak attempt. There is also no publicly established evidence that it was connected to the drug investigation.

But the combination of its location, the conflicting accounts surrounding its ownership and movement, and the prison security warnings raised weeks earlier has created a legitimate public-interest question.

An independent investigation could establish the facts without relying on competing narratives—determining the vessel’s ownership, registration, route, occupants, cargo, movements and circumstances surrounding its arrival at South Beach.

Until those questions are answered, the vessel behind the prison wall will remain what it became Thursday morning: a mystery sitting in plain sight.

World.title: Liberia: Expert Warns of Security Risks if Legislature Fails to Approve War Crimes Court Before U.N. Security Council Presidency
World.content:
Summary

Transitional justice expert Aaron Weah warns that failure to approve legislation establishing Liberia’s long-delayed War and Economic Crimes Court could create new security risks, particularly among a young generation raised on memories of the civil wars.

Liberia is preparing to assume the rotating presidency of the U.N. Security Council in December, putting a renewed international spotlight on the country’s unfinished transitional justice process.

Weah says Liberia must address how the wars are remembered and taught, warning that the absence of an agreed historical narrative, public memorials and museums has left younger Liberians exposed to disinformation about the conflict.

By Anthony Stephens, senior justice correspondent with New Narratives

Aaron Weah, the leading historian and transitional justice expert, has warned of security risks if the country fails to approve legislation establishing a War and Economic Crimes Court before it assumes the rotating presidency of the United Nations Security Council in December.

Despite years of advocacy, the push for a long-delayed court to prosecute those accused of “bearing the greatest responsibility” for atrocities committed during Liberia’s two civil wars, which the United Nations estimates left about 250,000 people dead, remains unfinished as the Legislature has so far failed to overcome opposition to the courts among lawmakers.

A recent poll by FrontPage Africa/New Narratives found 89 percent of survey respondents in 11 counties wanted to see the worst perpetrators tried in a war crimes court for atrocities committed during the war.

“You don’t want to raise expectations of people and let them down. I think it has a lot of security risk because we have a youthful population,” Weah, director of the Ducor Institute for Social and Economic Research, said in a FrontPage Africa/New Narratives interview.

Weah’s warning comes at a pivotal moment for Liberia’s unfinished transitional justice process. The country is preparing to preside over the Security Council for the first time while lawmakers consider competing proposals for the long-promised court. At the same time, a population dominated by young people who did not directly experience the wars is confronting unresolved questions about justice, reparations and how the conflict should be remembered and taught.

Weah said establishing the court is about more than prosecuting alleged perpetrators. He argued that it could help clarify Liberia’s wartime history and said abandoning the process after years of promises could create new resentment and security concerns.

His warning echoes concerns raised by the Liberian government and the United Nations. In an October 2025, statement to the U.N. General Assembly’s Sixth Committee, which deals with international legal issues, the government warned that “the absence of justice perpetuates the cycle of conflict.”

Liberia’s civil wars claimed an estimated 250,000 lives. Credit: Chris Hondros / Getty Images.

The United Nations has also linked the proposed court to preventing recurrence. Christian Mukosa, its top human rights official in Liberia, said that operationalizing a victim-centered court could “contribute to reconciliation and prevent recurrence.”

According to Liberia’s 2022 Population and Housing Census , three in every four of the country’s 5.25 million people were 35 or younger. Forty four percent of the population was born after the civil wars ended in 2003. Weah said many young Liberians have instead grown up with memories of the wars passed down by their parents. After taking the court process this far, he warned, abandoning it could have consequences beyond the justice debate.

Liberia’s official campaign graphic for its successful bid for a non-permanent seat on the United Nations Security Council for 2026–2027. Credit: Government of Liberia

Liberia previously served on the Security Council in 1961, but the December presidency will be its first time chairing the body. The 81st United Nations General Assembly began September 8, with President Joseph Boakai expected to deliver his third address during the General Debate, which begins September 22.

Jallah Barbu, executive director of the Office for the Establishment of the War and Economic Crimes Court, recently urged Boakai to recall lawmakers from their annual constituency break to act on the legislation.

Six proposals involving a War and Economic Crimes Court and a National Anti-Corruption Court are before the Legislature. They include proposals from the Liberian National Bar Association and a civil society coalition led by the Independent National Commission on Human Rights ; separate proposals from Senate President Pro Tempore Nyonblee Karnga-Lawrence and Senator Joseph Jallah; and two bills from the government’s court office.

Boakai reenergized the process when he renewed the Office’s mandate in May and later submitted its bills to the Legislature. But lawmakers went on their annual constituency break in July without approving legislation.

Before the recess, the Senate Judiciary Committee began consultations aimed at harmonizing the proposals, while more than 40 House members participated in a two-day technical session in Buchanan in June.

Some proposals have raised concerns among justice advocates over issues including the role of international experts and the appeals process. Senator Jallah has suggested international lawyers could serve as “consultants to Liberians” , rather than take direct roles.

“The final bill should include all benchmarks of fair, independent, meaningful and credible trials: crimes and modes of liability in line with international standards,” Michelle Reyes Milk, senior international justice counsel at Human Rights Watch, wrote in Just Security, a nonpartisan law and policy journal based at New York University School of Law. She also called for “full guarantees of due process for defendants” and “genuine participation and protection for victims and witnesses.”

Weah said Liberia’s Security Council role could showcase the country’s progress since the wars. He pointed to the success of international peacekeeping and the peaceful resolution of the closely fought 2023 presidential election as signs of the country’s resilience.

But he warned that sustaining that progress requires Liberia to confront how its wars are remembered and taught to younger generations.

“We have no public memorials. We have not agreed on a historical text on the war to teach kids in school,” Weah said. “And so much of what the children learn that’s passed for history is mostly the opinions of history teachers, is the opinions of civic teachers in school, and that’s dangerous.”

Weah said museums, memorials and other forms of public education could give younger Liberians a more structured understanding of the country’s past and help address violent memories transmitted from one generation to another.

Liberia has made some steps up efforts to address memorialization. A high-level government delegation has returned from a United Nations Development Program-supported study mission to Rwanda and South Africa in late August and early September, where it examined approaches to reconciliation, memorialization, peacebuilding and preserving national history. The lessons are expected to inform President Boakai’s proposed Liberia Peace, Reconciliation and Memorial Museum, envisioned as a national institution to preserve the country’s history, promote reconciliation and strengthen civic education.

TRC’s Controversial Decision to Sanction President Johnson Sirleaf Remains a Point of Debate

But Liberia’s efforts to establish an authoritative account of the wars have themselves generated controversy. More than 15 years after the Truth and Reconciliation Commission issued its final report, parts of its findings remain contested.

The commission recommended a 30-year public-office ban for a number of people, including then-President Ellen Johnson Sirleaf, because it said they had been associated with former warring factions. In 2011, Liberia’s Supreme Court struck down the sanction as unconstitutional , finding that it had been imposed without due process.

Liberian civilians flee Paynesville amid fighting between rebel forces and the Armed Forces of Liberia on Aug. 10, 1990, during the country’s first civil war. Credit: Pascal Guyot/AFP via Getty Images.

In testimony to the U.S. Congress in June 1990 , as Taylor’s rebellion was terrorizing people across the country, Sirleaf portrayed Taylor’s uprising as a broad-based struggle, saying people, “many of them children,” had joined what she called a “struggle for freedom,” and describing the rebellion as an opportunity to transform Liberia’s political system. (Taylor’s alleged use of child soldiers was seen as a particularly egregious act that was copied by other warring factions in years to come.)

Weah argued that the commission’s treatment of Sirleaf contributed to her reluctance to champion implementation of its recommendations and questioned whether the report sufficiently established the extent of her involvement in the conflict.

“I think she felt embarrassed. She felt stigmatized,” Weah said. “Before you mention the names of people in report, there has to be a duty of care to make sure that your work is thorough, is rigorous. It can stand up to basic scrutiny.”

John Stewart, a commissioner who chaired the committee that wrote the TRC report, rejected Weah’s criticism. He said Sirleaf was sanctioned because commissioners concluded that her testimony about when she distanced herself from Charles Taylor conflicted with evidence they had obtained.

“We did not do so because we wanted to embarrass Sirleaf,” Stewart said. “We did so because we wanted to be fair to all others. And her being president was no exception to the rule.”

The disagreement underscores the difficulty Liberia still faces in establishing a broadly accepted account of its violent past — the problem Weah says younger generations should not be left to navigate alone.

Against that backdrop, Weah recently co-launched Liberia: Remembering the Future with British journalist Gerry Naughton. The podcast, airing on 10 radio stations across Liberia, examines the country’s history, its transition from war to peace and its election to the Security Council.

Weah said the project aims to provide historical context and clarification for Liberians, particularly younger people, as well as international audiences seeking to understand the country as its global profile rises.

This story was a collaboration with New Narratives as part of the Investigating Liberia project. Funding was provided by the U.N. Office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights and the European Union. The funders had no say in the story’s content.

World.title: SpoonTV CEO Details Cooperation With U.S. Investigators That Led to Reduced Sentence and Early Release
World.content:
Monrovia — SpoonTV CEO Stanton Witherspoon has offered a detailed account of how his decision to cooperate with U.S. federal investigators ultimately helped secure his release from prison after he was convicted in a multimillion-dollar scheme involving fraudulent nursing diplomas and transcripts.

By Gerald C. Koinyeneh, [email protected]

Witherspoon, who pleaded guilty to conspiracy to commit wire fraud, was sentenced in November 2023 to 41 months in prison and three years of supervised release.

But on September 9, 2026, U.S. District Judge Rodney Smith granted a motion by federal prosecutors to reduce the sentence to time served, eliminating the supervised-release requirement and dismissing the remaining counts against him.

The reduction was granted under Rule 35(b) of the Federal Rules of Criminal Procedure, which allows prosecutors to seek a reduced sentence for a defendant who provides substantial assistance to the government after sentencing.

Witherspoon said Thursday that his cooperation was not simply a strategy to obtain a shorter sentence, but a decision he made after his lawyer and one of his Spoon Talk colleagues advised him that cooperating early could benefit his case and help investigators pursue others involved in the alleged fraud.

‘Cooperate’

Recounting the events on Spoon Talk, Witherspoon said panelist Abdullah Kiatamba advised him in 2023 to consider cooperating with investigators.

According to Witherspoon, Kiatamba told him that he was not making a judgment about his guilt or innocence but was speaking from his understanding of the U.S. legal system.

“He said, no matter what you do, I’m going to talk to you from experience. Cooperate,” Witherspoon recalled.

Witherspoon said he initially questioned the advice.

“I said, what are you talking about? He said, Stanton, I’m not saying you are guilty. I’m not saying you are not guilty. But I know the system. Talk to your lawyer.”

He said he followed the advice and consulted his attorney, who also recommended that he cooperate with investigators at an early stage.

According to Witherspoon, his lawyer warned that delaying cooperation could diminish its value if other defendants cooperated first.

“Every other day, the lawyer would say, Stanton, if you’re the last to cooperate, you are not needed. If you must cooperate, cooperate now,” he recalled.

Witherspoon said his lawyer subsequently explained the cooperation process and its potential implications to him step by step.

What Prosecutors Say He Provided

The government’s court filings indicate that Witherspoon’s cooperation went beyond simply providing information about his own conduct.

According to prosecutors, he was interviewed by agents from the FBI and the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services Office of Inspector General about individuals involved in nursing-school fraud schemes.

Prosecutors said his cooperation contributed to cases against several defendants, including Carleen Noreus, Cimoyne Alves, Lemuel Pierre and Cleophat Tanis.

Witherspoon testified against Noreus, who operated a separate fraudulent nursing program known as Carleen Health Institute. Following his testimony, prosecutors said Noreus pleaded guilty to wire fraud and money-laundering conspiracy charges and is awaiting sentencing.

Witherspoon also signed an affidavit identifying nursing students who received fraudulent degrees and transcripts. That information was provided to the National Council of State Boards of Nursing so state licensing authorities could take remedial action.

‘I Was a Star Witness’

Witherspoon described himself as a key witness for the government, saying investigators needed information and supporting documents that he possessed because of his involvement in the nursing-school business.

He said he had recruited students for multiple schools and therefore had knowledge of people involved in the operation.

“Now they have so many big, big people that were involved in this thing. And a lot of them came to me to recruit students for them,” Witherspoon said.

He said investigators already knew some of the individuals but needed additional evidence.

“The government knew them, but the government needed supporting documents from me.”

According to Witherspoon, one of the principal defendants initially refused to cooperate, leading prosecutors to call him to testify.

“I had to take the stand for the government. For four months, the woman couldn’t break. And the government called a star witness. And I was a star witness.”

Witherspoon said that after he testified, the defendant subsequently agreed to plead guilty.

“After I testified, the next day, the woman begged for the plea. She’s scheduled to be sentenced. It’s a public record.”

The account corresponds with prosecutors’ description of Witherspoon’s cooperation in the case involving Noreus.

A $5.17 Million Fraud

Federal prosecutors said Witherspoon was a 50% owner of Siena Education Center LLC and Siena College of Health II LLC and was also the founder and president of Nursing Education Resource Center LLC.

Prosecutors alleged that Witherspoon, working with Rene Bernadel, Alfred Sellu and Cimoyne Alves, used NERC to recruit and fraudulently train aspiring nurses.

He later worked with Eunide Sanon and Siena to provide fake nursing diplomas and transcripts, which students allegedly used to obtain fraudulent certification as registered nurses or licensed practical nurses.

Witherspoon was held responsible for approximately $5.17 million in losses.

His total offense level was calculated at 26, with a criminal history category of I, producing a federal sentencing guideline range of 63 to 78 months. He ultimately received a 41-month sentence.

‘I Wanted This to Stop’

Witherspoon said his decision to cooperate was motivated by more than his own legal circumstances.

He said he wanted to expose the broader operation and help prevent others from being harmed by fraudulent nursing credentials.

“I had to do it not because I was fighting for myself. I had to do it because I wanted this to stop,” he said.

“I had to do it because I want the system to be right.”

Witherspoon said the information he possessed was extensive and involved conversations with professionals and others connected to the business.

He also thanked his attorney for guiding him through the cooperation process.

Prosecutors Backed Sentence Reduction

The government’s motion to reduce Witherspoon’s sentence was supported by prosecutors and investigators from the FBI and HHS-OIG, who cited the scope of his cooperation.

Assistant U.S. Attorney Christopher J. Clark filed the motion on behalf of the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Southern District of Florida.

Judge Rodney Smith subsequently ordered Witherspoon released on time served and removed the three-year supervised-release component of his original sentence.

The remaining counts against him—Counts 2 through 6 and Count 8—were dismissed.

For Witherspoon, the sequence of events—from advice to cooperate, through interviews and testimony, to the government’s Rule 35(b) motion—ultimately culminated in his release.

“Yes, indeed, I cooperated with the government. And that’s why I took a plea. And today, the result of the plea is that Stanton is a free man,” he said.

He ended his account by thanking his lawyer and those who supported him during his legal battle.

World.title: Liberia: Ngafuan Highlights Gains in Health, Education and Energy, Admits More Work Remains
World.content:
Monrovia – In an appearance on the state-owned Liberia Broadcasting System, Liberia’s Minister of Finance and Development Planning, Augustine Kpehe Ngafuan, walked Liberians through progress in social delivery, especially in roads, education, health, and energy.

By Emmanuel Weedee-Conway

Minister Ngafuan told the audience how the government has been able to make life-touching progress over a little over two years, though he admitted that the government is still confronted with huge challenges amid competing priorities.

US$1.2 Billion Domestic Revenue On Course

He disclosed that, through the collaboration of the MFDP and the Liberia Revenue Authority, the country is nearing a US$1B revenue collection within days.
