World.title: Rubio doubles down on claims that cartels control large areas of Mexico, hinting at unilateral US action
World.content:
Listen to this article

U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Wednesday that Mexico isn’t doing enough to combat drug cartels and suggested that the United States could act unilaterally against such criminal organizations in Mexican territory.

In remarks to reporters outside the U.S. Embassy in Quito, Ecuador, Rubio also asserted that narco-terrorist organizations — i.e. drug cartels that the U.S. government has designated as foreign terrorist organizations — control large parts of Mexico.

SECRETARY RUBIO: There are territories, vast territories in Mexico, that are not governed by the state. They are controlled by these narco-terrorist organizations. pic.twitter.com/udRGZXv0xU — Department of State (@StateDept) September 9, 2026

The secretary of state, who traveled to Quito to speak with President Daniel Noboa about security cooperation between the United States and Ecuador, had been speaking about criminal threats in the Western Hemisphere when a reporter put it to him that if he was “talking about groups that are stronger than the state and fracturing the states, it sounds like a pretty similar situation to Mexico.”

“Mexico’s bad. It’s a bad situation,” Rubio responded.

The reporter then asked the secretary of state what the U.S. government’s plan was for combating organized crime in Mexico “given the fact that the Mexican government isn’t welcoming, or draws a pretty bright line about what it will accept in terms of U.S. military involvement.”

“How can you overcome that and have this kind of more tough approach that you’re describing?” she asked Rubio.

“The case of Mexico … [is] an even graver challenge because of the size of the country, because of the power of the cartels that are there,” he said.

“I don’t think it’s any mystery to anybody that there are territories, vast territories in Mexico, that are not governed by the state; they are controlled by these narco-terrorist organizations,” Rubio said.

He added that, “in fairness, the Mexicans have done more than they’ve ever done before to go after these groups.”

Indeed, the current Mexican government has captured or killed significant numbers of alleged cartel members and leaders, including Jalisco New Generation Cartel (CJNG) kingpin Rubén “El Mencho” Oseguera, sent scores of prisoners to the United States to face justice and seized more than 500 tonnes of drugs and over 34,000 firearms.

However, in Rubio’s view, what the Mexican government has done is “still not nearly enough.”

“They know that, we’ve expressed that to them,” he said.

“And we hope to work cooperatively with them to do more because … the head of the snake are these cartels in Mexico,” Rubio said.

“And they are a threat to the Mexican state, and the people of Mexico will tell you that. The number one issue in Mexico, poll after poll shows, is security. Political candidates are routinely assassinated in Mexico; judges — routinely assassinated; journalists who report on the cartels — routinely assassinated by these groups. So these groups pose an enormous threat right on our border. They have drones now. They’re using drones to try to traffic drugs and people across the border,” he said.

“These groups are very dangerous, they’re very well financed, they need to be confronted,” Rubio said, referring to criminal organizations such as the CJNG and the Sinaloa Cartel.

“Our hope and our intent is to do it in partnership with Mexico. That’s the ideal. But eventually, that threat will have to be confronted, one way or the other. But our hope is to do it cooperatively with Mexican authorities,” he said.

Rubio’s “one way or the other” remark alluded to the possibility of the United States taking unilateral action against cartels in Mexico. Asked about his comments at her Thursday morning press conference, President Claudia Sheinbaum characterized them as electorally motivated given that the U.S. midterms are coming up in November.

The secretary of state is by no means the first Trump administration official to suggest that the United States could act on its own against cartels in Mexico. U.S. Vice President J.D. Vance said in June that the United States “would take military action” in Mexico “if we feel like we have to to protect our people.”

Like Rubio, Vance said that the United States wants “to work with the Mexican government,” but he asserted that the U.S. has to “reserve the right” to take unilateral action against cartel threats.

For his part, U.S. Ambassador to Mexico Ronald Johnson told U.S. senators in March 2025, shortly before he took up his post, that on “any decision to take action against a cartel inside Mexico, our first desire would be that it be done in partnership with our Mexican partners.”

However, he added that, “should there be a case where the lives of U.S. citizens are at risk, I think all cards are on the table.”

In January, U.S. President Donald Trump said himself that the United States — whose military has targeted suspected drug boats at sea — was going to start “hitting” cartels on land. No confirmed U.S. attacks on Mexican criminal groups in Mexico have occurred since then, although CNN reported in May that the CIA facilitated a “targeted assassination” of an alleged Sinaloa Cartel member in México state in March.

Is Rubio’s cartel control claim true?

In asserting that cartels control “vast territories in Mexico,” Rubio echoed claims made by Trump and other current U.S. government officials, such as White House Deputy Chief of Staff Stephen Miller. In 2021, General Glen D. VanHerck, commander of the United States Northern Command at the time, asserted that criminal organizations operate in “ungoverned areas” of Mexico that account for 30% to 35% of national territory. President Andrés Manuel López Obrador promptly rejected his claim.

Sheinbaum has also rejected claims about cartel control in Mexico. However, there is, according to Ioan Grillo, a Mexico-based British journalist who specializes in organized crime, a “duopoly of power” in parts of the country.

A 2024 article published on Grillo’s site CrashOut is headlined “How Much of Mexico is Governed by Cartels?”

The subheading reads, “A: None 100%. But there is a duopoly of power in chunks of the country.”

“Cartels certainly exert an amount of control in chunks of Mexico. This can be seen in squads of gunmen operating openly, running checkpoints, ordering curfews, dictating what journalists can report, charging quotas on sales of avocados, moving votes for candidates, and controlling (or assassinating) mayors,” Grillo wrote.

“Yet unlike with the Islamic State caliphate, the Mexican government still operates in those turfs. It provides electricity, sends teachers and collects garbage. And the army can still go in (while the cartel gunmen hide) and then leave (and they come out again),” he wrote.

Later in his article, Grillo wrote that in his “subjective judgement,” about “a third of Mexican states have a severe cartel presence and high levels of violence; another third have a medium (but still important) level of cartel problems and bloodshed; and a last third have levels of violence compared with regular U.S. cities, and less serious problems from gangsters.”

Since that article was published in late January 2024 — around nine months before Sheinbaum took office — homicides and other high-impact crimes have declined, according to official statistics, suggesting that Mexico’s overall security situation has improved. Nevertheless, cartels continue to operate, fight turf wars and pose major challenges to authorities in various parts of the country.

World.title: Mexico gears up for Independence Day with a military parade, concerts and of course the Grito — all set for Sept. 15-16
World.content:
More than 18,000 members of Mexico’s armed forces are preparing to march, fly and roll out new equipment in Mexico City next week as the country marks the 216th anniversary of its independence.

On Wednesday, Defense Secretary Gen. Ricardo Trevilla Trejo reviewed the logistics for the capital’s Sept. 16 Independence Day parade.

In Mexico, Día de la Independencia commemorates the start of the rebellion against Spanish rule in 1810, although the nation’s War of Independence didn’t end until 1821.

The parade will include Army, Navy, Air Force and National Guard personnel, cadets, pilots, military engineers, medical workers, communications specialists, military police and special forces. It also will include horses, dogs and even eagles, according to El Heraldo de México.

Contingents will be designated “Justice and Peace,” “Sentinels of the Nation,” “Crucible of Patriots” and “Roots of Honor,” among other names, Trevilla Trejo said during his briefing on a military base in Naucalpan, México state.

The roughly 5-kilometer parade is scheduled to begin at 10 a.m. Sept. 16 with a flyover of nearly 100 Air Force and National Guard airplanes and helicopters above the Zócalo, Mexico City’s central plaza — including F-5 fighters performing a fleur-de-lis maneuver.

The ground procession will start near the Zócalo, pass the Palacio de Bellas Artes, continue along Juárez Avenue and Paseo de la Reforma, and end at the Campo Marte military complex near Chapultepec Park.

The capital’s celebrations begin the night before, when President Claudia Sheinbaum leads the traditional Grito de Independencia (“Shout” or “Cry” of Independence) from the National Palace balcony.

In conjunction, the Grammy-winning Texas-based band Intocable, whose Norteño-Tejano sound has landed them 21 No. 1 songs on Billboard’s Regional Mexican Airplay chart, will headline a free concert in the Zócalo.

Free concerts, food fairs and municipal Grito ceremonies are also planned across Mexico City’s 16 boroughs. The musical lineup includes norteño-banda group Calibre 50 (a record 27 No. 1 hits on Billboard’s regional Mexican chart) and Sinaloan balladeer Pancho Barraza (a headliner since the 1990s).

The observances will reach beyond the capital, as well, as the Grito tradition is replicated by governors and mayors nationwide.

In present-day Dolores Hidalgo, Guanajuato — then known simply as Dolores, where priest Miguel Hidalgo y Costilla called on residents to rise against Spanish rule in the early hours of Sept. 16, 1810 — Independence Day festivities are running nearly all month.

In nearby San Miguel de Allende, Sept. 16 observances include a reenactment of the start of the independence movement in 1810.

This year, the Sept. 16 national holiday falls on a Wednesday, meaning there will be no three-day weekend. Public schools and banks will close, as will many government offices and private workplaces, as it is a mandatory day of rest under federal labor law. Employees required to work are entitled to premium holiday pay. Sept. 15 remains a regular work and school day.

With reports from Milenio, Infobae, El Informador, El Heraldo de México, N+, El Sol de Bajío and ADN Noticias

World.title: María Fernanda Benítez Killer Receives Eight-Year Maximum Sentence in Paraguay
World.content:
PARAGUAY · JUSTICE

Key Facts — The verdict A Coronel Oviedo sentencing tribunal imposed eight years — the maximum under juvenile law — on the young man convicted of the femicide and abortion of María Fernanda Benítez, his 17-year-old ex-girlfriend.

— Why not more He was 17 at the time of the crime. Paraguay has since raised the maximum adolescent sentence from eight to ten years, in a reform born of this case — but it does not apply retroactively.

— The crime María Fernanda, four months pregnant, was killed on 27 May 2025; her burned body was found in a vacant lot four days later.

— Five more convicted A friend accused of instigating the killing received ten years; the teenager’s parents four and a half years each; a pharmacist five years; a fifth defendant three.

— The mother “It seems insufficient to me. My daughter is gone and he will walk free,” said Nilda Martínez.

— The legacy The case gave Paraguay the MAFE missing-persons alert system, named after her.

A Paraguayan court has sentenced the teenage killer of María Fernanda Benítez to eight years in prison — the most the law allowed. The verdict closes a case that horrified the country and changed its legislation, but not her family’s anger.

The Palacio de Justicia in Asunción, seat of Paraguay’s judiciary. The sentencing tribunal in the María Fernanda Benítez case sat in Coronel Oviedo, Caaguazú. (Photo: Felipe Méndez, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons)

María Fernanda Benítez was 17 years old and four months pregnant when she was killed in Coronel Oviedo, in Paraguay’s Caaguazú department, in May 2025. On Thursday night, the young man convicted of her femicide — her former boyfriend, himself 17 at the time — received the maximum sentence the country’s juvenile justice system allows: eight years.

The Sentence

The Tribunal de Sentencia of Coronel Oviedo, presided over by Judge Raúl Marecos with judges Vidal Santacruz Páez and Derlis Benítez, announced its decision at 10:15 p.m. on Thursday in a closed hearing, according to Última Hora’s correspondent in the city. The panel found the young man responsible for the femicide and abortion of María Fernanda after what it considered conclusive prosecution evidence.

Prosecutor Fermín Segovia had requested the maximum of eight years, arguing the evidence of authorship was overwhelming. The convicted man’s name is withheld because he was a minor at the time of the crime. Now 18, he has been held at the El Sembrador educational center for adolescents in Villarrica since May 2025; under the juvenile regime he will remain there until age 20, when he will be transferred to an adult penitentiary to serve the rest of the term.

The Crime That Shook Paraguay

María Fernanda — known to the country as “Mafe” — left her home on the afternoon of 27 May 2025 and never returned. According to the investigation, supported by the geolocation of the suspect’s phone, she was killed that same day during the siesta hours. Her body was found four days later, on 31 May, burned in a vacant lot in Coronel Oviedo. Forensic doctor Pablo Lemir established that she died from a strong blow to the head.

The prosecution’s case was that her ex-boyfriend killed her after learning she was pregnant. The brutality of the crime — a pregnant teenager murdered and her body set alight — dominated Paraguayan news for months and drew an unusual public statement of condolence from UNICEF, in a country that otherwise registers some of the region’s lower violent-crime rates.

Five More Sentenced

The teenager was tried separately under the adolescent criminal responsibility regime. In the parallel trial of five adults, the court sentenced Mikhaela Chiara Rolón Melgarejo, a friend of the convicted youth whom prosecutors described as the instigator who psychologically pushed him to act, to ten years in prison — the heaviest sentence of the case.

The young man’s parents received four and a half years each, as prosecutors had requested, for exposing the investigation to danger, filing a false missing-person report for their own son, and obstructing justice. Franco Antonio Acosta Céspedes, the owner of the pharmacy that supplied information on abortion medication to the accused teenager, was given five years — one more than prosecutors sought — for complicity in attempted abortion and frustrating criminal prosecution; he serves the sentence under house arrest. A fifth defendant, Ricardo Andrés León Villamayor, was sentenced to three years.

“Insufficient”

For the victim’s family, the maximum was not enough. “It seems insufficient to me. My daughter is gone and he will walk free,” Nilda Martínez, María Fernanda’s mother, told Channel 13 after the verdict. Her husband had told the court during final arguments: “I lost everything because of them. I want these monsters to go to prison.”

The legal saga may not be over. Prosecutor Noelia Montania confirmed that a separate case against the same young man, opened last year, remains active and could lead to another trial — he is also accused of instigating the abortion of another girl.

The Case That Changed the Law

Few crimes have left such a legislative mark. Outrage over the killing produced the MAFE Alert — a missing-persons alarm system named after María Fernanda — together with a National Registry of Missing Persons, fast-tracked through Congress from June 2025. This July, President Santiago Peña and Interior Minister Enrique Riera launched an alliance with Meta under the MAFE law to locate missing children and adolescents through notifications on social networks.

The case also moved Congress to raise the maximum prison term for adolescents convicted of extremely grave crimes from eight to ten years. The Chamber of Deputies sanctioned the reform in June and Peña promulgated it in July — weeks too late to apply to the man it was written for.

And it produced a corruption scandal inside the prosecution itself: Gloria Rojas, one of the prosecutors originally investigating the killing, was suspended by the Supreme Court and charged after an alleged agreement to accept 30 million guaraníes (about US$4,300) in exchange for a procedural exit for one of the defendants — a bribe documented in a watched delivery coordinated by anticorruption prosecutor Marlene González.

On Thursday night, after the verdict, the family said only that they will keep fighting. “Until the end of the world,” her father had promised during the trial, “I will go to know what they did to my daughter.”

World.title: Peru Bill Would End Sentence Reductions for Femicide, Kidnapping and Aggravated Robbery
World.content:
PERU · JUSTICE

Key Facts — The bill Deputy Norma Yarrow of Renovación Popular presented Bill 00033-2026-2031-CD on 13 August, targeting sentence reductions for three violent crimes.

— The mechanism A new clause in Article 51 of the Penal Execution Code would block “redemption of sentence through work or education” for aggravated convictions of femicide, kidnapping and aggravated robbery.

— The current math Inmates convicted of aggravated robbery can cut one day of prison for every five days of work or study; for grave crimes such as femicide the ratio is one day for seven.

— The scope The ban would apply only where a firm conviction establishes aggravated circumstances; extortion is already excluded from the benefit under a separate law.

— The status The proposal awaits committee assignment in the new Chamber of Deputies; no debate date has been set.

A Peruvian deputy wants people convicted of femicide, kidnapping and aggravated robbery to serve every day of their sentences — closing a benefit that lets inmates trade work and study for early release.

The Palacio Legislativo in Lima, seat of Peru’s Congress. A bill before the new Chamber of Deputies would end sentence-reduction benefits for three violent crimes. (Photo: Herwarth Morales, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons)

Peru femicide convicts would lose the right to work or study their way to an earlier release under a bill presented in the Chamber of Deputies by Norma Yarrow Lumbreras, a deputy of the conservative Renovación Popular party.

The initiative, registered on 13 August as Bill 00033-2026-2031-CD — registry entry 3710-CD — is formally titled “Legislative Proposal that Strengthens Restrictions on Prison Benefits for High-Harm Crimes.” It takes aim at one of the oldest features of Peru’s prison system: the redención de la pena, the redemption of sentence time through work or education.

What the Bill Would Change

The text adds a new clause, numeral 51.5, to Article 51 of the consolidated Penal Execution Code, the body of rules that governs how sentences are served. The clause declares sentence redemption through work or education inadmissible for those convicted of three crimes defined in the Penal Code: femicide (Article 108-B), kidnapping (Article 152) and aggravated robbery (Article 189).

The restriction is deliberately narrow. It applies only when a firm conviction establishes that the crime was committed in one of its aggravated modalities — not for every conviction under those articles. Where it does apply, the bill switches off the standard redemption rules of numerals 51.2 and 51.3 entirely. A final provision orders immediate application to current inmates under Constitutional Court doctrine on prison-benefit rules.

Two things the bill does not do: it does not ban work or study inside prison — only their conversion into reduced time — and it does not touch extortion, for which redemption is already absolutely inadmissible under Law 30077.

The Arithmetic of Redemption

Under the current regime, the trade-off is concrete. For aggravated robbery, special laws in force since 2013 and 2014 let a first-time inmate redeem one day of sentence for every five days of work or study. For grave crimes, including femicide, the ratio stands at one day for seven, under rates last adjusted by Legislative Decree 1737, issued in February 2026 under powers Congress delegated through Law 32527. A 2023 decree, Legislative Decree 1576, had set the earlier framework.

In practice, the math can cut years off long sentences. An inmate serving fifteen years for an aggravated femicide conviction who works or studies continuously can see the effective term shrink by roughly two years under the one-for-seven ratio — a gap between the sentence announced in court and the time actually served that victims’ groups have long denounced.

Why Now

The bill’s justification leans on Peru’s deteriorating security climate. It cites the national statistics institute INEI’s 2025 victimization figures, which showed crime touching more households, and the wave of extortion and kidnapping that has hit bus drivers and small merchants in Lima and the provinces — the same security crisis that brought down President Dina Boluarte in October 2025 and has defined Peruvian politics since.

“Femicide, kidnapping and aggravated robbery are crimes that destroy families and must be paid with the full sentence,” Yarrow wrote on X this week, presenting the initiative. “Whoever is convicted of these crimes must serve their sentence without prison benefits for work or education.”

The proposal lands as the Fujimori government makes security the center of its agenda. President Keiko Fujimori’s programme, presented to Congress in August, put the fight against organized crime first, and this week Peru joined the United States-led Escudo de las Américas security alliance during Secretary of State Marco Rubio’s visit to Lima. A benefits crackdown for violent convicts fits squarely in that current — and gives Renovación Popular, the conservative party founded by Rafael López Aliaga, its own banner on the issue.

What Happens Next

The bill now enters the machinery of Peru’s new bicameral Congress, restored for the 2026-2031 term after more than three decades of unicameral rule. As a Chamber of Deputies initiative, it must first be assigned to a committee — justice would be the natural destination — survive debate there, and then win approval in the chamber’s plenary before passing to the Senate. No committee assignment or debate date had been confirmed as of Thursday.

That path is long, and most bills in Peru never complete it. But the politics of this one are favorable: with extortion dominating headlines and every party competing to look toughest on crime, a proposal to make convicted femicides serve full sentences will be difficult for any bench to vote against — and difficult to ignore.

World.title: Trinidad and Tobago Frees 31 Emergency Detainees as Wage Deadline Looms
World.content:
TRINIDAD AND TOBAGO · SECURITY

Key Facts — The releases Thirty-one people held under preventive detention orders during the state of emergency were freed on Thursday from three prison facilities, security officials confirmed.

— Still inside Authorities have given no official total of how many SoE detainees remain behind bars, and releases at the Santa Rosa facility appeared slowest.

— The emergency The SoE, in force since 3 March and twice extended, expires on 17 September; a further extension would need a special majority the government does not control in the Senate.

— The wage clock The government has given the Public Services Association a final two weeks — until about 24 September — to accept its offer in an eight-year pay dispute worth an estimated TT$3.8 billion (about US$564 million).

— The gap The state offers 40 percent cash and 60 percent non-cash benefits; the PSA wants 60 percent cash, with the rest as deferred cash.

With six days left on the state of emergency, Trinidad and Tobago began emptying its detention wings on Thursday — while across Port-of-Spain, the same government handed its largest public-sector union a take-it-or-leave-it wage deadline. The twin moves sketch the outlines of an administration closing one emergency chapter and bracing for a labor fight.

Thirty-one people detained under preventive detention orders (PDOs) during Trinidad and Tobago’s state of emergency were released from three prison facilities on Thursday, security officials told CNC3 News, in the largest single-day release since the emergency powers were proclaimed in March.

Twenty-nine detainees walked out of Golden Grove Prison in Arouca, with one person each released from the Youth Training Centre and the Women’s Prison, also in Arouca. The releases began on Thursday morning and continued through the afternoon.

Families Camped at Santa Rosa

Word travels fast. From as early as 9 a.m., scores of relatives of PDO detainees gathered in vehicles along the access road to the Eastern Correctional and Rehabilitation Centre (ECRC) in Santa Rosa, hoping their family members would be among those freed, CNC3 reported. Heavily armed prison and police officers guarded barricades near the facility.

A senior police officer at the scene declined to confirm whether releases were under way at the ECRC, citing security concerns. A source told CNC3 that releases had begun at the Women’s Prison and the Youth Training Centre, while only a handful of detainees had left the ECRC by Thursday afternoon. As of Friday morning, there was still no official word on how many — if any — had been freed there.

No authority has published a figure for how many SoE detainees remain in custody. The preventive detention orders allowed police to hold people without charge on security grounds — the emergency’s most contested instrument — and each release is a reminder of how many were never charged at all.

The Emergency Behind the Releases

The state of emergency has been in force since 3 March 2026 and has twice been extended by Parliament, most recently on 10 June. It expires on 17 September, and pushing it further would carry the emergency past the six-month cumulative constitutional limit — requiring a three-fifths special majority in both Houses, a threshold the government cannot reach in the Senate without opposition or independent support, as The Rio Times reported. The National Security Council’s decision on the emergency’s fate was expected this week.

The government defends the emergency with results: official figures show murders fell from 626 in 2024 to 369 in 2025, the lowest annual toll since 2014. The opposition PNM, through senator Faris Al-Rawi, has warned it will challenge any attempt to extend the powers “by trick.” Thursday’s releases suggest the machinery is, quietly, already winding down whatever the council decides.

The Other Deadline: Wages

The day’s second story has nothing to do with gangs and everything to do with the state’s coffers. After a roughly hour-long meeting between Chief Personnel Officer Commander Dr Daryl Dindial and PSA president Felisha Thomas in Port-of-Spain, the government gave the Public Services Association a final two-week extension to accept its offer to settle wage negotiations for 2014–2016 and 2017–2019 — talks that have run for eight years, across two administrations, three PSA presidents and three chief personnel officers.

The offer itself will not move, Dindial said: 40 percent of the settlement in cash, 60 percent in non-cash benefits, with one concession — the arrears can be paid monthly over three years. The package is valued at an estimated TT$3.8 billion (about US$564 million). The PSA’s counter-proposal asks for 60 percent cash with the remainder as deferred cash. Dindial called the government’s position “a responsible and sustainable approach” that preserves public-service jobs; the non-cash items, he argued, carry real value and often require the state to forgo revenue.

Thomas acknowledged “slight movement” but declined to elaborate before consulting the PSA executive next week — a consultation that now doubles as a countdown. Former PSA president Clyde Weatherhead has warned that failure to agree could push the dispute beyond bargaining to a special tribunal.

For the government, the arithmetic of September is converging: an emergency that lapses on the 17th, a wage clock that runs out around the 24th, and a public watching both. Thursday’s prison gates opening was the visible part. The harder decisions are still on the table.

World.title: Bolivia Pushes Three-Month Extension of State of Exception as Reform Referendum Slips a Year Away
World.content:
BOLIVIA · POLITICS

Key Facts — The vote The Plural Justice Commission of Bolivia’s Chamber of Deputies unanimously approved a resolution on Thursday to extend the state of exception by three months.

— The next step The full Plurinational Legislative Assembly must still decide. The resolution asks Vice President Edmand Lara to convene it — and he is no ally of the government.

— The argument Backers cite a “latent risk against democracy”, claiming groups plan fresh unrest after 18 September; the opposition Libre bloc calls the move unconstitutional in spirit.

— The slow track Senate President Diego Ávila estimates the referendum on a partial constitutional reform is about a year away — a single, all-or-nothing vote.

— The stakes The reform menu includes the justice system, the autonomy model and the economic rules for hydrocarbons and mining — the framework every investor in Bolivia watches.

Bolivia’s emergency rule is about to outlive its 90 days — while the constitutional referendum meant to redraw the country’s rulebook recedes to the horizon of late 2027.

A session at Bolivia’s Plurinational Legislative Assembly in La Paz, July 2026. The full Assembly must still vote on extending the state of exception. (Photo: MagnoBlanco, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons)

The Bolivia state of exception declared in June is heading for renewal. The Plural Justice Commission of the Chamber of Deputies on Thursday unanimously approved a cameral resolution to extend it by three more months, deputy Manolo Rojas told Urgente.bo. The measure — identified in Bolivian reporting as Cameral Resolution No. 19/2025-2026 — is framed as a prior, exceptional and conditioned authorization for an eventual extension of up to 90 days.

“The thirty-sixth ordinary session approved it unanimously by those present — that was massive support,” Rojas said. The commission’s case rests on written reports sent to the Defense and Interior ministries asserting a risk to democratic stability. Rojas was explicit about the date driving the urgency: “There is a latent risk against democracy. There is a group waiting for 18 September to convulse the country again, and we will not allow it.”

A Commission Vote, Not Yet Law

The resolution is a first step, not a done deal. It instructs the Chamber’s president, Roberto Castro, to formally request that Vice President Edmand Lara convene the full Plurinational Legislative Assembly to debate the extension. That is a political problem in itself: Lara has broken with President Rodrigo Paz and commands his own faction in the legislature.

Rojas argued the mechanics are simple: no new bill is required, because that would amount to declaring a new state of exception; instead, the cameral resolution would modify the emergency law already in force. Government-aligned deputy Claudia Bilbao confirmed the sequencing and the expectation of friction. “It was already approved in commission yesterday, and let’s hope Edmand Lara puts no obstacles,” she told Urgente.bo, adding that the extension would give Bolivians “legal security to keep working” and help stabilize the economy. “We cannot have a state that is blocked.”

The opposition rejects the premise. “In Libre we do not agree with extending the state of exception. It is useless to us,” said Senator Elena Pachacute. “It worries me that the commission let political criteria prevail over constitutional ones.”

An Emergency Without a Visible End

The current state of exception dates from the early hours of 20 June, when President Paz decreed 90 days of emergency rule as the army moved to clear the road blockades that had strangled La Paz — a decree the Assembly later ratified, as The Rio Times reported when the emergency was declared. Those 90 days expire around the third week of September — precisely the cliff Rojas invoked.

The legal ground has also shifted since then. On 24 May the Senate, in a session led by its president Diego Ávila, voted to repeal Law 1341, the 2020 statute that regulated states of exception with time limits and procedural controls; Paz promulgated the repeal as Law 1732 days later, as The Rio Times reported at the time. Critics warned then that emergency rule had been stripped of its guardrails; a three-month extension will revive that debate, now inside a full Assembly where the government lacks a stable majority.

The extension bid lands on an agenda already crowded with the government’s financial lifelines — the IMF credit that floor managers say will be approved by October at the earliest, as The Rio Times reported this week in its Bolivia IMF calendar piece.

The Referendum That Slips Away

While the emergency track accelerates, the constitutional track slows. Senate President Ávila told Erbol on Thursday that he expects the referendum on a partial constitutional reform to materialize “in about a year” — meaning late 2027 at the earliest.

Ávila is backing the roadmap floated by deputy Carlos Alarcón, which he says is the fastest available: integrate the existing reform proposals, build consensus article by article, then pass a “law of necessity of constitutional reform” — which requires a two-thirds majority in parliament — before any question reaches the ballot. “In one year we could have the consultation and the referendum done, to see which articles of the Constitution would change,” Ávila said.

The topics on the table are the heaviest in Bolivian politics: justice reform, the autonomy model that distributes power between La Paz and the regions, and parts of the economic model, including the rules for hydrocarbons and mining. Because the constitution allows only one partial-reform referendum per five-year presidential term, Ávila stressed, everything must be bundled into a single vote — one reason the calendar stretches.

The reform debate has so far been driven more by Paz’s rivals than by the president himself, as The Rio Times documented in August: Alarcón first made headlines with an “extraordinary recall referendum” gambit against Paz, while businessman Samuel Doria Medina circulates an 11-point rewrite that would scrap presidential re-election and the popular election of judges. The Rio Times covered that landscape in “Bolivia Constitutional Reform: Everyone Wants It, Except President Paz”.

What It Means for Foreigners in Bolivia

For expats and investors, the two tracks frame the year ahead. A renewed state of exception would keep extraordinary powers in force through the end of 2026 — a tool the government says prevents blockades, and opponents call a blank check. The referendum calendar, meanwhile, means the rules governing courts, regional autonomy and the energy economy stay unsettled until at least late 2027. Between the IMF vote due by October and a constitution that will not be touched for a year, Bolivia’s stability now rests on an Assembly that has not yet been convened.

World.title: Amazon Cargo Plane Was Too Fast Before Deadly Miami Crash, NTSB Data Shows
World.content:
CARIBBEAN · AVIATION

Key Facts — The warning Cockpit recordings show a pilot warned of “excessive speed” one minute and 42 seconds before Amazon Air Flight 7598 crashed in Miami, and called for a go-around seconds before impact.

— The flight The Boeing 767-300 freighter, operated by 21 Air for Amazon, was arriving from San Juan, Puerto Rico, on Sunday 6 September when it overran runway 30 at 1:53 p.m.

— The victims Five people were killed, all of them workers in a cleaning-crew van the jet struck after leaving the runway. Five more were injured; both pilots survived.

— The data Flight recorders show the throttles were advanced to go-around thrust and the brakes reapplied, but the speed brakes and thrust reversers were never deployed.

— What next The NTSB interviewed both pilots this week and expects to publish a preliminary report within weeks.

One minute and 42 seconds before an Amazon cargo jet from Puerto Rico crashed at Miami International Airport, one of its pilots began warning that they were going too fast. He never stopped. Newly released recorder data now frames the central question of the investigation: why a crew that saw the problem coming could not stop the outcome.

A pilot aboard Amazon Air Flight 7598 repeatedly warned of the aircraft’s “excessive speed” in the final minutes before the Boeing 767 freighter overran a runway at Miami International Airport on Sunday 6 September 2026, killing five people on the ground, according to a cockpit voice recorder summary released by the US National Transportation Safety Board.

The NTSB readout, released on Wednesday 9 September, reconstructs the last moments of the flight from San Juan. About 30 seconds before the crash, sounds consistent with the jet touching down on runway 30 are heard. Roughly 15 seconds later, one pilot called for a “go-around” — an aborted landing. Five seconds after that call, the aircraft had already veered off the runway.

What the Recorders Show

The cockpit voice recorder captured more than two hours of audio. One minute and 42 seconds before the crash, one pilot warned the other that the aircraft was going too fast, and he “continued to make comments about the plane’s excessive speed throughout the remainder of the recording,” the NTSB summary says. Flight data cited in the investigation put the landing speed at 158 knots — about 292 kilometers per hour.

The flight data recorder tells the mechanical side of the story. Seconds before the recording ends, the throttles were advanced to a setting consistent with go-around thrust, NTSB investigator Chihoon Shin told reporters. The brakes were then reapplied and stayed applied until the end of the data. But there was no indication that the speed brakes or the thrust reversers — the two systems that slow a jet most effectively on the ground — were ever deployed.

Tracking service Flightradar24 recorded the aircraft still moving at roughly 128 miles per hour when it left the usable runway surface.

Five Workers Killed on the Ground

After leaving the runway, the freighter struck a 2012 Ford Econoline van inside the airport perimeter, then a small Toyota SUV on a road just outside the fence. The van belonged to Professional Ocean Service Corp., a contractor that cleans aircraft, and was carrying a seven-person cleaning crew. All five people killed were in that van, the Miami-Dade County Sheriff’s Office said; the victims, identified by name this week, were men aged 47 to 75.

Five more people were injured. As of Tuesday, three remained hospitalized — two in critical condition and one stable — Sheriff Rosie Cordero-Stutz said. The aircraft’s two pilots were treated and released, and both sat for interviews with NTSB investigators on Wednesday.

Both crew members survived a crash that NTSB Chairwoman Jennifer Homendy described after walking the site as “utter devastation.” A 32-person NTSB team has spent the week documenting tire marks, debris and the aircraft’s engines. The cargo was about 32,000 lb (14.5 tonnes) of freight, mostly contact lenses; nothing hazardous was aboard.

A Routine Caribbean Rotation

Flight 7598 was on the last leg of an ordinary working day: Cincinnati to Miami, Miami to San Juan, and back. The aircraft was a 32-year-old Boeing 767-300 built in 1994 and converted from passenger service to freight. It was flown by 21 Air, a Miami-based charter carrier operating the jet for Amazon’s air network — part of an outsourced cargo model in which Amazon owns the freight but contracts the flying.

That model, built around contractors such as 21 Air and Atlas Air, is now likely to face renewed scrutiny. 21 Air said it was “devastated by the accident” and offered condolences to the families. Amazon said its priority was the safety and care of everyone affected and that it was working closely with investigators. The FAA and the NTSB will examine weather, aircraft performance, crew actions and air-traffic communications; a preliminary report is expected within weeks.

The crash shut down Miami International for roughly three hours on one of the year’s busiest travel weekends; two of the airport’s four runways remained closed into the week, rippling delays across the US air system — as The Rio Times reported on Sunday. For the San Juan–Miami corridor — one of the Caribbean’s busiest freight routes — the question investigators now carry is a narrow and haunting one: a crew recognized the speed, called the go-around, and ran out of runway anyway.

World.title: OAS Chief Pushes Nicaragua Foreign Ministers Meeting: ‘Condemnation Is Not Enough’
World.content:
Nicaragua · Diplomacy

Key Facts —The push. OAS Secretary General Albert Ramdin said Thursday, September 10, that a Meeting of Consultation of the region’s foreign ministers on Nicaragua should happen “as soon as possible” — shortly after the UN General Assembly in late September. —The demand. Ramdin said the meeting must not end in a simple condemnation but produce measures — among them financial sanctions and travel bans against specific individuals. —The mechanism. The OAS Permanent Council voted 29-1 on August 19 to convoke the foreign ministers, with Brazil against and Mexico abstaining, invoking Articles 61–63 of the OAS Charter. The United States would host the session. —The trigger. Nicaragua’s National Assembly passed a constitutional reform on September 1 that bars the opposition from elections, extends the co-presidents’ term to seven years and eliminates the November 2026 vote. —The catch. Nicaragua formally left the OAS in 2023 — the organization is now deliberating measures against a non-member, and the reform’s second ratification vote is not due until January 18, 2027.

OAS Secretary General Albert Ramdin pressed on September 10 for a long-delayed foreign ministers’ meeting on Nicaragua to happen “as soon as possible” — and made clear it should deliver sanctions and travel bans, not just another condemnation of Daniel Ortega’s constitutional ban on the opposition.

“A Simple Condemnation Is Not Enough”

Speaking to international news agencies, including EFE, on Thursday, Ramdin said he expects the Meeting of Consultation of Ministers of Foreign Affairs to convene “as soon as possible, shortly after the United Nations General Assembly” at the end of September. Talks are continuing between the United States, the meeting’s host, and the other member states to fix “an acceptable date for all” that allows an optimal number of foreign ministers to attend.

“What is happening in Nicaragua is absolutely unacceptable,” Ramdin said. “But a simple condemnation is not enough. If we meet, it has to be to take measures.” Among the options he named: financial sanctions and travel bans against specific individuals in the Ortega-Murillo apparatus. The same day, the organization appealed more broadly for member states to work together to punish Nicaragua for banning opposition parties from its elections, AFP reported.

The statement is the sharpest signal yet from the OAS chief that the foreign ministers’ session — a mechanism the body rarely uses — is meant as an escalation step toward coordinated punitive action, not a talking shop.

The Rare Tool the OAS Reached For

The Permanent Council convoked the meeting on August 19 with the resolution “Convocation of a Meeting of Consultation of Ministers of Foreign Affairs to Consider the Situation in Nicaragua,” approved 29-1. Brazil cast the only vote against, Mexico abstained, and Haiti and Venezuela were absent. The resolution declares the developments in Nicaragua “a problem of an urgent nature and of common interest to the American States” and invokes Articles 61, 62 and 63 of the OAS Charter — provisions reserved for emergencies demanding a collective response.

Argentina, Panama, Paraguay, Uruguay and the United States advanced the measure after presenting it at a special session of the Permanent Council on August 5. Washington initially pushed for the foreign ministers to meet before September 1 — the date on which Managua was expected to codify its reforms — but delegations failed to agree on a date amid disagreements over what measures to take.

The meeting’s awkward premise is no secret: Nicaragua announced its withdrawal from the OAS in 2021 and completed its exit in November 2023, after years of resolutions criticizing Ortega’s re-elections and repression. The organization is now preparing collective measures against a government that no longer sits at its table.

What Managua Actually Passed

On the evening of September 1, the National Assembly — in a session held in León, at the foot of the colonial cathedral where the poet Rubén Darío is buried — gave the constitutional reform its first approval. The text bans from public office, party candidacies and party leadership anyone the regime considers “linked to coup attempts, foreign financing, international sanctions or acts against sovereignty,” including those labeled “traitors to the homeland.”

The reform extends the terms of the co-presidents, other elected officials and the heads of the army and police from six to seven years, eliminating the election scheduled for November 2026 and pushing the next vote to 2028. It moves the presidential inauguration from January 10 to January 18, in homage to Darío, and grants the Supreme Electoral Council broader powers to cancel parties and sanction candidates. Because it is a constitutional amendment, Nicaraguan law requires a second ratification in a separate legislative session: co-president Rosario Murillo announced that vote will start January 18, 2027.

Opposition lawyer Juan Diego Barberena, in exile, notes the text does not formally abolish elections — but in practice produces that effect, since Nicaraguans would only choose among options the regime deems eligible. Eliseo Núñez, a former opposition deputy, reads the extension as a calculation to outlast the Trump administration and postpone any negotiation over electoral conditions until 2028.

The Road Here — and What Comes Next

Ortega set the escalation in motion on July 19, declaring there would be “no more elections” for the opposition “to try to seize the government.” A 2024 reform had already extended the presidential term from five to six years, elevated Murillo from vice president to co-president and postponed the elections originally due that year to late 2027. The country has been in crisis since April 2018, when security forces repressed mass protests, leaving more than 300 dead; in 2023 the regime put more than 200 political prisoners on a plane out of the country and stripped them of their citizenship.

Washington’s response is already on record: Secretary of State Marco Rubio urged partners to stop “business as usual” with the Nicaraguan government after the September 1 vote; Panama had already withdrawn its ambassador from Managua over Ortega’s July announcement. After the August 19 OAS vote, eleven Nicaraguan opposition and civil society organizations sent letters to Brazil and Mexico asking both governments for a more active stance — urging Brasília to back “coordinated diplomatic and peaceful actions” and Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum to use her country’s “prestige and leadership” for a peaceful democratic transition.

For expats and investors in Central America, the trajectory matters practically: if the foreign ministers’ meeting produces the financial sanctions and travel bans Ramdin outlined, Nicaragua’s isolation would deepen well beyond its OAS exit — with direct consequences for banking, remittances and cross-border business in a country whose regime has now written the exclusion of all competition into its constitution.

Frequently Asked Questions

What did the OAS announce about Nicaragua on September 10, 2026?

Secretary General Albert Ramdin said the Meeting of Consultation of foreign ministers on Nicaragua should take place “as soon as possible,” shortly after the UN General Assembly, and that it must produce measures such as financial sanctions and travel bans — not just a condemnation. The OAS also appealed for member states to coordinate action over Nicaragua’s opposition ban.

What does Nicaragua’s September 1 constitutional reform do?

It bans opposition figures labeled “traitors to the homeland” or linked to foreign financing from elections and public office, extends the co-presidents’ and security chiefs’ terms from six to seven years, eliminates the November 2026 election and postpones voting to 2028. A second ratification vote is scheduled to begin January 18, 2027.

How did the OAS vote on the Nicaragua foreign ministers meeting?

On August 19, the Permanent Council approved the convocation 29-1, with Brazil voting against and Mexico abstaining; Haiti and Venezuela were absent. The resolution invokes Articles 61–63 of the OAS Charter. Nicaragua itself left the organization in 2023.

World.title: UNITAS 2026 Opens in Peru: 24 Navies Launch the Americas’ Largest Multinational Drill
World.content:
PERU · SECURITY

Key Facts — The opening UNITAS 2026 (UNITAS LXVII), the 67th edition of the world’s longest-running multinational naval exercise, opened this week at the Callao Naval Base, hosted and directed by the Peruvian Navy.

— The scale More than 5,300 personnel from 24 countries of the Americas, Europe, Asia and Africa, with 26 surface ships, three submarines, 21 aircraft and at least six unmanned systems.

— The calendar The operational phase runs 10–24 September, with actions in Callao, Ancón, Salinas, Junín and Iquitos — from the Pacific coast to the Amazon.

— The hardware Spain’s AEGIS frigate Álvaro de Bazán, Argentina’s destroyer ARA Almirante Brown, the US littoral combat ship USS Minneapolis-Saint Paul and P-8A Poseidon patrol aircraft are among the foreign units.

— The backdrop Peru confirmed its entry into the US-promoted “Shield of the Americas” security initiative this week, as Washington courts South America’s Pacific navies.

The Pacific off Lima is crowded with warships this week: Peru has opened UNITAS 2026, bringing two dozen navies together for the largest multinational naval exercise in the Americas — and one of the biggest military gatherings hosted by any Latin American country this year.

USS John P. Murtha and the Peruvian Navy’s BAP Pisco maneuver together during UNITAS LXII, the last edition Peru hosted, in 2021. The Pisco-class amphibious ships are again central to this year’s exercise. (Photo: US Navy, public domain, via Wikimedia Commons)

UNITAS 2026 is underway. The Peruvian Navy opened the 67th edition of the multinational exercise at the Callao Naval Base this week, with state news agency Andina broadcasting the inauguration of drills that bring together more than 5,300 military personnel from 24 countries.

The operational phase runs from 10 to 24 September, concentrated on the Pacific hub of Callao but extending to Ancón and Salinas on the coast, Junín in the Andes and Iquitos in the Amazon — a geography that lets the exercise train maritime, riverine, amphibious and even lake operations alongside cyber-defense scenarios, according to the Peruvian Navy.

Two Dozen Navies, One Command Structure

Opening-day coverage counted 23 participating navies; the Peruvian Navy’s final planning conference in June registered delegations from 24 countries, which signed a memorandum of understanding formalizing the commitments. Either way, it is the broadest multilateral military footprint on the region’s calendar this year.

The combined force includes 26 surface ships, three submarines, 21 aircraft and more than six unmanned aerial, surface and subsurface systems, according to Escenario Mundial. Peru is fielding its Pisco-class amphibious assault ships — built at the state SIMA shipyards — while foreign contingents include Argentina’s guided-missile destroyer ARA Almirante Brown with its embarked Fennec helicopter, Spain’s AEGIS-equipped frigate Álvaro de Bazán (F-101), the US littoral combat ship USS Minneapolis-Saint Paul and US Navy P-8A Poseidon maritime patrol aircraft.

Chile sent the offshore patrol vessel Cabo Odger, a marine infantry platoon, cyber-operations specialists and staff officers for the exercise’s Maritime Operations Center, the Chilean Navy confirmed. Colombia contributes a frigate of the Almirante Padilla class and an HH-65 Dauphin helicopter, Ecuador the missile corvette BAE Manabí, according to the Peruvian Congress’s authorizations for foreign forces published in El Peruano. The Rio Times reported Chile’s participation when it was first confirmed in July.

Submarines First: SIFOREX Set the Stage

The opening was preceded by SIFOREX XIV (Silent Force Exercise), the anti-submarine warfare phase run from 6 to 9 September off Callao, according to Zona Militar, in which allied ships and aircraft hunted Peruvian diesel-electric submarines to standardize detection and interdiction tactics. Argentina’s Almirante Brown took part with its embarked Fennec helicopter — the first time Argentina has joined SIFOREX with a ship, Zona Militar reported.

That sequence matters: diesel submarines are the Pacific coast’s quietest threat, and Peru operates one of the region’s most experienced conventional submarine forces, making it the natural host for this kind of training.

Sixty-Seven Editions and Counting

UNITAS — Latin for “unity” — was conceived at the first Inter-American Naval Conference in 1959 and has run annually since 1960, making it the world’s oldest multinational naval exercise still active. Peru last hosted in 2021, when UNITAS LXII brought 29 vessels, four submarines and 20 aircraft to Lima, according to the US Fourth Fleet. The 2025 edition was hosted by the United States at Camp Lejeune, North Carolina.

For the Peruvian Navy, hosting is a statement of institutional weight: it acts as “organizing and conducting country”, in its own words, running the combined command structure from its tactical training center in Callao. Rear Admiral Alfredo Osorio Bromberg, commander of the Surface Force, closed the June planning conference by calling the agreement a milestone for regional maritime security.

The Diplomacy Underneath

The exercise lands in a week of conspicuous alignment between Lima and Washington. On Thursday Peru confirmed its incorporation into the “Shield of the Americas” (Escudo de las Américas), the US-promoted coalition for coordinating intelligence and counter-narcotics efforts — the same initiative Colombia joined days earlier, as Escenario Mundial reported.

None of this is framed officially as directed at any power, and the Peruvian Navy’s language stays with interoperability and cooperation. But the optics — two dozen flags, US patrol aircraft on Peruvian tarmacs, a Spanish AEGIS frigate in Callao — speak for themselves at a moment when Washington and Beijing are openly competing for influence over South America’s Pacific ports.

What It Means for Foreigners in Peru

For expats, ship-watchers and anyone doing business through Callao — Peru’s main port and the country’s key foreign-trade gateway — the practical impact is modest: port calls, a visible uniformed presence around the bay and restricted waters during live phases through 24 September. The strategic takeaway is larger: Peru is positioning itself as the Pacific anchor of US-aligned maritime cooperation in the region, and its navy as the one force in South America that can convene two dozen others under its own command.

World.title: Costa Rica Boy Dies Waiting for Ambulance Flight; President Gives Agencies Three Days
World.content:
COSTA RICA · POLITICS

Key Facts — The case A 7-year-old boy was shot in an armed attack on Wednesday night in Pueblo Nuevo de Limón; a man and a woman in the same vehicle were also injured.

— The flight A private air ambulance was to fly from Tobías Bolaños airport in Pavas to Limón to take him to the National Children’s Hospital in San José. He died around 5:15 a.m. Thursday; the aircraft left about 5:30 a.m.

— The accusation Paramedic Ricardo Hernández says the Civil Aviation official who had to authorize the flight did not answer calls. The children’s hospital says the permit took three hours.

— The order President Laura Fernández gave the CCSS, the Public Security Ministry and the Civil Aviation Technical Council (Cetac) three days to deliver a full report to Casa Presidencial.

— The rebuttal Public Works and Transport Minister Efraím Zeledón said Friday that early Civil Aviation reports call it “completely false” that calls were ignored or the flight unauthorized.

— The context Costa Rica’s night-time air-ambulance rules have been criticized for years as bureaucratic and outdated; a December 2025 analysis called them a band-aid on a failed system.

A 7-year-old boy shot in Limón died while an air ambulance waited for a green light. President Laura Fernández has given three state institutions three days to explain why — and one of her ministers is already pushing back.

The ambulance flight never reached the child. A 7-year-old boy, wounded in an armed attack on Wednesday night in Pueblo Nuevo de Limón, on Costa Rica’s Caribbean coast, died at the Hospital Tony Facio Castro in the early hours of Thursday, September 10 — minutes before the private ambulance flight that was supposed to carry him to San José finally took off. By Thursday evening, the case had reached the top of the state: President Laura Fernández ordered an investigation and gave three institutions 72 hours to report to Casa Presidencial.

What Happened in Limón

According to the Judicial Investigation Police (OIJ), cited by Diario Extra, two people on a motorcycle opened fire on a vehicle in Pueblo Nuevo de Limón on Wednesday night. Three people were hit: the boy, a man and a woman. The child was taken to the Hospital Tony Facio Castro, the regional referral hospital in Limón city.

Doctors judged that he needed the Hospital Nacional de Niños, the national children’s hospital in San José — a three-hour drive over the mountains, or a short flight. With the public Air Vigilance Service reporting no aircraft available, a private air-ambulance service was engaged: its aircraft was at Tobías Bolaños airport in Pavas, west of the capital, and the plan was to fly to Limón’s international airport, pick up the boy and return.

That is where accounts diverge — and where the presidential investigation now aims. Ricardo Hernández, a paramedic with the private service, denounced that the operation stalled because the official of the Civil Aviation Directorate (DGAC) responsible for authorizing the flight did not answer the calls of the team coordinating it. Speaking to Teletica on Friday, he put it in five words: “We failed a child.” The National Children’s Hospital’s director, Carlos Jiménez, said the transfer experienced a delay of approximately three hours. The boy died around 5:15 a.m.; the ambulance flight departed at about 5:30.

The President’s Three-Day Ultimatum

On Thursday night, La Nación reported, Fernández signed off on formal letters to the Civil Aviation Technical Council (Cetac), the Ministry of Public Security and the CCSS — the Caja Costarricense de Seguro Social, the state institution that runs the country’s hospitals. The institutions have three days to hand Casa Presidencial a complete account: what each of them did during the coordination, a chronology of every step, whether the applicable protocols were correctly applied, and what circumstances affected response times.

The presidential letter also demands an answer to the hardest question: the boy’s medical state during the wait, and whether he was fit to fly at all while the paperwork and phone calls went on. Fernández instructed the three institutions to open a preliminary investigation and, if the findings justify it, to start the administrative procedures that determine legal responsibilities.

The Government Is Not Speaking With One Voice

By Friday, the political defense had begun. Efraím Zeledón, the Minister of Public Works and Transport — the ministry that oversees Civil Aviation — said that the first internal reports from the aviation authorities show it is “completely false” that the calls were not answered or that the flight was not authorized. The flight was authorized, the ministry insists; the dispute is over how long the ambulance flight took to clear, and why.

That sets up a direct collision between the paramedic’s account and the ministry’s — with a presidential deadline hanging over both. The three-day window closes early next week, and Fernández’s letter makes clear the reports are not the end of the matter but the basis for possible disciplinary and legal action.

A Warning the System Heard Before

The case has detonated in Costa Rica because it confirms a criticism that aviation and health specialists have made for years. A widely cited analysis published by Delfino.cr in December 2025 described the country’s air-ambulance regulation as a band-aid on a failed system: no modern framework for instrument flights by medical operators, night operations restricted to visual flight rules, and airports that effectively close to medical flights after dark. Its most quoted line reads like a premonition: the air resource is there, but it cannot take off because the sun has set — and in a medical emergency, every minute of waiting decides who lives and who dies.

Whether the Limón ambulance flight failed because of those rules, despite them, or because of individual error is precisely what the Fernández-ordered reports must establish.

What It Means for Foreigners in Costa Rica

Fernández, in office since May 8 as Costa Rica’s 50th president and its second woman in the job, has staked much of her political capital on security and state competence — she has accepted expanded U.S. security cooperation and presides over a country where illicit trade now funds organized crime at record scale. Limón, the Caribbean province, carries the heaviest burden of that violence; Wednesday’s attack fits its pattern.

For the large foreign community — retirees, remote workers, tourism operators — the practical lesson is narrower but real: emergency medical evacuation in Costa Rica depends on a regulatory chain that this week failed publicly and fatally. The Fernández government now has three days to say whose chain link broke. Expats with medical-evacuation coverage should ask their providers one question this week: does the policy cover the aircraft, or also the hours the system makes it wait?

World.title: Costa Rica Nears 49,000 Short-Term Rentals as Tourist Numbers Lag
World.content:
Costa Rica now has nearly 49,000 active short-term rental listings, more than double the number in 2019, while international arrivals have yet to return to pre-pandemic levels, according to a new study by the Center for Tourism Studies (CET). The report, prepared by CET director Víctor Umaña and released Wednesday, counts 48,985 active listings across 243 markets on platforms including Airbnb, Vrbo and Booking.com.

The CET estimates those listings generated about $813.5 million in revenue in the 12 months ending in June 2026. The average nightly rate stood at $204, with average occupancy of 43.7% and annual revenue of $16,606 per listing, according to the study. Entire homes account for 83.3% of listings in the sample analyzed, and 66.4% are tied to hosts who manage more than one listing.

The CET describes the market as professionalized, noting that short-term rentals are no longer mainly occasional exchanges between private individuals. The typical property has 2.3 bedrooms and supply has grown far faster than demand. The CET estimates that short-term rental inventory rose from roughly 22,500 listings in 2019 to 48,985 by June 2026, while traditional lodging tracked by the Costa Rica Tourism Board (ICT) grew 13.3%, from 50,264 to 56,950 rooms between 2019 and 2025.

Over a similar period, international arrivals fell 6.2%, from 3.14 million in 2019 to 2.94 million in 2025. The study calculates that the number of international visitors per available lodging unit dropped from about 43 in 2019 to 28 in 2025-2026. The CET says demand is becoming the main constraint on the market. In the 213 markets with year-on-year data, inventory was essentially flat at minus 0.2%, while revenue per listing rose 8.7%, growth the study attributes more to pricing and occupancy than to new supply.

The destination data show wide gaps in earnings. Cabo Velas, which covers Flamingo and Conchal, leads with average annual revenue of $28,800 per listing, followed by Tamarindo at $28,640 and Nosara at $26,100. Nosara also posts the highest average nightly rate, at $384, and the highest occupancy, at 53%. Jacó, with 3,786 listings, has the lowest occupancy among the main destinations, at 40%.

The Greater Metropolitan Area (GMA) has the largest single inventory, with 4,025 listings and 50% occupancy. It also has the lowest earnings, with an average nightly rate of $61 and $7,200 in annual revenue per listing, reflecting smaller units and shorter stays.

Destination Active listings Avg. nightly rate Avg. occupancy Annual revenue per listing Greater Metropolitan Area 4,025 $61 50% $7,200 Jacó 3,786 $306 40% $23,371 Cahuita / Southern Caribbean 3,779 $126 46% $13,400 Tamarindo 3,598 $336 47% $28,640 Cóbano / Santa Teresa-Montezuma 2,860 $274 50% $21,300 Sardinal / Playas del Coco 2,537 $214 48% $16,500 Bahía Ballena / Uvita 2,184 $217 46% $17,500 Quepos / Manuel Antonio 1,902 $259 47% $25,806 Cabo Velas / Flamingo-Conchal 1,678 $346 48% $28,800 Nosara 1,537 $384 53% $26,100 La Fortuna 1,397 $151 44% $14,900

Source: Center for Tourism Studies (CET), based on AirDNA data for the 12 months ending June 2026.

Nationally, the CET calculates a density of 9.4 short-term rentals per 1,000 residents. That places Costa Rica slightly above Barcelona, at 9.0, and above every large city in the comparison, including Rio de Janeiro, New York and Mexico City, though well below Mallorca, Hawaii and Crete.

The study places Costa Rica in the most permissive of four regulatory categories, alongside Belize, Rio de Janeiro and Cape Town. Hosts must register under Law 9742, but there are no national limits on nights rented, no zoning restrictions and no tax specific to short-term rental lodging, according to the CET comparison.

On housing, the report says short-term rentals can push up land values and residential rents in tourist destinations with limited housing supply, adding pressure on workers employed in tourism. It also notes that many coastal villas and condominiums were built specifically for visitors, so restricting them would not necessarily return units to the long-term housing market.

The CET ends by saying that effective policy would need to distinguish between homes converted into short-term rentals and properties developed for tourism from the outset. The study describes its analysis as descriptive and cautions that its market figures are third-party estimates built from public platform data, with methodologies that differ.

World.title: Billfish: Another Step Forward in the Eastern Tropical Pacific
World.content:
Some important decisions arrive with headlines, prohibitions, and grand speeches. Others seem much more modest. Last week in Lisbon, we saw one of the latter.

I participated as an observer representing FECOP at the 104th Meeting of the Inter-American Tropical Tuna Commission (IATTC). Amid discussions about tuna, sharks, bycatch, and other species that cross borders without asking permission, Central America managed to open a specific path forward on something many of us have been saying for years about billfish in the Eastern Tropical Pacific, we need to understand them better. It sounds like a simple conclusion. It is not.

Sailfish, marlins, and swordfish are highly migratory species. In a matter of weeks, they can move through the waters of several countries. They interact with industrial, artisanal, coastal, recreational, and sport fisheries. Some of these species also support an important tourism economy that sustains captains, crews, marinas, hotels, restaurants, transportation services, and coastal communities. Trying to manage them using information from only one country or one fishery is like trying to understand a movie by watching only a few scenes. That has been precisely one of our problems.

Information on billfish in the Eastern Tropical Pacific exists, but much of it remains fragmented. There are still gaps in catch and effort data, biological information, monitoring and data verification, post-release mortality, and our understanding of how different fisheries interact with these species. The proposal presented in Lisbon itself recognized many of these limitations.

For years, pieces that were once scattered have gradually been coming together. At FECOP, working alongside scientific partners and the sportfishing sector itself, we have sought to turn fishing records into useful information to better understand billfish.

Collaborations with researchers from Stanford University, for example, demonstrated the value of recreational fishing records from Costa Rica, Guatemala, and Panama for studying the occurrence of sailfish and blue marlin and their relationship with changing ocean conditions. We have also used historical data generated by sportfishing operations to examine changes in the local abundance of sailfish along Costa Rica’s Pacific coast.

Regional initiatives have added another layer to these efforts. The Pacífico Sostenible project, working with OSPESCA, governments, and private-sector actors, developed a regional pilot focused on recreational fisheries for sailfish and marlin. That process reached a conclusion that is particularly relevant to what later happened in Lisbon, our region needs to strengthen the collection, analysis, and standardization of data generated by recreational fisheries, and we need to do it in a coordinated way across countries and sectors.

An important change has also been taking place within the private sector. Sportfishing organizations in Central America have increasingly understood that asking governments to recognize the economic contribution of our activity is not enough. If we want to participate seriously in conversations about fisherie management, we also have a responsibility to help generate the information needed to make better decisions.

That principle has been part of the work of CASA, the Central America Sportfishing Alliance. Its 2026 agenda placed science and conservation among its strategic priorities and called for progress on regional information about sailfish and the creation of scientific spaces dedicated to billfish. This matters because fisheries discussions have too often fallen into a comfortable trap, each sector arrives at the table with its own numbers, its own experiences and, of course, its own certainties.

Science should help us get out of that trap.

In June 2026, the IATTC Scientific Advisory Committee recommended developing a work plan for billfish data collection and stock assessments, including the costs, staffing needs, and potential sources of external funding required to carry it out. Two months later, Panama, supported by Belize, Costa Rica, El Salvador, Guatemala, Honduras, and Nicaragua, arrived in Lisbon with a proposal to establish a specialized scientific working group on billfish.

What was ultimately agreed was more gradual, in 2027, a specialized workshop will be held to identify the main information and research gaps, establish priorities, and develop a draft work plan that will later be considered by the IATTC Scientific Advisory Committee. Is that enough? No. Is it important? Absolutely.

For the first time, a clear institutional pathway is opening to turn a concern that different actors have raised for years into scientific questions, research priorities and, eventually, better management decisions. And this is where we also need to accept our share of the responsibility.

Sportfishing holds something extremely valuable for science, thousands of days at sea, encounters with fish, locations, dates, sizes, ocean conditions, fishing effort, and releases. Much of that information is still lost or remains scattered across logbooks, phones, applications, databases, and the memories of captains. Turning that accumulated experience into useful scientific data must be part of the next stage.

But the same must happen with every fishery that interacts with billfish. This is not about proving in advance who is right. It is about building the information that will allow us to find out. That is why I left Lisbon thinking that perhaps the most important progress made at this meeting was the recognition of something quite basic, before we argue over the answers, we first need to agree on the questions.

Sailfish and marlins have been crossing the Pacific for millions of years without recognizing our borders, institutions, or sectoral differences. Perhaps it is time we learned to do the same.



Damián Martínez Fernández

Director de conservación y política pública Federación Costarricense de Pesca FECOP

World.title: Costa Rica Braces for Higher Fuel Prices as Oil Climbs Back Above $100
World.content:
Global oil prices climbed back above $100 a barrel this week, and the increase is on course to reach Costa Rica’s gas stations within weeks. Brent crude, the international benchmark, settled at $101.21 yesterday after a 3.4 percent single-session gain. West Texas Intermediate settled at $96.05.

The trigger was a fresh escalation in the US-Iran conflict, now in its seventh month. US Central Command said American forces destroyed five Iranian crude tankers on Tuesday after attempted attacks on a US warship. A senior Iranian official, speaking to Bloomberg on condition of anonymity, said Tehran was ready for a more intense war rather than back down in the face of the US naval blockade.

The rally is not new territory for this conflict as Brent traded around $72 a barrel on February 27, the day before the war began, and peaked above $126 at the end of April. By early July it had slid back to pre-war levels, and this week’s climb leaves it roughly 40 percent above where it started.

It also runs ahead of official projections. In its outlook released yesterday, the US Energy Information Administration forecast that Brent would average around $90 a barrel in the second half of 2026, already $8 higher than a month earlier. The agency noted that attacks on Saudi shipments through the Bab el-Mandeb strait had cut exports from the Red Sea port of Yanbu by about half in August.

Costa Rica imports all of its fuel through the state refiner Recope, leaving it directly exposed. The Regulatory Authority for Public Services (Aresep) sets pump prices monthly from Recope’s actual purchase invoices. International swings therefore reach consumers roughly one to two months later.

That lag explains why the adjustment Aresep approved on Tuesday moved in two directions. Regular gasoline falls ₡51 to ₡707 per liter (about $5.95 a gallon), while super rises ₡22 to ₡726 (about $6.11 a gallon). Diesel jumps ₡82 to ₡688 (about $5.79 a gallon), and the new prices take effect once published in the official gazette La Gaceta.

None of that reflects this week’s spike. Aresep’s monthly review opens on the second Friday of each month, which puts the next one on Friday, September 11, with new prices expected in early October. Based on the timing of previous reviews, it would capture fuel bought as prices rose through August, when Brent averaged $91 according to the EIA.

If crude holds near current levels, the following adjustment, due at the pump in November, would carry a full month of triple-digit oil. That would affect gasoline, diesel and liquefied petroleum gas alike.

The last spike shows how sharp the pass-through can be. The adjustment approved at the end of April, based on shipments from March 13 to April 9, raised diesel from ₡564 to ₡716 per liter and regular gasoline from ₡625 to ₡748. Energy Intendant Mario Mora attributed that increase directly to the Middle East conflict.

A stronger colón offers limited protection this time. The currency has gained about 6 percent against the dollar since early March, a fraction of the rise in crude over the same period. Its larger appreciation since 2022 cushioned gradual fuel increases but cannot absorb a shock of this size.

The stakes extend beyond the pump as the National Institute of Statistics and Census (INEC) reported year-on-year deflation of 0.17 percent in August, the 16th consecutive negative reading. Consumer prices have now run below the Central Bank’s 2 to 4 percent target range for 40 straight months.

Fuel has been central to that trend since INEC listed gasoline and diesel among the items that pulled prices down most in August. A sustained oil shock would turn fuel from a drag on prices into a source of upward pressure.

Transport costs are already moving in some categories. International airfares were among the things whose prices rose most in August, according to INEC, and airlines typically pass jet fuel costs through to fares. Higher diesel prices also raise costs for freight, public buses and tourism transport.

How long prices stay elevated depends on events in the Middle East. US President Donald Trump said this week the conflict would not end before the November midterm elections and that significant relief at the gas pump was unlikely before then. Goldman Sachs has warned Brent could exceed $120 a barrel if Gulf output stays well below pre-war levels, though that is not its base case. A de-escalation could pull prices down as quickly as they fell after the April peak.

World.title: Santa Elena’s Keon Mossiah makes history as Belize’s First IMMAF Pan Am Champion
World.content:
Santa Elena’s Keon Mossiah makes history as Belize’s First IMMAF Pan Am Champion

By Zoila Palma: Belizean mixed martial artist Keon Mossiah who proudly hails from Santa Elena, Cayo has made history, becoming the first Belizean to win a gold medal at the International Mixed Martial Arts Federation (IMMAF) Pan American Championships.

Mossiah secured the historic victory in Monterrey, Mexico, earning Belize’s first-ever IMMAF Pan Ams gold medal and putting the Belizean flag on top of the podium.
