World.title: Polish far-right leader Braun vandalises Ukrainian monument with hammer
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Polish far-right leader Grzegorz Braun has published a video of himself using a hammer to attack a monument in Poland dedicated to soldiers from the Ukrainian Insurgent Army (UPA), a World War Two partisan formation that fought against the Soviet Union but was also responsible for massacring Poles. Braun declared that the monument, which was also recently vandalised by other unknown perpetrators, should be removed as it “insults the memory of victims of the Ukrainian genocide against Poles” and “glorifies Nazism”. The incident comes amid recent tensions between Warsaw and Kyiv over World War Two history, and in particular the fact that the UPA continues to be honoured in Ukraine. Pomnik UPA w gminie Dołhobyczów w powiecie hrubieszowskim do likwidacji❗️ Obelisk obrażający pamięć ofiar ukraińskiego Ludobójstwa na Polakach powinien zostać usunięty profesjonalnymi narzędziami natychmiast po udokumentowaniu przestępstwa banderyzmu!#StopBanderyzacjiPolski… pic.twitter.com/8Q4QZ2z5vJ — Grzegorz Braun (@GrzegorzBraun_) September 10, 2026 The monument in question is located in the village of Liski, a few kilometres from the border with Ukraine, and marks the burial site of 41 UPA soldiers killed while fighting against the NKVD, the Soviet secret police, in 1946, in the aftermath of World War Two. The area previously had a large ethnic-Ukrainian population. The memorial was vandalised last month, when it was sprayed with black paint and its arch was damaged. On Monday this week, further damage was discovered to the inscription on the monument. Police announced that they had launched an investigation into vandalism, property damage and ethnic hatred, but had not yet identified the perpetrators, reported the Polish Press Agency (PAP). On Wednesday evening, Braun published a video showing himself and another man using a hammer to repeatedly strike the front of the monument, causing visible damage to the stone, which contains the names of the killed UPA soldiers. They also appear to attempt to remove a separate plaque. During the video, Braun, who is a member of the European Parliament and finished fourth in last year’s Polish presidential election, claimed that local residents are “afraid they would be set on fire” if they attempted to remove the memorial themselves. It is not clear when the video was recorded. Shortly after Braun published it, local police in Hrubieszów county, where the monument is located, issued a statement saying that officers were investigating damage to the monument. Interior ministry spokeswoman Karolina Gałecka shared their statement and declared that “the perpetrators will not go unpunished”. Sprawcy zniszczenia pomnika w Białymstoku nie pozostaną bezkarni. Policjanci zabezpieczają dowody i przesłuchują świadków. https://t.co/7HCApuhPZ1 — Karolina Gałecka (@K_Galecka) September 10, 2026 Braun regularly carries out stunts intended to demonstrate his anti-Ukrainian, antisemitic and anti-LGBT views, and is already facing multiple legal cases over such incidents. He is currently on trial for attacking a celebration of the Jewish festival of Hanukkah in parliament using a fire extinguisher. Last month, he was charged with the crime of denying Nazi crimes for claiming that the gas chambers at Auschwitz are “fake”. He was also charged with theft over incidents in which he tore down Ukrainian and European Union flags, and with vandalism of an LGBT+ exhibition. If convicted, some of the crimes Braun is charged with carry potential years-long prison sentences. Nevertheless, Braun’s party, Confederation of the Polish Crown (KKP), continues to enjoy support of around 8-9%, according to polling averages. That could make it a key player in deciding who can form a government after next year’s parliamentary elections. Polish far-right leader Grzegorz Braun has been charged with denying Nazi crimes, a criminal offence in Poland that carries a prison sentence of up to three years, for statements he made suggesting that the gas chambers at Auschwitz are "fake" https://t.co/PCssZt5eXD — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 25, 2026 At the time of writing, there had been no response from Ukrainian authorities to Braun’s latest stunt. However, when the same monument was vandalised last month, the Ukrainian embassy in Warsaw issued a statement expressing its “deep indignation”. “Regardless of the difficult and tragic chapters of our shared history, burial and memorial sites should remain outside the realm of political disputes and be treated with respect,” they wrote. The embassy also expressed “particular concern that this incident occurs against the backdrop of a rising number of hostile acts toward Ukrainians in Poland, including reports of aggression and attacks on Ukrainian citizens” “Any attempts to shift historical disputes into the realm of vandalism, intimidation or hostility toward modern Ukraine and Ukrainians are dangerous and must be met with an appropriate legal response,” they added. Poland and Ukraine have been embroiled in a diplomatic dispute since May, when President Volodymyr Zelensky named a military unit after the “heroes of the UPA”. His Polish counterpart, Karol Nawrocki, responded by stripping Zelensky of Poland’s highest honour. Tensions have since cooled, and Ukraine has made moves to defuse the crisis. However, significant differences remain, in particular over memory of the so-called Volhynia massacres, in which the UPA led the killing of around 100,000 Polish civilians. Poland regards the episode as a genocide. Ukraine strongly rejects that label, and also continues to honour the UPA for its role in fighting against Moscow-imposed Soviet rule. Recent months have also seen a rise in anti-Ukrainian sentiment in Poland, including a series of cases of verbal or physical attacks against Ukrainians, who are by far Poland’s largest immigrant group. Reported anti-Ukrainian hate crimes were up 30% in the first half of this year. Demonstrations took place in 25 Polish cities on Sunday against the “growing wave of hate and violence” against Ukrainians, who are Poland’s largest immigrant group. Reported hate crimes against Ukrainians in Poland are up 30% this year https://t.co/gGAEc6QZWT — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 10, 2026 In 2017, Ukraine responded to the dismantling of a UPA monument in Poland by introducing a ban on exhumations of Polish victims of the Volhynia massacres on its territory. It is believed that tens of thousands still remain buried in unmarked mass graves. However, last year, in a diplomatic breakthrough, Kyiv allowed such exhumations to resume, and since then the remains of dozens of victims have been found, researched and reburied. Earlier this month, Poland also granted Ukraine permission to conduct a search for the remains of Ukrainian civilians killed by Polish resistance fighters during World War Two. Following a crash between a train and a truck at a rail crossing that left one passenger dead and both drivers with serious injuries, Poland’s main train drivers’ union has announced a go-slow protest that will take place on Friday. They note that they have long been warning about a lack of sufficient safety measures at rail crossings, and say that a “red line has now been crossed”. In the wake of Wednesday’s tragedy, Prime Minister Donald Tusk has pledged that the government will introduce “very tough” new punishments for those who violate regulations at crossings. Poczułam takie jakby silne hamowanie, takie bardzo silne i nagle takie bujanie i do człowieka dociera, że zaraz się wykoleimy – mówiła pasażerka pociągu Intercity "Koziołek", jadącego z Lublina do Szczecina, który wykoleił się w miejscowości Sokolniki Suche w Mazowieckiem.… pic.twitter.com/enyjD2Wo6K — tvn24 (@tvn24) September 9, 2026 On Wednesday morning, a train travelling between the cities of Lublin and Szczecin partially derailed in the village of Sokolniki Suche in central Poland after colliding with a heavy goods vehicle that, initial findings suggest, had entered the tracks at a rail crossing despite warning lights flashing. The crossing had no barriers. The train was carrying at least 114 people, including three crew. One passenger in the first carriage, a 39-year-old woman, died in hospital from her injuries, prosecutors announced later on Wednesday. Four others, including the drivers of both the train and the truck, remain hospitalised in serious condition. Prosecutors say that, from the evidence collected so far, they will launch an investigation into the crime of unintentionally causing a rail disaster, which carries a prison sentence of six months to eight years. However, they have not yet been able to interview either driver due to their health conditions. On Thursday, the head of the Polish train drivers’ union, Leszek Miętek, announced that a protest would begin at midnight and last through the whole of Friday. “We are appealing to train drivers to travel at a safe speed of 20 km/h (12.4 mph) across every level crossing in Poland,” he said, adding that he had “received reports from across the country” that “there’s full support for this type of action”. Miętek noted that the Polish labour code allows employees to refrain from work if they believe it poses a threat to their life or health. While drivers would not go that far, they want to demonstrate in a bid to prompt “action from those responsible for safety.” He warned that train delays should be expected on Friday. Związek Zawodowy Maszynistów Kolejowych mówi "dość" i ogłasza ogólnokrajowy protest po tragicznej katastrofie w Sokolnikach Suchych. W piątek, 11 września, pociągi w całej Polsce będą zwalniać na przejazdach kolejowych do zaledwie 20 km/h. Więcej o tym: https://t.co/jj6jKm40X2 pic.twitter.com/ThqfLx3dEc — TVN Warszawa (@tvnwarszawa) September 10, 2026 The union chief said that Wednesday’s accident “was not a surprise to us, considering that statistically we have an accident at a railway crossing every two days”. However, “a red line has [now] been crossed”, he added, quoted by news website Interia. Miętek noted that, for over 18 months, the union has been running a campaign, titled “I Want To Live”, focused on safety. Just two days before the accident, it had issued a special appeal to drivers over “growing safety concerns on Polish railways”. “We have been doing everything we can in parliament and at the infrastructure ministry to make sure this problem is noticed,” added Miętek, who also welcomed the fact that, following Wednesday’s accident, Tusk has pledged to take action. 💬 Premier @donaldtusk ⤵️ Katastrofa kolejowa w Sokolnikach miała miejsce na przejeździe kolejowym, dlatego natychmiast rozpoczniemy prace nad zaostrzeniem przepisów dla tych, którzy wjeżdżają na przejazdy kolejowe, mimo zapór i czerwonych światel. pic.twitter.com/BgaZQLEPbR — Kancelaria Premiera (@PremierRP) September 9, 2026 In those remarks, the prime minister lamented that the accident in Sokolniki Suche was “yet another case of such a catastrophe happening at a rail crossing”. “We must immediately begin urgent work on tightening regulations,” he continued. This would include “very tough” punishments “for those who, unfortunately, quite systematically drive onto railway crossings despite barriers and red lights”. Infrastructure minister Dariusz Klimczak later confirmed that they were working on “radical” measures to toughen penalties for those who violate the rules at rail crossings. He revealed that one proposal being considered is suspending for three months the licence of any driver who ignores red lights at rail crossings. However, critics noted that the ministry had already announced such plans in July 2025, and had failed to implement them since then. – Chcemy wprowadzić przepis, na podstawie którego każdy kierowca, który wjedzie na przejazd drogowo-kolejowy kiedy jest zapalone czerwone światło, straci prawo jazdy, zostanie mu ono zatrzymane na trzy miesiące. Chcemy także zmienić kodeks karny we współpracy z ministrem… pic.twitter.com/RhE8pcvlJ9 — Ministerstwo Infrastruktury (@MI_GOV_PL) September 9, 2026 The latest data from Eurostat, the European Union’s statistics agency, show that in 2024 Poland recorded the second-highest number of rail accidents, 220, among all member states, behind only Germany (366). However, 24% of Poland’s accidents took place at rail crossings, compared to 16% in Germany. In total, Poland had by far the highest number of deaths caused by accidents at rail crossings (45), ahead of Germany (26), France (20) and Hungary (18). When taking into account the size of countries’ rail networks, Poland had 4.3 rail deaths (from all causes, not just accidents at crossings) per thousand kilometres of track, which was the fifth-highest figure in the EU, behind Portugal (6.2), Hungary (5.8), Slovakia (5.7) and Lithuania (4.6). Last week, in dramatic scenes captured on camera, a train carrying almost 300 passengers hit a truck at a rail crossing in Gdańsk, luckily resulting in no injuries. The driver of the truck, who is from Bosnia and Herzegovina, has been charged. A train crashed into a lorry stuck on a railway crossing in Gdansk, Poland, after the barriers closed while the vehicle was still on the tracks. World.title: Almost 80% of Poles support helping Baltic states if Russia attacks
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Almost 80% of Poles say that they would want their country to come to the aid of the Baltic states – Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania – if they were attacked by Russia. The new poll follows a controversy over comments by a senior opposition figure, former defence minister Mariusz Błaszczak, in which he refused to confirm his support for Poland fulfilling its NATO obligations by coming to the aid of the Baltic states if they were invaded. In a survey for broadcaster Radio Zet, the IBRiS agency asked: “In the event of Russian aggression, should Poland help Lithuania, Latvia and Estonia?” In response, 77.8% of those polled said that it should, while only 16.1% were opposed. Among respondents who identified as politically centrist, 92% were in favour. The figures were lower for those with left-wing (75%) or right-wing (73%) views, though in both cases a large majority still supported coming to the Baltic states’ aid. Commenting on the findings, Radio Zet wrote that “the survey shows that Poles feel responsible for the military security of their NATO allies – contrary to what some politicians have said”. That was a reference to remarks last week by Błaszczak, who is the head of the parliamentary caucus of the national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS), Poland’s largest opposition group. Between 2018 and 2023, Błaszczak served as defence minister in the former PiS-led government. In an interview with Radio Zet, Błaszczak was asked if, in the event of a Russian attack on the Baltic states, Poland should come to their aid. “Polish soldiers should defend Poland,” he responded. “We need to be strong in our alliances…We should prioritise cooperation with the United States.” The interviewer pointed out that Article 5 of the NATO treaty requires members of the alliance to come to the assistance of another member that is attacked, and again asked if Poland should help the Baltic states if such an attack occurred. “We border Russia directly, and we border a Russia that has effectively taken over Belarusian territory. So we’re also on the front line,” replied Błaszczak. “This article, of course, speaks of solidarity, but the point is that the government that governs Poland should establish the best possible relations with the United States.” With the interviewer continuing to press the question, Błaszczak simply said that “it all depends on the circumstances” and “it’s not a straightforward issue”. Błaszczak’s comments were criticised by figures from Poland’s ruling coalition, which ranges from left to centre right. They accused him of calling into question the validity of Article 5, on which Poland would rely if it were attacked. “A former defence minister who undermines the sanctity of Polish security, i.e. NATO’s Article 5, is a moron,” wrote deputy defence minister Cezary Tomczyk. Interior minister Marcin Kiewiński said that Błaszczak had “undermined the very purpose of NATO’s existence”. In response to the criticism, Błaszczak wrote on social media that, during the PiS government’s time in power, it had significantly enhanced security ties with the Baltic states, including stationing Polish forces in Latvia and contributing Polish F-16s to NATO’s air policing mission. “NATO’s Article 5 is activated collectively, and alliance commitments are binding, but every [Polish] defence minister’s priority should be the defence of Poland and ensuring the safety of Poles,” he added. Błaszczak to stan umysłu. Mało im było niszczenia SAFE, to dziś były szef MON podważył sens istnienia NATO wskazując, że Wojsko Polskie nie powinno bronić Litwy, Łotwy czy Estonii. Przyjaźń tego skompromitowanego środowiska z Orbanem to nie był przypadek… — Marcin Kierwiński (@MKierwinski) September 1, 2026 On Wednesday, Poland’s foreign minister, Radosław Sikorski, visited Latvia, including the base in Ādaži where a Polish military contingent has been based since 2017 as part of a multinational NATO brigade. “Poland and Latvia face similar threats in the security domain,” said Sikorski. “We must speak with one voice and take our security seriously. Only such actions can guarantee effective protection against the threat from Russia.” “We do not want an escalation of the conflict, but Putin must know that we are not going to sit idly by and wait for his next step,” he continued. “We understand that the defence of our allies also contributes to Polish security. We stand ready to share the burden of defending the eastern flank.” 📍 Ādaži 🇱🇻 Continuing visit to Latvia, Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Foreign Affairs @sikorskiradek visited the base of the Polish Military Contingent. World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Polish schoolchildren are the second best in the European Union at mathematics, the third best at reading comprehension, and the fifth best at science, according to the latest results from a major international study of pupils’ abilities. The Programme for International Student Assessment (PISA) is carried out every three years by the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) and measures the performance of 15-year-olds. The latest instalment, based on tests taken in 2025, was published on Tuesday this week. It includes results from 91 countries and territories across the world. A total of 760,000 pupils were assessed, including 7,103 in 217 Polish schools. In maths, Polish pupils obtained a mean score of 484, which was the 12th highest in the world. The top seven places were taken by Asian countries and territories. But the only other European Union country to exceed Poland’s score was Estonia (508). Poland was just behind the United Kingdom (488) and Canada (485), but ahead of the likes of Finland (469), Germany (464) and the United States (463). In reading comprehension, Poland’s mean score of 482 was 14th in the world and third best in the EU, behind Ireland (500) and Estonia (499). Polish pupils performed slightly worse, in relative terms, in science, where their mean score of 495 was 18th in the world and fifth best in the EU. A number of Polish media outlets and Prime Minister Donald Tusk wrongly reported that Poland was third best in the EU for science. In fact, it was significantly behind Estonia (527) and Finland (504) and marginally below Ireland (500) and Austria (497). Poland’s latest results continue its recent history of performing strongly in PISA. In the 2018 instalment, Polish pupils were the third best in the EU in both maths and science, and fourth best in reading. In 2022 (when PISA took place a year later than planned due to the Covid pandemic), Poland was fourth in the EU in maths and fifth in both science and reading. In 2021, a separate assessment of reading comprehension among fourth-grade pupils – called PIRLS and carried out every five years by the International Association for the Evaluation of Educational Achievement – found Poland had the joint best result among EU countries, equal with Finland Following the announcement of the new PISA data, Polish education minister Barbara Nowacka welcomed the fact that “Poland has maintained its high ranking among European Union countries”. However, she added a note of caution, pointing to the fact that, overall, test scores have been declining, both in Poland and globally. That shows “Polish education still has a lot of work ahead of it”. Nowacka said that her ministry’s efforts to reform the school curriculum had been based on results and recommendations from previous PISA reports. World.title: Poland secures further $4bn financing from US to buy American military equipment
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! We cannot do what we do without your support. Poland has signed an agreement for a further $4 billion (14.8 billion zloty) from the United States Foreign Military Financing (FMF) programme, which provides grants and loans to fund the purchase of American military equipment. Defence minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz called the development a “great honour”, because FMF is “granted only to the best allies”. The agreement is not only “another important step in the modernisation of the Polish armed forces” but also “strengthens the strategic partnership between Poland and the US”. The US embassy in Warsaw likewise hailed the agreement as “reaffirming the strength of the US-Poland partnership as we work together to strengthen NATO, deter aggression, and support peace and security in Europe”. .@UnderSecT took part in the signing of a $4 billion Foreign Military Financing (FMF) loan guarantee—an important step in U.S.-Polish security cooperation. Poland’s significant investments in its defense capabilities and the U.S. defense industrial base reflect our shared… pic.twitter.com/Dz3huAp8pj — US Embassy Warsaw (@USEmbassyWarsaw) September 9, 2026 Since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, Poland has embarked on an unprecedented military procurement spree, with its defence budget rising to the highest relative level in NATO. Between 2021 and 2025, Poland was also the largest importer of arms in NATO. Around 44% of those purchases came from the US, including Abrams tanks, Patriot air defence batteries, and HIMARS rocket artillery. The new agreement marks the sixth time Poland has received funds through FMF, for a total of almost $20 billion. Kosiniak-Kamysz said that the latest financing would be used to “accelerate the implementation of existing contracts, including for Apache helicopters”. In 2024, Poland signed a $10 billion deal to buy 96 AH-64E Apache attack helicopters, along with a logistics and training package and a stockpile of ammunition and spare parts. It will make Poland the second-largest operator of Apaches in the world, after only the US itself. Thomas DiNanno, the US under secretary of state for arms control and international security, said that the new agreement “signifies our commitment to assistance, but also Poland’s commitment to ensuring security, building defence capabilities, and ensuring the security of NATO’s eastern flank”. “Poland is not only a trusted partner; it is not only an ally on the front line; it is a model ally of the United States,” he added, repeating recent remarks by US defence secretary Pete Hegseth. The terms of the financing have not been revealed, but Marta Postuła, vice president of Poland’s national development bank, BGK, through which the funds will be channelled, said it was “on more favourable terms than the last two [FMF] loan guarantee agreements”. This, she added, was “due to the subsidisation of a portion of the financing costs through a grant awarded for this purpose by the US government”. 💬 Obecna umowa została zawarta na korzystniejszych warunkach niż dwie poprzednie umowy z gwarancjami pożyczkowymi dzięki subsydiowaniu części kosztów finansowania w ramach grantu przyznanego w tym celu przez Rząd USA. To kolejny wyraz bardzo bliskiej, transatlantyckiej… pic.twitter.com/Ipd4cYDeFo — Bank Gospodarstwa Krajowego 🇵🇱 (@BGK_pl) September 9, 2026 The issue of who Poland should buy military equipment from, and how such purchases should be funded, has become embroiled in domestic political disputes this year. President Karol Nawrocki and the right-wing opposition with which he is aligned have criticised the government for signing Poland up to the EU’s SAFE programme, which is providing €43.7 billion (188.7 billion zloty) in loans for defence and security spending. They argue that provisions requiring most of the money to be spent within Europe itself could damage Poland’s relations with the US and South Korea, who have in recent years been the main sources of military procurement. However, speaking today, Kosiniak-Kamysz said that the new loan agreement with the US shows that SAFE and FMF “do not compete with one another; they complement one another”. Amerykański sprzęt wojskowy ponownie wzmocni Wojsko Polskie i bezpieczeństwo Polaków! Właśnie zabezpieczyliśmy środki w wysokości 4 mld dolarów, czyli prawie 15 mld zł na jego zakup. Łącznie w ramach amerykańskiego programu Foreign Military Financing pozyskaliśmy już blisko 20… pic.twitter.com/hhzXcE1hoC — Magdalena Sobkowiak (@magdasobkowiak) September 9, 2026 While Nawrocki is a close ally of President Donald Trump, who endorsed him ahead of last year’s Polish presidential elections, the more liberal government, led by Prime Minister Donald Tusk, has at times clashed with Washington. In May this year, the sudden and unexpected cancellation of the rotational deployment of almost 4,000 US troops to Poland raised concern in Warsaw. Shortly afterwards, Trump declared that he would deploy 5,000 additional troops to Poland. However, since then, no clear details of that plan have been announced, although Poland has formally submitted a request for the US to establish a new permanent US military base on its territory. On Wednesday morning, Polish deputy defence minister Paweł Bejda told broadcaster TVP that an American delegation, including DiNanno, was in Poland this week to discuss potential locations for the base. World.title: “We remember where Germany in the hands of a far-right, pro-Russian party can lead,” says Polish FM
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Poland’s foreign minister has expressed concern over the rise of the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party at a time when Germany is rapidly rearming – suggesting that it has echoes of the build-up to World War Two. “We want Germany, under democratic leadership and as Europe’s largest economy, to play a strong role in ensuring our common security,” Radosław Sikorski told German newspaper Handelsblatt. “But we remember all too well where a rearmed Germany in the hands of a far-right, pro-Russian party can lead – and that is precisely what the AfD represents,” he added. Polens Außenminister Sikorski: „Wir wollen, dass Deutschland (…) eine starke Rolle bei der Sicherung unserer gemeinsamen Sicherheit spielt. Aber wir erinnern uns nur allzu gut daran, wohin ein wiederbewaffnetes Deutschland in den Händen einer rechtsextremen, prorussischen Partei führen kann (…)“ [image or embed] — Andreas Prause (@andreas-prause.eu) 8 September 2026 at 21:05 Poland was, on 1 September 1939, invaded by Nazi Germany, marking the start of World War Two and over five years of brutal occupation. The attack was launched in cooperation with the Soviet Union, which invaded Poland from the east two weeks later. After Hitler was defeated, Germany had no major far-right party for decades. However, that has changed in recent years. In 2024, the AfD came first in the Thuringian state election, with 33% of the vote. Last Sunday, it won in Saxony-Anhalt, with 44%. The party also came second in the federal elections of 2025, with 21%, making it the main national opposition. Opinion polls now show that the AfD is the most popular party nationally, with support of around 28%, well ahead of Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s Christian Democratic Union (CDU), on 21%. The AfD’s growth has been watched with particular concern in Poland, a country that suffered enormously under Nazi-German occupation. Some senior AfD figures have sought to downplay the significance of the Nazi era. In 2025, when the German parliament approved plans for a memorial in Berlin to Polish victims of World War Two, the AfD was the only party not to vote in favour. The AfD’s sympathy towards and links with Russia have caused further disquiet in Poland. Last year, AfD co-leader Tino Chrupalla said he “does not see any current threat to Germany from Russia” and that, in fact, “Poland could also be a threat to us”. This year, another senior AfD figure, Kay Gottschalk, called for Poland to pay his country €1.3 billion as reparations for its “complicity” in the sabotage of the Nord Stream gas pipelines that used to bring Russian gas to Germany through the Baltic Sea but were damaged by explosions in 2022. Germany’s parliament has passed a motion calling on the government to establish a permanent memorial in Berlin to Polish victims of the German-Nazi occupation. The measure was supported by all parties apart from the far-right AfD https://t.co/8dk0ZSpmjJ — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) December 3, 2025 In the wake of the AfD’s victory in Saxony-Anhalt on Sunday, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk declared that “only idiots or traitors” in Poland would celebrate an AfD victory. He claimed there were some such people in Law and Justice (PiS) and Confederation (Konfederacja), the two main right-wing opposition parties. However, PiS’s reaction to AfD’s rise has been mixed. On Tuesday, PiS MP Małgorzata Golińska told Polskie Radio that it represents a “kind of browning” of politics in Germany – a reference to the brown shirts of Hitler’s SA paramilitary forces that helped bring him to power in the 1920s and 1930s. “A return to very dangerous thinking is taking place there and we must observe in which direction it will all develop,” added Golińska. “From Poland’s perspective, we should not overreact with any particular emotion, but we also cannot be naive [in thinking] that nothing is happening there.” By contrast, another PiS MP, Jarosław Sellin, told Onet Radio that PiS and the AfD “say similar things” when it comes to EU climate and migration policies. But he added that “this does not mean we have to like what the AfD says about history, relations with Poland, and Russia”. Polish PM @donaldtusk has condemned as “idiots or traitors” right-wing opposition figures who have welcomed the far-right AfD's election victory in Germany However, the response from the Polish right to the election result has so far been relatively muted https://t.co/goSWlbeGA8 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) September 7, 2026 Responses from Confederation have likewise been mixed. The group is actually made up of two main factions, one of which, a libertarian party called New Hope (Nowa Nadzieja), is allied with the AfD in the European Parliament. New Hope’s spokesman, Wojciech Machulski, told the Fakt daily that they are “united [with AfD] in our opposition to EU migration and climate policies” but at the same time “we do not accept the anti-Polish statements”. Krzysztof Mulawa, an MP from the National Movement (RN), which makes up the other half of Confederation, told the newspaper that “several of the AfD’s demands are unacceptable from the Polish perspective”. But he said that there were areas of shared interest, such as abolishing the euro. A number of figures from PiS and Confederation have also expressed hope that the AfD’s rise at the expense of establishment parties can herald a similar development in Poland, which, like Germany, is ruled by a pro-EU coalition ranging from centre-left to centre-right. Europa się budzi, a establishment wpada w panikę. Wynik AfD pokazuje, że ludzie mają dość dyktatu Brukseli, Zielonego Ładu i niszczenia państw narodowych przez nielegalną imigrację. Polityczne trzęsienie ziemi dopiero się zaczyna. Piękna, biała Europa narodów wkrótce powróci. — Włodzimierz Skalik (@Wlodek_Skalik) September 7, 2026 One party that has been unambiguously positive in its response to AfD’s victory is the Confederation of the Polish Crown (KKP), a radical-right, pro-Russian group that broke away from Confederation last year and is currently polling support of around 9% “Europe is waking up, and the establishment is falling into panic,” wrote KKP’s deputy leader, Włodzimierz Skalik, on social media. “A beautiful, white Europe of nations will soon return.” Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. World.title: Robots “protest” in Warsaw to demand regulation of AI and automation
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Around 30 robots protested outside Poland’s digital affairs ministry on Monday, calling for tougher regulation of artificial intelligence and robotisation. The human organisers say there needs to be greater public debate over the impact of new technologies on the labour market. Digital affairs minister Krzysztof Gawkowski met with the demonstrators, telling them that his department is working on regulations. However, one of the organisers said that plans currently being discussed by parliament contain insufficient protection for workers. Around 30 robots joined a protest in front of Poland’s digital affairs ministry, calling for stronger AI regulations. The demonstration was organised by campaigners to spark debate on how AI and robots could replace workers. pic.twitter.com/QEbvchb2RS — Al Jazeera English (@AJEnglish) September 7, 2026 Standing in several rows, the robots waved Polish flags and chanted slogans such as “We want regulations, we want rules, we want law” and “Don’t wait, regulate, protect jobs”. The organisers, a group called Democratism, said the event was intended to highlight the need for debate and legislation before automation has a more profound impact on employment. “Some people will benefit from new opportunities, while others may need to retrain or adapt to completely different roles,” they wrote. Society needs to discuss “who is responsible for preparing people for these changes, how workers should be protected during the transition and how reskilling should work”. Democratism appears to have been launched shortly before the protest, with the announcement about the demonstration among the first material published on its social media accounts. The initiative was launched by Delta Robots, a company that rents robots for events. However, a website they have set up to gather support for greater debate over the impact of AI and robotisation has so far only obtained signatures from 61 people. Grzegorz Kuliś of Delta Robots admitted to news website Gazeta.pl that their “campaign also has public relations value” for the company. However, he added that, “even though we’re deploying robots, we’re also humans, and we have a whole host of concerns that, if we don’t regulate this, we’ll soon find ourselves in an unprecedented situation that no human being will be able to cope with”. “We are constantly debating the impact of migrants on our society, whilst the vast majority of ‘migrants’ will arrive either via undersea cables across the Atlantic in the form of AI agents, or as humanoid robots in shipping containers from China,” he warned. Gawkowski, who went out to address the organisers, said the ministry’s objectives were aligned with the protesters’ concerns. “People come first, and that is what matters most to us,” he said, quoted by broadcaster Eska. The minister also announced plans to establish a committee on AI development and safety as well as to introduce so-called sandboxes, where companies will be able to test AI solutions before deploying them more widely, reports local news website O!Polska. Kuliś, however, told Gazeta.pl that a draft law on AI systems currently being considered by the Sejm, Poland’s lower house of parliament, contains too little practical protection for workers affected by automation. A Polish radio station that launched a channel run almost entirely by AI – including its presenters – has decided to end the project after less than a week The head of the station admitted they were "surprised by the level of emotion" the idea had caused https://t.co/9iMlRVamSF — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 28, 2024 The rapid development of AI and robotics has sparked debate around the world on how such technologies will impact humans, including to what extent and in what ways they will replace human labour. However, a number of recent reports have found that the impact of AI on jobs has so far been smaller than many previously predicted. Analysis by the Institute of Economic Policy Research at Stanford University, published in July, found that “AI’s effects on overall employment are likely small”. A further concern has been the prospect of AI “going rogue” by starting to act without or beyond human control. Those fears were strengthened after it emerged in July this year that some of OpenAI’s AI agents had autonomously hacked Hugging Face, another AI company. The incident prompted more than 100 companies, including OpenAI, Anthropic, Microsoft and Hugging Face, to sign an open letter calling on companies and governments to step up cybersecurity efforts amid emerging threats. A recent rise in unemployment in Poland has raised concern. But that headline figure does not tell the whole story, with experts arguing that the Polish labour market is actually in good shape, writes @AlicjaPtak4 https://t.co/Pk4y7BqGrs — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) June 24, 2026 Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. World.title: Péter Magyar opens World Athletics Ultimate Championship in Budapest alongside Usain Bolt
World.content:
Budapest has welcomed some of the biggest names in athletics as the inaugural World Athletics Ultimate Championship got underway, with Prime Minister Péter Magyar joining athletics legend Usain Bolt and World Athletics president Sebastian Coe for the official opening.

Usain Bolt arrives in Budapest for new athletics spectacle

The three-day competition is being held at the Gyula Zsivótzky National Athletics Centre from 11 to 13 September, bringing together some of the world’s top athletes for a new-style global championship.

Magyar shared a photo on Facebook from the opening ceremony with Bolt, the eight-time Olympic champion, 11-time world champion and world record holder. Bolt is in Hungary as an ambassador for the event and is also attending the competition in person.

The Prime Minister wrote that he had welcomed the athletics legend to Budapest for the first-ever World Athletics Ultimate Championship.

The event is designed to present athletics in a new format, combining elite competition with a more spectacular presentation aimed at attracting audiences beyond the sport’s traditional fan base.

One event at a time, with a USD 10 million prize pool

According to Blikk, one of the biggest changes is the competition format. Rather than several events taking place simultaneously around the stadium, only one event will be held at a time, allowing spectators and viewers to focus entirely on the athletes competing.

The stadium itself has also undergone a striking transformation. The traditional red running track is complemented by a black competition surface, LED strips and extensive lighting effects, creating an atmosphere closer to a concert venue than a conventional athletics meeting.

The stakes are equally eye-catching. A total of USD 10 million will be distributed among the athletes, with each winner set to receive USD 150,000.

There will also be no traditional medals for the podium finishers. Only the winner of each event will receive a trophy, reflecting the organisers’ aim of putting the spotlight firmly on the athlete who reaches the top.

Sebastian Coe said the decision to abandon traditional medals was deliberate, arguing that the new global championship is about determining who is the single best athlete in each event.

Never miss a headline: join Daily News Hungary’s official WhatsApp channel!

New rules promise a different kind of competition

The Budapest championship also introduces several unusual rules. In the 200-metre final, athletes can choose their lane based on their world ranking. In the high jump and pole vault, ties for first place must be settled through a jump-off, ensuring that every event has a single winner.

The organisers have also introduced changes aimed at making controversial judging decisions more transparent. Appeals must be resolved before the television broadcast window closes, while major decisions will be announced inside the stadium. Spectators will also be able to watch replays of disputed moments on the big screen.

Broadcasts will feature another new element, with viewers able to see the competitors’ chances of winning the overall title based on the results as the competition progresses.

We wrote about the championship in detail earlier: Budapest is about to host an athletics event unlike any before – $10 million in prize money and no medals

Hungarian athletes among the global stars

Hungary is also represented at the championship, including by Olympic sprinter Boglárka Takács, who will compete in the newly introduced mixed 4×100-metre relay. Takács will race alongside Zita Szentgyörgyi, Lili Brucker, Krisztián Kalics, Dominik Pázmándi, Ábel Takács and Apor Jakab in the unusual event.

Meanwhile, the international field includes Swedish pole-vault superstar Mondo Duplantis, who will compete for the Absolute Champion title on the opening night. He is also set to perform the official anthem of the World Athletics Ultimate Championship during Sunday’s closing ceremony.

The event runs from 11 to 13 September at the Gyula Zsivótzky National Athletics Centre.

World.title: Viktor Orbán has returned from his summer vacation: “I’m back”
World.content:
Former Hungarian prime minister Viktor Orbán has announced his return to political work following the summer break, posting a short but striking message on Friday evening: “I’m back. Then let’s get cracking!”

Orbán set to speak at “Kötcse picnic”

The Fidesz leader did not provide any details about his plans, but accompanied the message with a fast-paced video featuring highlights from his previous political appearances, including scenes from earlier Fidesz gatherings and Kötcse picnics. The timing of the announcement comes just one day before Orbán is due to address an important Fidesz gathering.

Viktor Orbán is scheduled to deliver a speech at the Kötcse Picnic on Saturday, 12 September, where he is expected to outline his political strategy for the period ahead. The Kötcse meeting is considered one of the most significant events in the Fidesz political calendar.

It traditionally brings together senior party figures, politicians and members of the party’s wider intellectual and political circle. Orbán has typically used the occasion to assess the political situation and discuss the priorities and challenges facing the party, making his speech closely watched for indications of its future direction.

Never miss a headline: join Daily News Hungary’s official WhatsApp channel!

A message ahead of an important political gathering

Orbán’s latest video deliberately draws on his political past, combining footage from previous speeches and Fidesz events with music from the 2010 FIFA World Cup era. The post itself offered no indication of the specific issues he intends to address at Kötcse.

The upcoming gathering is also notable because attendance is reportedly no longer compulsory for members of Fidesz’s wider political circle, making this year’s event different from previous meetings. Critics of Viktor Orbán and Fidesz argue that the party is facing political and economic challenges and that the former prime minister needs to deliver a strong message to maintain support.

Whether Saturday’s speech will provide concrete policy announcements or focus primarily on political mobilisation remains to be seen. For now, Orbán’s message is brief but unmistakable: after the summer break, he says he is back in action.

World.title: Hungarian oil giant MOL reacted to the government’s diesel support decision
World.content:
Hungarian oil and gas company MOL has backed the government’s new diesel support scheme but warned that reintroducing a fuel price freeze could lead to petrol and diesel shortages within days.

The company said the monthly HUF 5,000 (EUR 13.76) support announced by the government was a better solution than restoring the previous regulated fuel price, as it provides targeted help to consumer groups most affected by rising diesel costs without discouraging fuel imports.

Price freeze could hit imports

According to MOL, bringing back a protected fuel price would immediately reduce imports because suppliers could no longer operate profitably at the artificially lower domestic prices. The company warned that this could result in petrol and diesel shortages within just a few days. MOL said the international fuel market has also become increasingly fragile. Conflict around the Strait of Hormuz and Ukrainian attacks on Russian energy infrastructure have contributed to tighter global supplies.

Based on July figures, MOL said global diesel exports were 21% lower than a year earlier, while petrol exports had fallen by 14%. Diesel deliveries from India and Turkey to the European Union have also declined, partly because of EU restrictions on products made from Russian crude. Lower water levels on important transport routes are creating an additional challenge, making it more difficult to move imported fuel into the interior of Europe, quotes Blikk.

Never miss a headline: join Daily News Hungary’s official WhatsApp channel!

Diesel demand set to rise

MOL also expects demand for diesel across Europe to increase significantly over the coming weeks, as the continent enters one of its strongest seasonal consumption periods. The company said the next two months are likely to bring particularly high demand at a time when supply is already constrained. The pressure is reflected in international prices. MOL reported that on 8 September, the global oil price was 53% higher, while the European diesel price was 89% higher than before the outbreak of the Iran war.

The company said maintaining a stable domestic fuel supply and ensuring continuous imports are therefore among its main priorities. Despite increasingly limited availability on international markets, Hungary has so far avoided fuel shortages.

Stay up-to-date: Péter Magyar would break away from Russian oil, but expects something in return from Brussels

MOL offers temporary premium fuel discount

MOL CEO Zsolt Hernádi and other company executives were recently invited to a government meeting to discuss how fuel prices could be contained without creating shortages or imposing an additional HUF 50–100 billion monthly burden on the state budget. Following the meeting, MOL announced a temporary HUF 35-per-litre discount on its EVO Plus premium fuels for customers using the MOL Move app and an eligible discount coupon.

The promotion is available during three weekends: 10–13 September, 17–20 September and 24–27 September. MOL said Hungarian retail fuel prices remain below the EU average, but argued that domestic prices must remain broadly aligned with those in neighbouring countries. If Hungarian fuel becomes significantly cheaper than the regional market, importers may no longer find it profitable to bring fuel into the country.

World.title: Former school guard jailed in Hungary for sexually abusing two vulnerable minors
World.content:
A former school guard and child-care worker has been sentenced to eight years in prison for sexually abusing two minors, the Budapest IV and XV District Court ruled at first instance on Friday.

Court hearing held behind closed doors

The man was found guilty of endangering a minor, repeated sexual violence and exploiting child prostitution. The court also ruled that he will not be eligible for parole. The trial was conducted behind closed doors, meaning only the operative part of the verdict was made public. The court’s reasoning has not been released.

According to the indictment, the man deliberately sought employment in institutions where he could come into contact with vulnerable children, first working as a school guard and later as a child-care worker at a Budapest children’s home.

Prosecutors said he exploited his position to establish sexual relationships with two minors who were in difficult and vulnerable circumstances.

First victim was approached at school

The defendant met the first victim while working as a school guard and gradually established a relationship of trust with the boy. He later invited the child to his home, where he provided alcohol and an intoxicating substance.

According to the indictment, he then exploited the situation and, on some occasions, his physical advantage, to force the boy to engage in sexual acts. The case later involved a second victim after the man began working at a Budapest children’s home.

Second victim was a 14-year-old girl

As a child-care worker, the man was responsible for supervising girls placed in the home, overseeing their work and providing care.

In spring 2023, prosecutors said he abused this position of authority to approach one of the girls, who was aged 14 or older, and subsequently engaged in sexual acts with her. The man then instructed the girl not to tell anyone about what had happened, according to the indictment.

The court found him guilty of the charges brought against him and imposed an eight-year custodial sentence. As the ruling was delivered at first instance, the case is not necessarily concluded.

World.title: Péter Magyar would break away from Russian oil, but expects something in return from Brussels
World.content:
Hungary could seek financial support from the European Union as it considers gradually reducing its dependence on Russian oil and gas, while analysts warn that replacing Russian energy could significantly increase costs for the Hungarian economy.

Speaking at a V4 summit press conference in Bratislava, Hungarian Prime Minister Péter Magyar said he wanted to see concrete, data-based EU proposals to support Central European businesses, help member states phase out Russian oil and gas, switch to alternative energy sources and develop energy-storage infrastructure.

Péter Magyar calls for EU support over energy transition

The Hungarian government is reportedly considering making compensation payments for countries phasing out Russian energy part of the EU’s next seven-year budget. Péter Magyar said the current global energy situation remained extremely difficult, with fuel shortages being reported in several countries. He also argued that national budgets could not absorb the financial burden indefinitely and that maintaining fuel price caps could ultimately lead to shortages.

The prime minister criticised what he described as a lack of concrete proposals from EU leaders, saying businesses in Central Europe were struggling with rising costs. The Tisza Party’s political programme has previously included a goal of ending Hungary’s dependence on Russian energy by 2035.

Replacing Russian oil would come at a cost

Hungary currently receives most of its Russian crude through the Druzhba pipeline, supplying MOL’s refineries. Around 5–5.5 million tonnes reportedly arrived through the route in 2025, with a similar volume expected in 2026. Analysts say Russian Urals crude has recently been around USD 15–20 per barrel cheaper than Brent, giving Hungary a substantial purchasing advantage.

Alternative supplies could be brought through Croatia, but analysts at Kpler say this would reduce at least part of the current price advantage. More expensive crude could squeeze MOL’s refining margins and raise costs across Hungary’s energy system, reports VG.hu.

Never miss a headline: join Daily News Hungary’s official WhatsApp channel!

Gas dependence presents an even bigger challenge

Hungary is also heavily dependent on Russian natural gas delivered through TurkStream under long-term agreements with Gazprom. A reported 7.8 billion cubic metres arrived through the route in 2025, while daily deliveries in 2026 have reached around 22 million cubic metres.

The precise pricing formula is not public, making the actual cost advantage difficult to calculate. However, previous reports have suggested that Russian gas could be significantly cheaper than prices on Europe’s TTF market.

More on the Hungarian government: Péter Magyar announces monthly diesel support for nearly one million car owners

Russia may also have an incentive to keep supplying Hungary

Analysts disagree over how Moscow might respond to a Hungarian shift away from Russian energy. Some argue that Russia benefits financially from continuing supplies and has an interest in retaining one of its remaining European customers. Others believe changing political relations could lead Moscow to reconsider prices or volumes.

For Hungary, a rapid transition could therefore mean substantially higher energy costs. Despite the reported political shift, the government has not indicated that it plans to abandon existing Russian energy agreements, while cooperation on gas supplies and the Paks II nuclear project is expected to continue.

World.title: Hungary announces monthly diesel support for nearly one million car owners
World.content:
Owners of eligible diesel cars in Hungary will receive HUF 5,000 (approximately EUR 13.75) a month in fuel support through December, with the first payment due in October. The scheme is expected to benefit nearly one million motorists.

Who qualifies for the support?

The payment will cover September, October, November and December, meaning eligible drivers can receive HUF 20,000 (EUR 55) in total. The scheme applies to private individuals who owned a diesel passenger car with a maximum output of 150 horsepower on 1 January 2026. Each person can receive support for one vehicle.

Small-scale farmers and sole proprietors can also qualify if the eligible diesel vehicle is registered in their personal name. People who purchased a diesel car after 1 January 2026 are not yet covered by the main system. A separate procedure is reportedly being prepared, although details and a timetable have not yet been announced.

No application expected for most drivers

Most eligible motorists will not need to submit an application. The National Tax and Customs Administration (NAV) will identify qualifying vehicles using its database for vehicle tax.

Payments will be made by the Hungarian State Treasury. The money will first be sent to the bank account used to pay the vehicle tax. If that account is unavailable, another account known to NAV may be used. Those without a suitable bank account may receive the money by post.

Never miss a headline: join Daily News Hungary’s official WhatsApp channel!

Farmers to receive additional diesel relief

Agricultural users will also be able to reclaim the full excise duty included in the price of diesel until the end of the year. The government says the measure is intended to help farmers cope with higher fuel costs during the harvest, autumn ploughing and sowing season, while limiting the impact on production costs and, ultimately, food prices.

Stay up-to-date: Fuel prices soar in Hungary, diesel hits 4-year high, but what does the government say about fuel price caps?

Why has the government chosen targeted support?

The announcement comes as diesel prices have risen sharply. The government says returning to Hungary’s previous regulated fuel price would be difficult, potentially discouraging imports and creating supply problems.

It estimates that restoring the former protected price could cost the state HUF 50–100 billion (EUR 137.5-275 million) per month. Instead, the government has opted for direct support targeted at diesel users. The authorities have attributed recent fuel-price pressures to international market developments, including tensions around the Strait of Hormuz and attacks on oil infrastructure linked to the Russia-Ukraine war.

World.title: Tragedy in Budapest: Woman jumps out the window after fire breaks out in 15th-floor flat
World.content:
A woman has died after a fire broke out in a flat on the 15th floor of a tower block in Budapest’s 14th district, Zugló, early on Friday morning.

Another fire broke out in Budapest’s District XIV

The blaze broke out in a flat in the Füredi housing estate in Rákosfalva Park. According to Budapest’s disaster management authorities, one room and a balcony were fully engulfed in flames. Firefighters extinguished the fire using two water jets.

As the report of BudapestKörnyéke claim, ten fire engines, three ambulances and several police units were dispatched to the scene. One firefighter was injured during the operation and was taken to the Honvéd Hospital for treatment. The resident of the flat, a mother of two, died at the scene.

Another case happened only a few hours before, in the same district, on Stefánia Road, where the roof of an apartment complex caught fire, where the flames spread to two neighbouring flats, and was also endangering nearby homes.

Woman fell from the 15th floor

According to local residents, the woman left the burning flat through a window after the fire broke out and died at the scene. However, it has not yet been established whether she deliberately left the building in this way or was attempting to escape the flames.

The Budapest Police Headquarters said an administrative procedure has been launched in connection with the death, while a separate fire investigation is underway to establish the cause and circumstances of the blaze.

Residents heard shouting before the fire

People living in the tower block told local media that residents on lower floors were woken by loud shouting and screaming in the early hours of Friday morning, followed by a loud impact. Neighbours said the woman had lived in the Füredi housing estate since childhood and was known by several people in the area, writes Blikk.

One neighbour said she had normally lived with her mother and two young daughters. The children were reportedly no longer living with her, while her mother was in hospital at the time of the incident. Residents also said the woman had experienced serious personal difficulties and that emergency services had been called to the property on previous occasions.

Investigation continues

The flat was severely damaged by the blaze and is currently uninhabitable. According to the building’s caretaker, the municipality is expected to arrange for the property to be cleared and repaired.

Relatives told reporters that police and ambulance services had previously been called to the property several times because of concerns about the woman’s condition. They said they had repeatedly asked authorities to provide her with appropriate help.

Two days before the tragedy, the woman had published a concerning message on social media in which she claimed that people were impersonating police officers and paramedics and said she was afraid to leave her flat. Authorities are continuing to investigate the circumstances of the fire and the woman’s death.

World.title: Huge Budapest traffic changes announced for the weekend
World.content:
Drivers and public transport passengers should expect significant traffic changes around Budapest’s Heroes’ Square on Saturday evening, 12 September, as an event takes place in the area.

The Budapest Festival Orchestra will give a free classical music concert at Heroes’ Square from 6:30 PM, prompting several road closures and changes to public transport services. The Budapest Transport Centre (Budapesti Közlekedési Központ, BKK) recommends using the M1 metro, which will run more frequently if demand requires, to reach the event.

Several roads to close from 4 PM

From 4 PM until approximately 8:30 PM, the following roads will be closed:

Állatkerti körút between Gundel Károly út and Heroes’ Square;

Heroes’ Square between Kós Károly promenade and Dózsa György út;

Kós Károly promenade between Hermina út and Heroes’ Square in the direction approaching from the M3 motorway.

From 6 PM until approximately 8:30 PM, further closures will affect the entire Heroes’ Square, Andrássy Avenue between Bajza utca and Dózsa György út, Kós Károly promenade in both directions, Olof Palme promenade between Zichy Mihály út and Heroes’ Square, and Dózsa György út between Városligeti fasor and Podmaniczky utca.

Never miss a headline: join Daily News Hungary’s official WhatsApp channel!

Buses and trolleybuses will be diverted

Several BKK services will operate on altered routes from 6 PM. The 105 and 210B buses will bypass Andrássy Avenue between Bajza utca and Dózsa György út, instead travelling via Podmaniczky utca and Szondi utca. They will not serve their usual Bajza utca or Heroes’ Square stops.

The 20E bus will be diverted through City Park and along Hungária körút, meaning it will not serve Heroes’ Square.

The 30, 30A, 79 and 230 buses will avoid Dózsa György út and travel via Zichy Mihály út, Hermina út, Állatkerti körút and Gundel Károly út. They will use affected trolleybus stops along the diversion, with stops near Heroes’ Square on Gundel Károly út.

The 75 trolleybus will also be diverted via Hermina út, Állatkerti körút and Gundel Károly út, using the relevant 72 trolleybus stops.

The 81 trolleybus will already be affected from 4 PM, with its stop near Heroes’ Square towards Dózsa György út M moved to Gundel Károly út.

This might interest you: Mayor Karácsony shared how Budapest would tackle social crisis

Check BudapestGO before travelling

BKK advises passengers to plan their journeys using the BudapestGO app. The application provides real-time public transport information and can calculate suitable routes around the temporary restrictions. Tickets and travel passes can also be purchased through the app.

With the closures expected to last until around 8:30 PM, passengers travelling through the Heroes’ Square and City Park area on Saturday evening are advised to allow extra time and check their route before setting off. For those attending the concert, BKK’s main recommendation is to use the M1 metro, which may operate at increased frequency according to passenger demand.

World.title: Kosovo Ex-President Thaci’s Defence Seeks Acquittal in Obstruction of Justice Trial
World.content:
The defence teams of former Kosovo President Hashim Thaci and four others co-accused of obstruction of justice in Thaci’s war crimes trial at the Kosovo Specialist Chambers in The Hague have called for their acquittal, accusing the prosecution of charging them based on conversations that did not result in any witness-tampering or intimidation.

The prosecution claims that that during visits at the Detention Centre in The Hague, where Thaci is being held, he told the other four defendants – Hajredin Kuci, Fadil Fazliu, Isni Kilaj and Bashkim Smakaj – to instruct certain witnesses in his war-crimes trial about what to say in court.

But Sophie Menegon, Thaci’s lawyer, told the court during closing statements on Thursday that Thaci was “on trial for having a conversation in the Detention Unit [where he is being held pending the verdict in his war crimes trial]. There is no allegation of a bribe, compulsion, or threat against witnesses.”

She added: “There is no allegation of actual interference with witnesses …There isn’t any victim in this case …The prosecution asks you to send Mr Thaci to prison for six years over conversations inside a detention unit that resulted in zero real-world impact.”

The claims are based on recordings of the visits as well as physical evidence found also at Kilaj’s home in November 2023 – less than a month after Kryeziu and Kilaj met Thaci – allegedly printed via the only printer at the detention centre that Thaci could use.

Thaci and his four-co-accused have denied wrongdoing.

Smakaj’s lawyer, Jonathan Elystan Rees, in his closing statements on Friday, called for the acquittal of all the defendants.

“You should find Mr Smakaj and all the other defendants not guilty, whether individually or collectively,” he said, because Smakaj’s actions did not obstruct or have an impact on the course of justice.

Smakaj “cannot be convicted on the allegation that he intentionally aided in disobeying court orders, because he was completely unaware of the court’s orders”, Rees said.

He added: “There is no evidence from the prosecution, nor any legal obligation, requiring my client to be aware of the operational guidelines and functioning procedures of the detention centres.”

The lawyer for Isni Kilaj, Ian Edwards, told the court on Friday that Kilaj did not take any action after visiting Thaci at the Detention Centre in The Hague, saying he “neither called nor met with any witnesses”, so showing a lack of intent to obstruct justice.

“Everything else is mud that the prosecution is throwing at Mr Kilaj, hoping that some of it will tarnish his reputation,” he added.

David Young, lawyer for Fadil Fazliu, highlighted that his client was not even questioned by the prosecution.

“We can infer that the prosecution adopted a strategic approach of not interviewing them, of not questioning these individuals regarding the allegations. Is this the right way to initiate investigations or bring charges? I believe not. I state clearly that it is not,” Young told the court.

Alexander Admiral, lawyer for Hajredin Kuci, told the court that his client had been charged based on a wrongful translation of a message he sent to one of the witnesses in Thaci’s war-crimes trial, former Kosovo Liberation Army, KLA fighter Rrustem Mustafa.

According to Admiral, the message had been misinterpreted as passing a note from a third individual when the rightful translation revealed that Kuci was passing his support to Mustafa and was basically “a man calming an old friend”.

During the prosecution’s closing statements on Thursday, it was claimed that Thaci tried to influence Mustafa and another former KLA, fighter, Bislim Zyrapi, both of whom were testifying in his war-crimes case.

The testimony of both men favoured Thaci’s defence.

The Kosovo Specialist Chambers was created specifically to try former members of the KLA; it is located in The Hague and staffed by international judges and prosecutors due to doubts about the Kosovo justice system’s own ability to try former KLA fighters, many of whom are considered heroes in Kosovo. Witness-tampering has been one of its key concerns from the outset.

World.title: Kosovo Parliament Hit by Fresh Dispute Over Deputy Speakers
World.content:
Kosovo parliament session on September 11, 2026. Photo: BIRN.

Kosovo’s parliament failed to find a way out of a fresh crisis on Friday when MPs reconvened in two attempts to elect new deputy speakers.

The legislature derived from the June 7 snap partliamentary elections has not yet been inaugurated because the ruling Vetevendosje party refuses to support proposed candidates from two opposition parties, Vlora Citaku, from the Democratic Party of Kosovo, PDK, and Kujtim Shala, from the Democratic League of Kosovo, LDK.

Under the constitutional rules, parliament cannot be considered inaugurated until the speaker and all five deputies are elected.

Albulena Haxhiu from Vetevendosje was elected speaker on Wednesday, Ardian Gola, from the same party, was installed as deputy on Friday.

When Citaku of the PDK received only 44 of a minimum of 61 votes on Friday, her party colleagues left the session and accused Albin Kurti’s Vetevendosje of blocking the inauguration of parliament.

“As of today, the PDK has no reason to participate in parliamentary sessions and we will take the case to the Constitutional Court,” Bedri Hamza, the PDK leader, said as soon as speaker Albulena Haxhiu interrupted the session.

In the June elections, Vetevendosje won 53 of the 120 seats in the chamber, well ahead of the next-placed PDK, which won 22 seats. The LDK came third with 18 seats.

Vetevendosje claims it can call on 62 MPs to form a new government, again relying on the support of MPs from ethnic minority communities – Roma, Ashkali, Egyptian, Turk and Bosniak – plus one of the Serb MPs.

However, the wider crisis that led to the June 7 elections has not been solved, as parliament needs to elect a new president of Kosovo within two months of its inauguration. Failure to do so would trigger another election, the fourth within less than two years.

As the post-election blockage enters its second month, Kurti and LDK leader Lumir Abdixhiku agreed on August 31 to nominate Bekim Sejdiu, a former Constitutional Court judge and former diplomat, as Kosovo’s president. But, days later, six LDK MPs refused to support his candidacy, making the necessary quorum impossible.

For a president to be elected, a candidate must win at least 80 votes in the first two rounds. In a potential third round, they need a simple majority of only 61 votes.

Arberie Nagavci, head of Vetevendosje’s parliamentary group, said its MPs would not support any candidate for deputy speaker who is against the deal on the new president. Both Citaku and Shala have announced their opposition to Sejdiu’s candidacy.

“Of course, the MPs who are in favour of the Vetevendosje-LDK agreement [on the president] have the support of our 53 MPs,” Nagavci said after the interruption of the session.

Parliament will resume work on Sunday.

World.title: Bosnia Charges Seven Over Deadly Fire at Tuzla Elderly People’s Care Home
World.content:
Investigators inspect the scene after the fire at the nursing home in Tuzla, November 5, 2025. Photo: EPA/NIDAL SALJIC.

Prosecutors in Bosnia and Herzegovina’s Tuzla Canton on Friday indicted seven people over the fire at a Tuzla nursing home in November 2025 that killed 15 elderly residents and injured more than 30 others.

The indictment charges former nursing home director Mirsad Bakalovic, service head Zinaida Razic Halilovic and Mustafa Azabagic, who was responsible for fire and occupational safety at the facility.

Three employees of the Tuzla-based company Inproz, which prepared the nursing home’s 2021 fire risk assessment, are also indicted: Nedim Dzambic, Mirsad Zukancic and Jasmin Softic. The seventh defendant is Ibrahim Sarajlic, a fire safety inspector in Tuzla Canton.

The defendants are charged with serious offences against public safety. Bakalovic is also charged with abuse of office and authority, the prosecutor’s office said.

Prosecutors allege that between April 2021 and November 4, 2025, the defendants failed to implement or order legally required fire safety and general safety measures, despite knowing the facility was classified as a high-risk building.

The nursing home run by the city of Tuzla housed 180 elderly residents, 110 of whom were seriously ill, immobile or living with disabilities.

According to the indictment, the failures included inadequate supervision of residents with limited mobility, inappropriate accommodation and allocation of residents according to their health and mobility, and an inadequate fire prevention and protection system.

Prosecutors said these failures prevented the timely detection and containment of the fire, the early detection and reporting of fire and carbon monoxide in residents’ rooms, the evacuation of residents, and the removal of smoke and heat from the building.

“As official and responsible persons, by failing to install prescribed fire protection equipment and by failing to act in accordance with regulations or technical safety rules, they caused a danger to people’s lives, resulting in the deaths of several people,” the prosecutor’s office said.

The fire broke out in a resident’s room on November 4 and quickly spread. Fifteen residents died, with autopsies establishing a direct causal link to carbon monoxide poisoning or other complications related to the fire, prosecutors said. More than 30 people were injured.

The indictment has been submitted to the Tuzla Cantonal Court for confirmation.

Prosecutors have also asked the court to ban all seven defendants from holding public or professional positions or performing certain activities for 10 years.
