World.title: Doha diary: A historian amid the Iran war
World.content:
(Renowned historian and author, Rila Mukherjee, was scheduled to fly from the USA to India by Qatar Airways [QA] on February 25, 2026. Her route—Shreveport–Dallas Fort Worth–Doha–Kolkata—was expected to bring her to Kolkata on the night of February 26 or in the early hours of February 27. However, as of March 8, she was still stranded in Doha. Qatar’s skies were closed due to the US-Israeli attack on Iran. QA’s commercial flights were suspended. At the time of writing, evacuation flights to India were scheduled to start soon. She reached home on 12 March.)

Today is 8 March. I am now camping out in Doha for the ninth day since 28 February. The Qatar airspace is shut and padlocked. The authorities have thrown away the key. Limited numbers of passengers are being flown to Europe and the Americas on evacuation flights (they are called ‘relief flights’) organised by QA, and relief flights to Africa and Asia will start from tomorrow. But for the time being, I am effectively marooned in Doha.

Doha is one of the largest airplane hubs in the world, and a cosmopolitan group of transit passengers has been put up by QA in the 4-star The Royal Riviera Hotel. The hotel is situated on Doha’s Corniche. It is an ageing hotel; not terribly posh, and the plumbing is a bit iffy. But it is well located, with comfortable rooms, and it is a clean and friendly hotel. I feel safe here. Its staff is composed of Asians (from Bangladesh, the Philippines, Sri Lanka, Nepal), North Africans (Algerians and Moroccans mostly) and some West Asians. All of them are helpful despite the pressures they are facing. They deal gracefully with the diverse demands and complaints of the passengers.

My room faces the Corniche and I can see the Persian Gulf from my window. As a maritime historian, this makes me very happy.

This country and its national airline are looking after us very well and, really, I have no complaints. QA’s representatives visit the hotel twice daily. There is no information forthcoming on my evacuation to Kolkata, and the greater part of passenger bags are still to arrive at the hotel. My South African neighbour says one of their bags has not been delivered; perhaps it is lost.

We are largely dependent on the clothes we have on our backs and those we had in our carry-on. Most of us are washing and drying them overnight. We have to use the hair dryer if they are still not dry.

My bags came in today, i.e., 8 March.

There are some elderly travellers. Many of them say that their medicines are running out. Mine will last another week.

Will I be able to get out by then?

We are told that a limited air corridor may open today; alternatively, we may be evacuated by the land route through Saudi Arabia to Riyadh (this would take around seven hours), where a leased QA aircraft may take us to India. But we have to make our own arrangements for the Saudi e-visa and overland travel. This seems a risky enterprise. And whether this potential leased aircraft would fly me direct to Kolkata is not known. There is no clarity to date.

***

But if I was scheduled to arrive in Kolkata on 27 February (and the war broke out a day later, on 28 February), how is it that I am still in Doha

Ah, thereby hangs a tale!

It is a cautionary tale on buying air tickets with multiple connections, and what ensues when the first connection does not take off as per schedule.

***

I had spent nine weeks in Shreveport with my son and daughter-in-law and was scheduled to leave on 25 February. Unfortunately, my flight from Shreveport to Dallas Fort Worth (DFW) by QA’s codeshare partner American Airlines (AA) did not take off. We were told that the incoming flight had nose gear problems and therefore could not land. Ultimately it made an emergency landing. Fire engines, firefighters, EMTs and ambulances were standing by. Luckily, there was no fireball and there were no casualties. The vice-chair of my daughter-in-law’s department was on that flight; I bumped into him in the terminal as he deplaned, and he said that the landing had been really scary.

There were no more AA flights to DFW that day. Roo and Stephanie came back to the airport and took me home. I spent a restless night. I hate flying at the best of times.

I was put on the same AA flight the next day, on 26 February, but when I reached DFW I was told that my connection flight to Doha was full. Apparently, the AA staff at Shreveport Regional Airport knew there were no seats on that flight; nevertheless they sent me on to DFW hoping I would ‘sort out’ the matter with AA’s customer care there. The only ‘sorting out’ that AA did at DFW was to put me on a later QA flight to Doha on the same day, that is, late evening on 26 February. It was a smaller aircraft (not the Airbus 350 on which I was ticketed), the flight was cramped and some of my co-passengers were not very well behaved. One lady kept on drinking; she skipped the meal service and was quite abusive. Another one, African American, told me that as an ‘American’ she was superior to Asians. Right, I thought, we all know how you as a Black person got there!!!

In all my years of travelling I have never encountered such blatant racism.

When we reached Doha very late on the night of 27 February (almost 24 hours later due to the time difference with DFW), I had missed that evening’s flight to Kolkata!

No problem, QA’s customer care said, we’ll talk with AA as it is their problem. This took a while, so I went off to buy myself a snack at Brioche Dorée in the airport’s food court.

By then it was early morning on 28 February.

Readers, note the date!

***

AA agreed to comp me a room for the remainder of the night at The Royal Riviera Hotel. I was granted a 48-hour emergency visa by Qatar Immigration and I was shifted to the hotel on 28 February at 2 AM. QA’s ground staff helped me throughout. The room was comfortable, the bed looked inviting, and I went to sleep, confident that my Kolkata flight would take off as scheduled at 18.45 hours on that day itself (that is, 28 February). At that point, I was going to reach only 24 hours behind my original schedule.

I informed Kolkata and asked my driver to collect me from the airport accordingly.

***

On 28 February, I was woken around 8 AM by a strange sound from my cell phone. It was a very loud, continuous screech. I don’t have international roaming and I wondered who was calling me and what was happening. I saw a ‘Security Alert’ on my screen but the text was in Arabic. I started hearing thuds and bangs. Another alert, still in Arabic, came in.

What was going on? I was mystified.

I was now getting alerts in English. It said the US and Israel had jointly attacked Iran. US bases and embassies and consulates across the Gulf were vulnerable. Qatar was in this critical area. Sirens were going off. I started watching Al Jazeera and Richard Engel on NBC.

This was Day 1.

Smoke rises following an explosion, after Israel and the US launched strikes on Iran, in Tehran, Iran, February 28, 2026. PHOTO: REUTERS

By Day 2, the Gulf was not just lying in a war zone; it had been converted into a theatre of war. Doha was undergoing regular drone strikes and missile attacks.

Day 3 was relatively quiet. Apparently, Qatar and Iran had a phone conversation, and Qatar urged Iran to stop the strikes. But our temporary visas were extended by Qatar. This was an indication that the phone call was not conclusive. This war was not going to end anytime soon.

The Qatar–Iran conversation does not seem to have yielded the desired result. There is no relief from Iranian attacks. These now form the backdrop to our daily life at The Royal Riviera. Drone attacks and missile strikes re-started from Day 4. None of them target the downtown area; they target only the US base and industrial areas in Qatar. Most of the drones and missiles are successfully intercepted; the few that are not cause localised fires. The attacks usually happen around breakfast and lunch, and sometimes they occur very late at night or in the early morning hours. This means we are always in a state of extreme alert. It is jarring on the nerves. We can neither eat properly nor rest. We are getting stressed out.

But I must also mention that the attacks and interceptions sound more like Diwali patakas than the very loud explosions that one expects.

*** Days 4 till 9 (that is, till date) have seen this regional war extending from land to sea: from the Hormuz Strait to the Indian Ocean. This is now becoming very serious. Critical choke points like this strait have become a curse. Ports across the Gulf are lying idle; almost no cargo is getting through. But we have had no alerts today. Does this mean that Iran will not strike Qatar for the time being? Is this a temporary reprieve? Will relief flights be able to take off? ***

Some bags arrived at the hotel on Day 5. Mine were not among them.

By Days 6 and 7 we have more or less settled into what is turning out to be our semi-permanent home. The hotel is no longer very ‘royal’; it has taken on the character of a London bedsit. Or a council housing estate in one of the UK’s inner cities! Children play noisy games in the corridors, an oddly comforting sound among the explosions, security alerts and sirens that go on regularly.

I see an enormous solidarity among the travellers, both on my floor and when we meet up at meal times. I have a very nice South African couple next door who check on me each morning, always asking how I am faring (‘please don’t hesitate to knock if you face any difficulties’). They have even offered to take me out to buy clothes (this was before my bags arrived). Elegant MENA (Middle East North Africa) people greet me each day at breakfast, a young Pakistani financial analyst from Toronto shares his insights with me at the breakfast table, and a British couple advise me to carry my passport with me at all times (especially when I leave my room in case of an attack and subsequent fire). They kindly offered to buy me my medicines, although they are at least a decade older than me. A young school teacher from Geneva shares my table at dinner. I have not seen her lately; perhaps she has already been repatriated on one of the relief flights to Europe which started operating from Day 7. The British couple and the South Africans are still here; the Pakistani man left for Toronto early this morning. He was given only two hours’ notice and he phoned my room to say goodbye at 1.15 AM this morning.

***

What does my daily schedule look like?

It is like what I imagine a day at boarding school would be. Because it is Ramadan, the hotel starts the breakfast buffet from 3 AM, lunch is from 12 noon, and dinner is over by 7.30. The food served (although mild in taste and quasi-institutional as regards the daily menu, which does not rotate much in terms of items), is nevertheless amazingly varied as regards the cuisine: Arabic, Turkish, Italian, Spanish and South Asian (the last is not good at all). A lot of lemon is used in the preparations, but practically no onions. This may be due to the fact that there was an onion shortage; onions came in from India only on Day 5. There are loads of different kinds of salads, some bland European cheeses and diverse types of hummus. In addition, there is feta cheese, stuffed vine leaves, green and black olives, veg and non-veg samosas and spring rolls, koftas, and baba ghanoush or baingan bharta. Good cappuccinos and lattes. Flaky croissants and brioches, pastries and amazing Arabian/Persian/Yemeni sweets. A decadent baked (and often caramelised) bread pudding called Umm Ali is served at dinner. Obviously, the Qatari supermarkets are still well-stocked with FMCG. The Indian-origin Lulu supermarket chain has flown in a whole lot of perishable and non-perishable food items.

Strangely, no fresh fruit!

***

Gas prices have shot up.

I have given up watching the death and destruction on TV, and watch Looney Tunes, Anthony Bourdain, Fawlty Towers and Mr Bean instead. Priyam Paul, my editor at The Daily Star, has sent me some e-books which help to pass the time.

When I am not reading, or watching sitcoms, cartoons and travel and food documentaries, I reflect on what brought us to this war. I see the Persian Gulf from my room; it is still a brilliant blue. But it is also desolate since the Hormuz Strait was closed off. I see no cargo ships or container vessels; there are no cruise ships or tankers. For a maritime historian like me, this is not the Persian Gulf I know. After all, it has been a crossroads since recorded history! My India in the Indian Ocean World (2022) documents this history of two thousand years at the very least. Now, mobility is severely constrained.

Persian Gulf. Photo: Collected

We are living now in a world of fragmented geopolitics, of accelerated climate degradation, and of critical demographic shifts. The world is undergoing these changes along with increasingly disaffected groups of peoples, perhaps terrorists, some of them. We are seeing the rise of AI which, to my mind, is linked, along with the toxicity of social media, with the increasing authoritarianism that we see worldwide. It horrifies me when I see a young nation declare it will bring ‘civilisation’ to Iran. It disregards the fact that Iran-as-Persia predates Arab culture and is one of the world’s oldest culture areas. Not just the glory of Shi’ite Safavid Persia (1501–1736), which political theorists and analysts invoke when describing this civilisational space and whose heritage modern Iran draws on: think of the period from c. 550 BCE to 651 CE (Muslim conquest and start of Islamisation by the Rashidun Caliphate), when four mighty Persian empires ruled a large portion of the then-known world: Achaemenid, Seleucid, Parthian and Sassanian. Persia challenged Egypt, Greece and Rome, and then it faced up to the Ottoman and Russian empires. This memory of resistance of 2500 years will not be easily erased.

However, the total disregard of international law and the collapse of the rules-based order will usher in a new regional order in West Asia. This will impact on the Gulf states. Once-biblical Lebanon is almost destroyed by a rampant Israel. Syria has closed its borders. As a rogue USA intimidates Persia and trains its eye on the Caucasus and Azerbaijan, it also destabilises Iraq. Iranian Kurds based in Iraq have been reactivated. How will this impact on the Turkish Kurds? Turkey, a NATO country, is already feeling threatened.

The relatively young post-WW1 statelets in the Gulf will lose out in the violent reshuffle in the greater region. The Dubai story was already over. And Oman had lost its sheen even earlier. Financial and service centres will shift eastward—to Singapore or perhaps to KL. As will global airline hubs. The Gulf states will see their importance in location, business and finance diminish. They will have to reconsider their dependence on the USA which has now become a double-edged sword. Iran will endure, but perhaps in a new form. But it will not be erased from the map of the world.

World.title: André Béteille: A sociologist Bangladesh should read
World.content:
My first encounter with the ideas of Professor André Béteille was in July 1966 in an introductory sociology course at the University of Dhaka (at that time in East Pakistan) through Professor Tom Bottomore’s book, Sociology: A Guide to Problems and Literature (1962). The emphasis on general theory of social stratification for an explanation of the Indian caste system found its empirical reflection, as Bottomore refers to, in the work of Béteille, especially in Caste, Class and Power: Changing Patterns of Stratification in a Tanjore Village (1965).

My second encounter with him was in the Fall of 1975 at Dalhousie University, Halifax where I was writing my Master’s thesis under Professor Bottomore, and he referred to read me Béteille’s “Closed and open social stratification” (1966). Reading Béteille after nine years under the Maple tree, I began to admire his empirical depth, comparative methodology, and theoretical clarity, which reshaped my understanding of social hierarchies in India.

In the Christmas of 1976, I had an occasion to share some of my understanding of Béteille’s work. At that time, I was at York University, Toronto where I was doing my PhD. Professor K. Ishwaran, one of our faculty members, who wrote Tradition and Economy in Village India (1966), invited me for Christmas dinner-- Turkey with cranberry sauce, cooked by his Dutch wife. There we talked about the contribution of both Béteille and his supervisor M. N. Srinivas towards understanding the impact of social change on Indian social stratification.

In order to realistically understand contemporary caste hierarchy, Béteille emphasised the “other factors such as class and power” that “have to be considered as independent variables” (1966). It appeared to me highly useful for comparative empirical research. It creates a distance from traditional essentialist and ideological perspective of inequality.

Borrowed from Max Weber, he focused on multidimensionality of stratification and examined how status, economic resources, and political control interact to shape multifarious social order. This was a tremendous contribution in the field of stratification studies. Though he focused on rural stratification, the model is also applicable to the study of urban social stratification.

It is puzzling that in Bangladesh universities, both sociology and anthropology disciplines overlooked and neglected the Weberian model of multidimensional stratification system: anthropology remained spell-bound under the dichotomous model of rural “ashraf-atraf”; and sociology was locked in the iron cage of simplistic Marxist model of “land ownership” under the name of peasant studies. In spite of teaching Weber’s “Class, Status, Party” (1922/1946) in the universities, there is a marked absence of the application of Weberian model in the study of rural and urban complex social hierarchy. Probably in Bangladesh, this shows the intellectual bankruptcy of these disciplines, which are suffering from morbidity.

In fact, in order to understand contemporary social change in Bangladesh, especially its regime of accumulation under crony capitalism, it is essential to understand the nexus between power and class. The determining power of traditional property ownership in the formation of classes and consequent class consciousness has diminished in Bangladesh.

The notion of political capitalism advanced by Max Weber is also useful in understanding Bangladesh social stratification, especially class formation. The party consciousness along with ruling party affiliation, may give legitimate or illegitimate access to economic resources, thereby determining class position in terms of life opportunities and life style. This in turn, heavily influence commodification of prestige and honour; and becomes marker of status.

André Beteille (1934 - 2026). Photo: Collected

The rural and urban dispossession, which is an integral part of neoliberal and crony capitalism’s regime of accumulation, is also the progenitor of emergent lumpen bourgeoisie, whose class position do not correspond with their demeaning status position. Again, the traditional status group in Bangladesh, as Béteille found in his Tanjore village study with respect to traditional caste, suffer from status dislocation, having less access to power and economic resources. The ontology of inequality and hierarchy can best be understood by the Weberian epistemology.

I think study of this process of social change, and its impact on inequality in Bangladesh, is vital towards understanding Bangladesh society. The internationally acclaimed Indian empirical model provided by Béteille can be one of the best guides to study the intersectionality of class, status and power in both urban and rural Bangladesh. It is unfortunate that social sciences in Bangladesh have neglected such a significant social dynamic that affects all our lives.

In March 1989, Professor Abhijit Dasgupta, a colleague of Professor Béteille, facilitated my direct meeting with him. Professor Dasgupta was kind enough to arrange a seminar talk by me in the sociology department of Delhi School of Economics. After the seminar, I paid a visit to Professor Béteille’s office room. He was very warm and hospitable to offer tea to me and my wife. He spoke in Bangla and affirmed his Bangali origin. I felt very comfortable to have a vibe of Bengal. I mentioned to him how I came to know of his work à la Bottomore and Ishwaran. I was so surprised to experience his stock of knowledge mediated by modesty and simplicity. The meeting with professor Béteille during the short-lived spring of Delhi was one of the most memorable events of my life. I wish his conceptual and methodological clarity inspire the young Bangladeshi sociologists to break the chain of ignorance, myopic framework, and the hegemony of intellectual infantilism.

A.I. Mahbub Uddin Ahmed is a professor in the Department of Sociology at the University of Dhaka.

World.title: In praise of Mymensingh’s Bangla folk ballads
World.content:
Folk-ballads are living archives that represent the imagination, values, ideas, and aesthetics of the people to whom they belong. Bangla literature has a rich repertoire of folk ballads. We are, however, quite oblivious of this treasure trove and, therefore, there is a dearth of research on these folk elements.

Czech Indologist Dusan Zbavitel's Bengali Folk-Ballads From Mymensingh And The Problem Of Their Authenticity can be called a wonderful exception in this regard. It is considered to be the first literary study of the beautiful folk-ballads from Mymensingh. The study was published by the University of Calcutta in 1963.

A brief background of the book may not be irrelevant here. In 1923, Rai Bahadur Dineshchandra Sen edited a volume of epic songs from the Mymensingh District of the then Eastern Bengal under the title Maimansimha-gitika. The ballads were mainly collected by Chandra Kumar De, a literary activist from the area. In the following years, Dineshchandra published three more volumes of balladic texts containing epic songs from different parts of Eastern Bengal. The beautiful ballads received enthusiastic response and admiration in India and abroad. However, for some scholars these ballads were too good, and they shared doubts about the ‍antiquity, authenticity and folk character of these lores. Dusan Zbavitel found this uncertainty "highly regrettable" and undertook a study to assign to the ballads their proper place—"one of the high points of Bengali literature". Dr Zbavitel tried to find out: "what is it that makes them so excellent?"

Zbavitel confined his analysis to the study of the ballads originating in Mymensingh—41 ballads containing more than 21,000 verses. He took an arduous effort of analysing each of these 41 ballads to prove their originality and, I must say, he achieved his goal with marked success.

One key argument put forward by Zbavitel in favour of the originality of the gitikas from Mymensingh is that these ballads are not collected by a single person and, still, there are similarities among the ballads: identical images, and similar artistic approach and common inventory of similes and metaphors. So these ballads couldn't be the creation of a modern poet as suggested by some detractors.

According to Zbavitel, the most significant aspect of these folk ballads is that they are devoid of any religious implications. They generally show harmonious co-existence of the Hindu and Muslim communities, without religious bias on either side. Zbavitel points out the fact that most of the Hindu ballads were collected from Muslim singers, which shows, according to him, that these folk poems were enjoyed and appreciated by both the communities with the same eagerness. The secular outlook of the folk ballads is diametrically opposite to the explicit religious connotation of the classical Bangla literary texts such as Mangal-kavyas and Vaisnava literature.

Zbavitel extensively discusses the ideological and artistic approach of the ballad writers, verse and rhyme technique, and use of similes and metaphors in chapter three and four of the book. The most dominant motif, according to Zbavitel, is love. Even the historical and heroic epics can be grouped into this category.

As to the literary techniques, the ballad writers, being true to the characteristics of folk epics, do not try to introduce innovations in their lyrical dictions. They are content with the poetic means offered by their predecessors. They want to tell an interesting and touching story in a simple garb, fresh with country scenes and feelings.

Zbavitel also discusses the manner of preservation of the folk ballads—preserved, in most cases, in torsos. Referring to two versions of the same ballad, Maishal Bandhu, he argues, "The 'original' ballads [were] sometimes rewritten by another folk poet, or other poets, quite freely, without any scruples; whole portions, as well as individual couplets and verses, were taken over, others were replaced by newly replaced passages, and the story itself was often changed." The reasons behind such changes, according to Zbavitel, might be an effort to offer listeners a 'better' story than the original one.

Due to this oral nature of preservation, it is always difficult to prove the originality of folk elements. If we undertake an effort to study the folklore of Bangladesh, Zbavitel's book will be an invaluable companion guide.

Rabindranath Tagore wrote to Dinesh Chandra Sen in appreciation of the book Maimansimha-gitika, "Classical Bengali literary texts such as Mangal-kavyas are ponds dug on by order and at the expense of the rich, but Maimansimha-gitika is a source of exuberance from the deepest level of the heart of rural Bengal, a clear stream of genuine pain. There has never been such a creation of self-forgetting rasa [aesthetic joy] in Bengali literature." [translation by the author]

While celebrating the Bengali new year this Pohela Boishakh, may we remember the melody and the essence of communal harmony embedded in Maimansimha-gitika.

Shamsuddoza Sajen is a journalist and researcher. He can be contacted at [email protected].

World.title: Fizz takes three in Mumbai rout
World.content:
Pace sensation Mustafizur Rahman recorded his best bowling figures of the Indian Premier League today when he finished with 3 for 16 in Sunrisers Hyderabad’s 85-run victory over Mumbai Indians at Vishakhapatnam.

The three-wicket haul took the left-armer to joint-second in the wicket-takers’ list with a total tally of 13 scalps from nine matches. He is one short of Mitchell McClenaghan, who has taken 14 wickets in 10 matches.

The 20-year-old currently has the best bowling average, 15.61, and best economy rate, 6.15, amongs bowlers who have played at least eight matches in the tournament.

The Sunrisers Hyderabad might have depended on Mustafizur a number of times in the ongoing Indian Premier League, but today was a collective effort. Ashish Nehra, Bhuvaneshwar Kumar and Barinder Sran had reduced the Mumbai Indians to 49 for 6 in nine overs before Mustafizur was given the ball.

The wily left-armer sent back Hardik Pandya with his first ball with a cutter which Pandya failed to adjust himself against. Pandya attempted a slice through point, but the ball curled away to the hands of the keeper, with the umpire judging that out even though the television replays were inconclusive.

Then in the very first ball of his second over again, Fizz bowled yet another slower delivery which moved away from the batsman, getting the edge of Tim Southee on the way to the keeper.

The man from Satkhira returned got the scalp of McClenaghan in the final delivery of his third over, getting the batsman to offer a loopy catch to midwicket.

Mustafizur did not get to bowl a fourth over as David Warner gave the other bowlers their chance to mop up the tail. And they did efficiently, bundling out the hosts for just 92 runs in 16.3 overs.

Earlier, brilliant performances from Hyderabad openers, Warner and Shikhar Dhawan helped the team post 177. Dhawan scored 82 off 57 while Warner smacked 48 off 33. Yuvraj Singh also had a good time with the bat, scoring 39 off 23.

World.title: Koizumi says Japan not ruling out nuclear subs, days after U.S. offers positive view
World.content:
Defense Minister Shinjiro Koizumi on Friday reiterated that Japan is not ruling out acquiring nuclear-powered submarines, days after a U.S. Navy official reportedly offered a positive assessment of the move.

“Regarding nuclear-powered submarines, we will proceed with our consideration of not ruling them out as an option,” Koizumi told a regular news conference. Tokyo is weighing acquiring such submarines in revisions to its three key security documents set to come by the year’s end.

Koizumi’s remarks came after an unidentified U.S. Navy official, citing Tokyo’s expertise in nuclear energy technology, told Japanese and South Korean media this week that Tokyo should consider acquiring nuclear submarines.

Asked about how the vessels might fit into Japan’s security strategy, the defense chief noted the pros and cons, saying that while nuclear-powered submarines are capable of extended patrols and are said to have several times the speed of conventionally powered submarines, they are less quiet underwater, expensive and require specialized expertise for maintenance, repair and operation.

Japan currently operates a fleet of 23 diesel-electric attack submarines, but has long avoided the more expensive and politically fraught option of nuclear-powered vessels.

Calls for Tokyo to acquire nuclear boats gained steam after an expert panel recommended in September last year that Tokyo develop vessels with “next-generation” power sources and vertical launching systems for long-range missiles. The ruling Liberal Democratic Party-Japan Innovation Party bloc effectively codified this push in their October coalition agreement.

Although neither the expert panel nor the coalition deal directly mentioned nuclear-powered submarines, Koizumi and other Japanese officials have repeatedly refused to rule out any options when it comes to nuclear submarines, as Tokyo looks to boost its defense capabilities.

Koizumi added to the speculation in November, when he touched on South Korea’s deal with the U.S. to secure nuclear vessels, noting that “all the surrounding countries have nuclear submarines.”

In June, the JIP also reignited the debate when it submitted a proposal to the government that called for the swift introduction of nuclear-powered submarines, citing China’s constant naval expansion into the Pacific.

World.title: Ratio of Japanese singles seeking marriage drops below 80% for first time
World.content:
The proportion of single Japanese men and women who said they intend to marry one day has fallen below 80% for the first time, a government survey showed Friday.

The result highlighted a declining desire for marriage as more people see few benefits to tying the knot.

“More people believe they will not feel lonely even if they continue living alone, while more people have never interacted with infants, and these trends are also linked to the low desire to marry and have children,” an official at the National Institute of Population and Social Security Research said.

The survey, conducted in June last year, covered unmarried people between the ages of 18 and 54, and married couples in which the wives were under 55. Valid responses were obtained from 6,756 unmarried people and 5,024 couples. The previous survey was conducted in 2021.

Among the 3,459 unmarried people age 18 to 34, 75.1% of men and 77.8% of women said they intend to marry eventually. Both figures fell by more than 6 percentage points from the previous survey, dipping below 80% for the first time since the survey of unmarried people began in 1982.

The proportion of men who said they never intend to marry rose 6.7 points to 24%, while the proportion of women rose 6.9 points to 21.5%, exceeding 20% for the first time.

The proportions of men and women who saw no benefits to marriage rose by about 7 points each to 42.8% and 36%, respectively. Fewer people said they believed marriage would enable them to have children or a family, gain peace of mind or achieve greater financial security.

Of the surveyed married couples, about 20% of those in their first marriage who had been married for less than five years said they met online, doubling from the previous survey and reaching around the same level as those who met through their workplaces or jobs and through introductions by friends or siblings.

The average ideal number of children for married couples was 2.18, a slight decrease from the previous survey. One in 4.4 couples had undergone infertility testing or treatment.

World.title: Digital Agency says personal information possibly leaked
World.content:
The Digital Agency said Friday that about 246,000 sets of personal information, including the names and email addresses of government employees, may have been leaked due to unauthorized access to a network system.

No misuse of the information has been confirmed so far, the agency said.

The unauthorized access occurred on the Government Solution Service, a system commonly used by government ministries and agencies.

The agency said it detected suspicious activity from the account of a system maintenance administrator on June 25. It then began investigating and found on July 9 that an external third party had repeatedly accessed the system since around late May.

“We take it seriously that the incident occurred despite our operations under multi-layered security measures and a 24-hours-a-day, 365-day-a-year surveillance system,” Chief Cabinet Secretary Minoru Kihara said at a news conference, adding that the agency would work to prevent a recurrence.

The breach affects some 189,000 government employees and around 57,000 private-sector workers involved in government duties. The information included their addresses and phone numbers, but not My Number personal identification numbers or bank account information.

The Digital Agency determined that the cyberattack exploited a vulnerability in virtual private network equipment to access the system remotely. The agency was aware of the vulnerability but yet to apply a patch.

Following the possible information breach, the agency warned of emails or phone calls from people posing as the agency.

World.title: Double-dipping: When one manga adaptation just isn’t enough
World.content:
When it was announced last year that the acclaimed manga “Look Back” by Tatsuki Fujimoto would be getting a live-action adaptation, I was both excited and confused. Excited because the film was being helmed by Hirokazu Koreeda, one of Japan’s best directors, and confused because an anime adaptation had already been released in 2024.

“Look Back,” which hits theaters Sept. 11, is far from the first double-dip in the long history of Japanese visual media. Popular manga titles have often been adapted into both live-action and anime films over the decades. While this can sometimes feel like a money grab, these releases also give audiences the chance to experience multiple takes on the same material.

A semiautobiographical manga by Fujimoto (“Chainsaw Man”), “Look Back” is a coming-of-age tale about two girls who team up to become professional manga artists. The anime film, directed by Kiyotaka Oshiyama, was both a financial and critical success, earning more than ¥2 billion (around $13 million) and bagging a number of awards, including best animated feature at the Japan Academy Awards.

World.title: Chubu Electric plans to abandon nuclear plant restart in wake of data scandal
World.content:
Chubu Electric Power is planning to withdraw its application to restart the No. 3 and No. 4 reactors of its Hamaoka nuclear power plant in Shizuoka Prefecture, following a scandal over the cherry-picking of earthquake risk data, it was learned Friday.

Regarding the scandal, Chubu Electric said the same day that it had received a report from an investigative committee of external lawyers. The company will hold a news conference on Monday that its president, Kingo Hayashi, will attend.

The company said that the scandal’s impact on its earnings has not yet been determined.

At a news conference on Friday, industry minister Ryosei Akazawa said that he had not learned the details of the report.

“Based on Chubu Electric’s response to our reporting order, we will take as strict action as possible,” Akazawa noted.

In the scandal, Chubu Electric is suspected of underestimating possible earthquake vibrations during the Nuclear Regulation Authority’s screening for the restart of the Hamaoka reactors.

Additionally, the company has been found to have attempted a cover-up even after the secretariat of the authority began investigating the matter in May last year.

World.title: Quake-hit Kumamoto Prefecture to offer travel discounts
World.content:
Kumamoto Prefecture will launch a travel discount campaign on Tuesday to stimulate tourism demand following a powerful earthquake that struck the prefecture in July, Kumamoto Gov. Takashi Kimura said Friday.

The discounts will apply to overnight stays in Kumamoto between Oct. 1 and Dec. 25.

“We want many people to visit Kumamoto,” Kimura said at a news conference, adding, “That will strongly support the recovery and reconstruction of the affected areas.”

The program will provide discounts of up to 60% on eligible travel packages.

For packages that include transportation fees, the maximum discount is ¥20,000 ($130) for one-night stays and ¥30,000 for stays of two nights or more.

For accommodation-only products, the maximum discount is ¥20,000, regardless of the length of stay. Tours that include both Kumamoto and other prefectures in the Kyushu region are eligible for discounts of up to ¥35,000.

About 190,000 people had canceled accommodation bookings in Kumamoto as of Aug. 21 due to the earthquake, resulting in losses of about ¥2.7 billion, according to the prefectural government.

Kimura expressed hope that the discount campaign will help generate 300,000 overnight stays.

World.title: U.S. women arrested over smuggling of $1 million worth of cannabis into Japan
World.content:
Tokyo police have arrested two American women for allegedly smuggling $1 million worth of cannabis into Japan, with one suspect claiming she was motivated by the idea of a free trip to the country, according to an official and local media reports on Friday.

The pair, both 25, arrived at Tokyo’s Haneda Airport from New York last Saturday with two suitcases in which “cannabis-like dried plants were secretly stored,” a police spokesperson said.

Japan has some of the world’s strictest drug laws, and smuggling or possession of illegal narcotics can result in a jail term.

The dried cannabis weighed around 30 kilograms and is valued at about ¥150 million ($970,000), local media reported.

One of the women told police that she took the job for the money and because “I was attracted by the fact I could go to Japan for free,” Nippon TV reported.

The other suspect denies the allegation, telling police she “didn’t know that cannabis was inside” the suitcase, the Tokyo Shimbun reported, citing unnamed police sources.

The women “conspired with someone else whose name is unknown,” the police spokesperson said.

The pair were arrested “on suspicion of violating the drugs and psychotropics control law, or, smuggling to gain profit,” the spokesperson said.

They also breached two other laws, he added.

Smuggling cannabis for the purpose of making a profit is punishable with up to 10 years in prison and a fine of up to ¥3 million.

World.title: Sentiment turns positive among big Japanese firms in July-September
World.content:
Business sentiment among large Japanese companies turned positive in the July-September quarter thanks to stronger semiconductor-related demand and more customers at hotels and restaurants, government data showed Friday.

The business survey index for large companies stood at plus 5.3, compared with minus 0.5 in the previous three months, according to the data released by the Finance Ministry and the Cabinet Office.

The index is calculated by subtracting the percentage of companies reporting deteriorating business conditions over the preceding three months from that of those reporting improved conditions.

The impact of the war in Iran had eased from the April-June quarter, a Finance Ministry official said. Citing the recent rise in crude oil prices, however, the official said, “We’ll continue to closely monitor corporate activities.”

The index for large manufacturers stood at plus 7.6. The production machinery manufacturing sector posted an index reading of plus 23.4 on increased demand for semiconductor manufacturing equipment.

The information and communications equipment manufacturing sector had a reading of plus 19.9, thanks to growing demand tied to artificial intelligence data centers.

The index for large nonmanufacturers was at plus 4.2. The service sector, including hotels and restaurants, posted a reading of plus 7.6, while finance and insurance companies recorded a reading of plus 3.4 as higher lending rates improved earnings.

The index for midsize companies was at plus 0.8, while that for small companies was at minus 10.9.

Companies across all sizes and industries expect to report higher sales and profits for fiscal 2026 from the previous year. Capital investment is projected to increase 11%.

World.title: Man arrested after allegedly refusing to share HK$30m Mark Six jackpot with group
World.content:
Hong Kong police have arrested a 36-year-old man suspected of having fled with a Mark Six jackpot worth around HK$30 million (US$3.8 million) that he should have shared with 14 colleagues.

A source said on Friday that a 53-year-old man had reported to police on Wednesday that he was one of 15 colleagues who had chipped in to buy a Mark Six ticket for the draw on Saturday.

The group reportedly comprised some staff members of the Food and Environmental Hygiene Department (FEHD).

His colleague, a 36-year-old man, bought the ticket and held the account into which the winnings were paid, the source said.

After the ticket won, the 36-year-old refused to evenly divide the prize money among the group, which prompted a dispute, the insider said.

A meeting was held on Wednesday evening in Aberdeen to try to resolve the dispute, but the source said the ticket-buyer allegedly insisted that he would not split the winnings during the roughly 30-minute negotiation.

Worried that the 36-year-old intended to keep the entire prize and disappear, the 53-year-old man filed a police report at 10.06pm the same day.

World.title: ‘Pillar of Shame’ sculptor to ask Denmark to negotiate for artwork’s return
World.content:
The creator of a sculpture commemorating those killed in the 1989 Tiananmen Square crackdown will ask Danish authorities to negotiate with Hong Kong for its return, with city officials disputing his claims of owning the confiscated artwork.

The fate of the “Pillar of Shame” sculpture has come back under the spotlight after the High Court on Friday handed jail sentences to three former leaders of the Hong Kong Alliance in Support of Patriotic Democratic Movements of China at the end of a high-profile national security trial.

In a reply to the South China Morning Post, Danish artist Jens Galschiot said he intended to ask his government to officially declare the eight-metre-tall (26-foot) sculpture a work of art and part of his country’s cultural heritage so it could be returned to “its rightful owner”.

He revealed he had raised the issue with the Danish parliament’s foreign policy committee, adding that a cross-party group of the European Parliament and the European Union’s Hong Kong office had also followed up on the matter.

“For me, the issue is quite simple: the ‘Pillar of Shame’ is my sculpture,” Galschiot said.

“It was never given away. It should not be confiscated or destroyed because of its political symbolism or because it commemorates the victims of the Tiananmen Square massacre.”

World.title: ‘Rest in eternal peace’: veteran horror actor, filmmaker Simon Loui dies at age 62
World.content:
Veteran Hong Kong actor and filmmaker Simon Loui Yu-yeung, better known to fans as the “King of Ghosts” for his prolific work in horror films, has died at the age of 62.

Long-time friend and fellow actor Frankie Ng Chi-hung revealed to reporters on Friday that Loui’s wife, TV and radio personality Ma Li, had confirmed the filmmaker had died in a hospital in Guangzhou on Monday after losing his battle with gastric cancer.

“The family hoped to stay low profile. There was no big announcement,” Ng said. “May he rest in eternal peace, free from all pain and sickness in heaven.”

Ng said he had known of Loui’s previous struggles with gastric cancer, which had been treated, but later learned the condition had come back in recent years.

Loui was born in 1964 and enjoyed an entertainment career spanning more than three decades across TV, radio and film and included his work as a filmmaker.

After finishing an artist training course at free-to-air broadcaster TVB in the late 1980s, he started with appearances in TV dramas and variety shows before moving to the film industry in the early 1990s.

World.title: Man dies in fall from scaffolding in 19th fatal construction accident this year
World.content:
A construction worker has died after falling while erecting scaffolding, marking Hong Kong’s 19th fatal accident in the construction industry and second to involve truss-out platforms this year, according to police and a concern group.

The force said it received a report at 11.39am on Friday that a male worker had fallen and was found lying on a podium along Yu Chau Street in Sham Shui Po.

The man was rushed to the nearby Caritas Medical Centre, where he was later declared dead. Police have classified the case as an industrial accident, with the exact cause of death to be determined by an autopsy.

The Labour Department said it had immediately deployed staff to the scene upon receiving the report, adding that it was investigating the cause of the incident.

The department also issued suspension notices to involved contractors, halting the erection, alteration, dismantling and use of scaffolds on the building’s external wall until the relevant risks were addressed.

Fay Siu Sin-man, chief executive of the Association for the Rights of Industrial Accident Victims , said the victim was a 50-year-old sub-subcontractor who had worked as a scaffolder for many years.

The man arrived at the site at around 8am and was putting up his second set of scaffolding when a support bracket was suspected to have come loose, causing him to fall, she said.

World.title: Over 60% of new dentists join Department of Health after mandatory internship
World.content:
About 60 per cent of Hong Kong’s first batch of dental graduates who underwent mandatory internship training have joined the city’s Department of Health, a move that has helped “significantly ease” the manpower crunch.

The development followed a controversial amendment to the Dentists Registration Ordinance in 2024, requiring all dental graduates in Hong Kong to complete a 12-month internship before obtaining a full licence starting in 2025. The measure aimed to enhance hands-on clinical experience in real-life settings.

Dr Kitty Hse Mei-yin, consultant-in-charge of the department’s dental services, said on Friday that the government had recruited 62 per cent, or 46 of the first batch of 75 interns.

The rest went on to work at the Prince Philip Dental Hospital’s teaching facility, at the University of Hong Kong (HKU), in non-governmental organisations or in the private sector.

“While students have learned a lot from their six-year undergraduate training, the internship allowed them to put what they learned in books into practice in the real world, meeting different kinds of patients in different roles under the support of experienced dentists,” Hse said.

“During the internship, they never know what kind of problems will be brought into the room by the next patients, which is different from their clinical training at school … that could enhance their clinical judgment and independent thinking skills.”

World.title: ‘The more, the better’: Hong Kong won’t cap talent scheme passes, labour chief says
World.content:
Hong Kong will not cap the number of admissions under its talent schemes, with the labour minister saying “the more, the better” amid a global race for skilled workers, despite rising concerns over whether the city can absorb the influx.

Wrapping up a five-day visit to Hong Kong by overseas innovation and technology (I&T) specialists, Secretary for Labour and Welfare Chris Sun Yuk-han said on Friday that no quota would be set for the two main categories of talent passes – one for professionals with job offers and the Top Talent Pass Scheme – but renewals were conditional on holders being employed or having set up companies in the city.

“Such requirements ensure arrivals contribute meaningfully to the economy. The more talent that comes to Hong Kong, the better,” he said.

Experts have raised concerns about whether the city can absorb the influx of non-local talent without putting strains on its population.

Hong Kong has rolled out a suite of talent schemes since late 2022, including the Top Talent Pass Scheme for top earners and graduates of leading universities, the points-based Quality Migrant Admission Scheme, and channels for professionals with job offers and technology specialists.

A member of the European delegation tries a virtual reality feature at Cyberport on Friday. Photo: Silvia Siu

Authorities have approved 126,942 applications since 2023, with 94.5 per cent, or 120,009, involving candidates coming from mainland China.

World.title: Hong Kong star Deanie Ip wins best actress at Venice Film Festival – from the SCMP archive
World.content:
This article was published on September 12, 2011.

Veteran Ip wins best actress in Venice

by Adrian Wan

Veteran Hong Kong movie star Deanie Ip Tak-han was named best actress at the Venice Film Festival for her portrayal of an ageing domestic servant in Ann Hui On-wah’s film A Simple Life (Tao Jie).

The award, a first for a Hongkonger, was a crowning achievement for the 63-year-old Ip, who returned to the big screen for the first time in a decade to take the film’s leading role.

The movie also stars Canto-pop heartthrob Andy Lau Tak-wah.

An emotional Ip said after receiving the award: “It’s great. I haven’t had my heart beat so heavily for so long, because I think it was more than 10 years ago that I had my best supporting actress award in Taipei.”

She won that Golden Horse Award for the 2000 film Crying Heart.

World.title: Alibaba mourns former independent director Tung Chee-hwa, hails his global vision
World.content:
Alibaba Group Holding has mourned the death of Tung Chee-hwa, who served as an independent director, saying the global perspective of Hong Kong’s first leader helped the e-commerce giant to remain rooted in the country while expanding internationally.

He joined Alibaba Group’s board as an independent director in 2014 and held the position until 2022. He died on Tuesday at the age of 89.

Alibaba, which owns the South China Morning Post, said on Friday that Tung’s “invaluable contributions and full support” during his tenure had played a vital role in the company’s development.

“His global perspective helped Alibaba stay rooted in China while expanding globally,” it said.

The company described him as a “visionary leader, steadfast patriot and also an elder of noble character, humility and kindness” who always had placed Hong Kong’s and the nation’s development at heart.

“During the critical period of Hong Kong’s historical development, he led the city forward with courage and foresight, remaining dedicated to the city’s long-term prosperity and stability,” it said.

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019013/Frog Gone: China’s Beloved Traveling Game Is Going Offline
World.title: Frog Gone: China’s Beloved Traveling Game Is Going Offline
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019013/Frog Gone: China’s Beloved Traveling Game Is Going Offline
World.content:
A mobile game beloved by millions of Chinese users about a traveling frog is set to shut down after the game operator and the IP holder failed to reach a licensing agreement.

Announced Tuesday by its official account on microblogging platform Weibo, the game, Travel Frog: China Journey, will discontinue on Dec. 8.

“This time, the little frog is going on a long journey, with no set date of return,” the announcement read. “But that quiet companionship will always remain in our hearts.”

A video game insider told domestic media that the IP holder, Japanese gaming studio Hit-Point, sought harsher terms from domestic operator Lingxi Games, including stripping it of its right to collaborate with other companies and sell game-related merchandise. After multiple rounds of negotiations, the companies could not reach an agreement, though the insider disclosed that they are in a final round of talks.

Travel Frog, released in 2017, is an idle game, meaning gameplay progresses with little player input. Chinese users began downloading the Japanese version before tech giant Alibaba secured authorization to publish it exclusively in the Chinese mainland under its gaming division, Lingxi Games, a year later. By then, the original version was already popular, with iOS downloads in China alone exceeding 30 million.

At its peak, the game was more popular than the domestic, Tencent-produced game Honour of Kings, topping the domestic App Store free chart. Lingxi Games was acquired by the private equity firm Trustar Capital in August this year.

In Travel Frog: China Journey, the protagonist, a frog who lives alone in a cave, passes its days reading, writing in its diary, eating, and whittling wood. It also travels around China, such as to the Great Wall in Beijing and West Lake in the eastern city of Hangzhou. While on the road, it meets fellow animal travelers, brings back local specialties, and sends home postcards, which devoted users post on WeChat.

After learning that the game would be discontinued, a graduate student in Shanghai surnamed Fang spent a day trying to redownload it. She had played since her first year of university but hadn’t reinstalled the game after changing phones, not thinking it would shut down permanently.

“(I will have to) think of it as a child growing up and setting off on a new journey — a solo trip where the parents don’t need to worry anymore,” Fang said. “I really loved my frog … It felt like a real little baby.”

Another player, surnamed Wang, in the southern city of Guangzhou, first tried the game’s Japanese version in 2018. The frog’s ability to travel, rest, and meet friends whenever it wanted — moved her, as she said that adult life is all about KPIs, responsibilities, and pressure.

When she learned the game would be taken offline, Wang told Sixth Tone that she was devastated. “This isn’t just a game,” she said. “It’s a second life.”

Online, some called the move the “tears of an era,” a Chinese internet slang term referring to something that evokes a strong sense of nostalgia. Others lamented that their “youth is over,” or said they could not bear to delete the game, hoping it might one day be restored.

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: A screenshot from Travel Frog: China Journey. From Weibo)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018994/She Preserved the Memory of the Mogao Grottoes. Now It’s All She Remembers.
World.title: She Preserved the Memory of the Mogao Grottoes. Now It’s All She Remembers.
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018994/She Preserved the Memory of the Mogao Grottoes. Now It’s All She Remembers.
World.content:
Chang Shana, one of China’s most treasured artists, is sitting on her living room sofa in Beijing, her eyes fixed on a TV documentary about Dunhuang, the northwestern oasis city where she spent much of her childhood. When a familiar face appears on screen, the 95-year-old breaks into a broad smile.

“That’s my father,” she says, pointing out Chang Shuhong, an accomplished painter best known for his research on the ancient Buddhist murals at the Mogao Grottoes.

Alzheimer’s disease, the most common cause of dementia, has robbed Chang Shana of most memories, yet her face still lights up the moment anyone mentions Dunhuang.

“Apart from Dunhuang, her family, and the caregivers who attend to her day and night, my mother has largely forgotten the people and things outside her immediate world,” says her son, Cui Donghui.

Gone are her memories of studying under world-renowned masters, of her mother walking out on the family, of helping design state gifts and landmark buildings like Beijing’s Great Hall of the People and the Cultural Palace of Nationalities, of losing her beloved husband, and of her tenure as the longest-serving president of the Central Academy of Arts and Design, now Tsinghua University’s Academy of Arts and Design.

On a desk in her bedroom is “Clothing Patterns of China Dunhuang Mural,” which compiles 328 color illustrations of cave murals and sculptures from various periods. “I drew this book. It’s all decorative motifs,” says Chang, standing up. After catching her breath, she points out another book: “This one, ‘Dunhuang! My Father’s Call,’ was written by my father, but I contributed many of the illustrations and written materials.”

Would she like to return to Dunhuang one day? “Yes,” she replies in a soft voice, without hesitation. Then, she slowly wanders back to the sofa to continue watching her documentary.

Life on the move

Chang Shana was born in Lyon, France, in 1931. Her father was among China’s first generation of French-trained artists, and both her parents went on to attend the prestigious Beaux-Arts de Paris school.

After being moved by a photobook about the Mogao Grottoes that he discovered in a secondhand book stall beside the Seine, Chang’s father returned to China alone in 1936 to head the fine arts department at the National Art School in Beiping, predecessor of Beijing’s Central Academy of Fine Arts.

However, as invading Japanese troops advanced toward Beijing, he was forced to flee, eventually moving with the academy to Nanjing in the eastern Jiangsu province — where he was joined by his wife, Chen Zhixiu, and daughter — and then to the southwestern city of Chongqing, which served as the nation’s wartime capital during the War of Resistance Against Japanese Aggression. In 1943, the family relocated again to Dunhuang in the northwestern Gansu province, where Chang Shuhong was appointed director of the National Dunhuang Art Research Institute.

Chang Shana found it difficult adjusting to their austere life among the arid dunes. In her 2013 memoir, “Yellow Sands and Blue Sky,” the artist recalls that first winter night, eating cold noodles with only salt and vinegar, and her father promising, “Things will get better.”

Yet despite the lack of material comforts, she instantly found an abundance of inspiration at the Mogao Grottoes. On days without school, she would walk the dirt roads, past the shimmering poplars, and climb into the grottoes to copy the murals. “I loved going into the caves to draw. I was always eager to do it. My parents never had to tell me to go,” she wrote. She would also chat with the many visiting artists and scholars, laying a strong foundation for her artistic development.

Previously, students had typically copied the murals with tracing paper, which they secured to the walls with thumbtacks, leaving tiny holes. Chang Shuhong prohibited this practice to prevent further damage to the relics, meaning his daughter had to recreate the originals stroke by stroke through observation alone. Although laborious, it helped her develop extraordinary levels of precision.

But the desert took as much as it gave. Under the strain of his responsibilities, Chang Shuhong was often irritable, and his relationship with his wife became fractious. She eventually left him and moved back east in 1945.

Chang Shana was 14. She dropped out of school and stayed home to help with the housework and to knit sweaters for her 4-year-old brother.

That same year, the Nationalist government ordered the Dunhuang Art Research Institute to close. As funding dwindled and workers left, Chang Shuhong traveled extensively to enlist fresh support, eventually recruiting a group of teachers and students from art academies in Chongqing and Chengdu, capital of the neighboring Sichuan province.

With the institute’s future secured, he instructed his daughter to make copies of representative murals covering various Chinese dynasties. In her memoir, Chang recalls her work to recreate the figures of warriors from the Western Wei dynasty (535–556): “The lines followed my feelings; my brushwork was especially free and expressive.”

Finding faith

When Chang turned 17, a Canadian friend of the family sponsored her to study in the United States at what is today Tufts University’s School of the Museum of Fine Arts. There, she took classes in drawing, anatomy, art history, perspective, color, painting, and design.

Although confident in French, she initially struggled with some of the highly specialized English terminology. What baffled her most, though, was the painting course. With abstract expressionism on the rise, her professors required students to create work without recognizable forms or subjects. In a letter to her father, she wrote, “Perhaps I just don’t understand.”

According to her son, Chang’s diary entries from the early 1940s are filled with confusion and unease. She occupied her time with sketching and knitting, often questioning the meaning behind such pursuits. Yet her letters home in 1950 reveal “a completely different person,” he says.

In one, she wrote about “finally finding faith,” and expounded on her belief that art should be accessible and serve the people. In other letters, she displayed a weariness with life overseas. “Staying here, depending on others for everything, life feels so empty,” she wrote. “I have a perpetual sense that something is missing, like I owe a debt.”

Chang returned to China in December 1950 without completing her degree. She immediately began helping her father organize an exhibition of Dunhuang cultural relics in Beijing, featuring copies of murals she and several art researchers had made.

The following year, she was introduced to the influential architects Liang Sicheng and Lin Huiyin, who agreed to recommend her for a teaching assistant position at Tsinghua University’s School of Architecture. Under Lin’s guidance, she and two other students applied traditional cloisonné enamelwork techniques and motifs to everyday items such as table lamps, cigarette cases, and plates.

With a growing portfolio, Chang was commissioned to design themed gifts for the 1952 Asia and Pacific Rim Peace Conference, held in Beijing. She created a silk headscarf and large cloisonné plate with peace dove motifs, inspired by Dunhuang cave paintings from the Sui dynasty (581–618).

When China began reforming its university system in the early 1950s, she transferred to the Department of Applied Arts at the Central Academy of Fine Arts before ultimately joining the Central Academy of Arts and Design in 1956.

Gone too soon

Chang met her first husband while studying in the U.S. The couple married in China in 1953 but divorced after just a few years. The artist barely mentions this time in her memoir, not even naming him.

Her second husband, Cui Taishan, was a Japanese-language interpreter. They met while part of a Chinese cultural delegation to Japan in 1961 and were married two years later, spending 26 years together until Cui’s death in 1989.

The artist’s friend, Huang Xuanzi, recalls that Chang often talked to her late husband’s photo before she developed dementia. “She’d grumble at him for leaving her too soon, then turn to me and say, ‘Look at him, always smiling at me like that,’” she says, adding that Chang still sometimes recognizes him in photographs. “One day, she suddenly smiled and said to me, ‘Cui Taishan was very handsome.’”

Huang recalls a thick stack of flower studies Chang had painted when she was pregnant, each accompanied by a short poem handwritten by her husband. “They were never published, so almost no one outside the family knows about them,” she explains. “You can clearly feel the depth of their affection in those paintings and poems.”

In 1983, Chang was appointed president of the Central Academy of Arts and Design, leaving her less time for family. Around the same time, Cui was diagnosed with diabetes and then liver cancer. Even during his final days, she was unable to stay with him full time, yet he would always reassure her, “You go ahead with your work. I’m fine.” He was just 62 when he died.

The artist struggled to cope with the combination of grief and work stress. “There were photos of her husband everywhere in the house,” says her sister-in-law, Wang Fulan. “She would always say, ‘He left us too soon. He was so young.’ She felt that she had devoted herself entirely to her work and left household matters to her husband, and that was what had worn him down.”

In later years, Chang told a friend: “I have done right by everyone and everything in my life. My father Chang Shuhong wanted me to carry on the cultural legacy of Dunhuang, and I spent my life doing so. Lin Huiyin mentored me to become a designer, and I devoted myself to that career. The only person I failed was my husband, Cui Taishan.”

Forever home

Shortly after losing her husband, Chang’s father was diagnosed with Alzheimer’s. His condition remained largely stable until he took a serious fall at age 92. After that, his memory began deteriorating rapidly, and he passed away two years later in 1994.

Huang says Chang Shana was also healthy and mentally sharp until her early 90s. She might forget small things, but a little prompting was enough to bring her back.

During the pandemic, her son Cui Donghui couldn’t visit in person; he could see her only through the security camera installed at her home. When he checked late at night, he often saw her lying alone on the sofa watching television. When he was finally able to return, she opened the door, looked at him, and said, “Who are you?”

Leafing through his mother’s book, “Clothing Patterns of China Dunhuang Mural,” he proudly remarks, “This is her life’s work. She systematically cataloged the motifs from different periods and defined their evolutionary progression. This foundational body of work is still essential today, whether for research or for the development of cultural products.”

All the detailed illustrations inside were completed during a special trip Chang took to the Mogao Grottoes in 1959 with two colleagues. For the artist, it was a joyous return to the place she once called home.

“We were young then,” she wrote in her memoir. “We rode horses and camels, climbed the Singing Sand Dunes barefoot, and had an absolutely wonderful time.”

At 95, the journey to Dunhuang is impossible. Yet smiling at that flickering TV screen, she is already back among the caves. The memories are gone, but the patterns remain.
