World.title: Foreign Media on Kazakhstan’s Economic Transformation, AIFC and Rybakina’s Rise to World No. 1
World.content:
ASTANA — The Astana Times has selected articles from global media outlets covering Kazakhstan. This week’s foreign media digest highlights the country’s economic and financial development, sovereign wealth strategy and global ambitions, alongside Elena Rybakina’s historic rise to world No. 1.

Elena Rybakina becomes world No. 1 for first time after U.S. Open win over Zheng Qinwen

Women’s tennis has a new world No. 1. Elena Rybakina took the top spot from Aryna Sabalenka on Wednesday at the U.S. Open with a quarterfinal win over China’s Zheng Qinwen, 3-6, 6-1, 6-4. It is her first time at the summit of women’s tennis, reported The New York Times on Sept. 9.

“It’s a great achievement, and I feel like you will appreciate and think about it even more when you finish your career,” Rybakina said in a news conference, when asked about the milestone.

Kazakhstan’s AIFC says other countries are seeking to replicate its model

Kazakhstan’s financial hub says its model is attracting interest abroad as competition between financial centres intensifies, while limited market liquidity remains a key challenge, reported Euronews on Sept. 9.

For two days, Astana Finance Days 2026 brought together representatives of global financial institutions that collectively manage more than $26 trillion in assets, as Kazakhstan seeks to strengthen its position in the global competition for capital.

How Kazakhstan’s economic reforms have turned the tenge into the best-performing currency in Europe and Asia

EU Reporter published an article on Sept. 7 examining the tenge’s strong performance in 2026 and highlights Kazakhstan’s accelerating economic transformation, driven by foreign investment, diversification, digitalization, infrastructure development, and the expansion of its financial and technology sectors.

“The Kazakhstani tenge has become the best-performing currency in Asia and Europe in 2026, according to the Financial Times. Since the beginning of the year, it has appreciated by nearly 10% against the US dollar, outperforming all other currencies worldwide except for several currencies of Latin American and African countries. This performance has been underpinned by economic growth driven by the transformation of Kazakhstan’s economic model. The country is rapidly evolving from a commodity-based economy into a financial and technology hub for Central Asia, amid growing inflows of foreign capital,” reads the article.

Erlan Karin’s appointment links reform and national identity

The Times of Central Asia published an article on Sept. 1 about Erlan Karin’s appointment as Vice President of Kazakhstan.

“When President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev put forward Erlan Karin for vice president on Aug. 31, he called him ‘a genuine patriot’ with long experience in government. He also stressed Karin’s part in implementing major reforms, his grasp of long-term state strategy and his understanding of Kazakhstan’s prospects for socioeconomic development.

Karin has spent seven years in senior posts under Tokayev. He also has a sustained interest in a question that runs through the president’s agenda — how Kazakhstan can modernize while remaining connected to its own history and national identity,” reads the article.

From oil reserves to infrastructure: How Kazakhstan invests in future generations

EU Reporter released an article on Sept. 8 examining how Kazakhstan can transform part of its sovereign wealth from financial savings into long-term national capital by investing in infrastructure, healthcare, education, and other assets that can generate lasting economic and social benefits for future generations.

“Savings from the National Fund are already being utilized directly in the interests of future generations. Since 2024, Kazakhstan has operated the National Fund for Children program: every young citizen of Kazakhstan is annually allocated a portion of the fund’s investment income, and upon reaching 18 years of age, the accumulated funds can be used for education or housing improvement. This program has already entered the phase of practical asset utilization. Between February 2024 and Aug. 1, payouts were received by more than 338,000 young Kazakhstanis, totaling approximately $67.8 million. Meanwhile, the funds belonging to minors remain within the National Fund’s assets and continue to be invested until they reach adulthood,” reads the article.

Almaty and Astana set to retain Central Asia’s economic lead

Almaty and Astana are likely to retain their position as Central Asia’s leading economic centers, even as Tashkent and Bishkek record rapid growth and invest heavily in their future expansion. Kazakhstan’s two largest cities benefit from an economic scale, financial infrastructure and established business ecosystems that have been built up over decades, reported the Times of Central Asia on Sept. 7.

“Almaty and Astana benefit from an economic scale unmatched elsewhere in Central Asia. Kazakhstan alone accounts for more than half of the region’s GDP and roughly two-thirds of its inward FDI stock, according to TCA’s Central Asia Balance Sheet. That scale helps generate the fiscal resources needed to build and maintain the municipal infrastructure that supports business activity,” reads the article.

World.title: Kazakhstan Looks to New Players and Products to Drive Next Phase of Digital Finance, NBK Governor Says
World.content:
ALMATY – Kazakhstan has built the core digital infrastructure for its financial sector and is now entering a new stage focused on developing new products, attracting new market participants and creating innovative business models, National Bank Governor Timur Suleimenov said at the Central Asia Fintech Summit 2026 in Almaty on Sept. 11.

Speaking at the opening of the third annual summit, Suleimenov said Kazakhstan’s financial sector has already reached a high level of digitalization, with more than 90% of payments made without cash and most basic banking and government services available through digital platforms.

The summit, held on Sept. 11, brings together regulators, financial institutions, technology companies and experts to discuss the future of financial markets, digital currencies, artificial intelligence, digital assets, cybersecurity and other areas of fintech.

Suleimenov said the National Bank’s approach has evolved from simply digitizing its own operations to actively encouraging innovation across the financial market.

“We decided to change the approach altogether – instead of being the one who is pushed, to become the one who pushes the market,” he said, describing the regulator’s role as creating a “push” for the market and encouraging participants to move faster.

Kazakhstan builds digital financial infrastructure

Kazakhstan has established a national digital financial infrastructure. It includes biometric identification, interbank payments, the digital tenge and mechanisms designed to protect citizens and businesses from financial fraud.

The infrastructure has been expanded through successive stages, with the digital tenge entering industrial use in 2023, the National Anti-Fraud Center launched in 2024 and new interbank and QR payment infrastructure introduced subsequently.

The digital tenge is gradually being integrated into government financial processes, including public procurement, budget planning and the management of state funds. Suleimenov said the National Bank, together with the government, intends to increase the volume of digital-tenge operations to 2 trillion tenge (US$4.4 billion) over the next 12 months.

Suleimenov pointed to the interbank mobile payment system launched this year as one of the latest developments. The system includes transfers by phone number and a unified QR code. Since its launch on July 19, it has processed more than 20 million transactions worth around 400 billion tenge (US$888 million), according to the National Bank.

He described the high level of digitalization as a major achievement, noting that in many countries reaching 50–60% of non-cash turnover remains a challenge.

From infrastructure to products

The next challenge, Suleimenov said, is no longer primarily about building the technological “rails” of the financial system but about using them to create products that meet the needs of businesses and consumers.

During the opening plenary, moderator Vitaliy Volyanyuk, co-founder and CEO of Digital Business, asked Suleimenov to assess what the measures introduced by the NBK and other regulators had actually delivered and how Kazakhstan’s financial sector looks today.

Suleimenov described the sector as bank-centered but increasingly diverse, with the domestic financial system, the Astana International Financial Center and emerging digital-finance initiatives creating complementary opportunities.

“Briefly, the system is strong, highly capitalized and digitalized, and it has a huge future,” he said.

But Suleimenov stressed that infrastructure alone would not be enough.

“The second step is, of course, financial infrastructure, on which these solutions have to run. We are also creating that. But now, probably, the main step is creating products,” he said.

“We cannot and will not create the products ourselves,” he added, calling on banks, traditional financial institutions and new financial companies to work both together and in competition to develop new products and business models. The objective, he said, is to make access to financing, payments and cross-border transactions easier for both businesses and individuals.

Digital maturity remains uneven

The transformation, however, is not taking place at the same pace across the entire financial sector, Chair of the Agency for Regulation and Development of the Financial Market Madina Abylkassymova said during the summit.

Volyanyuk also asked about the readiness of smaller banks, insurance companies and other financial institutions for digital and AI transformation, rather than focusing only on the largest banks with significant technological and financial resources.

Abylkassymova said the agency had assessed the digital readiness of 94 financial organizations this year, examining process digitalization, data quality, infrastructure, cybersecurity, AI use and employee competencies.

“Banks remain the leaders, with almost 75% already using artificial intelligence. However, a gap remains between banks and other parts of the financial sector, particularly insurance and microfinance,” she said, stressing that digital transformation is not simply about introducing technology.

“It is also about the competencies of employees,” Abylkassymova added, arguing that digital and AI tools need to be embedded into the actual processes of financial organizations.

According to her, the agency is now developing a strategy for large-scale digitalization and further AI adoption across the financial sector. It has identified 1,200 specific measures and prepared individual development plans for the 94 organizations assessed.

Kazakhstan looks to export financial services

Suleimenov identified exporting Kazakhstan’s financial industry as another strategic priority. This includes helping domestic financial companies enter foreign markets and attracting international players that can serve global customers through Kazakhstan’s jurisdiction and financial infrastructure.

He said the country has a strong domestic financial jurisdiction alongside the Astana International Financial Center, which he described as an additional driver of competition and investment.

The next stage, however, will depend on whether market participants can turn the established infrastructure and regulatory framework into products that can compete both domestically and internationally.

“We have a strong foundation, but now we need the market to become more active – with new products, partnerships and business models that will allow us to fully use these opportunities,” Suleimenov said.

The Central Asia Fintech Summit 2026 brings together more than 120 speakers and experts. It focuses on the development of digital finance, including payments, digital assets, AI, cybersecurity, tokenization and anti-fraud technologies.

World.title: Kazakhstan Highlights Middle Corridor Growth and Digitalization at Batumi Forum
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan highlighted the rapid growth of the Middle Corridor and the need to accelerate its digitalization at the Georgian International Maritime Forum in Batumi on Sept. 7-8.

Kazakhstan Deputy Minister of Transport Zhanibek Taizhanov said freight volumes along the Trans-Caspian International Transport Route (TITR) rose 22% in January-August, while East-West transit increased 55%.

Digitalization drives seamless transit

Speaking at the panel session From Seas to Corridors: The New Geography of Global Trade, Taizhanov stressed the importance of integrating maritime, rail and port infrastructure to make international supply chains more efficient and resilient, the ministry’s press service reported.

He also presented President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev’s initiative to develop a digital map of transport routes, providing an integrated view of transport infrastructure, logistics chains and cargo flows along international corridors.

The Middle Corridor currently has a capacity of 6 million tons, including 182,000 TEUs. Measures to streamline logistics have reduced cargo delivery times from 38 days to 13-17 days, with a target of 10-12 days from China to ports in Georgia and Türkiye.

Kazakhstan is also advancing the Digital Trade Corridor, which enables online cargo tracking and single-window contracting. Its Tez Customs module has reduced transit customs processing from eight hours to 30 minutes, the ministry told The Astana Times.

Infrastructure expansion

The forum brought together government officials, maritime administrations, international organizations, port operators, logistics companies and industry experts.

Discussions covered port infrastructure, maritime cooperation, digital transformation, navigation and shipping safety, and applying the single-window principle in the maritime sector.

Discussions on the Middle Corridor also highlighted the need for further infrastructure investment. Speaking at the 5th International Forum on Freight Transport in the Black and Caspian Regions 2026 in Baku, World Bank Senior Transport and Logistics Specialist Luis Blancas said a new comprehensive report on the Middle Corridor is scheduled for publication on Sept. 27, Trend reported.

The report covers all nine participating countries and identifies 16 critical investment priorities worth around US$25 billion. More than three-quarters of the required investment is already underway, Blancas said.

The report is expected to provide a broader assessment of infrastructure needs as cargo flows between Asia and Europe continue to grow.

World.title: Weekend Highlights: Discover Ballet, Music and Sport
World.content:
ASTANA – Looking for ways to spend the weekend? From cultural events to music and entertainment, Astana and Almaty offer plenty to explore. The Astana Times editorial team has curated a special list of events perfect for enjoying with friends and family.

“Swan Lake” ballet, Sept. 11

Experience the timeless beauty of Tchaikovsky’s “Swan Lake” in a breathtaking ballet performance. This beloved folk tale follows a maiden cursed by dark forces to live as a swan. Prince Siegfried vows to save her, but fate leads him to a tragic betrayal. A masterpiece of classical ballet, “Swan Lake” captivates both newcomers and longtime fans. With stunning grace and precision, the dancers bring this story of love and destiny to life.

Venue: Astana Opera; 1 Konayev Street. Tickets are available here.

Open Air, Sept. 12

Enjoy an energetic open-air music event featuring live performances and a lively atmosphere. The outdoor setting makes it a great choice for those looking to spend the day with music and entertainment.

Venue: Kazanat Hippodrome. Tickets are available here.

Ne Prosto pop concert, Sept. 13

Enjoy a high-energy show of 2000s hits, performed by a symphony orchestra and choir, featuring songs by Black Eyed Peas, Lady Gaga, Rihanna, Beyonce and Bruno Mars.

Venue: Qazaqconcert; 10/1 Mangilik El Avenue. Tickets are available here.

“Splendid Silk” exhibition, Sept. 11 – 20

“Splendid Silk” explores the beauty and craftsmanship of Chinese silk through a collection of elegant textile artworks, offering a glimpse into one of the country’s enduring artistic traditions.

Venue: National Museum of Kazakhstan; 54 Tauelsizdik Avenue. Tickets are available here.

“Living Paintings” exhibition, Sept. 11- Oct. 3

Discover the famous seascapes of Ivan Aivazovsky through a multimedia exhibition that combines classic art with immersive visual technology.

Venue: Lumiere-Hall Multimedia Museum; 8 Abay Avenue. Tickets are available here.

Leonardo da Vinci’s work exhibition, Aug. 21 – Sept. 30

An exhibition dedicated to Leonardo da Vinci invites visitors to discover the artistic and scientific legacy of one of history’s most influential minds. Through reproductions, multimedia elements and interactive displays, the exhibition explores the inventor’s creative vision, engineering ideas and masterpieces, offering a closer look at the Renaissance era.

Venue: Palace of Peace and Reconciliation; 57 Tauelsizdik Avenue. Tickets are available here.

Almaty

Steppe Fair, Sept. 12

Explore a lively mix of creativity, technology, culture and business, with talks, workshops, networking, art and live music.

Venue: Otzalt space; 36 Baribaev Street. Tickets are available here.

Football match, Sept. 13

Feel the excitement of top-flight football as FC Kairat faces FC Tobol in a highly anticipated league match.

Venue: Central Stadium; 48 Abay Avenue. Tickets are available here.

Classical Music Evening, Sept. 13

Celebrate the start of the new season with Gustav Mahler’s powerful Symphony No. 2, performed by a symphony orchestra and choir.

Venue: Jambyl Kazakh State Philharmonic; 35 Kaldayakov Street. Tickets are available here.

World.title: Tokayev to Outline Kazakhstan’s Goals and Priorities in October Address
World.content:
ASTANA – President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev will deliver a state-of-the-nation address in October, outlining Kazakhstan’s goals and priorities for the upcoming period, he said during a Sept. 11 ceremony honoring winners and medalists of the sixth World Nomad Games in Astana.

President Tokayev made the announcement at a ceremony at the Palace of Independence, where he congratulated Kazakhstan’s athletes and coaches on their performances at the World Nomad Games, praising the national team for demonstrating strong skills and strengthening Kazakhstan’s standing in traditional sports.

“Today, the authority of Kazakh sport is higher than ever, and the whole world recognizes this. Our athletes are always among the best,” he said.

Tokayev also highlighted sport’s broader role in strengthening public health and human capital, pointing to work underway to advance these principles enshrined in the Constitution. He said Kazakhstan is moving forward as a nation focused on the future, with ambitious goals and clear plans.

Tokayev also highlighted Kazakhstan’s growing role as a host of major international sporting events. Next year, the capital will host seven world championships, while Almaty is set to host the 10th Asian Winter Games in 2029.

“We have a huge amount of work ahead, but all these international events are extremely important for strengthening the authority and prestige of our country,” Tokayev said.

World.title: Kazakh FM Outlines Priorities to Accelerate Investment Projects and Attract Foreign Capital
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan’s Foreign Minister Mukhtar Tileuberdi has outlined key priorities for strengthening the country’s efforts to attract foreign investment during a Sept. 10 working meeting with the leadership of the Investment Committee of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and KAZAKH INVEST.

The meeting brought together Investment Committee Chairman Ardak Zebeshev, KAZAKH INVEST Chairman of the Board Sultangali Kinzhaкulov, as well as deputy chairpersons, managing directors and heads of key areas of the two organizations.

The minister was briefed on the current state of work to attract foreign direct investment, implement investment projects and engage with potential investors. The meeting also covered the development of Kazakhstan’s national digital investment platform and preparations for international investment events.

Focus on investor engagement and project implementation

Following the meeting, Tileuberdi identified improving the effectiveness of engagement with investors and accelerating the implementation of investment projects as key priorities for the upcoming period. Particular attention was also given to ensuring a coordinated approach to attracting capital into Kazakhstan’s economy.

The ministry, the Investment Committee and KAZAKH INVEST will continue work in these areas as part of a unified approach to implementing Kazakhstan’s investment policy and strengthening the country’s position as an attractive destination for international capital.

World.title: Rybakina Reaches US Open Final to Face Ex-No. 1 Sabalenka
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan’s Elena Rybakina has reached the U.S. Open final for the first time in her career and secured the world No. 1 ranking, becoming the first Kazakhstan’s singles player to top the WTA rankings.

Rybakina defeated American Coco Gauff 3:6, 6:4, 6:4 in the semifinal, with the match lasting two hours and eight minutes. The 27-year-old Kazakh athlete recorded five aces, two double faults and converted three of five break-point opportunities.

Rybakina to face Sabalenka in US Open final

Rybakina will face Aryna Sabalenka of Belarus in the final. Regardless of the outcome, Rybakina will become the new world No. 1 when the WTA rankings are updated on Sept. 14, reported the Kazakhstan Tennis Federation.

Her rise to the top marks a historic achievement for Kazakhstan. Rybakina secured the top ranking after reaching the U.S. Open quarterfinals, where she defeated China’s Zheng Qinwen 3:6, 6:1, 6:4. The result ended Sabalenka’s 99-week run at the top of the women’s singles rankings. Rybakina subsequently moved past Sabalenka in the live rankings after reaching the semifinal.

Asian swing could shape the battle for No. 1

The U.S. Open final will determine the size of Rybakina’s lead over Sabalenka heading into the next stage of the season, but she already holds a favorable position in terms of ranking points to be defended during the upcoming Asian swing.

The key tournaments in the coming weeks include the WTA 1000 China Open in Beijing, the WTA 1000 Wuhan Open and the WTA 500 Ningbo Open.

In Beijing, Rybakina has relatively few points to defend, having earned nearly 130 points from an early exit last season. Sabalenka did not compete in Beijing last year and therefore has no points to defend, meaning every match she wins would add points to her ranking total.

The situation is reversed in Wuhan. Rybakina is defending 215 points from last year’s quarterfinal appearance, while Sabalenka, the defending champion, will need to defend 1,000 points, according to the Kazinform news agency.

Ningbo presents another important difference. Rybakina is defending 500 points after winning the tournament last year, while Sabalenka did not compete there and has no points on the line.

Based on the points due to expire during the Asian swing, Rybakina would enter the China tournaments with a minimum advantage of 256 points over Sabalenka, according to the calculations provided.

The Asian series could therefore become an important stage in determining whether Rybakina can consolidate her position at the top of the WTA rankings after making history at the U.S. Open.

Rybakina currently has 13 WTA singles titles to her name. The U.S. Open final against Sabalenka will offer her an opportunity to add a first U.S. Open title to her collection while completing an unprecedented rise to the top of women’s tennis for Kazakhstan.

Zhalgasbay reaches junior doubles semifinals

Kazakhstan also recorded another strong result at the U.S. Open, with junior player Damir Zhalgasbay advancing to the semifinals of the junior boys’ doubles tournament.

Zhalgasbay, Kazakhstan’s No. 2 junior, is competing alongside American Safir Azam. The pair defeated Puerto Rico’s Yannick Alvarez and American Ryan Kozad 6:3, 6:7 (14:16), 10:6 in the quarterfinals.

The match lasted one hour and 22 minutes. Zhalgasbay and Azam recorded five aces, four double faults and converted three of six break-point opportunities.

In the semifinal, they will face the winners of the quarterfinal between the American duo of Tanishka Konduri and Marcela Lataca and the top-seeded pairing of Brazil’s Guto Miguel and Slovenia’s Ziga Sesko.

With Rybakina competing for the women’s singles title and Zhalgasbay advancing in the junior doubles draw, Kazakhstan remains represented in the closing stages of the 2026 U.S. Open.

World.title: How Will Kazakhstan’s Kurultai Work? New Rules Set Sessions, Ethics and Penalties
World.content:
ASTANA – Deputies of Kazakhstan’s Kurultai will face new rules governing their conduct inside and outside the legislative chamber, with violations ranging from inappropriate remarks and providing unverified information to breaches of parliamentary ethics that could result in public apologies, restrictions on speaking and other disciplinary measures.

Deputy Chair of the Kurultai Daniya Yespayeva outlined the rules at a briefing for media representatives after the plenary meeting of deputies on Sept. 10.

The new provisions form part of the Kurultai’s approved regulations, which establish the procedures for the legislative body’s work, including parliamentary sessions, the legislative process, government hours, hearings and the activities of parliamentary factions and committees.

Kurultai to meet Wednesdays and Thursdays

Under the new regulations, the Kurultai’s regular session will run from the first working day of September to the last working day of June. Plenary sessions will generally be held on Wednesdays and Thursdays, while hearings will take place on Fridays and government hours on Mondays.

Sessions will run from 10 a.m. to 6 p.m., with a break from 1 p.m. to 2:30 p.m. The Kurultai or its Bureau may decide to hold sessions at other times when necessary. A session is valid when at least two-thirds of the total number of deputies are present, meaning at least 97 deputies.

The regulations provide for open sessions as the general rule. Open meetings will be broadcast, including online through Kurultai’s internet resources. The legislative body will maintain transcripts and video recordings, and will also publish transcripts of open sessions on its website.

Between regular sessions, deputies will continue exercising their powers, including initiating legislation, preparing amendments to laws and working with constituents. Deputies may travel to the regions for up to 10 calendar days, and such visits must take place at least twice during a session.

Deputies are required to provide verified information

According to Yespayeva, violations of parliamentary ethics may include unjustified remarks directed at speakers and statements that insult or otherwise affect the honor and dignity of deputies or other individuals.

The ethical requirements will apply not only during Kurultai sessions and meetings of its factions, groups and other bodies, but also to deputies’ conduct outside the legislature. Specific requirements also apply to deputies’ interactions with the media. In public statements, responses and interviews, deputies are expected to provide verified and accurate information.

“Simply saying that something is not being fulfilled, or citing certain facts when they are not reliable, will also constitute a violation of parliamentary ethics,” Yespayeva said.

The provision emphasizes deputies’ responsibility for public statements, particularly because their comments to the media can influence public perceptions of government policies and legislative work.

Disciplinary measures range from reprimands to salary deductions

A Council on Parliamentary Ethics will be established to consider complaints concerning deputies’ conduct. The council will accept appeals from individuals and legal entities and will also conduct educational work on parliamentary ethics.

The council’s regulations were adopted the day before the briefing. Several types of disciplinary measures are available for violations. A deputy may receive a reprimand or be required to issue a public apology.

More serious measures include being prohibited from speaking at one Kurultai session or, in more severe cases, at three sessions. The law also provides for a deputy to be removed from one or three Kurultai sessions.

The most severe sanction among those outlined by Yespayeva is the withholding of one day’s salary. However, the Council on Parliamentary Ethics will not decide on sanctions independently. It will consider the alleged violation and issue a decision, after which the matter will be considered at a Kurultai session.

Council to focus on both enforcement and prevention

Yespayeva stressed that the Council on Parliamentary Ethics will have a broader role than simply reviewing complaints. It will also conduct explanatory work to help deputies understand the rules and standards governing their conduct.

The emphasis on guidance reflects the significant renewal of the Kurultai’s current composition. According to Yespayeva, nearly 70–80% of the deputies are new, meaning that many are working within the legislative framework for the first time.

The council’s explanatory function is therefore intended to help deputies understand the boundaries of acceptable conduct and their responsibilities before violations occur.

New regulations define Kurultai’s legislative work

The regulations also establish the procedures for considering draft laws. Most bills will be considered in three readings, while legislation on the ratification or denunciation of international treaties will be considered in two readings.

The first reading will focus on a bill’s goals, objectives and main provisions, as well as its potential social, economic, legal, environmental and other consequences. The second reading will consider amendments submitted by deputies, committees and party factions. The third reading will generally be limited to amendments needed to bring a draft law into compliance with the Constitution and legislation, eliminate contradictions and address editorial or legal-technical issues. Substantive changes will not be introduced at this stage.

Parliamentary opposition receives procedural guarantees

The regulations also establish procedures for the parliamentary majority and opposition. A political party holding the largest number of deputy mandates is recognized as the majority. Political parties represented in the Kurultai but not part of the majority may form a parliamentary opposition.

The opposition will have specific procedural rights. It may initiate hearings at least once during each session and determine the agenda of a government hour at least twice per session. The regulations also provide for opposition representation in the leadership of permanent committees.

The framework also regulates the work of party factions and deputy groups, requiring at least 15 deputies to establish a deputy group. The new rules thus combine procedures governing legislative work with requirements concerning deputies’ individual conduct and accountability.

World.title: EPRC: Wildberries expansion poses significant risks for Georgia
World.content:
According to the Economic Policy Research Center (EPRC), the expansion of the Russian online platform Wildberries in Georgia poses significant risks for the country.

The centre makes this assessment in a new report examining the threats that Wildberries-related activities could pose to Georgian brands represented on the platform, consumers, Georgian banks and Georgia’s economic and financial system as a whole.

Wildberries is an online marketplace often described as “Russia’s Amazon”.

According to EPRC, at least eight Wildberries warehouses were put out of operation by Ukrainian strikes in late August 2026, while more than 20 facilities were damaged. During the same period, part of the company’s financial ecosystem, Wildberries Bank, was placed under international sanctions.

The centre says that, while Wildberries’ warehouse infrastructure in Russia became a target for Ukrainian drones and the company’s banking arm was placed on a sanctions list, Wildberries used Georgia and other neighbouring countries to expand its trading network and logistics capabilities.

EPRC predicts that, as a result, Georgia could become part of a regional infrastructure helping a company linked to the Kremlin and sanctioned Russian businesses reduce losses caused by the war and sanctions.

The report notes that Wildberries’ official infrastructure in Georgia includes warehouses, sorting centres and collection points. According to the company’s instructions, updated on 4 June 2026, Georgian sellers can choose a warehouse or sorting centre and review the conditions for accepting products, logistics rates, sorting times and delivery times to consumers.

According to EPRC, this indicates that the company’s activities in Georgia are no longer limited to collection points. Local infrastructure is also being used to receive, sort and subsequently deliver products. However, open sources do not currently confirm the existence of a large logistics centre in Georgia. A similar situation exists in Azerbaijan.

According to the report, information spread in September 2025 that local businesses had been given the opportunity to sell their products directly through the Wildberries platform.

EPRC also publishes what it believes is an incomplete list of Georgian brands available on the platform. The centre explains that finding a complete list is difficult because Wildberries does not allow users to search for brands by country of origin.

At this stage, the list of Georgian products and brands on the platform is believed to include Borjomi, Nabeghlavi, Natakhtari, Zedazeni, Gurieli, Kula, Badagoni, Chateau Mukhrani, Askaneli, Sarajishvili, MACH & MACH, ANOUKI and Aleksandre Akhalkatsishvili.

EPRC stresses that Wildberries operates as a marketplace. The presence of a particular product on the platform does not automatically mean that the manufacturer or an official brand representative is selling it directly. The product may be listed either by the manufacturer or by an independent reseller.

According to the centre, if an independent retailer sells the product, the brand may restrict those sales by protecting its intellectual property or using contractual mechanisms.

In EPRC’s assessment, Wildberries’ expansion in Georgia is no longer solely a matter of developing online trade. The centre identifies several major risks.

In particular, the report says Wildberries is linked to Russia’s trading and financial system, and its ties to the Kremlin have also been confirmed. The company’s financial arm, Wildberries Bank, has been placed under UK and EU sanctions. According to EPRC, the sanctions are linked to the bank’s role in financially supporting the military and the Russian authorities’ aggressive interests.

The centre also says the Wildberries platform is used to purchase goods needed by the Russian military, including military equipment and dual-use goods. According to EPRC, independent journalistic investigations have also confirmed this.

Against this backdrop, the report’s authors question the effectiveness of controls over the trade and export of such products in Georgia. In their assessment, this increases the risk that sanctioned goods or dual-use items could enter or be re-exported through the country.

EPRC pays particular attention to the development of Wildberries’ logistics capabilities in Georgia. The centre believes that, after a significant part of the company’s warehouse network in Russia was damaged, infrastructure outside Russia has become even more important to Wildberries. Georgia could therefore become part of the company’s regional diversification network.

The report also describes the growing integration of Georgian businesses into the Wildberries system. Products from Georgian brands are already sold on the platform, and Georgian entrepreneurs can join it as direct sellers. EPRC believes this creates both reputational and potential financial risks for companies in the future.

According to the centre, Georgia’s financial sector is also at risk. Wildberries Bank came under UK and EU sanctions in 2026, while 5% of the bank is also owned by the sanctioned Russian bank VTB.

EPRC says that the fact that customers in Georgia pay for purchases on Wildberries using Georgian bank cards means that the local banking sector must comply with the sanctions regime and carry out additional transaction checks. According to the centre, after sanctions were imposed on Wildberries Bank, the National Bank of Georgia shifted responsibility to individual financial institutions, explaining that each bank must assess the risks of violating or circumventing sanctions independently.

In EPRC’s assessment, given these circumstances, the development in Georgia of infrastructure linked to a sanctioned financial institution, a business close to the Kremlin and a platform used to supply the Russian military cannot simply be viewed as foreign investment or the expansion of retail trade.

The centre suggests that if Wildberries continues to expand in Georgia without state oversight or proper customs and financial monitoring, and Georgian companies and banks deepen their cooperation with the platform, the country could become part of an economic and logistics network that helps Russian businesses continue operating amid war and international sanctions.

EPRC believes that such a process could have long-term economic and reputational consequences for Georgia.

EPRC on the risks posed by Wildberries in Georgia

World.title: Georgian Legion commander on former prosecutor general: ‘He is following directives from Russian intelligence services’
World.content:
According to a statement by Mamuka Mamulashvili, commander of the pro-Ukrainian Georgian Legion, former Georgian prosecutor general Otar Partskhaladze, who recently took command of a unit fighting on Russia’s side, is following directives from Russian intelligence services. Mamulashvili also said Partskhaladze’s value as a military figure was zero.

The Georgian Legion is a volunteer formation established in 2014 after Russia invaded eastern Ukraine. In 2016, the Georgian Legion officially joined Ukraine’s 25th Motorised Infantry Battalion. It is now subordinate to the Main Directorate of Intelligence of Ukraine’s Defence Ministry. The unit includes Georgian volunteers as well as fighters of other nationalities. It currently has around 2,000 members. In 2023, Russia’s Interior Ministry added Georgian Legion commander Mamuka Mamulashvili to its wanted list.

According to Mamulashvili, Otar Partskhaladze will try to draw ethnic Georgians living in Russia into his adventure — the war against Ukraine. However, his chances of success are doubtful, as very few Georgians fighting on Russia’s side are seen on the front line, and most of them have already been killed.

Former Georgian prosecutor general Otar Romanov-Partskhaladze, who is fighting on Russia’s side, told Russian pro-Kremlin media that members of the Georgian Legion are “war criminals” and will face prosecution under Russian law. Earlier, on 7 September, it became known that Partskhaladze would lead the international “St George” unit, which was created to take part in the war against Ukraine.

Mamuka Mamulashvili: “Partskhaladze will get a response. He will realise that he made a serious mistake by launching a campaign against the Georgian Legion.

No unit, not even Ukrainian ones, has faced the kind of pressure the Georgian Legion has endured. We are one of the oldest units, even compared with Ukrainian volunteer formations. Russia does not like the fact that so many Georgians are fighting on Ukraine’s side. That is why Russia has been fighting us for more than 12 years, both informationally and physically.

Since they failed to destroy the Georgian Legion physically, they have now tried to create a counterweight by forming another Georgian unit that supposedly will fight on Russia’s side. In reality, this is an attempt to discredit Georgia and bring it under the same sanctions that Russia faces. To do this, they are using people with Georgian surnames who live in Russia and who make all sorts of absurd claims that the Georgian Legion should be tried under Russian law.

In 2022, Russia designated the Georgian Legion as a terrorist organisation. This is hardly surprising, as the Georgian Legion has inflicted enormous damage on the Russian Federation. We can see that their disinformation machine has become much more active. Attempts to kill us physically and attacks have also increased. I have personally been attacked seven times and have survived three attempts to poison me.

Partskhaladze is following directives from Russian intelligence services because his own value as a military figure is zero. I doubt that this man knows which end of a weapon fires. Most likely, he was ordered to finance and create another battalion. He will then try to draw people with Georgian surnames who live in Russia into this adventure. I do not know how successful he will be, because over these 12 years I have encountered very few Georgians on the front line — and those I did encounter were already dead.

The battalion will most likely consist of Russians, with a few Georgian-speaking people who will claim that the unit is mainly made up of Georgians.”

Commander of the Georgian Legion on former prosecutor general

World.title: Mzia Amaglobeli: ‘All it takes to avoid asking the regime for pardon is self-respect’
World.content:
“I don’t need advice to avoid apologising to an aggressor or asking the regime for a pardon. A sense of self-respect is enough,” political prisoner Mzia Amaglobeli writes in response to a statement by Shalva Papuashvili, speaker of the parliament of Georgia. At a briefing on 9 September, Papuashvili called prisoners of conscience “prisoners of Brussels’ shamelessness”.

The publication Batumelebi published Amaglobeli’s letter.

Mzia Amaglobeli: “The briefing in parliament was a display of shamelessness and nothing else. The regime has no morals. They do not even want to take responsibility for the unjust verdict that, in the name of Georgia, sent us to prison and branded us dangerous criminals.

They point the finger at Brussels and European diplomats. Shame on them. I don’t need advice to avoid apologising to an aggressor or asking the regime for a pardon. A sense of self-respect is enough.

If two years in prison is not humiliating enough, it will not be difficult for you to come up with something else if you want to keep me behind bars.

Power and state institutions are in your hands.

As for me, I will wait for international justice. I will wait for the day when the European Court of Human Rights examines the legality of the charges against me and the sentence imposed on me for slapping someone.

And you wait too, Mr Papuashvili. The European Court will examine the fairness and legitimacy of the repressive laws you have adopted, as well as their compliance with the Constitution and democratic processes.”

What Shalva Papuashvili said

On 9 September, commenting on the situation of political prisoners and prisoners of conscience, Shalva Papuashvili said they were “prisoners of Brussels’ shamelessness”. Papuashvili also spoke specifically about convicted journalist Mzia Amaglobeli, claiming that the court had given her the lightest possible sentence.

“Under Georgia’s Criminal Procedure Code, a lesser sentence is possible only through a plea agreement. That is what both the law and practice provide. A plea agreement was offered to her. It required only one thing: for Mzia Amaglobeli to acknowledge that what she had done was a crime and that her conduct had been wrong.

Mzia Amaglobeli is a prisoner of the shamelessness of those ambassadors who sat in court, looked her in the eye and effectively told her: ‘Do not plead guilty. Stay in prison.’ It is also the fault of those who awarded her completely unjustified prizes, including the European Parliament, thereby encouraging her not to admit that attacking a police officer is a crime,” Papuashvili said.

Mzia Amaglobeli, founder of the well-known publications Batumelebi and Netgazeti, is the first female journalist in Georgia to become a prisoner of conscience.

Authorities arrested her in January 2025 in the city of Batumi during a protest after she slapped the head of the local police, Irakli Dgebuadze. The incident followed a confrontation between protesters and police, which the officers had provoked.

On 6 August 2025, Batumi City Court sentenced Mzia Amaglobeli to two years in prison. The court rejected her lawyer’s request to change her pre-trial measure.

Mzia Amaglobeli responds to the speaker of parliament

World.title: Armenia’s Anti-Corruption Commission did not open proceedings against Pashinyan
World.content:
Commission rejects case against Pashinyan

The Corruption Prevention Commission refused to open administrative proceedings against Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan. Commission members said the complaint contained no “obvious signs of violations of the code of conduct”.

Semyon Babayan, head of the human rights NGO Public Informant, had asked the commission to assess the prime minister’s alleged “violations of the code of conduct”.

“Pashinyan’s public rhetoric and the wording he often uses grossly violate the legally established integrity system and the ethical standards that public officials must follow,” the applicant said.

He presented the commission with 11 such examples. One of them was the word “immoral”, which the prime minister used to describe the Catholicos of All Armenians.

According to the human rights activist, “it insults the feelings of believers and violates the requirement for religious neutrality”.

However, the commission found that the wording remained within the permissible limits of freedom of expression.

For a long time, Nikol Pashinyan has demanded that Catholicos of All Armenians Garegin II step down. He claims that the Catholicos has broken his vow of celibacy and has a daughter. The prime minister also believes that the Catholicos has links to foreign intelligence services and follows their orders. On 24 August, Nikol Pashinyan called the Catholicos “immoral” while speaking in parliament. He also referred to the Patriarch by his secular name, Ktrich Nersisyan. He has used this name for him since launching his campaign to reform the Church. In protest, opposition MPs banged on their desks every time the Catholicos’s name was mentioned. “Your Catholicos is immoral. If you are not bothered by the fact that the man who heads the Mother See is sexually active, then keep banging your desks as much as you like. There is no other way to have a child — even in the Church. There is only one way to have a child: sexual intercourse,” Pashinyan said.

Commission says the word “immoral” falls within the bounds of political speech

The commission commented on the use of the word “immoral” against the Catholicos, citing case law from the European Court of Human Rights. It stressed that political speech enjoys a broader scope of protection.

Commission members assessed the prime minister’s wording as falling within what is permissible in the context of political debate:

“The use of exaggeration, generalisations and even shocking or striking expressions is characteristic of political speech during political debates — in this case, a speech delivered from the parliamentary rostrum.”

They also noted that, according to the European Court of Human Rights, freedom of expression covers not only positive and favourable statements, but also those that may “offend, shock or disturb”.

The Corruption Prevention Commission therefore concluded that the prime minister’s statement should be considered in the broader context of political debate.

The decision also gives the meaning of the Armenian word “պիղծ”, which Pashinyan used, citing academician Eduard Aghayan’s Explanatory Dictionary of the Modern Armenian Language. It notes that the word primarily means “unclean, immoral, vicious”, while in a religious context it means “heretical, unacceptable, ungodly”.

As for the statement “your Patriarch is immoral”, commission members found no attack on the faith or a religious group. In their view, Pashinyan made an “assessment of the alleged conduct” of a specific member of the clergy:

“Pashinyan’s statement sought to criticise not the person, but a specific phenomenon — namely, the alleged violation of the vow of celibacy.”

The commission also stressed that the word “immoral” carries a negative connotation but “does not cross the line into vulgarity or profanity”. Its members also found no calls for violence or threats in Pashinyan’s speech.

According to the decision, the prime minister’s speech was “predominantly critical in nature, as is characteristic of political debate”.

What other violations did the human rights activist identify?

Semyon Babayan also told the commission about 10 other “serious violations” that he believes the prime minister had committed:

“Violation of the principle of separation of powers: a public statement that ‘there is no judge who would not do what I tell them to do’, which directly undermines the independence of the judiciary and trust in democratic institutions.

Use of offensive language: using crude, street-level rhetoric in public against opponents or citizens — conduct that is clearly incompatible with the ethics expected of a senior public official.

Unsubstantiated assessments and ‘back-of-the-envelope estimates’: arbitrarily citing percentages related to corruption and bribery, such as 70% or 100%, without referring to official or verified factual data.

Erosion of public trust: using threats and divisive rhetoric from a high state platform, which contributes to the spread of intolerance.

Threats to ‘smear [people] across the asphalt’: publicly calling for the use of force in a personalised and punitive manner, outside the framework of legal procedures.

The phrase ‘whimpering judges’: humiliating members of the judiciary and systematically discrediting the institution.

Statements that citizens would be ‘brought to their knees’ because of their political views: entrenching a culture of communication based on force and a commanding tone that is unbecoming of a statesman.

Segregation of fellow citizens by labelling them ‘persons of Armenian origin’: violating the principle of national unity and artificially dividing society.

Showing preferential treatment towards members of his own team: violating the principle of equal integrity standards for the sake of political expediency.

Erosion of the integrity and image of a public official: maintaining a marginal, sarcastic and aggressive tone in public debate, undermining the duty of a public official to set an example of appropriate conduct.”

The commission found no signs of an obvious violation in any of the examples cited.

Commission rejects case against Pashinyan

World.title: Property prices in Armenia rise again: new wave of emigration from Russia and other factors
World.content:
Armenia is seeing another wave of people relocating to the country, amid reports over the past two months of a possible mobilisation in Russia. As a result, both rents and property prices have risen again. On average, prices for rentals and properties for sale have increased by 20%.

At one point, prices were rising almost every day. This was evident from listings on popular online property sales and rental platforms. The biggest boom has been in the rental market. Activity is also increasing in cities near Yerevan, including Abovyan, Masis and Nor Hachn.

Most of those arriving are Armenians who had been living in Russia. They say they are moving to avoid being called up for military service and because of the uncertainty they have faced in recent months.

Amid the large influx, it has become difficult to find affordable and mid-range rental properties. This is also linked to students from the regions moving to the capital as the new academic year begins.

A Russian man found a job but cannot find a flat

Dmitry Popov arrived in Armenia with friends three weeks ago. They first stayed in Yerevan, then moved to Lori Province, where they found jobs in the towns of Alaverdi and Tumanyan.

He decided to stay in Yerevan, where he has acquaintances who offered him a place to stay. He has already found a job as a courier with one of Yerevan’s companies. He is now negotiating his pay with his employer. Meanwhile, Dmitry has been looking for a one- or two-bedroom flat in the outer districts of the capital. He cannot afford a place in the city centre because rents there are very high.

“At first, I was looking for a place for up to $500. Now I’m looking for one for $700. I still haven’t found anything because I need basic amenities — furniture and household appliances. Even when I find a flat with an average-quality renovation, it turns out there is no fridge, washing machine or comfortable sofa,” the young man explains.

He knows that the latest influx of migrants from Russia is largely driving the rise in prices.

After the initial influx and surge in prices during the first months of the Russia-Ukraine war, the property market began to stabilise. Prices fell slightly as many Russians returned home or moved to other countries. Now they have risen again.

“To be honest, I really like Yerevan. The city has its own rhythm, an interesting cultural scene, good food, friendly people and convenient public transport. I managed to find a job within a few days. Now I just need to find a flat. If I can’t find one in Yerevan, I’ll look in nearby towns. I’m asking local people how public transport works in the suburbs, what rental options are available and how lively those places are,” Dmitry says.

He says he did not have many options: he could either move to Yerevan or Tbilisi:

“I’ve visited both cities many times and had already been considering moving to one of them before the recent tensions in Russia. My friends who have lived in both cities recommended Yerevan, even though it is more expensive than Tbilisi. They said people in Yerevan are friendly, welcoming towards Russians and willing to help. They also said it would be easier to find a job here. By the way, they also suggested moving to other Armenian cities, such as Gyumri, Dilijan and Vanadzor.”

He says relatives in Russia call him to ask whether they should move to Armenia for the long term. He recommends it, although he also tells them about the problems.

He has already decided that if he manages to earn more in the future, he will buy a one-bedroom flat in Yerevan.

Factors affecting prices

Andranik Harutyunyan, director of Silver REA real estate agency, says apartment rents have risen by around 15% compared with last year. This is an average estimate, as prices vary significantly between different parts of the city and types of apartments.

The same applies to the property sales market. According to the estate agent, it is difficult to establish a single rate of price growth and compare it with last year’s figures:

“It is quite difficult to assess price changes in the primary market because developers sell apartments in residential complexes at different prices depending on the stage of construction. The secondary market is also seeing a noticeable increase in demand.”

Harutyunyan notes that members of the Armenian diaspora are showing greater interest in apartments on the secondary market. For them, buying property is a form of business investment. By renting out a property, they can earn a higher annual return than they would by keeping the same amount of money in a bank.

“Those who moved to Armenia after the Russia-Ukraine war began are also active. Some have been living here for about a year and have decided to settle permanently. Another group consists of people who had ties to Armenia in the past but have now decided to move their businesses and families here.

Interest is also being driven by the growing value placed on property assets in Armenia in recent years. As a result, demand for housing remains high in both the primary and secondary markets,” the real estate agency director says.

Apartment price trends by administrative district

According to data from the Cadastre Committee, property prices continued to rise across all of Yerevan’s administrative districts in the second quarter of 2026. However, the pace of growth varied. The biggest increases came in Nork-Marash, Shengavit and Ajapnyak.

Nork-Marash recorded the sharpest increase, with the average price reaching 553,000 drams ($1,527) per square metre. Compared with last year, this represents a 24% rise.

Apartment prices in Shengavit rose by around 19% over the same period, while prices in Ajapnyak increased by 16%. More construction and relatively affordable prices have helped drive demand in these districts.

Price changes were more moderate in other parts of the city. Growth has been relatively slow in the Small Centre and neighbouring Arabkir, largely because prices there were already high.

Overall, property prices in Yerevan continue to rise. However, the strongest growth is occurring in districts with development potential and relatively more affordable prices.

World.title: How does Georgia’s parliament work? SJC analyses current legislative processes
World.content:
The Social Justice Center (SJC) analyses the work of Georgia’s 11th Parliament between 25 November 2024 and 26 June 2026. It notes that the parliament’s work has, on the one hand, undermined democratic institutions and rights and, on the other, expanded the executive branch’s discretionary powers and strengthened the centralisation of power.

The organisation’s director, Tamta Mikeladze, published the report’s main findings:

During this period, parliament adopted 276 legislative packages or initiatives. Almost half went through an accelerated procedure, while around 10% followed a simplified procedure. This means parliament adopted around 60% of legislative acts through accelerated or simplified procedures. The executive branch submitted more initiatives than parliament itself, showing that the legislative agenda was largely driven by government initiatives.

Almost half went through an accelerated procedure, while around 10% followed a simplified procedure. This means parliament adopted around 60% of legislative acts through accelerated or simplified procedures. The executive branch submitted more initiatives than parliament itself, showing that the legislative agenda was largely driven by government initiatives. During the same period, the parliament, which was almost entirely made up of members of the ruling Georgian Dream party, did not adopt a single opposition legislative initiative , including those submitted by the Gakharia for Georgia parliamentary party. After Gakharia for Georgia entered parliament, lawmakers formally opposed legislative initiatives in only 38 cases. In all other cases, they adopted the initiatives unanimously.

, including those submitted by the Gakharia for Georgia parliamentary party. After Gakharia for Georgia entered parliament, lawmakers formally opposed legislative initiatives in only 38 cases. In all other cases, they adopted the initiatives unanimously. The quality of the legislative process is also problematic. Explanatory notes generally did not indicate that broad consultations had taken place and often lacked relevant sectoral or comparative legal analysis. Of the 276 initiatives, local or international experts took part in only six cases, while just eight initiatives provided for the harmonisation of Georgian legislation with legal instruments of the Council of Europe, the EU or the UN.

Against this backdrop, the parliament’s work can be divided into several main areas:

● Restrictions on civil society and repressive controls – 7 legislative changes. Alongside the laws on “transparency of foreign influence” and “registration of foreign agents”, parliament amended the law on grants. These changes effectively placed civil society organisations under full state control and criminalised certain forms of their activity. Parliament also created an Agency for the Management of State Grants, restricted NGOs’ participation in state decision-making, tightened the rules for issuing and receiving grants, broadened the legal definition of a grant, and introduced new criminal and financial sanctions.

● Media and freedom of expression – 6 direct changes: rules on foreign funding changed, the Communications Commission gained wider powers, new requirements for broadcast content were introduced, coverage of court proceedings was restricted, and financial oversight mechanisms were strengthened.

● Five separate changes concerned freedom of assembly and expression, increasing administrative and criminal liability for actions related to protests.

● Public service – 8 changes. Institutional safeguards for civil servants were weakened, while political appointments and the discretion of senior officials gained greater importance. The Civil Service Bureau was abolished, and opportunities for employment under administrative contracts were expanded. At the same time, new financial benefits and mechanisms for obtaining permission to engage in certain activities were introduced, with access to them largely dependent on decisions by senior officials. This creates a risk of not only politicisation but also clientelist governance.

● Education and academia also became targets of centralisation. Changes adopted in 2025-2026 strengthened the government’s influence over university funding, student numbers, academic programmes, and the reorganisation and institutional structure of universities. The limited involvement of academics in the process points to a broader problem with academic freedom.

● Ideological and propaganda-related measures – 7 major legislative changes. These included the introduction of a new crime, “treason against the state”; the removal of the term “gender” from legislation; tougher drug policies; changes to labour and immigration rules for foreigners; and expanded mechanisms of state control. What these changes have in common is not only tougher policies in specific areas, but also the incorporation of political and ideological concepts into the legal framework.

It is also important to look not only at what parliament adopted, but at what it left off its agenda. During the reporting period, issues concerning the rights of children and prisoners, public procurement and corruption prevention, environmental protection and civil safety, healthcare, urban planning and construction, education, regional policy, agriculture and tourism were pushed into the background or postponed. As a result, parliament’s agenda was clearly dominated by restrictive and controlling legislation. At the same time, its positive legislative agenda, covering a broad range of public interests, was significantly weakened.

Tamta Mikeladze: “The parliament’s work is therefore, on the one hand, directed against democratic institutions and rights, while on the other, it strengthens the executive branch’s discretionary powers and centralisation.

The theoretical frameworks of ‘autocratic legalism’ and ‘sham law’ are important for describing this process. In such a system, a law may formally meet the technical requirements of a legal act, but it loses its primary function: limiting state power and reducing arbitrariness. The law no longer acts as a mechanism for constraining power. Instead, it becomes a tool for maintaining and consolidating power.

In short, Georgia’s process of autocratisation, after years of oscillating between hybrid democracy and hybrid authoritarianism, is now aggressively and systematically affecting the legal sphere itself for the first time. It is fundamentally changing the law’s substance and nature.

We still have no adequate understanding of how difficult it will be to rehabilitate the state, political system, legal system and society after the crisis and the authoritarian period that Georgian Dream has inflicted on them.”

On legislation in Georgia

World.title: Georgian blogger says Interior Ministry wants to punish him for insulting Russian propagandists
World.content:
Civil rights activist and blogger Tornike Razmadze says Georgia’s Interior Ministry has summoned him to court to impose a fine or administrative detention because he insulted Kremlin propagandists Margarita Simonyan and Vladimir Solovyov in response to their insults against Georgian King Erekle II.

Georgia’s recently established Hate Speech Unit at the Interior Ministry has accused Razmadze of violating Article 166, Part 1 of the Code of Administrative Offences. The provision covers swearing in a public place and carries a fine of 500 to 3,000 lari ($185–1,110) or administrative detention for up to 20 days.

According to the activist, the case concerns a video he posted several weeks ago in which Russian propagandists discussed Erekle II, calling him a “king who crawled on his knees”. Margarita Simonyan, in particular, claimed that King Erekle had begged the Russians for help “on his knees” and that modern Georgians would likewise get down on their knees and ask Russia to take them under its protection.

Tornike Razmadze explains that this was why he used obscene language against Simonyan and Solovyov — more precisely, against their mothers.

According to the blogger, Simonyan and Solovyov effectively insulted the ruling Georgian Dream party as well. What angers him most is that, instead of taking offence at the Russian propagandists, the government wants to punish the person who insulted them. Razmadze sees this message from the authorities as the most important aspect of the whole case.

The activist also appealed to Georgia’s Public Defender (Ombudsman):

“I am not asking you for protection or support. I have one simple request: record your position on the case opened against me. I simply want to hear your position.”

However, the Interior Ministry’s Hate Speech Unit said the case had nothing to do with kings or propagandists. It said Tornike Razmadze was accused of insulting Georgian Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze.

“Insulting comments on social media by citizen Tornike Razmadze and Anna Bdeyan directed at Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze were identified. Administrative proceedings have been launched against them under Articles 166 and 173,” the Interior Ministry said.

The blogger’s lawyer, Mikheil Zakareishvili, in turn, says the Interior Ministry deliberately added Article 173, which concerns insulting a public official, to the charges. He says the original reports did not contain such wording. The lawyer is convinced that the case was opened specifically because of the insults directed at Simonyan and Solovyov.

The Georgian Young Lawyers’ Association (GYLA) considers the case against Razmadze another example of restrictions on freedom of expression. The association says prosecuting people over statements made on social media violates their fundamental constitutional rights and freedom of expression.

What is the Hate Speech Unit

The new Hate Speech Unit at Georgia’s Interior Ministry began operating on 1 June 2026. According to the ministry, its main task is to identify public statements that demean human dignity or are offensive and may constitute administrative offences.

Over the past three months, the unit has fined dozens of people. Vakhtang Sanaya, a journalist and presenter on Formula TV, became the first person to receive a two-week administrative detention sentence. Activist Giorgi Akhobadze also received a one-month detention sentence for a Facebook post.

World.title: Russian Orthodox Church calls on pilgrims to ‘boycott’ New Athos Monastery in Abkhazia
World.content:
The Russian Orthodox Church (ROC) has called on pilgrims not to visit the New Athos Monastery in Abkhazia.

The ROC considers the monastery’s abbot, Father Dorotheus, a schismatic.

However, this did not stop Sergei Kiriyenko, first deputy chief of staff of the Russian presidential administration and the Kremlin’s point man for Abkhazia, from visiting the monastery.

The Moscow Patriarchate’s chancellor, Metropolitan Grigory, has sent a circular letter to all bishops of the Russian Orthodox Church warning that Russian pilgrims must not attend services at the New Athos Monastery. The services there are led by defrocked hieromonk Dorotheus (Dbar).

“We are concerned about cases in which Orthodox pilgrims from dioceses of the Russian Orthodox Church visit the New Athos Monastery and take part in services held there. Pilgrims often go to confession and receive communion there without knowing that they should not.

I ask you to take measures to ensure that pilgrims travelling to holy sites in Abkhazia with your blessing are always informed that they must not engage in prayer or Eucharistic communion with the monk Dorotheus. They should also be informed that the sacraments performed in schism have no spiritual grace,” Metropolitan Grigory wrote.

Archimandrite Dorotheus

Archimandrite Dorotheus heads the Holy Metropolis of Abkhazia, one of two unrecognised Orthodox churches operating in the republic. A graduate of Aristotle University of Thessaloniki in Greece and a doctor of theology, he is highly popular in Abkhaz society and well known in church circles.

His “rival” is Father Vissarion, who heads the Abkhazian Orthodox Church (AOC). He is the only serving Abkhaz cleric ordained by the Georgian Orthodox Church during the Soviet era. Despite its unrecognised status, the AOC enjoys the active support of the Russian Orthodox Church.

The ROC, by contrast, has opposed Archimandrite Dorotheus and officially defrocked him in 2023 for refusing to submit to its authority.

The Holy Metropolis of Abkhazia and the AOC have been engaged in a long-running and bitter conflict.

Father Vissarion has also addressed not Russian but Abkhaz believers, saying they should not take part in services at New Athos.

Father Dorotheus himself believes that the Moscow Patriarchate’s letter was prompted by Archpriest Nikolai Balashov, an adviser to Patriarch Kirill of Moscow and All Russia. According to Dorotheus, Balashov has consistently worked in the interests of the Georgian Orthodox Church for decades.

“Similar circulars have appeared repeatedly. Yet their authors stubbornly refuse to acknowledge the main point: pilgrims who visit the New Athos Monastery are not there ‘out of ignorance’. The overwhelming majority of them knowingly take part in the services I conduct.

These people know the church bureaucracy well and can see that it contains no spiritual truth — only political and administrative manipulation,” Father Dorotheus wrote on his social media page.

Dorotheus believes another factor also prompted the AOC leadership to step up its activity. On 28 August 2026, Abkhaz President Badra Gunba and Sergei Kiriyenko, first deputy chief of staff of the Russian presidential administration, made an unofficial visit to the New Athos Monastery.

According to Dorotheus, this was the first time since 2011 that such high-ranking officials had visited their monastery.

The terminology, place names and views expressed in this article are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the editorial position of this website.

World.title: First day of diplomatic corps visit to Karabakh and East Zangezur concludes (PHOTO/VIDEO)
World.content:
SHUSHA, Azerbaijan, September 11. On September 11, the first day of the visit by representatives of the diplomatic corps accredited in Azerbaijan to Karabakh and Eastern Zangazur included visits to and inspections of a number of sites in the cities of Khankendi and Shusha, Trend's correspondent reports from the event.

In accordance with the visit program, representatives of the diplomatic corps first familiarized themselves with the ongoing works at the Khankendi Railway and Bus Terminal Complex. The participants were briefed on the work being carried out at the complex.

The delegation then visited the Cultural Center in Khankendi, where Assistant to the President of the Republic of Azerbaijan Hikmet Hajiyev welcomed the participants of the visit.

Representatives of the diplomatic corps visited the Victory Park and took a commemorative photograph in front of the Victory Arch.

As part of the visit, the participants also familiarized themselves with Karabakh University. They were briefed on the facilities created at the university and its activities. The representatives of the diplomatic corps then visited the sewing factory of *AzCotton LLC*, operating in Khankendi, and familiarized themselves with the enterprise’s activities.

The visit continued in the city of Shusha. Representatives of the diplomatic corps were briefed on the restoration and reconstruction works being carried out in the city. The diplomats inspected the construction of the New Shusha Mosque. They then visited Jidir Duzu, Karabakh Street and Shusha Central Square, as well as the “House of Sadigjan” and the Upper Govhar Agha Mosque. They also inspected the shot-up busts located in Shusha Central Square.

The diplomats viewed the exhibition “Heydar Aliyev and Karabakh” at the Shusha Creative Center. Afterwards, they visited the Shusha fortress walls and took a commemorative photograph in front of the walls. Representatives of the diplomatic corps familiarized themselves with the facilities created in the first residential quarter and met with residents of Shusha.

The participants of the visit attended an official reception held in Shusha on the occasion of the Independence Day of the United Mexican States.

The visit will continue on September 12.
