World.title: Hajiyev: Azerbaijan, Mexico have major potential to expand economic ties
World.content:
SHUSHA, Azerbaijan, September 11. There is significant potential for further developing economic, trade and investment ties between Azerbaijan and Mexico, Hikmet Hajiyev, Assistant to the President of Azerbaijan and head of the Foreign Policy Affairs Department of the Presidential Administration, made the remarks at an official reception in Shusha marking the Independence Day of the Republic of Mexico, Trend’s correspondent deployed to Karabakh and East Zangazur reports.

Hajiyev said there are broad prospects for developing relations between the two countries in economic, trade, cultural, humanitarian, investment, energy and other areas.

“There is a certain geographical distance between our countries, but this geographical distance is certainly not a problem for us. Both countries are firmly determined to ensure that our relations develop successfully across various areas,” he said.

According to the presidential aide, contacts between the relevant institutions of the two countries are continuing, particularly in the development of economic, trade and investment ties.

“There are the necessary opportunities to unlock this rich potential and develop it in the interests of our countries,” Hajiyev emphasized.

He added that Azerbaijan highly values Mexico’s dynamic development in Latin America and its role as one of the leading countries in the G20.

World.title: Azerbaijan highly values Mexico’s steadfast support for its territorial integrity – Hikmet Hajiyev
World.content:
SHUSHA, Azerbaijan, September 11. Azerbaijan highly values Mexico’s continued and steadfast support for the country’s territorial integrity and sovereignty.

Hikmet Hajiyev, Assistant to the President of Azerbaijan and head of the Foreign Policy Affairs Department of the Presidential Administration, made the remarks at an official reception in Shusha marking the Independence Day of the Republic of Mexico, Trend’s correspondent deployed to Karabakh and East Zangazur reports.

“We highly value Mexico’s determined position in supporting our country’s territorial integrity and sovereignty when Azerbaijan’s lands were under occupation, and the Azerbaijani people greatly appreciate this,” Hajiyev said.

He noted that these principles play an important role in the foundation of friendly relations between Azerbaijan and Mexico.

The presidential aide emphasized that Azerbaijan and Mexico currently maintain close political ties and an active political dialogue, with regular political consultations held between the two countries.

“Regarding most of the fundamental issues on today’s international agenda, the positions of Mexico and Azerbaijan are almost identical. Our countries support friendship, partnership, interstate relations based on the norms and principles of international law and mutual respect, as well as justice and fairness in international relations,” Hajiyev added.

World.title: US marks 25th anniversary of 9/11 attacks
World.content:
The United States has commemorated the 25th anniversary of the devastating September 11 attacks with a poignant ceremony in New York that was marked by Donald Trump's absence and searing criticism from victims' relatives.

In an unusual move, the US president paid his respects at the Pentagon, where hijacked planes destroyed the World Trade Center and most of the 2,977 victims were killed, up-ending the global status quo.

The Republican billionaire sought to link the "war on terror" that followed 9/11 with the conflict in Iran.

"Today we renew the sacred oath that we first swore in their names a quarter of a century ago. We will never, ever forget. That's why we fight today," Mr Trump said.

" We don't have a choice. There can only be victory. We fight hard. We fight to win. "

Donald Trump and first lady Melania Trump attended the ceremony at the Pentagon. (AP: Manuel Balce Ceneta)

Vice-President JD Vance and Mr Trump's four living predecessors — Republican George W Bush, who was in office during the attacks, and Democrats Joe Biden, Barack Obama and Bill Clinton — attended the event at Ground Zero in Lower Manhattan.

A huge crowd gathered for the sombre annual ceremony, which retraced the events of 9/11 minute by minute, concluding shortly before 1pm, local time.

The names of the victims were read out and a bell was rung to mark major moments in the attack.

The event is generally apolitical with no speeches.

But several bereaved family members who read out the names of those killed criticised Saudi Arabia and US leaders' closeness to the kingdom.

'We have no justice'

Terry Strada, whose husband Tom Strada died in the Twin Towers, unleashed a stinging attack on Riyadh, accusing it of complicity in the attacks and denouncing former presidents who were in attendance.

"You are missed more with each year that passes, but how can it be 25 years and still we have no justice for the role that Saudi Arabia played in your murder?" she said.

Terry Strada is the national chair of the group 9/11 Families United. (Reuters: Adam Gray/Pool)

The September 11, 2001 attacks were carried out by mostly Saudi hijackers and orchestrated by Al-Qaeda leader Osama bin Laden, a wealthy Saudi.

"For 25 years, administration after administration — including leaders in front of us here today — chose to protect the Saudis instead of standing with a 9/11 family," Ms Strada said, calling for action from the absent president.

25 years on, the twin brothers left behind still carry weight of 9/11 The September 11 terror attack reshaped more than just national security and geopolitical forces. In Australia, it ripped apart 10 families.

In New York, Democratic Mayor Zohran Mamdani, the city's first Muslim leader, attended the Ground Zero event despite a campaign urging him to stay away.

That effort was spearheaded by the right-wing New York Post newspaper and former mayor and Trump ally Rudy Giuliani, who led the city through the crisis and was also present on Friday.

The petition gathered more than 100,000 signatures.

A small anti-Islam protest gathered at City Hall and marched towards Ground Zero, flanked by police and counter-protesters.

Zohran Mamdani met with people after the memorial in New York. (AP: Adam Gray, Pool)

Mr Mamdani won plaudits for revealing thousands of documents showing what city officials knew about toxicity levels of the air in Lower Manhattan following the attacks.

After the initial dust cloud that followed the collapse of the World Trade Center, pollution lingered for months, causing cancers from which thousands of New Yorkers still suffer today.

The CIA also declassified and published dozens of 9/11-related presidential intelligence briefs to coincide with the 25th anniversary.

'New York did recover'

Nineteen Al-Qaeda operatives hijacked four airliners on the nearly cloudless autumn day in 2001.

Two of the jets slammed into the World Trade Center's Twin Towers and the iconic skyscrapers collapsed.

Images of firefighters who died during the September 11 attacks were displayed on buildings in Times Square. (Reuters: Eric Lee)

A third plane struck the Pentagon, while a fourth — believed to have been aiming for Congress or the White House — crashed into a field near Shanksville, Pennsylvania, after passengers fought back.

Some 100 million Americans have been born since or are too young to remember the traumatic day.

Sophia Rotunno, 58, recalls watching the first tower fall with colleagues back in 2001 and also remembers helping those affected in the aftermath.

"All we could do is support them, and be there for when they went to memorials, or be there for when they came home, and hug them, and pray for them," she said.

"It was a hard time for everybody afterward — and New York did recover."

Al-Qaeda meanwhile marked the anniversary by releasing a video showing images of the late Bin Laden and his son Hamza, who Mr Trump said in 2019 had also been killed.

AFP

World.title: Fremantle Dockers show they have the steel to be best in AFL
World.content:
Legendary NFL coach Vince Lomabrdi once said: "It's not whether you get knocked down, it's whether you get up."

The Fremantle Dockers got up, twice, to claim a 14-point win and breathe life into the club's best-ever chance of winning the AFL Premiership.

After the Dockers semi-final shocker against Hawthorn, the question was whether this young group, right at the beginning of their Premiership window, would be able to get off the canvas and land a blow.

History was against them in surviving a straight-sets exit, which would have been nothing short of humiliating after being crowned minor premiers just weeks ago.

Crows' quest for premiership glory just beginning as they prepare to take on Lions The Crows have snapped their September shackles, but the team's next assignment is in Brisbane, where they will take on the reigning premiers at a venue where they've been winless since 2018.

Were they mature enough to handle the pressure, whether it was from a self-imposed sense of expectation, the external commentary or the actual on-field action?

Against Geelong, they delivered an emphatic response.

Shai Bolton's two goals in two minutes to start the match, and the Dockers five in the opening quarter — after just five all game against the Hawks — dismissed fears they were scarred from last week's loss.

Fremantle's opening half was a reminder of the football that saw them win 14 games in a row on their way to a club record 19 wins for the season.

The Dockers pressure was intense in the first half. (AAP Image/Richard Wainwright)

They laid 45 tackles in a half of football, compared to 47 for the entire game against Hawthorn. It was a measure of the intensity they brought to the game, and they were rewarded with a 31-point lead.

That was the Dockers getting up from last week's loss.

But 23 minutes into the third term, they were down again.

Their mettle was tested, but their stars shone

Great sides — and Geelong is a great side — don't go down without a fight.

A lesser team, with a lesser coach, would have struggled to get a grip on the rampaging Fremantle as they surged to a five-goal lead.

But the Cats know a game isn't over until the final whistle. When Shannon Neale goaled just before half-time, there was a sense Geelong was getting going.

When Ollie Henry kicked his second just after the main break, that sense became a reality. Geelong took complete control of the game, as they kicked six goals to one to take the lead.

That was the moment the Dockers showed the steel that could land them an illusive Premiership.

It was also the moment Fremantle stars, who have earnt plaudits all season but were poor last week, got to work.

Luke Jackson and Shai Bolton were among the Dockers best as they held off the Cats. (AAP Image/Richard Wainwright)

Luke Jackson tore the game apart with a five-minute burst that yielded eight disposals, three clearances and two goals. He finished the game with 25 disposals and eight clearances to live up to his moniker of "The Unicorn".

Caleb Serong drove his side into attack time and again and Andrew Brayshaw hunted the football like a man possessed.

The Dockers' three-headed monster in attack, which kicked just two goals and took five marks between them against Hawthorn, showed why they should be considered among the most feared forward line in the competition.

Patrick Voss booted four goals, Jye Amiss slotted two, while Josh Treacy took eight marks and booted one.

Handling the momentum shifts

Momentum is an intangible of sport. A side, for no discernible reason, gets on top for a period of time.

The Dockers enjoyed the momentum in the opening stages, but the Cats challenged after half-time.

Justin Longmuir's side avoided the embarrassment of a straight-sets exit from the AFL finals (AAP Image/Richard Wainwright)

"Our games against Geelong this year have had those momentum shifts," Fremantle coach Justin Longmuir told Channel 7 after the game.

"If you don't handle the contest well, which we didn't in the third quarter, gave up field position, lacked a bit of dare with the ball, we let them back in the game.

"I'm really proud of the way the players got back on top of the contest and thought Luke [Jackson] and Caleb [Serong] late in that third quarter were outstanding for us."

The Dockers lack of big scores in finals had been highlighted in the build-up to this game, but the 120 points they put on Geelong was the most they have ever scored in September.

Fremantle fans can continue dreaming after their side fought off Geelong in Perth (ABC/Briana Shepherd)

"A lot has been mentioned about our scoring in finals and I think it's because we haven't trusted ourselves," Longmuir said.

"We trusted our way from the very start."

The Dockers will be hoping that trust travels with them to Sydney to face the Swans, with a berth in the Grand Final just one win away.

World.title: This water scored a perfect 100. Now it's being served like wine
World.content:
Passionate South Australian surfer Damien Smith moved to the rugged western coast of Yorke Peninsula for the waves.

What he didn't expect to find was water beneath his property that was worth bottling.

Mr Smith and his wife Gretchen Scinta became interested in the underground aquifer after buying the property in 2008.

"The tip for us was [the] freshwater crayfish down in the back paddock, but you're so close to the ocean, so you're starting to go, what's going on here?" Mr Smith said.

The couple initially extracted the water for their house and to grow vegetables.

But after having it tested, they realised they were sitting on something special.

Mr Smith said a water engineer told him, "This is a unicorn."

"He said it's the balance of the minerals in it, but it's pristine because it's so isolated, so no-one's touched this water."

Taking water beyond hydration

After years in the wine industry, the couple recently launched their mineral water, joining a growing global market challenging the idea that water is a commodity.

One of the people driving this movement is food anthropologist Michael Mascha, who co-founded the Fine Water Society after a heart condition forced him to give up alcohol.

Damien Smith says there is more to water than hydration. (ABC Landline: Tony Hill)

"I looked around the table, and there was another bottle there, which was water," he said.

" I applied all my curiosity I had for wine; I applied that to bottled water. "

After an initially hostile reception, Mr Mascha said premium water was now being taken more seriously.

"Salt has made a transition from a commodity to a product with terroir, olive oil, chocolate, other products like this and I think water is now in the process of making exactly the same transition."

Australia is playing an increasingly important part in this evolution.

"Australia is definitely a brand that started very early … then there was a little bit of a lull, but I see now Australia is a country that's really up and coming," Mr Mascha said.

The source is everything

Mr Smith and Ms Scinta access their water from an aquifer in the Carribie Basin, through a sealed extraction point.

To be called mineral water, it must naturally contain soluble matter.

While Australia does not specify a minimum amount, in the United States mineral water must contain at least 250 milligrams per litre of dissolved solids.

The couple got more than they bargained for when they bought a property on the Yorke Peninsula in SA. (ABC Landline: Tony Hill)

The couple protects the mineral make-up by moving the water through food-grade pipes underground into holding tanks.

"The important thing here is, limit oxygen, limit light, and limit changes in temperature … so we do literally do nothing," Mr Smith said.

While harvesting is now straightforward, getting it to market is trickier, with the water trucked in bulk to a bottling plant near Adelaide.

"If you look at Europe they've got strict rules; you need to bottle on site," Mr Smith said.

"We decided we're not going to do that because glass in, glass out is not a good footprint."

This is the extraction point where water is pulled from the ground. (ABC Landline: Tony Hill)

The footprint of the business isn't just about what leaves the property, it's also about how much should be extracted.

Mr Smith says the amount is guided by government reports and engineers.

"We probably need to be twice the size of Sanpellegrino to actually potentially do any damage to this basin, and we're not that. We're far, far, far from that," he said.

A market under scrutiny

The premium bottled water industry is growing, but so is scrutiny over how it's sourced and processed.

In 2024, it was publicly revealed Nestlé Waters in France had used prohibited treatment methods on contaminated water.

"People naturally are asking these questions of us as well in terms of what's your process, what's your ethos behind how you bring the water to market and so forth," Mr Smith said.

Damien Smith has turned his drinking water into premium bottled water. (ABC Landline: Tony Hill)

" So, rightly consumers are very, very wary about where things come from and how things are managed. "

Yet the thirst for premium water remains strong.

An international fine-water-tasting event in Canada attracted more than 100 entries.

Yorke Peninsula's Carribie still water scored a perfect 100 points from one of the judges and its sparkling water scored 99.

Mr Smith said the event showed him water was being taken as seriously as wine.

Gretchen Scinta is training to be a water sommelier. (ABC Landline: Tony Hill)

"Going to Montreal in May was a real eye-opener in terms of how intricately people were analysing all the different waters and, I guess, how far they were looking at it in terms of food and wine matching as well," he said.

Local water gains ground as drinking habits change

That approach is now making its way into some Australian restaurants.

At Adelaide's 2KW, sommelier Dan McEvoy serves Carribie water for $10 a bottle.

"I've seen other water brands go a lot higher than that, and they're coming from Italy, they're coming from France," he said.

Dan McEvoy has added the Yorke Peninsula water to his restaurant's drinks list. (ABC Landline: Kerry Staight)

"We can get something in our backyard, which I think objectively is better for a lesser cost."

And as alcohol consumption declines, water is being given a more prominent place.

"I'm seeing a lot more demand for non-alcoholic beverages, lot of waters, lot of mocktails, not only being asked for, but almost demanded in the restaurant," the sommelier said.

As for the couple that got more than they bargained for when they moved to Yorke Peninsula, they're now waiting to see what future vintages yield.

The sweeping dunes and rugged coastline sit on top of a fresh water source worth bottling. (ABC Landline: Kerry Staight)

However, cellaring takes a little longer than they're used to.

"That rainfall now that we've experienced this week, for us to take that out of the ground, I'll be 95 [years old]," Mr Smith said.

" I hope I'm here at 95 to actually taste the rains from 2026. "

Watch ABC TV's Landline at 12:30pm AEST on Sunday or stream anytime on ABC iview.

World.title: Court hears how Mexican police found bodies of Australian brothers
World.content:
Mexican authorities have revealed how they found the bodies of two Australian brothers and their American friend after they were killed on a surfing trip on Mexico's Pacific Coast.

Jake and Callum Robinson were with Carter Rhoad in Baja California when they went missing in April 2024.

A court in Ensenada has heard from authorities involved in finding the men, including homicide detectives and forensics officers.

The chief of the state missing persons unit told the court investigators acquired their first clue on May 1, 2024, about four days after the men went missing.

The officer said a search was conducted in the area where the victim were camping near Punta San José, a remote surfing location about 80 kilometres south of Ensenada.

"We located a house in front of the ocean, like a ranch, apparently abandoned. Approximately 100 to 120 metres from the house, there was a well that caught my attention," the officer told the court.

" Upon approaching, we detected foul odours. "

The officer said the case was referred to the homicide unit when burned human remains were found inside the well.

Forensic evidence at the crime scene

Three Mexican men — Jesús Gerardo, also known as "El Kekas", Irineo Francisco and Ángel Jesús — are charged with aggravated homicide, aggravated burglary, violent robbery and grand theft auto.

Last year the former girlfriend of El Kekas, Ari Gisell, was sentenced to 20 years' jail for her role in connection with the murders. She is expected to testify in the trial next week.

A forensics specialist who testified on Thursday, local time, told the court they located blood-stained clothes in the abandoned home near the well.

Among the items found at the crime scene were a pair of brown boots and a sweater, a .45-calibre bullet, blood smears and a tooth.

The forensics specialist said all items were severely burned.

Local media, citing local police sources, reported at the time of the brothers' disappearance, this burnt out car was believed to have belonged to the missing men. (Supplied)

The defence lawyers questioned whether items such as the bullet were "old" and pointed out discrepancies in timelines recorded by authorities.

The forensics specialist told the court they had been unable to confirm when the items may have been burned, as they did not have access to laboratory results of items from the scene.

The trial was expected to last about a month, but a last-minute judge replacement has potentially thrown that timeline into disarray. It will continue next week.

Once the trial is finished, the judge will have 24 hours to make a judgement, and another week to hand down his verdict.

World.title: Pack the umbrella as cooler days and showers loom for Qld this weekend
World.content:
After sweltering days across parts of the state, a cool change has begun for the weekend.

Senior meteorologist at the Bureau of Meteorology Shane Kennedy said cloud cover would keep temperatures slightly down, particularly along the state's east coast, where scattered showers were likely.

"It should be a little bit lighter over the north tropical coast compared to Friday, now that the wind surge has moved a bit further north and weakened," he said.

"But there still is that expectation we'll see a few rounds of showers throughout the day."

Up to 10mm in some areas

Between 2 and 10 millimetres of rainfall was expected across the eastern regions, Mr Kennedy said, with more than 10mm expected in some isolated areas, most likely on the north tropical coast or south-east coast.

Most coastal wind warnings have contracted to the far north-eastern waters, and the weather bureau says the worst of the surges have passed. (ABC Far North: Miriam Mazurek-Kaminska)

Inland, he said there was also a chance of isolated showers and even a thunderstorm in the Channel Country, but the risk of rain would ease by the end of the weekend.

While much of the state might enjoy the promise of cooler conditions, the weather would be much warmer inland.

"[We're] expecting the south-west to get more up into the mid-30s by the end of the weekend, generally in the low to mid-30s elsewhere in western Queensland," Mr Kennedy said.

"For the rest of the state, typically getting up to the low to mid-20s in the south-east and then into the mid to high 20s for central Queensland and the Far North."

On Saturday afternoon though, temperatures will start climbing for the far south west.

"That will be as the winds swing around more to the north-north-east ahead of a new trough system expected early next week," Mr Kennedy said.

Winds to ease

For those heading for the boat ramp, Mr Kennedy said wind conditions were now easing.

He said coastal warnings have eased for waters in the far north, and were likely to be cancelled on Sunday.

After a hot start to September in the south-east, this weekend will bring cooler temperatures and occasional showers. (Supplied: Therese Sherley)

It was the trend for more coastal areas, with winds easing as the ridge of high pressure continues to weaken.

Mr Kennedy did caution that there were hazardous surf warnings for northern New South Wales; however, they were not expected to affect beaches and surf north of the border.

"The worst of the waves should stay offshore, but worth being aware of if anyone's planning to head well offshore this weekend."

Fire risk remains

Mr Kennedy said there were still some fire danger ratings in place for parts of the west and north-west of the state.

He said this was due to winds combining with warm and dry conditions.

"That may make fires a little bit more difficult to control in those parts of the state, but not expecting it to push up to extreme or give us any fire weather warnings at this stage," he said.

World.title: No longer safe as houses: Why no-one is rushing to Bathla's rescue
World.content:
More than two weeks after Bathla Group entered voluntary administration, the company is still standing.

But only just.

Since Teneo took control of the Western Sydney developer, the administration has lurched from one deadline to the next as it scrambles for cash.

At several points in these frantic first weeks, shutdown loomed.

Each time, Bathla found enough money to survive a little longer.

Its latest reprieve came on Monday, when five lenders agreed to provide between $3 and $5 million to keep a much smaller Bathla running for another two weeks.

A $40,000 Bathla promise in doubt May bought her apartment on the promise that property developer Bathla would knock $40,000 off the price at settlement. Now with the company in administration, she has no guarantee it will be honoured.

Construction on projects not backed by the five participating lenders has been suspended by the company, although individual lenders may take control of projects and continue construction separately under a different building licence.

More than 60 per cent of Bathla's roughly 350 staff have been stood down.

The reprieve is a long way from the roughly $20 million the administrators initially said was needed to keep construction operating for five weeks.

What remains is a substantially smaller operation keeping about 14 projects moving while the fate of the rest of the group is increasingly decided elsewhere.

Bathla has several construction sites across western Sydney. (ABC News: John Gunn)

The break-up is already underway

With only five of around 40 lenders funding Bathla's continued operation, others are increasingly taking control of the projects securing their loans.

This week, 360 Capital Mortgage REIT escalated efforts to recover $31.7 million across four Bathla-linked loans, with receivers appointed over three and being pursued over the fourth.

For most of the properties, the strategy is to sell them down. But one loan is secured against 72 near-complete apartments, where lenders are working to get the project to occupancy so existing pre-sales can settle before the remaining apartments are sold.

ABC Business Daily: Breaking down Bathla Bathla Group has collapsed owing billions, with hundreds of projects caught up in the fallout. Was it simply a company that grew too fast and took on too much debt — or is it a sign of deeper pressure across property and construction?

Ray White Capital, billionaire property investor Bob Ell’s Leda, Balmain and Woodbridge Capital are some of the lenders that have appointed receivers or otherwise taken control of individual projects.

There is nothing unusual about secured lenders enforcing their rights in a property insolvency.

Property development is often financed project by project, with lenders holding security over particular land or developments.

What sets Bathla apart is the sheer scale on which that process is now playing out; dozens of lenders, hundreds of companies and more than 200 sites.

The future of residential developer Bathla is becoming increasingly uncertain. (AAP: Dan Himbrechts)

So while Bathla remains in voluntary administration as a group, what happens from here is increasingly being decided project by project.

That means there may be no single outcome for subcontractors and buyers caught up in the collapse.

A subcontractor owed money for work already completed may still have to pursue that debt through the administration, even if a receiver takes control of the project and hires someone else to finish it.

For buyers, the outcome will depend heavily on their individual development, including whether it continues, is sold or refinanced, and the terms of their contract.

And the further that project-by-project process advances, the harder it may become to put Bathla back together in anything resembling its previous form.

Loading...

Is there still another way out?

That does not mean parts of Bathla cannot still be rescued or restructured.

Under voluntary administration, Teneo must investigate the options for Bathla's future and ultimately recommend the course it believes would produce the best outcome for creditors compared with liquidation.

That has included considering proposals to refinance or restructure parts of the group.

Do you know more? If you have more information about this article or any other tips, you can securely contact reporter Lin Lin at lin.lin@abc.net.au or linreporting@proton.me.

One such proposal emerged this week, involving around 25 land-only Bathla sites worth about $1 billion and funding from an unidentified Japanese investor-backed syndicate, according to Renown Wealth, which had been coordinating the proposed refinance on behalf of the investors.

The proposal would have refinanced debt attached to those projects through Buildwell Australia Pty Ltd, whose directors include Rohit Bathla, the son of Bathla founder Bhart Bhushan. Buildwell Australia is not in administration.

But on Friday afternoon, the private credit investment manager said the offer had been withdrawn.

Renown said the parties had been unable to agree on key conditions, including the corporate structure of the proposed deal and obtaining fresh valuations of the sites. It also raised concerns about the proposed continuing involvement of Bathla founder Bhart Bhushan.

The government is not offering a circuit-breaker

The NSW government has made clear it sees Bathla's future as a matter for its lenders.

Treasurer Daniel Mookhey said the government would focus on protecting buyers and keeping homes under construction where possible, but would not use taxpayer money to bail out private-credit lenders.

Loading

That leaves Teneo and Bathla's lenders to work through interests that do not always align.

For the administrators, the task is to preserve value across the group.

For individual secured lenders, the question is narrower — whether continuing to fund Bathla or a particular project will produce a better recovery than taking control of the secured asset itself.

Increasingly, some are choosing the latter.

World.title: Germany's election and the UK's sanctions signals political warfare
World.content:
The complexity of the differing forms of warfare being employed in conflicts around the globe these days has seen analysts increasingly try to organise them under the headings of 'kinetic' and 'economic' warfare.

Kinetic warfare is the sort that involves shooting things at each other. Economic warfare employs weapons like sanctions.

There's been an escalation in both sorts this week: a resurgence in missile exchanges in Ukraine and the Middle East; and new rounds of sanctions employed against Israel, Iran and Cuba.

The US House of Representatives is also scheduled to vote next week on sweeping new tariffs on countries buying Russian oil and gas, though it is unclear whether the vote will proceed or not.

There have also been developments which represent both kinetic and economic warfare: notably the Iran-backed Houthis gaining control of the strategically crucial city of Mocha on the Red Sea coast of Yemen, just 50 kilometres from the Bab el-Mandeb Strait.

Saudi Arabia has been getting around the blockade of the Strait of Hormuz on its eastern flanks by shipping oil via pipeline to its west coast, in order to ship it out through the Red Sea.

The Iran-backed Houthis have gained control of the strategically crucial city of Mocha on the Red Sea coast of Yemen, just 50 kilometres from the Bab el-Mandeb Strait. (Reuters)

Far-right party triumphs in Germany

The spectre of shipping through the Bab el-Mandeb Strait coming under more lethal Houthi fire sent a shudder through world markets on Thursday night.

But the new player that has erupted on the warfare block this week is political warfare.

That is, shifting internal politics within countries which are changing the geopolitical landscape.

The conspicuous latest examples of this came in an election in the German state of Saxony-Anhalt, and the equally important shift by the UK government of Andy Burnham in its position on Israel.

The success of the far-right Alternative for Deutschland (AfD) party in winning 44 per cent of the vote in the state election — while the ruling CDU's vote halved to just 17.2 per cent — has shaken national German politics, even though the rise of the AfD has been underway for some time.

A 'serious moment in Europe' The weekend win by Alternative for Germany in the state of Saxony-Anhalt has sent shivers across the continent, and could embolden the right across Europe.

As this week ends, German media is widely reporting that the position of German Chancellor Friedrich Merz is in mortal danger, because — like former UK PM Keir Starmer — he has proved both an ineffective communicator, and a disliked leader. He has not been able to fend off the rise of the AfD, after pledging he would see the party's vote halved.

The pressure is also only going to continue on Merz, and on German politics, with two more state elections due next weekend in Berlin and another state that was once part of the old East Germany: Mecklenburg-Vorpommern.

The result saw fiery clashes in the Bundestag in Berlin, in which Merz conceded that voters had spoken "pretty clearly" in the state election last weekend with a result that had shocked his "to its very foundations".

"They also sent us, and me personally, a clear message," Deutsche Welle reported him saying.

"We must try, myself included, to reach people more effectively, in the full range of their emotions."

However, a more combative chancellor hit back at the AfD's co-leader Alice Weidel likening the AfD's "remigration" policy —the mass deportation of irregular migrants and foreigners who are required to leave the country — to "nothing other than ethnic cleansing based on skin colour and origin".

AfD's policy makes even right-wing parties anxious

Merz said there was agreement within his governing coalition that many people without a right to remain permanently in Germany should be deported.

"But we distinguish carefully between those who work in Germany, who contribute to our prosperity, who are welcome in Germany, and those who do not have a permanent right to remain and who must leave our country again," he said.

The AfD's remigration policy is only one of the policy positions which leave many in Germany, and in Europe more broadly, deeply anxious, even right-wing parties in other countries.

German media is widely reporting that the position of German Chancellor Friedrich Merz is in mortal danger, because he has proved both an ineffective communicator, and a disliked leader who has not been able to fend off the rise of the AfD. (Reuters: Christian Mang)

Le Monde described the AfD's victory as "particularly embarrassing" for Marine Le Pen's Rassemblement National (RN).

RN had been part of a coalition in the European Parliament with the AfD until 2024 when it broke away "after ambiguous statements by the German party about the role of the SS during World War II and disagreements over remigration".

But it is the AfD's hostility to Ukraine and calls for closer ties with Russia which is of greatest concern in Europe.

Germany, Europe's largest economy, has been the major European backer of Ukraine under Merz, who has also been overseeing the biggest rearmament of his country since World War II, under the perceived threat coming from Russia.

As the former head of MI6, Sir John Sawers, told the Financial Times this week that "it's been a real testament to European support and solidarity that we've kept the Ukrainians going".

But he acknowledged that with changes in the wind in the politics of Germany, France and Italy in the next year, this could significantly change.

The more prosaic issue of gas supply may have a major role to play in the political warfare over Ukraine in coming months.

Europe currently holds its lowest gas stocks in 20 years. With about one third of the world's LNG supplies knocked out by attacks on Qatari production facilities, and facing another bleak winter, the pressure in Europe to start buying more gas from Russia will be intense, including in Germany where the AfD explicitly advocates for this to occur.

Ukraine will need all the friends it can get as European support wobbles, which is why the recent UK move to announce a defence deal with Ukraine, and now a deal between Canada and Ukraine to provide military support in the form of military drones and air defence interceptors, is so significant.

Under new prime minister Andy Burnham the UK is taking a more assertive position on foreign policy issues. (Reuters: Kin Cheung)

UK takes more assertive stance

Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney has been the poster boy this year for the call for Middle Powers to take on more active independent roles in world affairs.

This week has seen another shift in the UK's international position which reflects that trend.

The UK likes to still think itself as a 'Great Power' but it is at best a middling one these days, even it does still possess nuclear weapons.

But under new prime minister Andy Burnham, and his foreign secretary Ed Miliband, the UK is taking a more assertive position on foreign policy issues, this week releasing legislation for tougher sanctions against Iran, and most notably announcing trade sanctions against West Bank settlements in Israel.

The importance of the West Bank move is not just about the actual trade sanctions. It lies in the upgrading of the language the UK is using about the actions of the Netanyahu government in the West Bank.

Loading...

Just as Merz attacked the AfD in Germany for a policy he says amounts to ethnic cleansing, Miliband accused Israel of doing the same thing in the West Bank.

What is more, he made explicit the view that the UK regards Israel's occupation of the entire West Bank as unlawful — adopting the findings of the International Court of Justice — rather than continuing with the almost 60-year-old claim that it is just temporarily "occupied".

It is a particularly big turnaround for a party that was defending itself against claims of antisemitism only a few years ago.

Australia stands still on Israeli sanctions After joining other countries in recognising the state of Palestine, Australia has broken from the pack of other nations in not adopting trade sanctions against West Bank businesses.

Whether the trade sanctions can be implemented by the UK, or the other 11 countries who also indicated this week that they would impose similar measures, is yet to be seen.

Commemorations of the 25th Anniversary of the terror attacks of September 11, 2001 have seen a number of analysts observe that Al Qaeda had eventually been contained.

But those threats have been replaced with state-sponsored terror, notably from Iran and Russia. And Europe has been confronting the cost of the mass wave of refugees that era of terror unleashed.

Along with the transformation of the United States from global policeman to global disruptor, middle power countries are having to write their own rules rather than just hiding behind America in this new world.

Unfortunately, it is not clear whether Australia has yet mastered the dexterity to engage in this new era of political warfare.

Laura Tingle is the ABC's Global Affairs Editor.

World.title: Hastie emerges as genuine conviction politician
World.content:
People who lead us in public life can often sound like one of those dead-eyed "large language models" many are so worried about.

Politically-optimised LLMs jerry-rigged to flesh-and-bone "neural networks". Sprouting reasonable-sounding nonsense.

All that's missing is a silly name like Llama or Rufus.

This column has no real understanding of how AI works. But the way LLMs are fed on data in Silicon Valley's dark satanic mills reminds one of how the French force-feed ducks and geese to expand their livers for foie gras. It's illegal to produce this artery-clogging delicacy in Australia because the ducks really don't like it.

But as with AI we're allowed to import foie gras in whatever quantities we fancy.

Barnaby Joyce this week said he "was not Jesus Christ" on ABC's 7.30 program. (ABC News: Callum Flinn)

One Nation's failed super sell

Politicians feed their personal internal LLMs with polls and focus groups and by watching how voters react to the things they and their colleagues do and say. Then then hold up the mirror to the audience, hoping they like what they see.

As with any circular self-fertilising system it pays to keep your guard up for when these political AI machines make stuff up. Or worse still, hallucinate.

Barnaby Joyce springs to mind after this week declaring on 7.30 that he "was not Jesus Christ". And that he should therefore not be asked too many questions about One Nation's latest superannuation policy.

The uncharitable interpretation of this — certainly one that Treasurer Jim Chalmers suggested — is that Joyce was bluffing his way around the fact that he didn't know the details. An interpretation, by the way, that some Liberals privately agree with.

There's a strong view that One Nation's policy was leaked by someone inside the Coalition which was preparing to announce a very similar idea.

But we've digressed somewhat. Back to politicians who sound like automated simulacra of intelligence and meaning.

Andrew Hastie this week launched a blistering public assault on Pauline Hanson for calling him a "traitor" in a social media cartoon. (ABC News: Callum Flinn)

Hastie launches blistering assault

Sometimes you get a flash of lightning. An insight into someone being more genuine and honest.

This week raised the possibility that Andrew Hastie might be an example after he launched a blistering public assault on Pauline Hanson for calling him a "traitor" in a social media cartoon.

The former SAS veteran who served three tours in the Middle East slammed Hanson as a "lying coward" for failing to take responsibility and deleting the film, which called him a traitor eight times. He said her accusation was an attack on all veterans.

"The question I have for Senator Hanson is: are you calling them traitors as well? Because if you are, just own it. You don't get to redefine ANZAC. You don't get to redefine the profession of arms."

The row between Hastie and One Nation continues to rumble, but it's generated plenty of online heat.

Tassie senator Jacqui Lambie, another veteran, was equally scathing of Hanson, who by Friday was telling everyone to take a "chill pill".

As of late yesterday the offending video was still pinned to the top of her social media feeds.

Hastie's fightback — which has been buttressed by a string of Coalition voices — is both targeted and deliberate. The MP for Canning knows he has a difficult fight on his hands keeping his southern Perth-based seat in the face of a resurgent One Nation. And he's long ago decided that rather than work with Hanson — as some Liberals have advocated — he wants to take her on directly.

It's all complicated by the fact that Hastie is up against it given WA's insular media ecosystem is largely arrayed against him over the Ben Roberts Smith case. So it's a bold experiment and we'll have to wait to see if it works.

But the unique thing about what Hastie is doing is that he's fighting fire with fire against Australia's most prominent populist. It's part of an ongoing transformation over recent months.

Loading

Remember when we made big cars

A year ago Hastie was making headlines with a fairly hokey social media campaign that was harking back to a distant past, a sepia-coloured Hills Hoist idyll. Remember when we made big cars. Economists — inside and outside the Coalition — shook their heads in disbelief.

Then Hastie learnt the hard way what it means to be burnt by the flaming pit of hell that is online engagement.

Originally pitching himself as a libertarian against political censorship, Hastie was against the tide of Labor's post-Bondi anti-vilification legislation. After switching to a more centrist view that there should be limits on saying terrible things about minorities, Hastie was excommunicated by many of his previous boosters, outraged at this transgression.

In response, Hastie has been busy trying to build support from different constituencies.

The question for Hastie, and those who want him to lead the Liberal Party, is whether he can make his momentum last.

There's no way to know at this point and there are many examples abroad of how such an approach has failed. Particularly in the United States where Donald Trump tore down column after column of Republican opponents.

Hanson is no Trump, but it's a dangerous fight. In the US, Republicans who couldn't beat Trump either joined him or quietly faded away, though there are some exceptions.

At the very least, Hastie has established that he's an institutionalist, with a clear set of values and that he's prepared to defend them, even if its uncomfortable and may upset his own base. But hat's what genuine conviction politicians do.

Loading...

Meanwhile, the Greens' splinter

Which brings us to the Greens, who were quietly having their own internal meltdown this week.

The surprise is that it happened on an issue of core business; the question of whether to support a new method for generating carbon credits from turning land that was earmarked for logging into national park. For many in the environmental movement opposition to this idea was hard to understand. Why die on this remnant old growth forest covered hill?

ABC Politics in your inbox Sign up to the ABC Politics newsletter with Courtney Gould

But for others, including Bob Brown and Christine Milne, it was selling out the environmental movement to neoliberalism.

In the end the Greens partyroom voted six votes to five to support the government's policy. Three Greens then dissented on the Senate floor, the first time anyone can remember such a thing happening at such scale.

In most other political parties the sight of 27 per cent of the party room crossing the floor would trigger a leadership spill. It's not clear that's what will happen this time. But one does have to wonder.

Either way, it's a tough business being a political leader. Not something you'd want done by Claude or Gemini or Grok.

Jacob Greber is political editor of ABC's 7.30 program.

World.title: They’re an AFL powerhouse. So why can’t Collingwood’s women’s team find success?
World.content:
Analysis SportAFLAFLW They’re an AFL powerhouse. So why can’t Collingwood’s women’s team find success? Hannah Kennelly September 12, 2026 — 6:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

For nearly four quarters, Collingwood captain Ruby Schleicher was on the verge of an unwanted statistical milestone. With just three minutes left in last weekend’s game against Carlton, her career-high personal tally of three goals and four behinds would ordinarily have been cause for celebration. But the disappointing fact for Schleicher and her Magpies was that she had contributed 100 per cent of her team’s score. Ruby Schleicher during Collingwood’s clash with Carlton Getty Images Teammate Georgia Knight offered a reprieve with a behind, followed by a goal to Dominique Carbone, which made the 39-point loss to the undefeated Blues sting a little less. To put the loss in perspective, the injury-marred Pies were missing key players, including last-minute drop-outs from star Ash Centra and Jemma Rigoni and were facing Carlton – a team that made finals last year and will likely to do the same in 2026.



Still, Sunday’s defeat marks their fourth consecutive loss —a streak that, compounded by several years of poor results, should be sounding alarm bells at Collingwood headquarters. In 2019, this masthead published a piece, titled ‘What’s wrong with Collingwood’s AFLW side’, which examined the club’s poor performance after high-profile players Jasmine Garner, Moana Hope, Emma King and Jess Duffin defected to North Melbourne during W’s rapid expansion period. Collingwood coach Sam Wright and his team. AFL Photos At the time, critics questioned the Pies list management, draft and recruiting strategy. Staff turnover was also cited as a concern, after the club had employed three women’s football operations managers in three years. That was seven years ago. Even the brightest of optimists and diehard Pies fans would concede not enough has changed since then.



Collingwood are currently second-last on the ladder and – like Essendon, St Kilda and West Coast – yet to record a win ahead of their match on Saturday against Gold Coast at People First Stadium. Related Article AFL 2026 Jeremy Howe changed his mind on retirement. Now his mate’s daughter is a Collingwood clubmate So why single Collingwood out, when three other clubs have the same 0-4 start? Essendon, St Kilda and West Coast entered AFLW at later stages of the competition, with the latter two reaching finals for the first time last year. Collingwood are one of the inaugural teams of the competition, but – despite showing glimpses of promise – seem to have gone backwards.



Their first and only preliminary final was in 2021 against the Brisbane Lions, followed by a semi-final appearance in 2022. Since then, Collingwood have finished 11th in 2023, last in 2024 and 15th in 2025 with only three wins. Collingwood should be a successful AFLW club. They have up-to-date facilities and a strong history of success in the men’s program, plus a large membership pool to tap into. View post on X The Pies have also been adamant they are improving. Coach Sam Wright told media after their round 12 loss in 2025 the Pies would have a “tough and prescriptive” off-season. “While we only got the three wins this year, we don’t feel like we are far away from progressing,” he added. So why can’t Collingwood’s AFLW program find success?



The club has had steady leadership over the past few years, poaching Wright from North Melbourne in 2023 and promoting highly regarded performance analyst Jess Burger to general manager of women’s football in 2024. Burger and Collingwood declined to comment for this article. However, support from Collingwood’s upper echelons has been less straightforward and more cautious. Collingwood CEO Craig Kelly has been publicly and privately vocal about the financial risks of expanding the AFLW program. Collingwood Football Club chief executive Craig Kelly. AAP Last year, the AFL met with all 18 clubs for a conference exploring the priorities for the future of the AFLW for its 10-year anniversary. Columnist Caroline Wilson, reported Kelly urged the league to consider the heavy cost of expanding the AFLW competition too quickly, arguing the game should not invest too heavily in the women’s competition at the expense of upgrading the MCG, creating better facilities for the game across Australia and improving the AFL experience for fans. AFLW commentator Chyloe Kurdas said it was important for clubs to remember the women’s game was still “playing catch-up” to the men’s – a chase that requires investment in staffing, resources and most importantly mindset.



“I can’t speak specifically about Collingwood, but I think what is a problem is that not all 18 clubs have got a consistent mindset across the whole club of the value of the women’s program and the level of investment that’s required to ensure that there’s success in it” she said. Kurdas – a former AFL Victoria football development manager – said the most successful AFLW clubs established cultures that the best players wanted to be a part of, pointing to the long-term success of Brisbane, Adelaide and reigning premiers North Melbourne. View post on X “You can throw lots of money at a program, but if it’s not part of your heart and soul, and ... you don’t believe in its capability, then it doesn’t matter how much money you spend,” she said. From a list perspective, Collingwood are lacking key players in their forward line. The Pies have consistently struggled to find a consistent path to goal, arguably since Chloe Molloy’s departure in 2022. Superstar Molloy signed with the Sydney on a five-year-deal – the longest contract in the history of the competition.



After receiving a list assistance package from the AFL Commission in 2025 – including two additional spots for the 2026 season and one for 2027 – Collingwood’s list went under an extensive turnover Eleven players left the program and 13 new players were introduced; including delisted free argent Jemma Rigoni and two cross-code Super Netball players Maisie Nankivell and Olivia Lewis. The recruits have helped build versatility and height in Collingwood’s list, but the Magpies still lack experienced players in their forward line. Through the 2025 draft, the Pies brought in six young players, injecting a noticeable boost of energy into their side. But it’s also left the overall playing group relatively inexperienced and young. Kurdas said, while Collingwood’s young players looked exciting and the team had shown some improvement this year, the Pies needed to recruit more A-grade quality players.



“Collingwood probably just don’t have enough depth of mature-age elite level talent, and they need more of those in each zone,” she said. There’s also concern about Collingwood ability to retain senior players. The club has strong leadership from veteran captain Schleicher, but it’s worth noting she and a number of senior players come out of contract this year. Collingwood coach Sam Wright is in his third year as senior coach. Getty Images Schleicher has been offered a deal, but is yet to sign, while, Tarni White, Sarah Rowe, Mattea Breed, Lauren Butler and Bri Davey are others coming out of contract. Vice-captain Jordyn Allen signed a three-year deal in 2024, but tried to seek a trade to Brisbane last year. After their loss to Carlton last weekend, Wright conceded the Pies were “under some duress from a list point of view with injuries”, but said there were opportunities for young players to step up.



When asked specifically by this masthead, what was missing from the Collingwood program and list, Wright said Collingwood were still working that out. “It certainly throws some challenges when you’ve got this many injuries to significant key players as well,” he said. “As a club, we are working through it right now, to put our finger on it, but certainly part of it is luck. But the other part [is] we want to be the best program we can be in that area, and we are working really hard. “In terms of list, it’s more around just continuing to get our processes right, push our processes.” Both Richmond and Carlton initiated comprehensive independent reviews into their AFLW’s programs after periods of poor performance. Carlton’s review in 2022 led to the departure of coach Daniel Harford and other key staff, while Richmond’s review at the end of 2025 prompted the departure of senior coach Ryan Ferguson.



Since then, Carlton have surged, playing in the finals last year and opening thisd season with four straight wins. It’s too early to examine Richmond’s progress, but the Tigers have got two wins on the board so far this season. Related Article AFL 2022 ‘A global reckoning is coming’: The toll of trolls on footballers No one can dispute Collingwood’s desire to get better. As Wright put in his press conference, “I think every player in our program and every staff member is committed to winning”. Kurdas said Collingwood have “the potential to be a great W side”, and said any club that wasn’t getting the success they wanted should consider evaluating their program. “The ability to self-reflect honestly; that’s a non-negotiable ingredient of being successful,” she said. World.title: ‘Made for finals’: The interstate gun with the AFL’s No.1 ranking
World.content:
Analysis SportAFLAFL 2026 ‘Made for finals’: The interstate gun with the AFL’s No.1 ranking Michael Gleeson September 12, 2026 — 6:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Loading

Isaac Heeney thought he had space. He turned to goal and took a step. Braeden Campbell had dinked a loopy handball to him over a Crows player just as he was about to be tackled and Heeney was clear. He was inside 50, tight to the boundary on his left and caught Izak Rankine in his peripheral vision closing fast from the right. You could almost hear Heeney thinking, “I can get through him. I can shrug him”. It was late in the last quarter, with about seven minutes to go, on a wet SCG in round 19 and the home team was surging. Izak Rankine’s big tackle on Isaac Heeney in round 19. Channel Seven Rankine slammed into Heeney and wrapped his arms around him. Heeney, comfortably 15 kilograms heavier and stronger than Rankine, stood in the tackle. It looked like David Attenborough footage from a savannah. Heeney wriggled an arm free to try to handball. Rankine lunged and surprisingly managed to spin Heeney as they cuddled, and the pair tumbled to the ground. The ball spilt free. The Crows cleared it, and they hung on to win the game.



The significance of the tackle in that moment in the game, and in the context of Rankine’s season and career, cannot be underestimated. “That was the complete midfielder’s game. As a coach, I thought that was the game that he had a turning point,” Adelaide assistant coach Scott Burns said of the Sydney game. “Two weeks earlier against West Coast he had started to really influence games in the midfield, but that tackle in the wet against Sydney at that time of the game was such a big play. He’d had a great game, but that tackle was where you saw how competitive he is – how much he hates to lose. Izak Rankine celebrates a goal. AFL Photos “That game was a real turning point. It was a complete midfielder performance – inside and out, 30 touches, tackles, inside 50s.”



And he only kicked one goal. Ordinarily, good Izak Rankine games had to include him kicking three, four or five goals. Related Article Analysis

AFL 2026 Bring on the the Zak attack: The Cats’ semi-final showed they sorely need it Rankine only moved to a permanent midfield role in round nine this year after being primarily a forward and part-time mid. Last year the idea of him as a midfielder was better than the reality, and this year was tracking along similarly: he was good but not great in the way he can be as a forward. The first big change came in round 17 against West Coast, and then the next week against the Suns when he had high numbers and his impact was profound. But that was beating up two teams that were poor at the time. This was Sydney in Sydney. Since round 17, Rankine has not gone from good to great – he has gone from good to elite. Champion Data ranks him the No.1 player in the competition since round 18. He is averaging 150 Champion Data points per game. The next best are Errol Gulden on 129 and Max Gawn on 123.



The question on hyper-attacking, dangerous mid-forwards like Rankine, Petracca, “Dusty” and “Kozzy” Pickett can be about their sleight of hand. The freakish goal can be the magician’s distraction from what they are not doing defensively. Jeremy Clarkson and his Italian luxury tractor on his farm, Diddly Squat, in West Oxfordshire. Amazon Prime Typically, the theory is you don’t want your stars to do the grunt inside midfielder work – that you use a tractor to plough a field, not a Lamborghini. Rankine, like Jeremy Clarkson on his farm, doesn’t understand why you can’t have a Lamborghini tractor. “He is made for finals,” said one former coach. “He is a difference-maker. There are plenty of role players in finals who do their job well, but there are not many players who can change the game. In finals, you need players who can kick you two in two minutes and change the game. Rankine is that.”



Another Gold Coast coach said: “The one player we missed last year in finals was Izak Rankine”. The difference-maker could make no difference last year. Or, perhaps, he made a profound difference to two clubs by not being there. Rankine barely played in his first year in the AFL after being drafted by Gold Coast. At the time, it was said he was struggling with repeated hamstring issues. In fact, he had rheumatoid arthritis, which took a long time to diagnose. The autoimmune disease causes swelling and severe pain in the joints, normally to the same joint on both sides of the body. Relatively rare in people under 30, it took some time to diagnose him and then get him on the right (WADA compliant) medication. This time last year, Rankine was suspended for four matches – including the Crows’ entire finals series – after admitting to using a homophobic slur during a game against Collingwood.



“I want to start by saying how deeply sorry I am for what I said. There was no excuse, it was wrong, and I take full responsibility,” Rankine said later. “I’m disappointed in myself and I know I have let a lot of people down. I want to apologise to anyone who I have hurt and offended. I understand that word was offensive, harmful, it’s hurtful and has no place in our game or our society.” Rankine was not a victim, but the length of his ban was the product of an AFL determination to eliminate homophobic language in the game by continuing to escalate punishments for any players using such terms. The consequence was Rankine was not there last year as they lost to Collingwood by 24 points in week one of the finals and then were eliminated altogether when they lost to Hawthorn by 34 points the next week.



View post on X It’s academic what might have been last year, had he been there. The evidence of the first final this year against the Bulldogs, when Rankine had 34 touches, seven clearances, four tackles and two goals – one of them one of the most artful goals of the year – shows is he is not only in dominant form, he is indeed made for finals.
