World.title: He’s one of pop’s great technological disruptors. But the AI era fills him with anxiety
World.content:
Haruomi Hosono: “We don’t use our brain muscles because AI does it for us. What will happen to us before long?”

Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

In the studio of the 79-year-old Japanese pop icon Haruomi Hosono is a bust of Ludwig van Beethoven, some flowers and a small bowl of water. He pulled the bust out of storage when it came time to record the track Figlio Perduto for his new album Yours Sincerely, his first collection of new music in seven years. Hosono’s 23rd studio album features gently soothing electronics and acoustic guitar that feels whimsically reflective, like he’s reaching for his inner child late in life. “Maybe because of my age I might have gone back to being a child. I do have quite a lot of those memories from my childhood,” says Hosono, contemplating the idea. Haruomi Hosono (right) with his Yellow Magic Orchestra bandmates – Yukihiro Takahashi and Ryuichi Sakamoto – in 1982. Gentle Look via Getty Images “Rather than being stories of the past, they are still continuing even now. For example, Beethoven has been glaring at me since I was a child … Now it’s sitting here and I’m praying to it. Until then I had left it alone because I was a bit scared.” Summing up Hosono’s career is almost impossible. His early work in the band Happy End (1969-1972), then as a solo artist on his debut Hosono House (1973), is frequently cited as a touchstone by indie artists, most notably the similarly prolific Mac DeMarco (the title of Harry Styles’ Grammy-winning album Harry’s House was a homage, too). His later outfit Yellow Magic Orchestra is one of the most influential synth-pop groups of all time. But if there’s one consistent thread, it can be found on Figlio Perduto, a cover in Japanese of a track by Sarah Brightman that sets an Italian translation of Johann Wolfgang von Goethe’s poem Erlkonig to Beethoven’s Symphony No. 7.



This iterative, memetic layering of cultures, often with technology, has been a through line of Hosono’s entire career. Born in 1947, Hosono grew up in post-WWII Japan, after nuclear devastation in Hiroshima and Nagasaki, when US popular culture worked its way off military bases and into Japanese life. “My mother is no longer with us; it’s been about five or six years now. She really loved Hollywood movies and music, and I was heavily influenced by that. From a young age she would play movie soundtracks for me. Her idol was Fred Astaire. I watched those movies a lot as I grew older. My father probably liked it, too; he even said he wanted to be a dancer because of my mother’s influence. That’s the kind of person my mother was. I’m very grateful,” says Hosono. Happy End was a Japanese approximation of American roots rock. Next, as a solo artist, Hosono began a reflexive reappropriation of 1950s exotica records on his albums Tropical Dandy, Bon Voyage co. and Paraiso, the album on which he first worked with Ryuichi Sakamoto and Yukihiro Takahashi. The three men became Yellow Magic Orchestra, Japan’s most influential band, whose first major hit in 1978 was a subversive synth-pop cover reclaiming the “oriental” melody of the 1959 exotica recording Firecracker by Martin Denny. Hosono pioneered the use of electronic instruments with his YMO bandmates – each hugely influential solo musicians, producers, session musicians and composers in their own right – and Japanese popular music became increasingly dominated by electronic compositions in the wake of YMO’s peak 1970s and 1980s popularity. Some middle-aged Japanese businessmen still sport the group’s “techno cut” undercut hairstyle. The first record Hosono bought as a boy was a version of Mon Oncle by the Japanese singer Jun Nakajima, taken from Jacques Tati’s film of the same name. The film is a comedic account of one man’s struggle at confronting modernity and technology – a prophetic first purchase for a pioneering technologist with his own questions about today’s technological advancements. “For Jacques Tati I think there was some irony in how things would break down, but now we have entered an era where it is no longer a carefree matter. After all, with the Industrial Revolution of the 18th and 19th centuries, moving into the 20th century from the age of oil, machines began to work so that human workers didn’t have to use their muscles,” says Hosono.



“But now we’ve stopped using our heads, too. We don’t use our brain muscles because AI does it for us. What will happen to us before long? It is an era filled with anxiety that our heads might become completely empty.” It’s no surprise, then, that Yours Sincerely finds Hosono turning to matters of the soul and the natural world. Rojiura (Walking Vibration) is a new version of a track originally recorded for the 2006 television drama Walkers, about a group of adults undertaking Ohenro – the 88-temple, esoteric Buddhist pilgrimage around Shikoku island. (This elicits his wide-eyed approval when I share that I completed Ohenro in 2023, with YMO records stuffed in my backpack, and he asks me to listen to Rojiura if I ever walk the trail again.) Yellow Magic Orchestra’s Ryuichi Sakamoto, Yukihiro Takahashi and Haruomi Hosono at the Toji Buddhist Temple in Kyoto in July 2007. Both Takahashi and Sakamoto died in 2023. WireImage Hosono attended an Anglican school but has been interested in Buddhism since reading the popular Chinese story Journey to the West as a boy. “I’ve always loved stories about various gods,” he says. Yours Sincerely’s guiding principle is laid out on its opening track, Note of Mothership – a gently bubbling acknowledgment of the maternal force Hosono believes envelopes the planet. It’s a concept informed in part by an ongoing interest in the British chemist James Lovelock, who, along with the microbiologist Lynn Margulis, developed the Gaia theory in the 1970s. The theory posited that Earth is a self-regulating superorganism composed of both living organisms and their inorganic surroundings. “Within [the Gaia hypothesis] there is an idea called ‘Daisyworld’. Daisies of various colours bloom on Earth. Why are there so many colours? If it were just a single colour, light would concentrate and the climate wouldn’t be right, which is why they are so diverse,” says Hosono. “Ever since then I’ve always loved that [maternal] world-view.”

World.title: The true story behind the record label that defined pop in the ’80s and ’90s
World.content:
CultureMusicPodcasts The true story behind the record label that defined pop in the ’80s and ’90s Barry Divola September 12, 2026 — 5:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Siân Pattenden still remembers her life flashing before her eyes. This was back in the early ’90s, when she was a young writer for English pop magazine Smash Hits. She was doing a story on boy band East 17. The bad boy of the group, Brian Harvey, realised he had to move his car, as it was illegally parked, and encouraged Pattenden to accompany him. He proceeded to put the pedal to the metal and the car careened down the street at dangerously high speed, Pattenden hanging on for dear life, visions of being a footnote in a pop star’s obituary in her head. East 17: The hard-living British boy band was a key act of London Records, which is the subject of a hit new podcast. Pattenden survived to tell the tale, and went on to write for The Face, Select and The Guardian, and became a broadcaster, visual artist and children’s book author. Her latest venture is a podcast about London Records, the UK label that was a hit machine in the ’80s and ’90s, signing not just East 17, but Bronski Beat, Bananarama, Fine Young Cannibals, The Communards, Shakespears Sister, All Saints and more. Sian Pattenden, a former Smash Hits writer, is the host of Hit That Perfect Beat: The London Records Story podcast.



“It really was a unique label,” Pattenden says. “As it was owned by PolyGram, it had major label money, but the way it operated was maverick. It was run by people who wanted hits, but they didn’t try to be lowest common denominator to get them. They were truly passionate about music.” Across the five episodes of Hit That Perfect Beat: The London Records Story, we hear about the ambitious execs at the core of the label: Roger Ames, Tracy Bennet, Colin Bell and Pete Tong. One of their first signings was Bronski Beat, a trio fronted by Jimmy Somerville. Their debut single, Smalltown Boy, was accompanied by a music video that not only didn’t shy away from the fact that the group was gay, it highlighted it and embraced it. Colin Bell, who is gay, appears in the video as a police officer, and was supportive of the band and what it was trying to do. “Colin fought for his acts,” Pattenden says. “He knew that Bronski Beat wanted to make a political and personal statement, and he wanted to help them do that. I really think other labels would have squashed that, or tried to change it.”



The podcast doesn’t shy away from some of the dodgier practices that London, along with many other UK record labels, indulged in back then. One episode covers “record hyping”, where employees travelled to record shops around England buying the label’s new releases to boost sales, getting them into the charts so that the bands were eligible to appear on the influential weekly TV show Top of the Pops. Pattenden also interviewed many of the artists about the insanity of those years and the surreal nature of pop stardom. Siobhan Fahey of Bananarama (and later Shakespears Sister) remembers signing on for the dole each week, even as her group’s records climbed the charts in the ’80s. Bronski Beat embraced its queer identity in an era when it was still fraught for pop acts to do so. London threw around lots of money, while having a slightly alternative take on commercial pop. Just as All Saints were marketed as a more relatable, less glossy Spice Girls, East 17 were touted as a cheekier, street-smart Take That. “Even when I interviewed them back in Smash Hits days, East 17 were mental,” Pattenden says. “But I have a lot of respect for [songwriter and band member] Tony Mortimer being so honest in the podcast about those days and the effect they had on him.



“Excess and bad behaviour were encouraged back then, even though we now know it was destructive for many of those people who were teenagers when they became stars. I think that now it’s taken more seriously and there’s a duty of care.” Some didn’t make it through unscathed. In 1990, London signed Flowered Up for an advance of £250,000. They were touted as the south’s answer to the north’s Happy Mondays. Their rise was swift and their fall even swifter. Two of them died of heroin overdoses. London Records pop duo Shakespears Sister. One of the most erudite and entertaining of Pattenden’s interviewees was Richard Coles from The Communards. His unusual life path led him from being a pop star to ordination as an Anglican priest. He is self-effacing about the hedonism and the ridiculous lifestyle he adopted back in his chart-topping days. This included buying a speedboat in Ibiza, then forgetting where he left it. He still has no idea what happened to it. Which raises the question: exactly how does one lose a speedboat?

World.title: Why am I feeling sorry for rich nepo babies? Next Gen NYC achieves the impossible
World.content:
CultureTV & radioThe Verdict Why am I feeling sorry for rich nepo babies? Next Gen NYC achieves the impossible In this column, we deliver hot (and cold) takes on pop culture, judging whether a subject is overrated or underrated. Nicole Elphick September 12, 2026 — 5:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Bravo’s newish addition to the reality TV pantheon manages the near-impossible: Next Gen NYC makes one feel sympathy for that most maligned of creatures, the nepo baby (and their spiritual cousin, the trust fund baby). Launched in 2025, the series kicked off following a bevy of twenty-somethings, many spawned from famous Real Housewives cast members, as they ran around the Big Apple partying and bickering. The titular next generation’s lofty ambitions include such totally relatable goals as being an influencer, model, DJ, fashion designer, influencer, nightclub impresario, cleaning supplies entrepreneur and influencer. Next Gen NYC, Bravo’s most-watched series premiere ever, is wildly enjoyable (and slightly tragic) viewing. Next Gen NYC was an instant success upon launching, becoming Bravo’s most-watched series premiere ever. It is both wildly stupid and wildly enjoyable viewing. The four Real Housewives children might have come to the show already famous (at least in the Bravo-verse) but the series does show an insight into the downsides of being a reality TV nepo baby. They had to grow up on camera when they were too young to consent to it or truly know what it would entail. Their most awkward moments are forever immortalised on television to later be dissected on Reddit forums.



It’s especially hard not to feel sorry for Next Gen NYC face Ariana Biermann, daughter of The Real Housewives of Atlanta star Kim Zolciak, who in the first season alleges that money she earned from social media deals (she had her first brand deal at 14 years old) was taken by her parents. The show has smartly cast a few youngsters from non-famous families as foils to the Housewives progeny – there’s even an heir to a billion-dollar fried chicken fortune! (I swear I am not making this up.) Georgia McCann, the intellectual of Next Gen NYC, with Brooks Marks, son of The Real Housewives of Salt Lake City star Meredith Marks. Charles Sykes/Bravo The greatest of these is loveable kook Georgia McCann, who is basically the intellectual of the crew; she’s even written her own book of poetry. McCann endearingly and constantly mentions her love of the 1989 romcom When Harry Met Sally on a show where having even a passing knowledge of any cultural artefact released prior to one’s birth is akin to being a Tolstoy scholar. To give a clearer idea of how comically clueless this Gen Z crew is, in an episode where they all attend a Rocky Horror Picture Show-themed party, rather than just watching the 1975 camp classic, they instead suggest to one another seeing Glee’s 2010 tribute episode to familiarise themselves with the movie.



The daughter of Brooke Shields was cast in the second season, and anyone born in the 1980s or earlier will be aghast to hear her contribution to pop culture constantly being described as … being “Hannah Montana’s mother”. Poor, beautiful Brooke. It’s interesting to see how their young ambitions play out among the cast. The non-nepo babies seem to have an easier time of it; if they fail, they will presumably just have to move back in with their (still mostly rich) families. Meanwhile, decades of internet criticism seem to have made the Housewives kids scared to take any real risks on their various ventures and postpone doing anything besides posting on their social media channels. And if you’re not watching Next Gen NYC, you are missing out on possibly the greatest “villain” of modern-day reality television: Charlie Zakkour. He’s the 31-year-old son of a wealthy banking executive, and cast members say he gets an allowance from his father – though he bills himself as a cryptocurrency trader. Charlie is a chaos merchant who loves to meddle in relationships and try to pull power plays on the others. He goads Georgia that she is only on the show because she was his friend, as if the fact that he was first cast for being from wealth, while she was then cast for being interesting, is some sort of flex.



In the first season Charlie is shown as yearningly desperate for the approval of his father but seemingly unwilling to do the main thing that would earn his dad’s respect: stop his hard-partying ways and get a proper job. He would almost be a figure of deep tragedy, prevented from ever properly growing up in his trust fund gilded cage, except for the inexcusable fact that he is constantly spewing sexist, racist, transphobic nonsense to his friends. He then follows up with the weakest apologies where he vaguely requests forgiveness for his statements, saying he meant them with no malice, before repeating the cycle all over again. While Next Gen NYC is an escapist delight to binge, it makes one thing clear. Being a trust fund baby? You couldn’t pay me. Next Gen NYC streams on Hayu.

World.title: ‘Is this something I want?’: Tove Lo, pop’s messy genius, ponders motherhood and domesticity
World.content:
Pop’s party girl Tove Lo is considering settling down: “My body is telling me ‘It’s time!’ and my brain is like, ‘No!’”

Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

It took a decade, but the world finally caught up with Tove Lo. For years, the Swedish musician has been pop’s professor of provocation, its scholar of squalor, its expert in excess, carving out a niche of gorgeously explicit filth with breakthrough albums like Lady Wood and Blue Lips (its title a feminine take on “blue balls”) that spun art from the personal chaos of drugs, drinking and wanton sex. And then Charli XCX’s Brat Summer happened, sending messiness mainstream and making the internet’s prevailing “clean-girl aesthetic” a relic of a naive age. In a culture where electroclash is the defining influence (again), Slayyyter is pop’s new trashbag star, and hedonism is celebrated, it seems the world is finally vibing with ideas Lo has been playing with all along. Does it feel that way for her? “Um … it kind of does,” she laughs coyly. “It’s nice to get to sing about these things without needing to defend myself any more. “It’s in the ether right now. I don’t know if it has to do with female artists taking control of their own narrative, or if it’s just the state of the world. Whenever our feelings are in a pressure cooker for too long, they tend to explode, and I think that’s what’s happened.” Few modern pop stars have turned sex into such a vital driver of their artistic process as Lo. Why is it so creatively inspiring? “It’s something I’ve been trying to put my finger on – if it’s me just being a sexual person, or if it’s just the fact I do think music and sex have always gone hand in hand for me,” she says. “Maybe it’s because it comes from the body and it’s an instinctual form of expression; singing and dancing and working with emotions and everything that’s running through your body naturally makes it sexual.”



She grew up in the northern suburbs of Stockholm, among family and friends who were progressive and open-minded. “It never occurred to me that saying I’m a feminist and I’m bi and being sexual were political. To me, that was just the baseline of what everyone should be. But when I started touring the world and going to places where that wasn’t the baseline, I realised, oh, maybe it is political. “But in terms of how I choose to express myself – the bluntness, directness, and it being provocative to some people – I just think it feels good to express desire without being judged. Or even if you do get judged, just having the freedom to play with that anyway.” Lo is speaking from her home in Los Angeles, following a brief stint in Stockholm where she’s been rehearsing for an upcoming world tour around her new album, Estrus. The biological reference behind the title is to a female animal “in heat” and ready to procreate. ‘I’m still messy and I party too much and I say the wrong thing a lot.’ It’s funny, and perhaps typically defiant, that just when the world has caught on to her trashy wavelength, Lo is pivoting. On Estrus, the pop star – on the verge of turning 39 – is singing about settling down and contemplating the logistics of having a child. “I’m thinking about these things, but I’m in no way ready for it,” Lo explains. “I feel I’m being told by the outside world that I’m a grown woman now and I’m supposed to set roots and settle down and act accordingly and be responsible and have answers for everything, and I’m just not there at all. I’m still quite messy, and it’s the only thing I’m good at.” Inspired by her long-term relationship with husband Charlie Twaddle – a Kiwi producer and creative director she married in 2020 – the album finds Lo contemplating domestic malaise, and the expectations around 30-something women, with her usual brand of outrageous humour. On highlight I’m the Cake, her pent-up desire explodes to the point she’s yelling at (presumably) her husband for taking for granted what he’s got at home: “Babe, I’m a pop star, did you just forget?” she sings with carnal frustration.



She’s called Estrus her “Peter Pan record” – driven by a desire to never grow up, but feeling the burden that she might have to. “Being in a relationship for this long and having found someone I want to be with for the rest of my life is quite a new feeling for me in terms of my creativity. But I’m still messy and I party too much and I say the wrong thing a lot. So there’s some growth but this album is thinking about, ‘Is this even something I want? And what does growth look like when I still want to be me and I don’t really want to change?’ ” Lo ponders with a laugh. The album closes with Source of Life (“the place between my thighs”), a moving song where Lo explores her anxiety about motherhood. As a man, I’m self-conscious about asking Lo to discuss her apprehension about something that obviously doesn’t affect us in the same social, physical or biological way – so, instead, I tell her that before I had two kids, I was so nervous about becoming a parent that I once Googled “I regret having children” just to see how many search results came up. It wasn’t many, which was very reassuring. Lo bursts into laughter. “I mean, [parenting] does feel like the ‘final boss’ of adventures, right? So I am very curious about it. But, for me, I have a hard time picturing it. I’ve never dreamt about it, it’s never been something I’ve wanted, but now my body is telling me ‘It’s time!’ and my brain is like, ‘No!’ So I’m in that place … but also, I have said that if my husband could get pregnant, we probably would have a few kids by now. I think there’s a toll on the body that’s also clearly challenging for me. But everyone seems to be doing it, so I don’t know!” Lo had already explored the idea on Suburbia, the conflicted centrepiece from her last album, 2022’s Dirt Femme. It’s a song that presaged the current wave of Millennial pop stars exploring their mixed feelings around impending motherhood, from Charli XCX and Taylor Swift to Carly Rae Jepsen and Robyn. “It’s cool to see all my peers working through this, and no one’s shying away from talking about something that wasn’t that common to sing about in pop. Because I remember when I sang about it on Suburbia, I got a lot of different reactions – there was a lot of ‘oh my God, I relate to this so hard’, but also a lot of ‘how the f--- can you talk like this, you’re such a selfish bitch’,” Lo recalls drolly. “Women speaking about struggling with this picture of motherhood as only a positive seems to really trigger something in people. So I love that the topic is just out there, and in pop as well. It’s really beautiful to see.”

World.title: ‘It’s hard to tell anyone’: The debilitating, hidden injury affecting thousands of Australians
World.content:

This story is part of the September 12 edition of Good Weekend. See all stories .

Early one Saturday morning in July, 2021, Gold Coast triathlete Alexa Leary set off on a training ride with a group of elite cyclists in the hills behind Noosa, on Queensland’s Sunshine Coast. The route was demanding; an undulating 90-kilometre ride, including a 2.5-kilometre climb to the summit of a local landmark called Black Mountain. Her father, Russell, would tag along as a support rider. Her fellow cyclists had a reputation for riding fast and even for being a little reckless. But Leary, who was 19, had ridden the route before and was a fierce competitor: two years prior, she had won silver at the Women’s Under 18-19 World Triathlon finals in Switzerland in 2019 and she had her sights set on the Paris Olympics. Leary kept pace with the group up Black Mountain and down the other side, then on to the top of the next hill, just above Cootharaba. Exhilarated, she texted Russell, who had fallen behind. “I made it with them,” she wrote. He replied: “Great effort. The universe is changing, keep trusting it.” Leary then began her descent, pushing herself to stay with the group. She was charging downhill at 75 kilometres per hour when, in a split-second miscalculation, she clipped the wheel of the rider in front. She immediately catapulted over the handlebars before landing on the right side of her head, causing her helmet to fly off. She then flipped, slamming the left side of her head onto the bitumen with a cracking sound so loud that a fellow rider later likened it to a tree splitting. Related Article Good Weekend She nearly quit the pool at 14. Now, Mollie’s the face of a new Australian era When Russell arrived at the scene, some 30 minutes later, he saw a crowd of people, and two ambulances. He had no idea who was injured. As he approached, one of the paramedics remarked, “They don’t think she’s going to make it.” It wasn’t until he got closer that he saw it was his daughter. “She was unconscious, her eyes were rolled back,” he tells me. “There was blood everywhere, and her knee was ripped to pieces.” Alexa was rushed to Sunshine Coast University Hospital, where she was put in the ICU. By the time her parents made it to the hospital, the pressure on her brain was already so great that, as Russell remembers it, “her eyes were bulging out of her head.” The doctors told Russell and his wife Belinda that their daughter had suffered what was called a TBI – a traumatic brain injury. It was so severe that if she survived, she would be a vegetable, unable to walk or talk.



Leary was placed in an induced coma and airlifted to Royal Brisbane and Women’s Hospital. In order to relieve the pressure on her brain, part of her skull was removed and placed in a freezer in the basement. (Unrestrained, Leary’s swollen brain bulged 20 millimetres outside her head.) Two weeks later, she emerged from the coma. Three months of rehab lay ahead, during which Leary, with the aid of doctors and therapists, would relearn the rudiments of human functioning, from how to chew, swallow and communicate, to the difference between a knife and fork and how to use them. After 111 days, she walked out of the hospital, against all the odds, alive and breathing. The after-effects of triathlete Alexa Leary’s traumatic brain injury were both mysterious and terrifying. Paul Harris Her family was traumatised, but Leary had survived. In November 2021, as a celebration, her parents took her to a cafe in Noosa for her favourite treat, an iced coffee. She took one sip, curled up her nose and told the cafe owner it was “shit”. Leary could be moody and intense, but she had never been rude or abusive. But other, more bizarre behaviours would follow. Soon after the cafe incident, Leary’s grandmother, Shirley, paid a visit. The minute Shirley walked through the door, Leary walked up and grabbed her breasts. She did the same thing with a waitress on a trip to Sydney. “I was grabbing random ladies’ boobs,” she tells me. “I just couldn’t control it.” Leary’s parents would try to explain that their daughter had a brain injury, but strangers found it hard to reconcile. Leary looked fine. Her physical scars had healed. For all intents and purposes, she was back to her old self. But, as was becoming apparent, her brain was full of broken wiring. The fragile snow-dome of her mind had been shaken violently and beyond repair, with consequences that were both mysterious and terrifying. Brains in museums often look rubbery and plasticised, but they are in fact, surprisingly squishy, with a consistency that has been likened to soft tofu or custard. The average specimen weighs 1.5 kilograms and is thought to contain about 88 billion neurons, including galaxies of axons and synapses, all variously connected by electrical signals and neurotransmitters. Different parts of it do different things, from the temporal lobes, which are located behind the ears, near the temple, and play a role in hearing and language, to the frontal lobes, which are involved in problem-solving, abstract thinking and how we act upon our emotions and impulses. Roughly the size of two clenched fists, your brain floats in a sea of cerebrospinal fluid housed in a helmet of bone, up to 10 millimetres thick in places, otherwise known as your skull. If you get hit hard in the head, your brain can bounce around inside your skull, or twist and ricochet, causing the pathways between brain cells to tear and snap and your brain to start bleeding. This is followed by a secondary trauma, known as a neurotoxic cascade, when the injured neurons secrete free radicals and glutamate that further kill healthy cells.



“No traumatic brain injury is the same,” says Melinda Fitzgerald, deputy vice-chancellor (research) at Curtin University and CEO of Connectivity Traumatic Brain Injury Australia, a not-for-profit that advocates for people with TBIs and supports research. “The damage depends on where you’re hit and how hard, and everyone responds differently.” TBIs are on the rise. A 2022 report from the Lancet Neurology Commission estimated that 55 million people worldwide live with a TBI and described it as a major global health problem. According to the Australian Institute of Health and Welfare, 450,000 Australians have brain injury: TBIs account for 142,000 hospitalisations annually, placing significant strain on emergency departments. Most are caused by falls, car crashes, sports injuries and assaults. The accidents that occasion TBIs tend to be extraordinarily violent: one man I spoke to for this story was driving at night on a lonely stretch of highway when he hit a bull. The animal came straight through the windscreen, colliding with his face. “My doctor told me that I didn’t so much as break the bones in my face as totally shatter everything.” Fortunately, victims rarely, if ever, remember what happened. Invariably, large chunks of their memory are erased. In Leary’s case, five years of her life prior to her accident were wiped clean. When she woke up, she didn’t recognise her mother – “I thought she was Dad’s best friend” – or her longtime boyfriend. “I had to look at photos on my phone to fill in the blanks, but I couldn’t date him any more because I felt I didn’t know who he was.” Leary has a love-heart tattoo on her wrist and a lightning bolt on her ankle, but she couldn’t remember how they got there. “My parents told me I got them with my best friend.” TBIs commonly affect the brain’s processing speed. “When I woke up in the ICU, my husband, Eric, was talking to me, saying, ‘It’s Eric, your husband,’ over and over,” says Eloise Zoppos, a 39-year-old researcher in Melbourne, who was struck by a car during her morning walk in 2024. “But he seemed to be talking incredibly fast and I couldn’t understand why. In fact, as I found out later, he was talking very slowly, but my processing speed had been so damaged.” Zoppos, who has soft brown eyes and dark, straight, shoulder-length hair, underwent several marathon surgeries and was in a coma for two weeks. “Eric was told that every minute I was alive was a win.” Today, her main challenge is cognitive fatigue. “It’s not the same as simply being tired,” she tells me. “Because of my injury, my brain has to work harder to compensate for deficits. This means I need an extremely high level of sleep and rest every day to even be able to do simple tasks and activities. Without adequate sleep, I can have trouble concentrating, mix up my words, forget words, slump, feel physically weak, forget to eat and drink, and drop things. I can have seizures. I’m even more sensitive to bright lights and loud sounds.” While TBIs cause a bizarre range of symptoms, the injury itself remains hidden.



She can no longer work or socialise as much as she used to. “And if I do, it takes meticulous planning so that the days immediately before and after are extremely quiet to allow for more sleep.” She doesn’t drive long distances or at night, watch much TV (it’s too stimulating), or read to or play with her two young children. “My cognitive fatigue is so debilitating that it feels like my family’s entire life revolves around managing it, and to me, it can feel like it casts a fog over almost every aspect of our lives.” And yet no one, save for her close friends and family, knows what she is going through because, as she puts it, “a TBI is invisible”. Indeed, while TBIs cause a bizarre range of symptoms – from volcanic rage to giggling fits – the injury itself remains hidden. This can have its advantages, says Zoppos. “It means that I can decide how much of my injury I want to share with others.” Some people with TBIs carry cards in their wallet explaining their disability to strangers, and asking that they speak slowly and remain patient. Others prefer to disclose nothing: “It’s hard to tell anyone that you’ve had brain injury because you have to expect that you’ll never have a job again,” says Ian Lacy, who was working as a strategy consultant with Citibank when he was involved in a life-altering car crash in Queensland in 2005. “I was employed by Fortune 500 companies to tell them where to take their business. But would you like someone with a brain injury giving you advice about what to do with your business?” On the other hand, not sharing your condition makes it hard for strangers to understand or empathise. This becomes especially problematic when the TBI has caused behavioural changes. According to studies from the UK, between 50 and 70 per cent of people with a TBI experience personality changes. Some of these can seem relatively benign. “Before my accident, I was a serious person,” says Rosey Morrow, a former journalist who was hit by a car in Sydney in 2016. “Now sometimes I’ll get the giggles and I can’t stop. I’ll laugh at stuff other people don’t find funny at all, but I just find it hilarious.” But most people with TBIs, and their carers, report that the personality changes are negative. People can become more self-centred, narcissistic, colder to loved ones or less affectionate. Disinhibition is common, especially with people who damage their prefrontal cortex, the region sitting directly behind your forehead, which governs, among other things, impulse control. When Alexa Leary’s skull hit the tarmac at 75 kilometres per hour, one of the things it obliterated was her social filter. She would tell people in the street that they were ugly. If she didn’t like their outfits, she would tell them they “should go home and change”. If she didn’t like a meal, she would throw it back at the staff. If her parents were present, they would try to explain, to make excuses and smooth things over. If they weren’t, their daughter was on her own. “After a while, I had to accept that I would never be the same,” says Rosey Morrow. “That was a very hard moment.” Paul Harris At the same time, her social world steadily shrunk. “If my friends said one word to me [that she found annoying], I’d say, ‘You’re a c---!’ ” says Leary. “I lost a lot of friends that way.” Those close to a person with a TBI – including family members – can find it hard to accept that the person they knew before the accident no longer exists. After a time, even Leary’s best friend – the girl with whom she’d got her wrist and ankle tattoos – stopped inviting her out. “I would see her on social media saying, ‘Hanging out with friends’, and it broke me,” says Leary. “I’d unfollow her, but then refollow her and get hurt all over again.” Such social isolation is both a by-product and a cause of TBIs. “When people get isolated, they’re more prone to develop drug and alcohol problems,” says Adam Schickerling, acting CEO of the brain injury organisation, Synapse. “And when they develop drug and alcohol problems, they’re more prone to violence, which is one of the main causes of TBIs.”



It’s no accident that a large number of prisoners are thought to have a brain injury – research in the US suggests it’s somewhere between 40 to 60 per cent. But inmates are unlikely to get a formal diagnosis, let alone treatment. “Most people go, ‘These people need a psychiatrist,’ but actually, their brains are broken.” Women subject to domestic violence are especially vulnerable. If a woman has been abused for an extended period and never been to hospital, “her rehab prospects are long gone,” says Schickerling. “That window has closed, and often she doesn’t even know.” It’s tempting to see your brain as a central command, a kind of flight deck for our executive functions. But the brain is also the seat of our identity. Somewhere in that ball of gluggy mush is a matrix of memories, beliefs, inclinations and values, all mediated, in ways we are barely aware of, by raw genetics and the passage of time. A study published in the journal Social Cognitive and Affective Neuroscience in 2021 suggests that much of our identity, that ineffable sense of self, may be located in the ventral medial prefrontal cortex, a small region at the very bottom of the frontal lobe, behind our eyes. Some people with damage in and around this area report no longer fully recognising themselves. “Memories of my prior self feel complete but inaccessible,” writes Bruce Powell, a former doctor who sustained a TBI in 2018 and now blogs extensively about the condition. “I know who I was, but I do not feel like him any more.” This is not “a change in personality”, he adds, “but the traumatic termination of one life, reincarnated as another”. Tall and beefy, with thick, snowy-grey hair, Powell, who is 59, lives in Perth with his wife, Anita. He was taking part in a bicycle race on the Great Ocean Road (bicycles feature prominently in TBIs) when he collided head-first, at 65 kilometres per hour, with a metal road sign. “I hit the pole so hard that it bent in half,” he tells me. Before his accident, he was Western Australia’s director of organ and tissue donation, a highly experienced anaesthetist and head of department in the intensive-care unit in Rockingham hospital, south of Perth. All that was taken from him in a split second: his injury meant he could no longer practise medicine. It was like the loss of a loved one and has involved a similar mourning process. He cites “acceptance” – the last of the five stages of grief, according to Swiss-born psychiatrist Elisabeth Kübler-Ross – as being particularly important. “We don’t get to choose when that acceptance comes,” he says, “nor any of the other stages.” Former anaesthetist Bruce Powell can no longer practise medicine – and feels like a different person. Paul Harris

World.title: They’re an AFL powerhouse. So why can’t Collingwood’s women’s team find success?
World.content:
Analysis SportAFLAFLW They’re an AFL powerhouse. So why can’t Collingwood’s women’s team find success? Hannah Kennelly September 12, 2026 — 6:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

For nearly four quarters, Collingwood captain Ruby Schleicher was on the verge of an unwanted statistical milestone. With just three minutes left in last weekend’s game against Carlton, her career-high personal tally of three goals and four behinds would ordinarily have been cause for celebration. But the disappointing fact for Schleicher and her Magpies was that she had contributed 100 per cent of her team’s score. Ruby Schleicher during Collingwood’s clash with Carlton Getty Images Teammate Georgia Knight offered a reprieve with a behind, followed by a goal to Dominique Carbone, which made the 39-point loss to the undefeated Blues sting a little less. To put the loss in perspective, the injury-marred Pies were missing key players, including last-minute drop-outs from star Ash Centra and Jemma Rigoni and were facing Carlton – a team that made finals last year and will likely to do the same in 2026.



Still, Sunday’s defeat marks their fourth consecutive loss —a streak that, compounded by several years of poor results, should be sounding alarm bells at Collingwood headquarters. In 2019, this masthead published a piece, titled ‘What’s wrong with Collingwood’s AFLW side’, which examined the club’s poor performance after high-profile players Jasmine Garner, Moana Hope, Emma King and Jess Duffin defected to North Melbourne during W’s rapid expansion period. Collingwood coach Sam Wright and his team. AFL Photos At the time, critics questioned the Pies list management, draft and recruiting strategy. Staff turnover was also cited as a concern, after the club had employed three women’s football operations managers in three years. That was seven years ago. Even the brightest of optimists and diehard Pies fans would concede not enough has changed since then.



Collingwood are currently second-last on the ladder and – like Essendon, St Kilda and West Coast – yet to record a win ahead of their match on Saturday against Gold Coast at People First Stadium. Related Article AFL 2026 Jeremy Howe changed his mind on retirement. Now his mate’s daughter is a Collingwood clubmate So why single Collingwood out, when three other clubs have the same 0-4 start? Essendon, St Kilda and West Coast entered AFLW at later stages of the competition, with the latter two reaching finals for the first time last year. Collingwood are one of the inaugural teams of the competition, but – despite showing glimpses of promise – seem to have gone backwards.



Their first and only preliminary final was in 2021 against the Brisbane Lions, followed by a semi-final appearance in 2022. Since then, Collingwood have finished 11th in 2023, last in 2024 and 15th in 2025 with only three wins. Collingwood should be a successful AFLW club. They have up-to-date facilities and a strong history of success in the men’s program, plus a large membership pool to tap into. View post on X The Pies have also been adamant they are improving. Coach Sam Wright told media after their round 12 loss in 2025 the Pies would have a “tough and prescriptive” off-season. “While we only got the three wins this year, we don’t feel like we are far away from progressing,” he added. So why can’t Collingwood’s AFLW program find success?



The club has had steady leadership over the past few years, poaching Wright from North Melbourne in 2023 and promoting highly regarded performance analyst Jess Burger to general manager of women’s football in 2024. Burger and Collingwood declined to comment for this article. However, support from Collingwood’s upper echelons has been less straightforward and more cautious. Collingwood CEO Craig Kelly has been publicly and privately vocal about the financial risks of expanding the AFLW program. Collingwood Football Club chief executive Craig Kelly. AAP Last year, the AFL met with all 18 clubs for a conference exploring the priorities for the future of the AFLW for its 10-year anniversary. Columnist Caroline Wilson, reported Kelly urged the league to consider the heavy cost of expanding the AFLW competition too quickly, arguing the game should not invest too heavily in the women’s competition at the expense of upgrading the MCG, creating better facilities for the game across Australia and improving the AFL experience for fans. AFLW commentator Chyloe Kurdas said it was important for clubs to remember the women’s game was still “playing catch-up” to the men’s – a chase that requires investment in staffing, resources and most importantly mindset.



“I can’t speak specifically about Collingwood, but I think what is a problem is that not all 18 clubs have got a consistent mindset across the whole club of the value of the women’s program and the level of investment that’s required to ensure that there’s success in it” she said. Kurdas – a former AFL Victoria football development manager – said the most successful AFLW clubs established cultures that the best players wanted to be a part of, pointing to the long-term success of Brisbane, Adelaide and reigning premiers North Melbourne. View post on X “You can throw lots of money at a program, but if it’s not part of your heart and soul, and ... you don’t believe in its capability, then it doesn’t matter how much money you spend,” she said. From a list perspective, Collingwood are lacking key players in their forward line. The Pies have consistently struggled to find a consistent path to goal, arguably since Chloe Molloy’s departure in 2022. Superstar Molloy signed with the Sydney on a five-year-deal – the longest contract in the history of the competition.



After receiving a list assistance package from the AFL Commission in 2025 – including two additional spots for the 2026 season and one for 2027 – Collingwood’s list went under an extensive turnover Eleven players left the program and 13 new players were introduced; including delisted free argent Jemma Rigoni and two cross-code Super Netball players Maisie Nankivell and Olivia Lewis. The recruits have helped build versatility and height in Collingwood’s list, but the Magpies still lack experienced players in their forward line. Through the 2025 draft, the Pies brought in six young players, injecting a noticeable boost of energy into their side. But it’s also left the overall playing group relatively inexperienced and young. Kurdas said, while Collingwood’s young players looked exciting and the team had shown some improvement this year, the Pies needed to recruit more A-grade quality players.



“Collingwood probably just don’t have enough depth of mature-age elite level talent, and they need more of those in each zone,” she said. There’s also concern about Collingwood ability to retain senior players. The club has strong leadership from veteran captain Schleicher, but it’s worth noting she and a number of senior players come out of contract this year. Collingwood coach Sam Wright is in his third year as senior coach. Getty Images Schleicher has been offered a deal, but is yet to sign, while, Tarni White, Sarah Rowe, Mattea Breed, Lauren Butler and Bri Davey are others coming out of contract. Vice-captain Jordyn Allen signed a three-year deal in 2024, but tried to seek a trade to Brisbane last year. After their loss to Carlton last weekend, Wright conceded the Pies were “under some duress from a list point of view with injuries”, but said there were opportunities for young players to step up.



When asked specifically by this masthead, what was missing from the Collingwood program and list, Wright said Collingwood were still working that out. “It certainly throws some challenges when you’ve got this many injuries to significant key players as well,” he said. “As a club, we are working through it right now, to put our finger on it, but certainly part of it is luck. But the other part [is] we want to be the best program we can be in that area, and we are working really hard. “In terms of list, it’s more around just continuing to get our processes right, push our processes.” Both Richmond and Carlton initiated comprehensive independent reviews into their AFLW’s programs after periods of poor performance. Carlton’s review in 2022 led to the departure of coach Daniel Harford and other key staff, while Richmond’s review at the end of 2025 prompted the departure of senior coach Ryan Ferguson.



Since then, Carlton have surged, playing in the finals last year and opening thisd season with four straight wins. It’s too early to examine Richmond’s progress, but the Tigers have got two wins on the board so far this season. Related Article AFL 2022 ‘A global reckoning is coming’: The toll of trolls on footballers No one can dispute Collingwood’s desire to get better. As Wright put in his press conference, “I think every player in our program and every staff member is committed to winning”. Kurdas said Collingwood have “the potential to be a great W side”, and said any club that wasn’t getting the success they wanted should consider evaluating their program. “The ability to self-reflect honestly; that’s a non-negotiable ingredient of being successful,” she said. Keep up to date with the best AFL coverage in the country.

World.title: ‘Made for finals’: The interstate gun with the AFL’s No.1 ranking
World.content:
Analysis SportAFLAFL 2026 ‘Made for finals’: The interstate gun with the AFL’s No.1 ranking Michael Gleeson September 12, 2026 — 6:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Loading

Isaac Heeney thought he had space. He turned to goal and took a step. Braeden Campbell had dinked a loopy handball to him over a Crows player just as he was about to be tackled and Heeney was clear. He was inside 50, tight to the boundary on his left and caught Izak Rankine in his peripheral vision closing fast from the right. You could almost hear Heeney thinking, “I can get through him. I can shrug him”. It was late in the last quarter, with about seven minutes to go, on a wet SCG in round 19 and the home team was surging. Izak Rankine’s big tackle on Isaac Heeney in round 19. Channel Seven Rankine slammed into Heeney and wrapped his arms around him. Heeney, comfortably 15 kilograms heavier and stronger than Rankine, stood in the tackle. It looked like David Attenborough footage from a savannah. Heeney wriggled an arm free to try to handball. Rankine lunged and surprisingly managed to spin Heeney as they cuddled, and the pair tumbled to the ground. The ball spilt free. The Crows cleared it, and they hung on to win the game.



The significance of the tackle in that moment in the game, and in the context of Rankine’s season and career, cannot be underestimated. “That was the complete midfielder’s game. As a coach, I thought that was the game that he had a turning point,” Adelaide assistant coach Scott Burns said of the Sydney game. “Two weeks earlier against West Coast he had started to really influence games in the midfield, but that tackle in the wet against Sydney at that time of the game was such a big play. He’d had a great game, but that tackle was where you saw how competitive he is – how much he hates to lose. Izak Rankine celebrates a goal. AFL Photos “That game was a real turning point. It was a complete midfielder performance – inside and out, 30 touches, tackles, inside 50s.”



And he only kicked one goal. Ordinarily, good Izak Rankine games had to include him kicking three, four or five goals. Related Article Analysis

AFL 2026 Bring on the the Zak attack: The Cats’ semi-final showed they sorely need it Rankine only moved to a permanent midfield role in round nine this year after being primarily a forward and part-time mid. Last year the idea of him as a midfielder was better than the reality, and this year was tracking along similarly: he was good but not great in the way he can be as a forward. The first big change came in round 17 against West Coast, and then the next week against the Suns when he had high numbers and his impact was profound. But that was beating up two teams that were poor at the time. This was Sydney in Sydney. Since round 17, Rankine has not gone from good to great – he has gone from good to elite. Champion Data ranks him the No.1 player in the competition since round 18. He is averaging 150 Champion Data points per game. The next best are Errol Gulden on 129 and Max Gawn on 123.



The question on hyper-attacking, dangerous mid-forwards like Rankine, Petracca, “Dusty” and “Kozzy” Pickett can be about their sleight of hand. The freakish goal can be the magician’s distraction from what they are not doing defensively. Jeremy Clarkson and his Italian luxury tractor on his farm, Diddly Squat, in West Oxfordshire. Amazon Prime Typically, the theory is you don’t want your stars to do the grunt inside midfielder work – that you use a tractor to plough a field, not a Lamborghini. Rankine, like Jeremy Clarkson on his farm, doesn’t understand why you can’t have a Lamborghini tractor. “He is made for finals,” said one former coach. “He is a difference-maker. There are plenty of role players in finals who do their job well, but there are not many players who can change the game. In finals, you need players who can kick you two in two minutes and change the game. Rankine is that.”



Another Gold Coast coach said: “The one player we missed last year in finals was Izak Rankine”. The difference-maker could make no difference last year. Or, perhaps, he made a profound difference to two clubs by not being there. Rankine barely played in his first year in the AFL after being drafted by Gold Coast. At the time, it was said he was struggling with repeated hamstring issues. In fact, he had rheumatoid arthritis, which took a long time to diagnose. The autoimmune disease causes swelling and severe pain in the joints, normally to the same joint on both sides of the body. Relatively rare in people under 30, it took some time to diagnose him and then get him on the right (WADA compliant) medication. This time last year, Rankine was suspended for four matches – including the Crows’ entire finals series – after admitting to using a homophobic slur during a game against Collingwood.



“I want to start by saying how deeply sorry I am for what I said. There was no excuse, it was wrong, and I take full responsibility,” Rankine said later. “I’m disappointed in myself and I know I have let a lot of people down. I want to apologise to anyone who I have hurt and offended. I understand that word was offensive, harmful, it’s hurtful and has no place in our game or our society.” Rankine was not a victim, but the length of his ban was the product of an AFL determination to eliminate homophobic language in the game by continuing to escalate punishments for any players using such terms. The consequence was Rankine was not there last year as they lost to Collingwood by 24 points in week one of the finals and then were eliminated altogether when they lost to Hawthorn by 34 points the next week.



View post on X It’s academic what might have been last year, had he been there. The evidence of the first final this year against the Bulldogs, when Rankine had 34 touches, seven clearances, four tackles and two goals – one of them one of the most artful goals of the year – shows is he is not only in dominant form, he is indeed made for finals. Keep up to date with the best AFL coverage in the country.

World.title: He’s one of pop’s great technological disruptors. But the AI era fills him with anxiety
World.content:
Haruomi Hosono: “We don’t use our brain muscles because AI does it for us. What will happen to us before long?”

Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

In the studio of the 79-year-old Japanese pop icon Haruomi Hosono is a bust of Ludwig van Beethoven, some flowers and a small bowl of water. He pulled the bust out of storage when it came time to record the track Figlio Perduto for his new album Yours Sincerely, his first collection of new music in seven years. Hosono’s 23rd studio album features gently soothing electronics and acoustic guitar that feels whimsically reflective, like he’s reaching for his inner child late in life. “Maybe because of my age I might have gone back to being a child. I do have quite a lot of those memories from my childhood,” says Hosono, contemplating the idea. Haruomi Hosono (right) with his Yellow Magic Orchestra bandmates – Yukihiro Takahashi and Ryuichi Sakamoto – in 1982. Gentle Look via Getty Images “Rather than being stories of the past, they are still continuing even now. For example, Beethoven has been glaring at me since I was a child … Now it’s sitting here and I’m praying to it. Until then I had left it alone because I was a bit scared.” Summing up Hosono’s career is almost impossible. His early work in the band Happy End (1969-1972), then as a solo artist on his debut Hosono House (1973), is frequently cited as a touchstone by indie artists, most notably the similarly prolific Mac DeMarco (the title of Harry Styles’ Grammy-winning album Harry’s House was a homage, too). His later outfit Yellow Magic Orchestra is one of the most influential synth-pop groups of all time. But if there’s one consistent thread, it can be found on Figlio Perduto, a cover in Japanese of a track by Sarah Brightman that sets an Italian translation of Johann Wolfgang von Goethe’s poem Erlkonig to Beethoven’s Symphony No. 7.



This iterative, memetic layering of cultures, often with technology, has been a through line of Hosono’s entire career. Born in 1947, Hosono grew up in post-WWII Japan, after nuclear devastation in Hiroshima and Nagasaki, when US popular culture worked its way off military bases and into Japanese life. “My mother is no longer with us; it’s been about five or six years now. She really loved Hollywood movies and music, and I was heavily influenced by that. From a young age she would play movie soundtracks for me. Her idol was Fred Astaire. I watched those movies a lot as I grew older. My father probably liked it, too; he even said he wanted to be a dancer because of my mother’s influence. That’s the kind of person my mother was. I’m very grateful,” says Hosono. Happy End was a Japanese approximation of American roots rock. Next, as a solo artist, Hosono began a reflexive reappropriation of 1950s exotica records on his albums Tropical Dandy, Bon Voyage co. and Paraiso, the album on which he first worked with Ryuichi Sakamoto and Yukihiro Takahashi. The three men became Yellow Magic Orchestra, Japan’s most influential band, whose first major hit in 1978 was a subversive synth-pop cover reclaiming the “oriental” melody of the 1959 exotica recording Firecracker by Martin Denny. Hosono pioneered the use of electronic instruments with his YMO bandmates – each hugely influential solo musicians, producers, session musicians and composers in their own right – and Japanese popular music became increasingly dominated by electronic compositions in the wake of YMO’s peak 1970s and 1980s popularity. Some middle-aged Japanese businessmen still sport the group’s “techno cut” undercut hairstyle. The first record Hosono bought as a boy was a version of Mon Oncle by the Japanese singer Jun Nakajima, taken from Jacques Tati’s film of the same name. The film is a comedic account of one man’s struggle at confronting modernity and technology – a prophetic first purchase for a pioneering technologist with his own questions about today’s technological advancements. “For Jacques Tati I think there was some irony in how things would break down, but now we have entered an era where it is no longer a carefree matter. After all, with the Industrial Revolution of the 18th and 19th centuries, moving into the 20th century from the age of oil, machines began to work so that human workers didn’t have to use their muscles,” says Hosono.



“But now we’ve stopped using our heads, too. We don’t use our brain muscles because AI does it for us. What will happen to us before long? It is an era filled with anxiety that our heads might become completely empty.” It’s no surprise, then, that Yours Sincerely finds Hosono turning to matters of the soul and the natural world. Rojiura (Walking Vibration) is a new version of a track originally recorded for the 2006 television drama Walkers, about a group of adults undertaking Ohenro – the 88-temple, esoteric Buddhist pilgrimage around Shikoku island. (This elicits his wide-eyed approval when I share that I completed Ohenro in 2023, with YMO records stuffed in my backpack, and he asks me to listen to Rojiura if I ever walk the trail again.) Yellow Magic Orchestra’s Ryuichi Sakamoto, Yukihiro Takahashi and Haruomi Hosono at the Toji Buddhist Temple in Kyoto in July 2007. Both Takahashi and Sakamoto died in 2023. WireImage Hosono attended an Anglican school but has been interested in Buddhism since reading the popular Chinese story Journey to the West as a boy. “I’ve always loved stories about various gods,” he says. Yours Sincerely’s guiding principle is laid out on its opening track, Note of Mothership – a gently bubbling acknowledgment of the maternal force Hosono believes envelopes the planet. It’s a concept informed in part by an ongoing interest in the British chemist James Lovelock, who, along with the microbiologist Lynn Margulis, developed the Gaia theory in the 1970s. The theory posited that Earth is a self-regulating superorganism composed of both living organisms and their inorganic surroundings. “Within [the Gaia hypothesis] there is an idea called ‘Daisyworld’. Daisies of various colours bloom on Earth. Why are there so many colours? If it were just a single colour, light would concentrate and the climate wouldn’t be right, which is why they are so diverse,” says Hosono. “Ever since then I’ve always loved that [maternal] world-view.”

World.title: The true story behind the record label that defined pop in the ’80s and ’90s
World.content:
CultureMusicPodcasts The true story behind the record label that defined pop in the ’80s and ’90s Barry Divola September 12, 2026 — 5:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Siân Pattenden still remembers her life flashing before her eyes. This was back in the early ’90s, when she was a young writer for English pop magazine Smash Hits. She was doing a story on boy band East 17. The bad boy of the group, Brian Harvey, realised he had to move his car, as it was illegally parked, and encouraged Pattenden to accompany him. He proceeded to put the pedal to the metal and the car careened down the street at dangerously high speed, Pattenden hanging on for dear life, visions of being a footnote in a pop star’s obituary in her head. East 17: The hard-living British boy band was a key act of London Records, which is the subject of a hit new podcast. Pattenden survived to tell the tale, and went on to write for The Face, Select and The Guardian, and became a broadcaster, visual artist and children’s book author. Her latest venture is a podcast about London Records, the UK label that was a hit machine in the ’80s and ’90s, signing not just East 17, but Bronski Beat, Bananarama, Fine Young Cannibals, The Communards, Shakespears Sister, All Saints and more. Sian Pattenden, a former Smash Hits writer, is the host of Hit That Perfect Beat: The London Records Story podcast.



“It really was a unique label,” Pattenden says. “As it was owned by PolyGram, it had major label money, but the way it operated was maverick. It was run by people who wanted hits, but they didn’t try to be lowest common denominator to get them. They were truly passionate about music.” Across the five episodes of Hit That Perfect Beat: The London Records Story, we hear about the ambitious execs at the core of the label: Roger Ames, Tracy Bennet, Colin Bell and Pete Tong. One of their first signings was Bronski Beat, a trio fronted by Jimmy Somerville. Their debut single, Smalltown Boy, was accompanied by a music video that not only didn’t shy away from the fact that the group was gay, it highlighted it and embraced it. Colin Bell, who is gay, appears in the video as a police officer, and was supportive of the band and what it was trying to do. “Colin fought for his acts,” Pattenden says. “He knew that Bronski Beat wanted to make a political and personal statement, and he wanted to help them do that. I really think other labels would have squashed that, or tried to change it.”



The podcast doesn’t shy away from some of the dodgier practices that London, along with many other UK record labels, indulged in back then. One episode covers “record hyping”, where employees travelled to record shops around England buying the label’s new releases to boost sales, getting them into the charts so that the bands were eligible to appear on the influential weekly TV show Top of the Pops. Pattenden also interviewed many of the artists about the insanity of those years and the surreal nature of pop stardom. Siobhan Fahey of Bananarama (and later Shakespears Sister) remembers signing on for the dole each week, even as her group’s records climbed the charts in the ’80s. Bronski Beat embraced its queer identity in an era when it was still fraught for pop acts to do so. London threw around lots of money, while having a slightly alternative take on commercial pop. Just as All Saints were marketed as a more relatable, less glossy Spice Girls, East 17 were touted as a cheekier, street-smart Take That. “Even when I interviewed them back in Smash Hits days, East 17 were mental,” Pattenden says. “But I have a lot of respect for [songwriter and band member] Tony Mortimer being so honest in the podcast about those days and the effect they had on him.



“Excess and bad behaviour were encouraged back then, even though we now know it was destructive for many of those people who were teenagers when they became stars. I think that now it’s taken more seriously and there’s a duty of care.” Some didn’t make it through unscathed. In 1990, London signed Flowered Up for an advance of £250,000. They were touted as the south’s answer to the north’s Happy Mondays. Their rise was swift and their fall even swifter. Two of them died of heroin overdoses. London Records pop duo Shakespears Sister. One of the most erudite and entertaining of Pattenden’s interviewees was Richard Coles from The Communards. His unusual life path led him from being a pop star to ordination as an Anglican priest. He is self-effacing about the hedonism and the ridiculous lifestyle he adopted back in his chart-topping days. This included buying a speedboat in Ibiza, then forgetting where he left it. He still has no idea what happened to it. Which raises the question: exactly how does one lose a speedboat?

World.title: Why am I feeling sorry for rich nepo babies? Next Gen NYC achieves the impossible
World.content:
CultureTV & radioThe Verdict Why am I feeling sorry for rich nepo babies? Next Gen NYC achieves the impossible In this column, we deliver hot (and cold) takes on pop culture, judging whether a subject is overrated or underrated. Nicole Elphick September 12, 2026 — 5:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Bravo’s newish addition to the reality TV pantheon manages the near-impossible: Next Gen NYC makes one feel sympathy for that most maligned of creatures, the nepo baby (and their spiritual cousin, the trust fund baby). Launched in 2025, the series kicked off following a bevy of twenty-somethings, many spawned from famous Real Housewives cast members, as they ran around the Big Apple partying and bickering. The titular next generation’s lofty ambitions include such totally relatable goals as being an influencer, model, DJ, fashion designer, influencer, nightclub impresario, cleaning supplies entrepreneur and influencer. Next Gen NYC, Bravo’s most-watched series premiere ever, is wildly enjoyable (and slightly tragic) viewing. Next Gen NYC was an instant success upon launching, becoming Bravo’s most-watched series premiere ever. It is both wildly stupid and wildly enjoyable viewing. The four Real Housewives children might have come to the show already famous (at least in the Bravo-verse) but the series does show an insight into the downsides of being a reality TV nepo baby. They had to grow up on camera when they were too young to consent to it or truly know what it would entail. Their most awkward moments are forever immortalised on television to later be dissected on Reddit forums.



It’s especially hard not to feel sorry for Next Gen NYC face Ariana Biermann, daughter of The Real Housewives of Atlanta star Kim Zolciak, who in the first season alleges that money she earned from social media deals (she had her first brand deal at 14 years old) was taken by her parents. The show has smartly cast a few youngsters from non-famous families as foils to the Housewives progeny – there’s even an heir to a billion-dollar fried chicken fortune! (I swear I am not making this up.) Georgia McCann, the intellectual of Next Gen NYC, with Brooks Marks, son of The Real Housewives of Salt Lake City star Meredith Marks. Charles Sykes/Bravo The greatest of these is loveable kook Georgia McCann, who is basically the intellectual of the crew; she’s even written her own book of poetry. McCann endearingly and constantly mentions her love of the 1989 romcom When Harry Met Sally on a show where having even a passing knowledge of any cultural artefact released prior to one’s birth is akin to being a Tolstoy scholar. To give a clearer idea of how comically clueless this Gen Z crew is, in an episode where they all attend a Rocky Horror Picture Show-themed party, rather than just watching the 1975 camp classic, they instead suggest to one another seeing Glee’s 2010 tribute episode to familiarise themselves with the movie.



The daughter of Brooke Shields was cast in the second season, and anyone born in the 1980s or earlier will be aghast to hear her contribution to pop culture constantly being described as … being “Hannah Montana’s mother”. Poor, beautiful Brooke. It’s interesting to see how their young ambitions play out among the cast. The non-nepo babies seem to have an easier time of it; if they fail, they will presumably just have to move back in with their (still mostly rich) families. Meanwhile, decades of internet criticism seem to have made the Housewives kids scared to take any real risks on their various ventures and postpone doing anything besides posting on their social media channels. And if you’re not watching Next Gen NYC, you are missing out on possibly the greatest “villain” of modern-day reality television: Charlie Zakkour. He’s the 31-year-old son of a wealthy banking executive, and cast members say he gets an allowance from his father – though he bills himself as a cryptocurrency trader. Charlie is a chaos merchant who loves to meddle in relationships and try to pull power plays on the others. He goads Georgia that she is only on the show because she was his friend, as if the fact that he was first cast for being from wealth, while she was then cast for being interesting, is some sort of flex.



In the first season Charlie is shown as yearningly desperate for the approval of his father but seemingly unwilling to do the main thing that would earn his dad’s respect: stop his hard-partying ways and get a proper job. He would almost be a figure of deep tragedy, prevented from ever properly growing up in his trust fund gilded cage, except for the inexcusable fact that he is constantly spewing sexist, racist, transphobic nonsense to his friends. He then follows up with the weakest apologies where he vaguely requests forgiveness for his statements, saying he meant them with no malice, before repeating the cycle all over again. While Next Gen NYC is an escapist delight to binge, it makes one thing clear. Being a trust fund baby? You couldn’t pay me. Next Gen NYC streams on Hayu.

World.title: ‘Is this something I want?’: Tove Lo, pop’s messy genius, ponders motherhood and domesticity
World.content:
Pop’s party girl Tove Lo is considering settling down: “My body is telling me ‘It’s time!’ and my brain is like, ‘No!’”

Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

It took a decade, but the world finally caught up with Tove Lo. For years, the Swedish musician has been pop’s professor of provocation, its scholar of squalor, its expert in excess, carving out a niche of gorgeously explicit filth with breakthrough albums like Lady Wood and Blue Lips (its title a feminine take on “blue balls”) that spun art from the personal chaos of drugs, drinking and wanton sex. And then Charli XCX’s Brat Summer happened, sending messiness mainstream and making the internet’s prevailing “clean-girl aesthetic” a relic of a naive age. In a culture where electroclash is the defining influence (again), Slayyyter is pop’s new trashbag star, and hedonism is celebrated, it seems the world is finally vibing with ideas Lo has been playing with all along. Does it feel that way for her? “Um … it kind of does,” she laughs coyly. “It’s nice to get to sing about these things without needing to defend myself any more. “It’s in the ether right now. I don’t know if it has to do with female artists taking control of their own narrative, or if it’s just the state of the world. Whenever our feelings are in a pressure cooker for too long, they tend to explode, and I think that’s what’s happened.” Few modern pop stars have turned sex into such a vital driver of their artistic process as Lo. Why is it so creatively inspiring? “It’s something I’ve been trying to put my finger on – if it’s me just being a sexual person, or if it’s just the fact I do think music and sex have always gone hand in hand for me,” she says. “Maybe it’s because it comes from the body and it’s an instinctual form of expression; singing and dancing and working with emotions and everything that’s running through your body naturally makes it sexual.”



She grew up in the northern suburbs of Stockholm, among family and friends who were progressive and open-minded. “It never occurred to me that saying I’m a feminist and I’m bi and being sexual were political. To me, that was just the baseline of what everyone should be. But when I started touring the world and going to places where that wasn’t the baseline, I realised, oh, maybe it is political. “But in terms of how I choose to express myself – the bluntness, directness, and it being provocative to some people – I just think it feels good to express desire without being judged. Or even if you do get judged, just having the freedom to play with that anyway.” Lo is speaking from her home in Los Angeles, following a brief stint in Stockholm where she’s been rehearsing for an upcoming world tour around her new album, Estrus. The biological reference behind the title is to a female animal “in heat” and ready to procreate. ‘I’m still messy and I party too much and I say the wrong thing a lot.’ It’s funny, and perhaps typically defiant, that just when the world has caught on to her trashy wavelength, Lo is pivoting. On Estrus, the pop star – on the verge of turning 39 – is singing about settling down and contemplating the logistics of having a child. “I’m thinking about these things, but I’m in no way ready for it,” Lo explains. “I feel I’m being told by the outside world that I’m a grown woman now and I’m supposed to set roots and settle down and act accordingly and be responsible and have answers for everything, and I’m just not there at all. I’m still quite messy, and it’s the only thing I’m good at.” Inspired by her long-term relationship with husband Charlie Twaddle – a Kiwi producer and creative director she married in 2020 – the album finds Lo contemplating domestic malaise, and the expectations around 30-something women, with her usual brand of outrageous humour. On highlight I’m the Cake, her pent-up desire explodes to the point she’s yelling at (presumably) her husband for taking for granted what he’s got at home: “Babe, I’m a pop star, did you just forget?” she sings with carnal frustration.



She’s called Estrus her “Peter Pan record” – driven by a desire to never grow up, but feeling the burden that she might have to. “Being in a relationship for this long and having found someone I want to be with for the rest of my life is quite a new feeling for me in terms of my creativity. But I’m still messy and I party too much and I say the wrong thing a lot. So there’s some growth but this album is thinking about, ‘Is this even something I want? And what does growth look like when I still want to be me and I don’t really want to change?’ ” Lo ponders with a laugh. The album closes with Source of Life (“the place between my thighs”), a moving song where Lo explores her anxiety about motherhood. As a man, I’m self-conscious about asking Lo to discuss her apprehension about something that obviously doesn’t affect us in the same social, physical or biological way – so, instead, I tell her that before I had two kids, I was so nervous about becoming a parent that I once Googled “I regret having children” just to see how many search results came up. It wasn’t many, which was very reassuring. Lo bursts into laughter. “I mean, [parenting] does feel like the ‘final boss’ of adventures, right? So I am very curious about it. But, for me, I have a hard time picturing it. I’ve never dreamt about it, it’s never been something I’ve wanted, but now my body is telling me ‘It’s time!’ and my brain is like, ‘No!’ So I’m in that place … but also, I have said that if my husband could get pregnant, we probably would have a few kids by now. I think there’s a toll on the body that’s also clearly challenging for me. But everyone seems to be doing it, so I don’t know!” Lo had already explored the idea on Suburbia, the conflicted centrepiece from her last album, 2022’s Dirt Femme. It’s a song that presaged the current wave of Millennial pop stars exploring their mixed feelings around impending motherhood, from Charli XCX and Taylor Swift to Carly Rae Jepsen and Robyn. “It’s cool to see all my peers working through this, and no one’s shying away from talking about something that wasn’t that common to sing about in pop. Because I remember when I sang about it on Suburbia, I got a lot of different reactions – there was a lot of ‘oh my God, I relate to this so hard’, but also a lot of ‘how the f--- can you talk like this, you’re such a selfish bitch’,” Lo recalls drolly. “Women speaking about struggling with this picture of motherhood as only a positive seems to really trigger something in people. So I love that the topic is just out there, and in pop as well. It’s really beautiful to see.”

World.title: ‘It’s hard to tell anyone’: The debilitating, hidden injury affecting thousands of Australians
World.content:
Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

This story is part of the September 12 edition of Good Weekend. See all stories .

Early one Saturday morning in July, 2021, Gold Coast triathlete Alexa Leary set off on a training ride with a group of elite cyclists in the hills behind Noosa, on Queensland’s Sunshine Coast. The route was demanding; an undulating 90-kilometre ride, including a 2.5-kilometre climb to the summit of a local landmark called Black Mountain. Her father, Russell, would tag along as a support rider. Her fellow cyclists had a reputation for riding fast and even for being a little reckless. But Leary, who was 19, had ridden the route before and was a fierce competitor: two years prior, she had won silver at the Women’s Under 18-19 World Triathlon finals in Switzerland in 2019 and she had her sights set on the Paris Olympics. Leary kept pace with the group up Black Mountain and down the other side, then on to the top of the next hill, just above Cootharaba. Exhilarated, she texted Russell, who had fallen behind. “I made it with them,” she wrote. He replied: “Great effort.
